Years of experience (β = 0.198, p = 0.004) and bachelor's degree or above compared with a technical nursing diploma (β = -0.255, p < 0.001) were significant predictors. The other education contrast, AI training/support and MISSCARE Reasons were not statistically significant. In interviews, nurses described AI-related tools as potentially helpful for alerts, information review, workflow, and communication while also raising concerns about trust, overreliance, empathy, and training. CONCLUSION: Nurses perceived potential benefits from AI-supported tools, but the quantitative findings did not establish an independent effect of AI or a statistically significant adjusted association between decision-making orientation and MNC. These findings support cautious, nurse-centered implementation and further longitudinal evaluation. IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING MANAGEMENT: Managers should pair any AI-supported CDS implementation with role-specific training, clear accountability, usability monitoring, and safeguards that preserve clinical judgment and humanistic care.

articles.title: Response to "Fragility of Observed Associations in Selection of Empirical Antifungal Therapy for Critically Ill Non-Neutropenic Patients" [Response to Letter].
Feeding practices during high-flow nasal cannula: current evidence and clinical implications for respiratory care.
articles.abstract: High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy is increasingly used as a noninvasive respiratory support modality across acute and critical care settings. Although nutritional management is integral to the care of patients with respiratory failure, established guidelines for feeding patients receiving HFNC are lacking, and clinical decisions vary widely, reflecting persistent uncertainty about HFNC's effects on swallowing function, airway protection, and aspiration risk. This narrative review found that HFNC may alter swallowing biomechanics, particularly at flow rates >40 L/min, potentially increasing the risk of choking and aspiration. Evidence on aspiration risk is heterogeneous, deriving largely from healthy volunteers and pediatric bronchiolitis cohorts. Adult evidence is limited to retrospective studies; the largest found no increase in respiratory deterioration with enteral feeding. Most institutions lack formal feeding protocols, and practice is driven by individual clinician judgment. Areas of consensus include the safety of early enteral feeding in hemodynamically stable patients and the avoidance of routine prolonged withholding of nutrition based solely on HFNC use. Disagreement persists regarding routine swallowing assessment, optimal flow thresholds during feeding, and the prioritization of oral versus tube feeding. Safe feeding in patients receiving HFNC requires a multidisciplinary, individualized approach that balances respiratory support against nutritional adequacy. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to define safe flow thresholds, validate bedside assessment tools, and establish standardized feeding guidelines, particularly in adult and critically ill populations.

articles.title: Clinical evaluation of AI Chatbots' performance and safety for total parenteral nutrition planning in critically ill patients: a simulation-based benchmarking study.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is essential for critically ill adults unable to meet their nutritional needs via the gastrointestinal tract. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sparked interest in their potential to support healthcare providers in complex clinical decisions. Nonetheless, no prior research has systematically compared publicly accessible chatbots to pharmacist-developed reference TPN plans across a diverse patient cohort, using a predefined, guideline-based rubric assessing accuracy, completeness, safety, error types, and numerical precision. This study presents a simulation-based benchmarking to evaluate (i) the accuracy and comprehensiveness of chatbot-generated TPN plans, (ii) their safety, acceptability, and error profiles, and (iii) the numerical agreement and concordance with expert pharmacist references. METHODS: This benchmarking study, based on simulations and cross-sectional analysis, evaluated the performance of four publicly accessible AI chatbots-ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and Perplexity-in formulating TPN plans for critically ill adults. Copilot declined to generate patient-specific TPN plans; this refusal was retained as a performance outcome, while Copilot was excluded from analyses requiring an analyzable TPN prescription. Each chatbot produced one plan for each of 10 standardized clinical cases, resulting in a total of 30 TPN plans. Friedman tests, Kendall's W, and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used for comparative analyses. RESULTS: ChatGPT produced comprehensive plans for all 10 cases, compared to 6 plans from Gemini and 4 from Perplexity. The median accuracy was 57.7% for ChatGPT, 43.9% for Gemini, and 38.5% for Perplexity, with no statistically significant overall difference (p = 0.124). However, ChatGPT performed better than Perplexity in pairwise comparison (adjusted p = 0.035). There was a significant difference in completeness among the chatbots (p = 0.003; Kendall's W = 0.57), with median scores of 64.6, 41.9, and 32.3%, respectively. All 30 plans had at least one major or critical safety issue, 7 (23.3%) contained a critical concern, and 19 (63.3%) were rejected. The most common errors were related to electrolytes (90.0%), micronutrients (70.0%), and monitoring (66.7%). Recommendations from chatbots often exceeded pharmacist-derived values, with median relative differences of +47% for energy, +120% for lipids, and +100% for potassium. Bland-Altman analysis revealed considerable variability in the agreement. CONCLUSION: ChatGPT produced the most comprehensive TPN plans among chatbots. However, none showed enough accuracy, safety, or concordance for independent use. All plans had critical issues, especially with electrolytes, micronutrients, monitoring, and refeeding precautions. AI chatbots can support education or planning but require review by a well-trained clinician before clinical use.

articles.title: The Impact of 12-Hour Versus 8-Hour Shifts on Intensive Care Unit Nurses' Physical and Mental Well-Being and Job Satisfaction: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Twelve-hour shifts have been widely implemented in intensive care units (ICUs), where nurses work in high-acuity environments requiring sustained clinical attention. However, evidence regarding the impact of shift length on ICU nurses' physical health, mental well-being, job satisfaction and patient-care outcomes remains limited and inconsistent. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the impact of 12-h compared with 8-h shifts on ICU nurses' physical health, well-being and job satisfaction. DESIGN: This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251021178). METHODS: A systematic search of CINAHL, Ovid MEDLINE and Embase was conducted in February 2025 and updated in June 2026. Additional searches of Scopus and Web of Science were undertaken in June 2026. Eligible studies included ICU nurses and compared 12-h with 8-h shifts. Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed using design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach. Findings were synthesised narratively due to the heterogeneity of the included studies. RESULT: Of 815 records identified, five studies met the inclusion criteria. Findings on fatigue, sleep and burnout were inconclusive across studies. Twelve-hour shifts were generally associated with greater roster satisfaction, flexibility and work-life balance, while evidence for sick leave was limited or mixed. CONCLUSION: Evidence did not consistently favour either 12- or 8-h shifts for ICU nurses, with low to very low certainty of evidence. Shift duration should therefore be considered alongside overall roster design, staffing needs and nurses' well-being when planning ICU schedules. IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING MANAGEMENT: Nurse managers should avoid a one-size-fits-all approach to shift duration, as evidence does not clearly favour 12- or 8-h shifts. Shift-length decisions should consider roster design, staffing needs, workload, recovery time and nurses' preferences. Managers should also monitor staff well-being, satisfaction, absenteeism, retention and patient-care outcomes when reviewing shift patterns. Given the low certainty of evidence, ongoing local evaluation is essential to ensure rosters support workforce sustainability and safe, high-quality care.

articles.title: CT-Assessed Sarcopenia Combined with Laboratory Inflammatory Markers for Outcome Prediction in Critically Ill, Pulmonary, and Geriatric Patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sarcopenia, assessed via computed tomography (CT), is an emerging prognostic tool in critically ill, pulmonary, and geriatric patients. Laboratory inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) are routinely obtained in these populations. Whether CT-assessed sarcopenia combined with laboratory markers offers superior prognostic accuracy over either measure alone remains unclear. OBJECTIVES: To systematically evaluate the prognostic value of CT-assessed sarcopenia, alone or combined with laboratory inflammatory/nutritional markers, for predicting mortality, mechanical ventilation duration, and ICU length of stay in critically ill, pulmonary, and geriatric patients. METHODS: MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to December 2024. Observational studies (prospective or retrospective cohorts, case-control) that reported CT-based sarcopenia assessment alongside at least one laboratory inflammatory marker and at least one clinical outcome were included. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Random-effects meta-analysis was performed; heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. RESULTS: Twenty-five studies encompassing 12,347 patients were identified. The pooled odds ratio for mortality in sarcopenic versus non-sarcopenic patients was 2.28 (95% CI: 1.83-2.83; I² = 22.1%) across critically ill ICU cohorts. In COVID-19 pulmonary populations, pooled OR for in-hospital mortality with low skeletal muscle mass was 5.84 (95% CI: 1.07-31.83). CT-derived muscle measurements correlated inversely with CRP (r = -0.315), fibrinogen (r = -0.392), D-dimers (r = -0.363), and WBC count (r = -0.287). Combined CT-sarcopenia and inflammatory marker models outperformed conventional scoring systems (APACHE II, SOFA, CURB-65, PSI). CONCLUSIONS: CT-assessed sarcopenia, when integrated with laboratory inflammatory markers, provides a robust, mechanistically grounded, and clinically accessible multimodal prognostic framework across critically ill, pulmonary, and geriatric populations.
articles.ai_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the prognostic value of CT-assessed sarcopenia, alone or combined with laboratory inflammatory markers, for predicting mortality and other outcomes in critically ill, pulmonary, and geriatric patients. The results showed that CT-assessed sarcopenia, when integrated with laboratory inflammatory markers, provides a robust prognostic framework. The pooled odds ratio for mortality in sarcopenic patients was 2.28, and 5.84 in COVID-19 pulmonary populations.
articles.ai_significance: This study provides a clinically accessible multimodal prognostic framework for critically ill, pulmonary, and geriatric populations, which can help clinicians make more informed decisions.

articles.title: Endotracheal tube size selection in critically ill patients: a 4-year single-center experience in Saudi Arabia.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intubation is a critical aspect of airway management and supportive care for intensive care unit (ICU) patients. Inappropriate size of endotracheal tubes (ETT) affects the patient's airway, it is crucial to choose an appropriate size for each patient. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to assess current practices of ETT size. SELECTION: for adult ICU patients and to explore factors associated with it. DESIGN AND SETTINGS: Single-center, retrospective cohort study at King Fahad Hospital of the University, Saudi Arabia. PATIENTS AND METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted for adult patients admitted to ICU from January 2020 to January 2024 at King Fahad Hospital of the University. Inclusion criteria included patients aged 18 years or older, underwent intubation and was followed by tracheostomy. Those with missing data, had laryngeal or thyroid masses, had upper airway obstruction by any cause and upper airway surgery were excluded. MAIN OUTCOME AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was compliance of ETT size selection with established guidelines. Secondary outcomes included associations between ETT size (mm), patient demographics and intubation indications. RESULTS: A total of 228 ICU patients were analysed [mean (standard deviation) age of 61.8 (19.6) years]. The median internal diameter of the ETT size was 7.5 mm, with neurological causes being the most common indication for intubation. ETT size showed a significant positive correlation with height (rs=.341; P<.001) and weight (rs=0.190; p=0.004), but not with body mass index (rs=.050; P=.456). In multivariable analysis, larger ETT size was significantly associated with male sex (adjusted odds ratio, aOR 2.38, 95% confidence interval, CI 1.12-5.05), pulmonary indication for intubation (aOR 2.31, 95% CI 1.10-4.86), older age (aOR 1.20 per 10 years, 95% CI 1.02-1.42), and height (aOR 1.95 per 10 cm, 95% CI 1.20-3.16), whereas weight was not independently associated after adjustment (aOR 1.04 per 10 kg, 95% CI 0.85-1.26). Overall, 77% of ETT size selection did not comply with height-based guidelines. CONCLUSIONS: No standardized ETT size selection guidelines were followed for adult ICU patients. Male sex, height, older age, and pulmonary indication were independent predictors of larger ETT size, supporting the implementation of more structured, height-informed ETT sizing protocols.
articles.ai_summary: This study reviewed endotracheal tube (ETT) size selection in critically ill patients over 4 years at a Saudi Arabian hospital. The researchers found that ETT size was not consistently chosen according to established guidelines and was associated with patient demographics such as height, sex, and age. They also identified factors that predicted larger ETT size.
articles.ai_significance: This study highlights the need for more structured and evidence-based approaches to ETT size selection in ICU patients, which could improve patient outcomes and reduce complications.

articles.title: Effects of Integration Sedation Interruption With Early Mobility on Patient Outcomes and Prevention of Intensive Care Unit-Acquired Weakness in Critically Ill Ventilated Patients.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early mobilization and sedation reduction are critical strategies for improving patient outcomes. AIM: This study assessed the effects of integrating daily sedation interruptions with an early progressive mobility strategy on outcomes in critically ill, ventilated patients. STUDY DESIGN: A quasi-experimental research with a control group was conducted on a sample of 60 mechanically ventilated adult patients who met the inclusion criteria. We randomly divided the patients into 30 groups, with each representing the control and study groups. Data were gathered using 4 tools. RESULTS: The intervention group showed significant improvements (P < .001) in Medical Research Council strength scores, progressive mobility milestones, and functional assessment. Moreover, the intervention group showed significant improvements in clinical outcomes (P < .001), including shorter hospital stays, fewer adverse events, improved discharge status, and better weaning outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: The protocol for integrating sedation interruptions with early progressive mobility is associated with improved outcomes of critically ill ventilated patients. Further randomized controlled trial studies are suggested to improve patients' clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Effectiveness of Quality Improvement Strategies in Preventing Healthcare-Associated Infections Among Neurosurgical Patients Admitted to Intensive Care Units: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) remain a major and largely preventable cause of morbidity, excess mortality, prolonged hospitalization, and escalating healthcare costs in intensive care units (ICUs) worldwide. Neurosurgical patients are particularly vulnerable because of frequent exposure to invasive devices such as external ventricular drains (EVDs), central venous catheters, urinary catheters, and mechanical ventilation, combined with impaired neurological status and prolonged ICU stays. Although quality improvement (QI) strategies have been widely implemented across critical care settings, evidence specific to neurosurgical and neurocritical care populations remains fragmented. OBJECTIVES: To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of QI interventions in reducing HAI incidence among neurosurgical and neurological ICU patients and to assess their impact on secondary outcomes including ICU length of stay, device utilization, and bundle compliance. METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science from January 2010 to May 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Eligible studies for the primary evidence synthesis included randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, and observational cohort studies evaluating structured QI interventions for HAI prevention in neurosurgical or neurological ICU populations, or mixed ICU settings with extractable neurocritical care data. Systematic reviews identified during screening were retained for contextual interpretation and reference screening but were excluded from the primary evidence synthesis to avoid duplication of overlapping primary data. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I, Cochrane RoB 2, and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale according to study design. RESULTS: Seventeen primary studies from 14 countries met eligibility criteria and were included in the primary narrative synthesis. Three systematic reviews were retained for contextual interpretation. Structured QI interventions consistently reduced device-associated infection rates across studies. The strongest evidence was observed for EVD-specific care bundles, with EVD-related infection rates decreasing from 14.35 to 3.21 per 1,000 catheter-days following bundle implementation, and one study reporting 20 consecutive infection-free months after interprofessional bundle adoption. Device-associated infection prevention bundles also demonstrated clinically meaningful reductions, including VAP rates decreasing from 68.2 to 47.4 per 1,000 ventilator-days and CAUTI rates from 24.9 to 13.4 per 1,000 catheter-days following structured educational interventions. CLABSI rates declined substantially following standardized central venous catheter bundle implementation, reaching zero in one study with sustained monitoring. Risk of bias was predominantly low to moderate across included primary studies. CONCLUSIONS: Structured QI interventions, particularly EVD-specific care bundles, device-associated infection prevention protocols, and staff education programs with compliance monitoring, consistently reduce HAI incidence in neurosurgical and neurological ICU settings. Although the evidence base is predominantly non-randomized, findings are directionally consistent across diverse healthcare systems and institutional contexts. Universal adoption of evidence-based infection prevention frameworks in neurocritical care is strongly supported.

articles.title: Rapid Response System Escalation During Recovery of Hospital Bed Occupancy: An Observational Longitudinal Study.
articles.abstract: Early warning scores (EWS) identify patient deterioration, but their impact depends on how they are integrated into workflows and escalation culture, particularly as hospitals recover from pandemic-related bed pressures. To evaluate changes in rapid response system (RRS) escalation processes and rare safety outcomes after embedding an EWS within proactive Critical Care Outreach Team (CCOT) rounds as hospital bed occupancy recovered. Observational longitudinal study at a single tertiary hospital in Japan comparing one pre-intervention year (2021) with three post-intervention years (2022-2024). In January 2022, a standardised EWS was embedded into proactive CCOT rounds and used as a prompt for shared clinical reasoning rather than a strict numeric trigger. Monthly aggregated ward-level data were analysed using Poisson regression, adjusting for seasonality, patient characteristics and bed occupancy. Across 71 985 admissions and 692 942 general-ward patient-days, rates of nurse-initiated escalations, RRS activations and resuscitation-status updates per 1000 patient-days increased in post-intervention analyses, but these differences were attenuated after full adjustment. In fully adjusted models, post-intervention incidence rate ratios (IRRs) were close to 1.0 for all process outcomes. For nurse-initiated escalations, IRRs ranged from 0.94 to 1.14, and all 95% confidence intervals included 1.0. Rates of unexpected in-hospital cardiac arrest and unplanned ICU admission remained low and stable. Bed occupancy increased over the study period, but within-year associations with outcomes were weak. After adjustment for patient characteristics and hospital bed occupancy, embedding an EWS within proactive CCOT rounds was associated with broadly stable escalation process indicators and no clear evidence of deterioration in rare safety outcomes. These findings suggest that approaches to the RRS afferent limb that embed EWS use within structured dialogue between ward nurses and outreach teams may provide one plausible mechanism for sustaining escalation behaviours under operational pressure.

articles.title: Post-norepinephrine fluid volume and clinical outcomes in septic shock: a landmark retrospective cohort analysis of MIMIC-IV.
articles.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
articles.abstract: Fluid administered after norepinephrine initiation may reflect both resuscitation decisions and evolving illness severity, making observational comparisons susceptible to confounding and reverse causation. To evaluate associations between fluid volume during the first 6 h after norepinephrine initiation and mortality and incident invasive ventilation. We reconstructed an adult MIMIC-IV cohort with coded sepsis and norepinephrine initiated during ICU hours 0-24. Eligibility required complete pre-norepinephrine physiology and initial norepinephrine rate, survival, and ICU observation through a 6-hour landmark. Fluid exposure was ≤1,000 versus >1000 mL. Stabilized inverse-probability weights were truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Doubly adjusted logistic models used patient-clustered robust standard errors. The cohort included 2696 ICU stays from 2493 patients; 1572 received ≤1,000 mL. Maximum weighted standardized mean difference was 0.033. Twenty-eight-day mortality occurred in 1117 stays. Lower-volume exposure was not associated with mortality (odds ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.89-1.31; adjusted risks 42.6% versus 41.1%). Results were similar for other mortality analyses and thresholds. Among 1356 stays not ventilated at baseline, incident ventilation was not clearly associated with exposure (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.53-1.13). The spline showed no dose-response association (p = 0.983). After source-level cohort construction and expanded adjustment, post-norepinephrine fluid volume was not associated with mortality or incident invasive ventilation.

articles.title: Determining the Prevalence of Hospital-Acquired Anemia in the Intensive Care Unit at a Florida Hospital.
articles.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
articles.abstract: Hospital-acquired anemia (HAA), which negatively affects morbidity, mortality, and resource use, is a common iatrogenic effect of hospitalization, especially in intensive care units. Contributing factors include phlebotomy, intravenous fluid resuscitation, and medications. To determine the prevalence of HAA among adult patients in a southwest Florida intensive care unit and evaluate the relationship between decline in hemoglobin level and length of intensive care unit stay. A retrospective, exploratory medical record review of a 6-month convenience sample (N = 151) was conducted. Hospital-acquired anemia was defined as a 10% or greater decline in hemoglobin level from admission to discharge. Of 108 patients meeting inclusion criteria, 69 (64%) developed HAA. Stays were significantly longer for the 69 patients with HAA than for the 39 patients without HAA (mean [SD], 5.9 [5.8] days vs 3.3 [3.6] days; P = .005). The mean (SD) decline in hemoglobin level was 20% (8%) for patients with HAA and 4% (2%) for patients without HAA (P < .001). A sensitivity analysis excluding 6 outliers (n = 102) confirmed that stays were significantly longer for patients with HAA than for patients without HAA (mean [SD], 5.1 [4.2] days vs 2.8 [1.7] days; P < .001). Hospital-acquired anemia is prevalent in this intensive care unit and correlates with longer stays. Although causality regarding phlebotomy was not directly measured, the high prevalence of HAA supports implementing blood conservation strategies to improve clinical outcomes and reduce iatrogenic blood loss.

articles.title: Evaluating cardiopulmonary resuscitation in "The Pitt": accuracy, clinical realism, and adherence to international resuscitation guidelines.
articles.abstract: Medical television dramas shape public perceptions of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). The Pitt has been praised for its clinical realism but has not been systematically evaluated. We assessed adherence of televised CPR to current European Resuscitation Council (ERC) and American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines. All cardiac arrest (CA) scenarios requiring chest compressions or defibrillation in seasons 1 & 2 (30 episodes) of The Pitt were prospectively analysed using a standardized assessment via an electronic case report form based on Utstein-style variables by at least 2 emergency and/or intensive care physicians experienced in CA management. Seventeen CA were identified. Most occurred in hospital (65%, n = 11/17) and had medical causes (59%, n = 10/17). ROSC was achieved in 56% (n = 9/16), and survival to discharge in 46% (n = 6/13). Key elements of the initial assessment, including consciousness and pulse checks, were fully guideline compliant, and correct hand placement was observed in 94% (n = 15/16). In contrast, guideline-compliant compression rate were achieved in only 19% (n = 3/16) of assessable cases, respectively, and pre-airway 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratios were absent. Immediate post-shock rhythm reassessments were observed in 78% (n = 7/9) of appropriate cases. Nevertheless, no inappropriate shocks were delivered during asystole, and rhythm-based pharmacotherapy was appropriate, although medication timing and sequence could not be reliably assessed. The Pitt provides a highly realistic portrayal of cardiac arrest, although manual CPR technique and some algorithmic details remain imperfect.

articles.title: Sense of Coherence in Patients After Intensive Care Treatment: A 1-Year Follow-Up Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Patients endure physical, mental and cognitive symptoms after critical illness, and coping is vital to their healing process. Little research exists on associations between sense of coherence (SOC) and patients' health improvements after intensive care unit (ICU) discharge. To describe the trajectory of SOC and how demographic, clinical and psychosocial variables affect SOC in discharged ICU patients during 12 months of follow-up. A prospective cohort substudy of a neutral randomized controlled trial in Norway involving discharged ICU patients receiving nurse-led follow-up consultations or standard care. Data were collected in the ward (baseline) and after 3, 6 and 12 months. Univariate and multivariate linear mixed models for repeated measures were fitted with SOC-13 score as the dependent variable. We included 523 patients with a median of three ICU days, median age 57 years, 47% females, 54% receiving mechanical ventilation and stable SOC during follow-up. Higher SOC was associated with increased age (B = 0.12, 95% CI [0.05, 0.18]), no prior mental health problems (B = 6.69, 95% CI [4.19, 9.19]), no prior use of psychotropics (B = 2.37, 95% CI [0.16, 4.58]) and lower post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) at baseline (B = 5.56, 95% CI [3.50, 7.61]). Low educational level (B = -2.25, 95% CI [-4.10, -0.40]), higher pain interference at baseline (B = -0.46, 95% CI [-0.84, -0.08]) and less social support 3 months later (B = -5.93, 95% CI [-7.87, -3.99]) were associated with lower SOC. During 12 months after ICU discharge, SOC remained stable. Higher age, no previous mental health problems or use of psychotropics, and lower PTSS were associated with higher SOC. Low education, more pain and low social support were associated with lower SOC. More vulnerable patients deserve greater attention during general rehabilitation after ICU treatment due to low SOC.

articles.title: The Relationship Between Caring Roles and Fatigue in Intensive Care Nurses: A Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.abstract: Intensive care nurses experience significant levels of fatigue while providing care to their patients. High levels of fatigue may negatively impact nurses' orientation to their caring roles, and this orientation may also be a cause of fatigue. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between intensive care nurses' orientations towards their caregiving roles and their fatigue levels. The sample of this cross-sectional and correlational study was conducted with nurses working in the intensive care units of a hospital in northwestern Turkey. The 'Personal Information Form', 'Chalder Fatigue Scale' and 'Nursing Care Role Orientation Scale' were used for collecting research data. In this study, conducted with 110 nurses, the average fatigue score for intensive care nurses was 19.00 ± 7.60, with a physical fatigue score of 13.13 ± 5.20 and a mental fatigue score of 5.87 ± 2.81. The average score of nurses' orientation towards caregiving roles was 82.00 ± 7.68. Female nurses and those working in critical care for less than a year experienced greater fatigue levels (t = 2.131, p = 0.035 and F = 2.858, p = 0.041, respectively). Nurses' orientation towards caregiving roles differed based on their education level and professional experience (p < 0.05). There was a positive correlation between nurses' fatigue scores and orientation towards caregiving roles (p < 0.05). Intensive care nurses were able to effectively adapt to their nursing care roles despite high levels of fatigue and there was a positive relationship between nurses' physical and mental fatigue levels and their adaptation to their care roles. The results of this study, which cannot be generalised to all intensive care nurses because it was conducted in a single hospital, reveal that as nurses' orientation towards their caring roles increases, their fatigue levels also increase. For intensive care nurses to effectively care for their patients, they need to be well oriented in their caregiving roles. However, efforts to be well oriented in caregiving can increase nurses' fatigue levels. Considering that reducing physical and mental fatigue will increase the success of the care nurses provide, the importance of providing work environments that will facilitate intensive care nurses' orientation to their caregiving roles in reducing the fatigue levels they experience becomes evident.

articles.title: Intensive Care Unit Patients' Perspectives and Experiences in Using Virtual Reality Technology: A Qualitative Meta-Synthesis.
articles.abstract: As Intensive Care Unit (ICU) survival improves, attention has shifted towards patients' psychological well-being and recovery. Although Virtual Reality (VR) is increasingly used in critical care, patients' experiences of VR interventions have not been comprehensively synthesised. To synthesise qualitative and mixed-methods evidence regarding ICU patients' perceptions, experiences and implementation-related considerations associated with VR interventions. A qualitative systematic review and thematic synthesis following Thomas and Harden's three-stage approach was conducted. Eight databases were searched from inception to September 2025. Studies employing qualitative methods or components of mixed methods exploring ICU patients' firsthand VR experiences were included. Methodological quality was appraised using the JBI checklist. Eight studies involving 247 participants were included. Four analytical themes were synthesised: (A) VR as a restorative escape, (B) VR as a route from passive endurance to active participation, (C) Patient readiness and personal preference shape VR engagement, and (D) VR as a co-produced intervention requiring contextual and relational adaptation. ICU patients perceived VR as a valuable tool that provided restorative escape and enabled active recovery, yet multiple barriers shaped its feasibility. Implementation should consider comfortable devices, customisable content and staff training. These findings inform patient-centred VR design in the ICU. VR offers a non-pharmacological approach that may support patient well-being and recovery during an ICU stay. It can provide meaningful focus and relief from distress, while encouraging engagement with rehabilitation. Nurses play a key role in facilitating sessions and assessing patient readiness. Implementation may be enhanced by comfortable, bed-compatible devices, customisable content and staff training. While not all patients may be suitable candidates, VR appears generally acceptable and could be integrated into individualised care plans. The review protocol had been registered in PROSPERO (International prospective register of systematic reviews). The registration number is CRD420251074650.

articles.title: Efficacy and Safety of Low-Dose Versus Standard-Dose Alteplase to Treat High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism.
articles.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
articles.abstract: The optimal dosing of alteplase in patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism is widely debated. To evaluate outcomes in patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism who received alteplase at a low dose or a standard dose. This was a retrospective cohort analysis of 65 patients who received alteplase for high-risk pulmonary embolism at a large academic medical center between June 1, 2011, and August 31, 2022. Patients were placed in 2 cohorts according to initial dose: low-dose alteplase (50 mg) and standard-dose alteplase (100 mg). The primary outcome was sustained hemodynamic stability within 24 hours of the start of alteplase infusion. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, hospital and intensive care unit length of stay, and major bleeding. The primary outcome of sustained hemodynamic stability within 24 hours did not differ significantly between the 2 cohorts (achieved in 32% of patients in the low-dose group and 38% in the standard-dose group; P = .65). In-hospital mortality did not differ significantly between groups (48% in the low-dose group vs 45% in the standard-dose group; P = .81). Patients in the low-dose group had fewer days of mechanical ventilation than patients in the standard-dose group (1.5 vs 6 days; P = .03) and a smaller percentage had major bleeding (12% vs 25%; P = .34). In patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism, sustained hemodynamic stability within 24 hours did not differ significantly between low-dose and standard-dose alteplase treatment strategies. Low-dose alteplase may be an appropriate alternative dosing strategy for patients with high-risk pulmonary embolism.

articles.title: Management of Intensive Care Unit Admission of Patients With Blood Cancer.
articles.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
articles.abstract: Patients with blood cancer are at high risk of complications requiring intensive care. Admission to the intensive care unit (ICU) involves ethical and organizational complexities. To investigate the perspectives of hematologists and intensivists making ICU admission decisions in France. A nationwide survey of French hematologists and intensivists was conducted using clinical vignettes to assess ICU admission criteria. The influence of institutional practices, individual experiences, and cancer status on ICU transfer decisions was explored. All 174 participating physicians agreed on ICU admission for patients with immediately life-threatening conditions. Although the general principle of early ICU admission was supported by 75% of hematologists and 54% of intensivists, responses to specific clinical scenarios showed that intensivists recommended broader ICU access and earlier involvement, particularly for patients with noncritical but high-risk conditions. Hematologists more often deferred ICU discussions until clinical deterioration had occurred. Structural barriers such as lack of shared protocols, variations in training, and absence of ICU staff members in hematology decision-making contributed to inconsistent practices. Ethical guidelines were underrecognized and unevenly applied. Neither physician group routinely included nurses in discussions despite nurses' critical role in ICU care. In France, ICU admission practices for patients with blood cancer vary between hematologists and intensivists. Harmonizing practices through common training, early multidisciplinary discussions, risk assessment models, and improved knowledge of ethical standards is urgently needed. These findings may reflect global challenges in aligning ICU triage with evolving cancer care.

articles.title: The Experiences and Needs of Nursing Staff During Patients' ICU-To-Ward Transition: A Meta-Synthesis of Qualitative Studies.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) transitional care ensures continuous care for patients transferring from the ICU to general wards. Relevant qualitative studies show that nurses play a vital role here, so exploring their real experiences and needs is essential for nursing development. To summarise the current qualitative evidence on the experiences and needs of nursing staff during ICU transitional care. A meta-synthesis of qualitative studies retrieved through a search conducted in China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang, VIP Database, Cochrane Library, PubMed, Web of Science, CINAHL and Embase from inception to June 2025. All studies that presented qualitative findings on the experiences, feelings and needs of nursing staff, based on participants' reports, were included. Data extracted included publication year, location, sample size, study design, data collection method, phenomenon of interest and all qualitative themes identified. Thirteen studies were selected for inclusion, resulting in four synthesised findings: the practical challenges faced by nursing staff during the ICU transition period, their perceptions and attitudes towards transitional care, their supportive needs for transitional care and recommendations for improving transitional care. The provision of transitional care services by nursing staff is influenced by factors such as existing medical resources, psychological support, workflows and organisational structures. These can guide nursing administrators and healthcare institutions in addressing the occupational needs of nursing personnel, optimising transitional care interventions and promoting the high-quality development of transitional care practices. Despite cultural differences, the experiences and needs of nursing staff during the transition period in the ICU reflect commonalities across cultures. The review gives specific advice for ICU transition care, including establishing effective communication models, psychological support and professional training, establishing ICU liaison nurses and formulating standardised ICU transition procedures.

articles.title: Family Engagement and Shared Decision-Making in Adult Intensive Care Nursing: A Bibliometric Review and Thematic Analysis.
articles.abstract: Family members contribute information, emotional support, bedside care and surrogate decision-making in adult intensive care, yet the nursing literature on family engagement remains conceptually and geographically fragmented. To map the development, intellectual structure, collaboration patterns and thematic evolution of research on family engagement and shared decision-making in adult intensive care nursing. This study was a bibliometric review with complementary thematic content analysis. Following the framework of Donthu et al., Scopus was searched on 16 July 2026 from inception, with bibliometric coverage restricted to complete calendar years through 31 December 2025. Scopus was used because it provides the cited-reference data required for co-citation and bibliographic-coupling analyses. Eligible records were journal articles and reviews concerning adult intensive care that examined family engagement or shared decision-making and included an identifiable nursing component. Performance analysis, co-authorship analysis, reference co-citation, bibliographic coupling, and keyword co-occurrence analysis were conducted using Python and VOSviewer, while cluster content was interpreted using inductive qualitative content analysis. Reporting followed the BIBLIO guideline. The review included 278 publications (1993-2025) from 117 journals and 47 countries. Annual output increased from two publications in 1993 to 32 publications in 2025; 141 publications (50.7%) were published during 2020-2025. Nursing journals produced most publications, whereas two multidisciplinary critical care journals produced 23 publications (8.3%) but 3090 of 11 220 citations (27.5%). The United States led with 104 publications; 23.9% were internationally co-authored. Co-citation analysis identified four intellectual foundations and bibliographic coupling five research fronts, led by family participation and nurse-family engagement. Thirty-nine author keywords formed six themes spanning end-of-life communication and ethics, family-centred nursing engagement and surrogate participation, family support and visitation, family presence in high-acuity care, caregiver experience and bereavement. Keyword trends moved from family needs and withholding treatment towards active engagement, implementation barriers and family nursing. The field has progressed towards partnership but continues to under-specify nurses' roles, use inconsistent terminology and draw disproportionately on high-income Western settings. Critical care services should formalise nurses' responsibilities in family assessment, communication, advocacy and decision support while developing culturally responsive and implementable engagement models.

articles.title: From Framework to Toolkit: Practical Guidance for Using the PrOcess Evaluation of Trials In Critical care (POETIC) Framework.
articles.abstract: The PrOcess Evaluation of Trials In Critical care (POETIC) framework was developed to support systematic evaluation of Context, Fidelity, Dose, Reach, and an integrative assessment of Quality of Delivery (QoD). Its practical use, however, requires explicit guidance on selecting measures, constructing QoD, assessing changing context, and governing prospective use. We undertook a retrospective comparative synthesis of process evaluations embedded in four randomized U.K. critical care trials: Biomarker-guided antibiotic stewardship in suspected ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAPrapid-2), Provision of Psychological Support to People in Intensive Care (POPPI), Sedation AND Weaning In CHildren (SANDWICH), and Alpha-2 agonists for sedation to produce Better outcomes from critical illness (A2B). We selected them because they informed POETIC's development or application and provided sufficiently detailed quantitative and qualitative evidence. We mapped the reports, protocols, and process evaluation findings to the five dimensions; compared recurring and contradictory patterns, quantitative-qualitative agreement, measurement and interpretation problems, and mechanism-specific limitations; and translated our learning into guidance for applying the framework. The relevance and measurement of POETIC dimensions varied according to how each intervention was expected to work. Contextual influences changed over time and differed between sites. Combined assessments of QoD required explicit decisions about component selection, weighting, thresholds, aggregation, and missing data. VAPrapid-2 showed why a separate Dose measure and a QoD composite were not meaningful for a one-off diagnostic recommendation; POPPI used a weighted site composite; SANDWICH summarized delivery of four intervention components, staff training, and patient Reach; and A2B combined four equally weighted indicators in a 0-12 site score. This cross-trial learning informed practical guidance on selecting measures, assessing context over time, integrating quantitative and qualitative findings, constructing QoD, and governing prospective use. POETIC is best used as a mechanism-aligned, mixed-method scaffold rather than a requirement to measure every dimension or calculate a universal composite. Prospective use is feasible when outputs, recipients, review times, permitted actions, and safeguards are prespecified. The framework and accompanying toolkit support reproducible assessment while protecting trial integrity.

articles.title: Dysphagia in Patients With High-Flow Nasal Cannulas: Risk and Practice Implications.
articles.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
articles.abstract: High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy is often used in critical care, but its effects on swallowing function remain unclear. Dysphagia in hospitalized patients is associated with complications and prolonged length of stay, yet screening and referral practices vary widely. Limited evidence exists to guide evaluation of dysphagia risk factors among patients receiving HFNC therapy. To identify patients most at risk for developing dysphagia during HFNC therapy and to examine differences in clinical outcomes based on dysphagia status. This retrospective chart audit reviewed adult inpatients (≥21 years) who received HFNC therapy between 2022 and 2024. Of 1038 eligible patients, 210 were randomly selected for chart audit; 195 were included after exclusions. Data included HFNC settings, dysphagia status, and clinical outcomes. No dose-response relationship was identified between dysphagia and HFNC settings, including flow rate, fraction of inspired oxygen, or duration. Dysphagia during admission was not associated with mortality (all P's > .36) or preexisting dysphagia status (χ2 = 3.7, P = .16). However, patients with dysphagia had longer intensive care unit stays than patients without dysphagia and patients with unknown dysphagia status (P = .04 and P = .09, respectively), and dysphagia status was associated with intubation (χ2 = 13.6, P = .001), with intubation most common among patients with dysphagia. This cohort showed no association of HFNC settings with dysphagia status, and no specific triggers were identified to inform standardized dysphagia screening protocols for patients receiving HFNC therapy. Dysphagia was associated with intubation and prolonged intensive care unit stay.

articles.title: Intensive Care Nurses' Experiences and Attitudes Towards Family Involvement in Delirium Care: A Qualitative Descriptive Study.
articles.abstract: Delirium is a common neuropsychiatric complication among critically ill patients, particularly those who are mechanically ventilated. Evidence suggests family involvement may improve delirium-related outcomes in adult intensive care units (ICUs). However, limited evidence exists on intensive care nurses' (ICNs) experiences and attitudes towards family involvement in delirium care in South Africa. The study aimed to explore intensive care nurses' experiences and attitudes towards family involvement in the care of mechanically ventilated patients with delirium in adult ICUs. A descriptive qualitative study design was utilised. Four focus group discussions were conducted with 32 ICNs from two adult ICUs at a tertiary academic hospital in Johannesburg between April and August 2022. Participants who had at least 2 years of intensive care experience were purposively sampled. Data were analysed using inductive qualitative content analysis. The study adhered to Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Studies guidelines. Three categories were identified: emotional burden and psychological demands of delirium care, communication and psychosocial support for families in delirium care and barriers to effective family involvement in delirium care. While recognising the therapeutic value of family engagement, the nurses reported experiencing emotional stress related to family expectations and anxiety. They adopted strategies such as structured communication, empathetic listening and technology-assisted contact to support families. However, barriers such as time constraints, limited intensive care space, staffing shortages and restrictive policies limited sustained involvement. This study provides context-specific insight into how ICNs facilitate family involvement in the care of patients with delirium in a public tertiary ICU. ICNs recognise the therapeutic value of family involvement in the care of patients with delirium and are willing to facilitate engagement. However, systemic and environmental barriers limit consistent implementation. Therefore, strengthening institutional policies and supporting nurses through structured training and team-based approaches may enhance sustainable family-centred delirium care. This study's findings demonstrate the need for ICNs to adopt structured communication strategies, flexible visitation policies and empathy towards families and their patients in the ICU. Perhaps incorporating family-centred care into daily intensive care practices could strengthen family involvement in critical care, particularly for patients with delirium.

articles.title: Olanzapine for the Prevention and Treatment of ICU Delirium: Protocol for a Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) delirium is a multifactorial acute brain dysfunction associated with prolonged hospitalization, increased morbidity and mortality, and higher healthcare costs. Despite these substantial negative impacts of delirium, the optimal prevention and treatment strategies are unclear. Olanzapine, an atypical antipsychotic drug, is commonly used for delirium management. We will perform an updated systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the benefits and harms of olanzapine for the prevention and treatment of ICU delirium. This protocol is developed in accordance with the recommendations of The Cochrane Collaboration and is reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) guidelines. We will include all randomized clinical trials (RCTs) evaluating prophylactic or therapeutic olanzapine versus any comparator, including pharmacological, non-pharmacological, placebo, or routine care/no specific delirium-directed intervention (treated as a single comparator) in ICU patients. Observational studies will be included solely to address potential harms. We will systematically search the following databases: Embase, MEDLINE, The Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CINAHL, Scopus, and PsycINFO, as well as clinical trial registries. We will perform meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis (TSA) to investigate the risk of both Type I and II errors. We will assess the risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool (RoB-2). The quality of trials will be evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations (GRADE) approach. The review is registered in the PROSPERO database (CRD420261474813). The primary outcome is days alive and out of the hospital. The secondary outcomes include all-cause mortality at 90 days, number of CAM-ICU (Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit) negative days at 30 days, number of days without pharmacological treatment for delirium other than study drug during the intervention period and serious intervention-related harms. This protocol outlines the methodology we will use in a systematic review with meta-analysis designed to evaluate the beneficial and harmful effects of olanzapine for prevention and treatment of delirium in ICU patients. The findings of the systematic review will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication. We hope this review will inform future RCTs and improve clinical practice.

articles.title: Postoperative Delirium in Intensive Care Units: A Bibliometric Analysis of Nursing Studies.
articles.abstract: Delirium is a common and serious postoperative complication in intensive care units, associated with increased morbidity, mortality and long-term cognitive impairment, and despite the pivotal role of nurses in its assessment and management, variations in prevalence and gaps in intervention-focused nursing research persist, underscoring the need for a bibliometric evaluation of the literature. The aim of the study was to quantitatively analyse and visually map trends, citations, key terms and country contributions in nursing research on postoperative delirium in intensive care as well as to characterize the overall structure of the literature. This study was conducted as a retrospective and descriptive research using the bibliometric analysis method on December 1, 2025. No time restrictions were imposed on the literature. Data analysis was performed using R Studio software. The earliest study on postoperative delirium in intensive care units within the field of nursing was published in 2001, and the analysed publications covered the period from 2001 to December 2025. In addition, 55.96% of all publications have been released in the past 7 years. The journal with the highest number of publications is Nursing in Critical Care, while the United States stands out as the country with the highest research output. It can be suggested that topics such as 'cardiac surgery', 'nursing care', 'postoperative delirium', 'postoperative care' and the 'Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit' represent areas that warrant further investigation and development in future research. The analysis showed a marked increase in publications on postoperative delirium in intensive care nursing in recent years. The United States and the Journal Nursing in Critical Care were identified as the leading contributors to the literature. Thematic mapping indicated that the literature primarily focused on delirium assessment and intensive care nursing, with several interconnected research areas. The findings emphasize the critical role of nurses in delirium screening and management in intensive care units. While assessment tools are well represented in the literature, further research is needed to develop and evaluate nurse-led interventions aimed at delirium prevention and care. Enhancing nursing education and institutional support may contribute to improved patient outcomes and quality of postoperative intensive care.

articles.title: Global Research Trends in Sleep Quality, Sleep Deprivation and Sleep Promotion Among ICU Patients: A Descriptive and Evaluative Bibliometric Analysis.
articles.abstract: Sleep deprivation and poor sleep quality are critical problems among intensive care unit (ICU) patients, with significant implications for recovery, delirium onset and clinical outcomes. Despite growing scientific interest, no bibliometric study has systematically mapped the intellectual structure and thematic evolution of this field. To analyse the bibliometric characteristics and thematic structure of publications on sleep deprivation, sleep promotion and sleep quality in ICU patients indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database between 1983 and 2026. A descriptive and evaluative bibliometric analysis was conducted. Data were retrieved on April 26, 2026, from the WoS Core Collection using a comprehensive search strategy. Publications were filtered by document type, WoS categories (nursing, critical care medicine, anaesthesiology) and index (SCI-EXPANDED, SSCI, ESCI). Data were analysed using R software with the Biblioshiny interface, and annual publication trends were evaluated using Microsoft Excel. Of 11 418 publications retrieved, 379 met the inclusion criteria, spanning 37 years (1983-2026). Linear regression revealed a statistically significant positive trend in publication output (β = 0.643, R2 = 0.704, r = 0.839, p < 0.001), with mean annual publications of 10.24 ± 8.83 and notable acceleration from the 2000s onwards. Thematic mapping identified 'sleep', 'sleep deprivation' and 'delirium' as motor themes both highly central and well developed. Emerging concepts included circadian rhythm, actigraphy, fatigue, pain and anxiety. ICU sleep research has grown substantially over four decades, with sleep deprivation and delirium emerging as co-dominant research priorities. Thematic gaps and emerging clusters identified in this analysis highlight important directions for future nursing research and evidence-based practice development in critical care. This bibliometric analysis identified sleep deprivation and delirium as the co-dominant motor themes of ICU sleep research, and intervention-related concepts such as earplugs, eye masks and melatonin as emerging clusters. These evidence-based trends can guide ICU nurses in prioritizing targeted sleep promotion protocols and support policymakers in directing resources toward the most scientifically mature intervention areas in critical care.

articles.title: Incidence of Intensive Care Unit Delirium After Heart Surgery: A Feasibility Study of a Forest Environment Intervention.
articles.abstract: Postoperative delirium is a serious complication in intensive care units (ICUs), particularly following cardiac surgery. It is associated with circadian rhythm disruption, sleep disturbances and adverse outcomes. ICU environments often lack natural time cues, which may exacerbate circadian misalignment and increase delirium risk. The primary aim of the study was the evaluation of the implementation of two chronotherapeutic ICU interventions regarding recruitment, implementability and safety. Its secondary aim was to descriptively assess postoperative delirium across intervention groups. This randomized feasibility study was conducted in a tertiary cardiac surgery ICU in Austria. Adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery were allocated to one of three groups: (1) forest environment, (2) light exposure or (3) standard ICU care. Interventions were applied for 12 h daily. Delirium was assessed at three postoperative time points using the confusion assessment method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) and intensive care delirium screening checklist (ICDSC). This study was conducted between March 2020 and 2025. Seventy-seven patients were enrolled, and 64 remained in the final analytical cohort. Interventions were delivered within routine care. Patients and ICU staff did not report intervention-related concerns. Implementation challenges included ICU restructuring, patient transfers due to COVID-19 and deviations from randomized allocation because of operational constraints. No intervention-related adverse events occurred. Delirium assessments were limited at several time points because of sedation, early ICU discharge or transfer. Across all groups, postoperative delirium was detected in 5 of 130 CAM-ICU completed assessments (3.8%) and 8 of 115 ICDSC completed assessments (6.9%), precluding inferential group comparisons. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions were feasible and safe in ICU care. Feasibility results highlighted challenges related to ICU logistics, sedation-related assessment limitations and pandemic-related disruptions. The unexpectedly low delirium incidence limited conclusions regarding intervention efficacy. Future trials should include larger high-risk populations and prospectively defined feasibility outcomes. Optimized ICU environments, including noise reduction and light management, may support delirium prevention. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions are feasible additions to routine ICU care.

articles.title: Post-intensive care syndrome at 6 months and 1 year among survivors of severe COVID-19 requiring invasive mechanical ventilation: a single-center observational study.
articles.journal: Journal of infection and chemotherapy : official journal of the Japan Society of Chemotherapy
articles.abstract: Long-term multidomain impairment after critical coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) overlaps with post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) and post-COVID-19 condition. We assessed PICS at 6 months and 1 year after hospital discharge and explored associated clinical factors in Japanese patients with COVID-19 requiring invasive mechanical ventilation. This single-center observational study included adult patients with COVID-19 who required invasive mechanical ventilation and survived to discharge. PICS was assessed using the Barthel Index, Short-Memory Questionnaire, and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale. Exploratory multivariable logistic regression examined factors associated with 1-year PICS. Of 67 discharged survivors, 37 completed both 6-month and 1-year assessments; 17 (45.9%) received extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. PICS was present in 22 (59.5%) patients at 6 months and 21 (56.8%) at 1 year, and 15 (40.5%) had cognitive impairment at both assessments. Delirium was more frequent in patients with PICS than in those without at 6 months (63.6% vs 26.7%, p = 0.045) and 1 year (66.7% vs 25.0%, p = 0.020). In the exploratory multivariable analysis, delirium was associated with 1-year PICS after adjustment for age and mechanical ventilation duration (odds ratio, 7.09; 95% confidence interval, 1.54-32.7; p = 0.012). PICS was common 6 months and 1 year after hospital discharge among survivors of severe COVID-19. In an exploratory analysis, delirium was associated with 1-year PICS after adjustment for age and mechanical ventilation duration. This hypothesis-generating finding requires confirmation in larger prospective cohorts.

articles.title: Ultrasonographic Pupil Assessment in Patients With Severe Traumatic Brain Injury.
articles.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
articles.abstract: In patients with severe traumatic brain injury, accurate pupillary assessment is critical for neurological monitoring but is often hindered by periorbital edema, trauma, or dressings that preclude direct visualization. To validate the feasibility and accuracy of ultrasonographic pupil assessment performed through the closed eyelid as an alternative to direct pupillometry in patients with traumatic brain injury. This prospective study enrolled 45 intensive care unit patients (36 male; mean [SD] age, 67.1 [12.9] years). Both direct pupillometry and ultrasonographic pupil assessment were sequentially completed within a 3-minute interval under standardized low-light conditions for both eyes. Direct pupillometry involved video recording of the exposed pupil with a calibrated reference scale. Ultrasonographic pupil assessment was performed by using a high-frequency linear probe placed on the closed eyelid. The primary outcome was the agreement between methods for calculating the percentage of pupillary constriction. Secondary outcomes included agreement on resting and minimum pupil diameters. Ultrasonographic pupil assessment showed excellent agreement with direct pupillometry for percent pupillary constriction (median [IQR] difference, 0.44% [-2.78% to 2.83%]; Wilcoxon P ≥ .48). Bland-Altman analysis showed narrow limits of agreement. Strong correlations were also noted for resting and minimum pupil diameters (0.6 ≤ r2 ≤ 0.873). Ultrasonographic pupil assessment is a reliable and accurate method for objective pupillary evaluation when direct visualization is obstructed. By enabling quantitative measurement of the pupillary light reflex through the closed eyelid, ultrasonographic pupil assessment addresses an important monitoring gap in the management of patients with severe traumatic brain injury and periorbital swelling.

articles.title: Effect of preoperative video-based digital educational program on incidence of delirium and length of hospital stay following coronary artery bypass grafting: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
articles.abstract: Postoperative delirium is common after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and is associated with prolonged hospitalization and delayed recovery. Non-pharmacological educational interventions may improve outcomes, but evidence on structured video-based education for delirium prevention remains limited. To evaluate the effect of a preoperative video-based educational program on postoperative delirium incidence and hospital length of stay among patients undergoing CABG surgery. A parallel-group randomized controlled trial was conducted at Queen Alia Heart Institute, Jordan, between October 2025 and January 2026. Adult patients scheduled for elective first-time CABG surgery were randomized into intervention and control groups. Both groups received standardized multidisciplinary preoperative education through the institutional Preoperative Clinic, while the intervention group additionally received an 8-minute structured Arabic video-based educational program. Postoperative delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU). Among 226 randomized participants, 213 were analyzed (105 intervention; 108 control). Delirium incidence was lower with intervention (7.6%vs 25.0%, p < .001) and remained significantly associated with study group after adjustment (OR = 3.14, 95% CI: 1.08-9.14, p = .036). Hospital stay was shorter in the intervention group unadjusted (8.38 vs 10.58 days, p < .001), but not after adjustment (B = -0.656, p = .182). Preoperative video-based education was associated with lower postoperative delirium incidence, while its association with shorter hospital stay was not maintained after adjustment. Larger multicenter trials are warranted.

articles.title: Application of Combined Gastric Tube Tip Manometry and Auscultation for Nasogastric Tube Positioning in Neurocritical Care Patients With Artificial Airways: A Prospective Diagnostic Pilot Study.
articles.abstract: Nasogastric tube placement is central to enteral nutrition support in neurocritical care patients. However, tube malposition, particularly accidental placement into the airway, can lead to fatal complications. To assess the accuracy of a combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation approach for confirming nasogastric tube placement in neurocritical care patients with artificial airways. This prospective study enrolled patients who underwent nasogastric tube insertion in the neurocritical care unit of a tertiary hospital in China between January 2025 and May 2025. Using chest X-ray as the reference standard, we compared the sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), positive likelihood ratio (PLR) and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) for gastric tube tip manometry alone, auscultation alone and their combination. In total, 120 patients participated. X-ray confirmed correct nasogastric tube positioning in 119 patients and malposition in 1 patient. For gastric tube tip manometry alone, the sensitivity was 97.48%, with a specificity of 0%, a positive predictive value (PPV) of 99.15% and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 0%. Auscultation alone yielded a sensitivity of 90.76%, a specificity of 100%, a PPV of 100% and an NPV of 8.33%. The combined manometry-plus-auscultation approach had a sensitivity of 88.24%, a specificity of 100%, a PPV of 100% and an NPV of 6.67%. The combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation method might serve as an adjunctive bedside strategy for confirming nasogastric tube placement in neurocritical care patients with artificial airways. However, only one malpositioned tube was observed in this study; the specificity and NPV should be interpreted with caution. When gastric aspirate cannot be obtained or immediate chest radiography is impractical, combined gastric tube tip manometry and auscultation provide a feasible, radiation-free bedside pathway for confirming nasogastric tube position; equivocal or negative bedside findings should still be verified radiographically before feeding. The study was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2300078001).

articles.title: Inhaled nitric oxide: Expanding indications beyond traditional boundaries.
articles.abstract: Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) is a selective pulmonary vasodilator that improves ventilation-perfusion matching with minimal effect on systemic blood pressure. Although the FDA approval is restricted to neonatal hypoxic respiratory failure associated with pulmonary hypertension, many clinicians now use iNO in adults with conditions where elevated pulmonary vascular resistance, right ventricular dysfunction threaten stability and hypoxic respiratory failure. This review examines both the mechanistic rationale and the available evidence for such off-label use. Examples range from acute RV failure in the ICU to perioperative support in cardiac surgery, heart and lung transplantation, and severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, including COVID-19-associated acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). In these settings, iNO offers rapid afterload reduction and short-term improvement in oxygenation, but randomized trials are lacking and limited studies to date have failed to consistently show outcome benefits. Adverse effects such as methemoglobinemia, nitrogen dioxide toxicity, rebound pulmonary hypertension, and a potential increase in acute kidney injury risk in certain non-cardiac surgical populations. Additionally, cost considerations and other practical limitations must be weighed carefully. Overall, current evidence supports the use of iNO as an adjunctive therapy in carefully selected critically ill patients.

articles.title: Clinical Impact of Haemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis Among Patients With HIV/AIDS and Disseminated Histoplasmosis in a Hyperendemic Region of Northeastern Brazil.
articles.abstract: Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome that may occur in people living with HIV/AIDS (PLWHA), often triggered by opportunistic infections such as disseminated histoplasmosis (DH). The substantial overlap in clinical and laboratory features between HLH and DH complicates timely diagnosis. To describe HLH among PLWHA with DH and compare clinical, laboratory and outcome characteristics between patients with and without HLH. A retrospective observational study was conducted at São José Hospital of Infectious Diseases, Fortaleza, Brazil, between March 2023 and June 2024. Hospitalised PLWHA with DH were evaluated for HLH based on the presence of ≥ 3 HLH-2004 criteria and an H-Score ≥ 169. Baseline clinical, laboratory and outcome parameters were compared between patients with and without HLH. Among 61 patients diagnosed with DH, 11 (18.0%) met the study criteria for HLH. Patients with HLH were more likely to present with hepatomegaly (p = 0.036), haemoptysis (p = 0.030) and lower platelet counts (p = 0.029). In-hospital mortality was significantly higher among patients with HLH (54.5% versus 18.0%; p = 0.019). These patients more frequently required renal replacement therapy (p = 0.028) and intensive care unit admission (p = 0.048). Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank testing demonstrated significantly reduced in-hospital survival among patients with HLH (p = 0.015). HLH represents a severe complication in PLWHA with DH and is associated with increased mortality and greater need for intensive care. Early recognition and use of adjunctive diagnostic tools may facilitate timely management and improve clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Clinical Phenotypes, Machine-Learning Risk Stratification and Treatment Outcomes of Constipation in Stroke Patients Receiving Enteral Nutrition: A Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract: Stroke-related complications and frequent feeding interruptions often compromise nutritional intake, making enteral nutrition (EN) a cornerstone therapy to improve nutritional status and support recovery. Nevertheless, constipation is highly prevalent and clinically consequential among stroke patients receiving EN, particularly in critically ill populations, where enteral nutrition-associated constipation can impede rehabilitation, increase complications and prolong intensive care unit (ICU) stay. This study aimed to explore potentially important determinants of enteral nutrition-associated constipation (ENAC) in patients with stroke using artificial intelligence approaches, characterise relevant clinical subgroups, compare internally validated machine-learning models and examine how the temporal availability of candidate predictors may influence model performance. Clinical data from patients admitted to a neurological intensive care unit between December 2019 and December 2023 were retrospectively analysed. K-means clustering was used to identify clinical subgroups. Six algorithms-logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting tree, XGBoost, LightGBM and Table PFN-3-were compared under temporally restricted and expanded retrospective feature frameworks using five repeats of nested five-fold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using ROC-AUC, average precision, Brier score, calibration and decision-curve analysis. Treatment outcomes were summarised descriptively. Among 362 patients, 233 (64.4%) had documented constipation. Table PFN-3 achieved the highest discrimination in both frameworks. The temporally restricted model yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.629 (95% CI 0.567-0.689), whereas the expanded retrospective model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.771 (95% CI 0.715-0.820), average precision of 0.857, Brier score of 0.177 and calibration slope of 0.965. The ROC-AUC increased by 0.142 (95% CI 0.090-0.201) after full-hospitalisation information was included. K-means clustering retained three subgroups (K = 3; silhouette coefficient = 0.108), with constipation frequencies of 67.35%, 56.98% and 88.89% in Clusters 0, 1 and 2, respectively. Among evaluable patients, observed relief was 80.3% with glycerin enema, 60.0% with lactulose, 72.7% with combination treatment and 65.7% with neither treatment; these treatment comparisons were descriptive. Table PFN-3 achieved the strongest internally validated performance, with the expanded retrospective framework combining good discrimination, strong precision-recall performance and close calibration. The 0.142 increase in ROC-AUC after completed hospital-course variables were incorporated quantifies the substantial discriminative information that emerges as hospitalisation evolves. Together with the distinct clinical phenotypes and descriptive treatment findings, these results establish a clinically relevant framework for trajectory-aware bowel monitoring and provide a clear rationale for developing dynamic, time-updated prediction models. By integrating machine-learning benchmarking, clinical phenotyping and observed treatment outcomes, this study identifies prolonged, treatment-intensive hospital trajectories as a particularly high-burden constipation phenotype and demonstrates that classification performance changes materially as hospital-course information accumulates. These findings support structured reassessment of bowel risk during neurological intensive care rather than reliance on a single static evaluation and provide a practical rationale for future dynamic monitoring tools.

articles.title: Reducing Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infections in ICUs: A Systematic Review of Barriers and Facilitators and Intervention Measures.
articles.abstract: Despite established guidelines, central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI) remains a severe ICU complication due to cognitive and resource barriers hindering healthcare worker compliance. A systematic evaluation of these barriers and facilitators is currently lacking but is important for informing targeted implementation strategies for CLABSI prevention. To explore the barriers and facilitators to implementing CLABSI prevention in ICUs using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to provide evidence-based strategies for improvement. A PRISMA-guided systematic review was performed using PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, VIP, Wan fang, and CBM databases, up to August 2026. Eligible studies included qualitative, quantitative, or mixed-methods research on the barriers and facilitators to CLABSI prevention implementation among ICU healthcare workers. Two researchers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Data synthesis and intervention development were guided by the CFIR, with targeted strategies mapped using the CFIR-ERIC (Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change) matching tool. The literature search identified 1,780 records, of which 28 studies were ultimately included. The review identified 28 barriers and facilitators, which were synthesized into four major themes and mapped to 16 CFIR constructs across the catheter-care continuum. The most prominent barriers involved staff knowledge gaps, inconsistent adherence to recommended practices, limited resources, and insufficient leadership support. CFIR-ERIC mapping identified 11 Level 1 expert-endorsed implementation strategies, of which four were represented in the included literature and seven were identified as potential implementation gaps. CLABSI prevention in ICUs is influenced by multilevel implementation determinants spanning individual, organizational, and practice-related factors.
