A structured implementation-science approach may help healthcare organizations identify context-specific barriers and prioritize targeted strategies to support more consistent implementation of evidence-based CLABSI prevention practices. Improving CLABSI prevention may require multilevel strategies that combine targeted education and training, adequate resource allocation, leadership engagement, standardized clinical procedures, and ongoing audit and feedback. These strategies may help strengthen adherence to evidence-based practices, improve quality of care, and enhance patient safety in ICUs.

articles.title: A nomogram for predicting in-hospital mortality in patients with coagulase-negative staphylococcus bloodstream infections.
articles.journal: Journal of infection and chemotherapy : official journal of the Japan Society of Chemotherapy
articles.abstract: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) have emerged as significant pathogens in bloodstream infections (BSIs). Currently, no validated models exist for specifically predicting in-hospital mortality in patients with CoNS-BSIs. A retrospective study was conducted on adult patients with CoNS-BSIs using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-III) database. Participants were randomly allocated into a training set (n = 366) and a validation set (n = 157). Demographic characteristics, severity scores, comorbidities and laboratory examinations from the first 24 h of ICU admission were analyzed. The optimal predictive variables for establishing a nomogram were screened through univariate, multivariate logistic regression and stepwise regression analyses. Model performance was evaluated by receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curve, calibration curve, decision curve analysis (DCA) and clinical impact curve (CIC). Among 523 patients enrolled, the overall in-hospital mortality was 22.9%. Four independent predictors were incorporated into the nomogram: age (OR = 1.04), anion gap (AG: OR = 1.11), total bilirubin (TBil: OR = 1.26) and respiratory failure (OR = 1.97). The area under the curve (AUC) values in the training set and validation set were 0.758 and 0.823, respectively. The P-values of the calibration curve in two sets were 0.258 and 0.432. The DCA curves were above the two extreme curves. The CIC analysis revealed a high concordance between predicted high-risk cases and observed clinical events when the risk threshold exceeded 60%. Age, AG, TBil and respiratory failure were independent risk factors for in-hospital mortality among patients with CoNS-BSIs. The nomogram based on these four parameters demonstrated good performance and clinical utility for risk assessment.

articles.title: Clinical factors associated with noninvasive ventilation-associated pneumonia in acute respiratory failure: a prospective cohort study.
articles.journal: Heart & lung : the journal of critical care
articles.abstract: Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is preferred to invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) as treatment for acute respiratory failure due to its lower complication rate, but NIV may still be associated with serious complications such as nosocomial pneumonia. However, risk factors associated with NIV-associated pneumonia remain insufficiently characterized. To investigate factors associated with NIV-associated pneumonia in patients treated with NIV for acute respiratory failure in a respiratory intensive care unit. In this prospective cohort study, we followed adult patients who were admitted to a respiratory intensive care unit in a tertiary hospital for acute respiratory failure. None of the patients had pneumonia on admission. All patients were treated with NIV and monitored daily for the development of nosocomial pneumonia, which was defined using standardized criteria. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with NIV-associated pneumonia. Among 191 eligible patients admitted between March 2023 and May 2024, 84 developed NIV-associated pneumonia. Age was not independently associated with pneumonia development. In multivariable analysis, poor oral hygiene, poor secretion control, and longer NIV duration were independently associated with NIV-associated pneumonia. Patients who developed pneumonia also had longer ICU stay and higher rates of antibiotic modification. In patients receiving NIV for acute respiratory failure, poor oral hygiene, poor secretion control, and prolonged NIV exposure were independently associated with NIV-associated pneumonia, whereas chronological age, sepsis, and frailty were not. These findings suggest that clinical factors related to bedside care and NIV exposure may be more relevant to pneumonia development than age alone.

articles.title: Persistent Endothelial Glycocalyx Disruption in Sepsis: Translational Evidence for Melatonin-Mediated Vascular Protection.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome driven by a dysregulated host response to infection, with endothelial dysfunction and glycocalyx disruption playing central roles in vascular failure. Despite growing recognition of the glycocalyx as a therapeutic target, its temporal dynamics and potential pharmacological modulation remain poorly understood. We performed a translational study combining longitudinal clinical observations in septic patients with mechanistic investigations in a murine cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) model. Plasma from patients was collected at intensive care unit admission and after clinical recovery to assess inflammatory mediators, coagulation parameters, and glycocalyx-related biomarkers. In parallel, the CLP model evaluated systemic and tissue-specific glycocalyx alterations and the effects of injectable melatonin. Acute sepsis induced marked alterations in multiple glycocalyx-related biomarkers in patients, with several changes persisting despite normalization of organ dysfunction and standard inflammatory indices, indicating ongoing endothelial injury and repair. In the CLP model, sepsis reproduced these alterations, while melatonin treatment significantly attenuated systemic cytokine responses and partially restored circulating and tissue glycocalyx components in an organ- and gene-specific manner. These results highlight persistent, dynamic glycocalyx disruption as a key driver of sepsis pathology and support pharmacological stabilization of the glycocalyx as a promising therapeutic strategy. Melatonin emerges as a potential endothelial-protective agent capable of promoting vascular recovery and homeostasis, providing translational insight for interventions targeting microvascular integrity in sepsis.

articles.title: [Sepsis-induced coagulopathy].
articles.abstract: Sepsis-induced coagulopathy (SIC) represents a frequent and prognostically highly relevant complication of sepsis, characterized by a dysregulated interaction between inflammation, endothelial activation and coagulation. Pathophysiologically, the excessive host immune response to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMP) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMP), activation of the complement cascade, formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NET) and disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx collectively promote a prothrombotic and antifibrinolytic microenvironment, resulting in microvascular thrombosis, organ dysfunction and increased mortality. Approximately 20-25% of critically ill patients with sepsis fulfil the diagnostic criteria for SIC. Current diagnostic approaches rely on scoring systems such as the International Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis (ISTH)-SIC, ISTH overt-disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and Japanese Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis (JSTH)-DIC scores; however, their clinical utility remains limited as they predominantly collate hemorrhagic parameters even though sepsis is typically characterized by a thrombotically dominated phenotype. Viscoelastic point-of-care assays enable dynamic bedside assessment of coagulation and fibrinolysis, including the frequently occurring hypofibrinolysis or fibrinolytic shutdown, which is associated with an unfavorable outcome; however, for this specific purpose, these methods have not yet been sufficiently validated or established as a diagnostic standard. Data and recommendations on specific therapeutic options are limited. A consistent pharmacological thromboprophylaxis remains the cornerstone in patients with sepsis, with low-molecular weight heparins demonstrating advantages over unfractionated heparin regarding venous thromboembolic complications. Coagulation modulating treatment, such as antithrombin, recombinant thrombomodulin or activated protein C, have thus far failed to demonstrate consistent survival benefits in large randomized clinical trials. Experimental approaches targeting NET formation, complement activation or fibrinolytic modulation appear mechanistically promising but require further clinical validation. Overall, SIC necessitates an individualized, pathophysiology-driven diagnostic and therapeutic approach integrating inflammatory, endothelial, thrombotic and fibrinolytic alterations.

articles.title: Investigating Fibrinolysis Resistance in Sepsis Using High-Multiplex Plasma Proteomics: A Statistical Analysis Plan.
articles.abstract: Sepsis-induced coagulopathy is characterised by consumptive coagulation abnormalities and resistance to fibrinolysis, which is increasingly recognised as a driver of microvascular thrombosis, organ dysfunction and mortality. The molecular determinants of the fibrinolysis-resistant phenotype remain incompletely defined. To present a pre-specified statistical analysis plan for a plasma proteomic investigation of fibrinolysis resistance in 89 samples collected serially from 32 critically ill patients with sepsis, using the Olink Explore HT platform (approximately 5400 proteins). The plan is designed to characterise protein associations with a validated bedside measure of fibrinolysis resistance, the ratio of tissue plasminogen activator-induced lysis time to fibrin clot amplitude (TPA-LT/FIBA10). The associations will be examined across the fibrinolysis resistance severity continuum and between three ordinal severity grades, and over time within individual patients. The analytic framework combines five complementary approaches: (i) limit-of-detection-based data filtering, (ii) continuous-variable modelling of protein abundance against TPA-LT/FIBA10 using limma-trend regression, (iii) categorical comparison across severity grades using empirical Bayes moderated statistics, (iv) linear mixed-effects modelling of longitudinal intra-patient trajectories and (v) pathway-level enrichment analysis to translate statistical associations into mechanistic hypotheses. A semi-supervised pathway clustering analysis will describe how proteins change by fibrinolysis resistance in eight a priori defined domains. This multi-model design is intended to define genuine biological signals in a high-dimensional dataset while remaining transparent about the exploratory nature of several components. The statistical reasoning behind each method is discussed alongside anticipated limitations. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06680180.

articles.title: The First 48 Hours: Incidence, Timing and Predictors of Adverse Events After ICU-To-Ward Transfer: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: The transition from the intensive care unit (ICU) to a general ward is a period of heightened vulnerability, yet the precise timing and modifiable predictors of adverse events remain poorly defined. To determine the incidence, timing and types of adverse events following ICU-to-ward transfer, evaluate the predictive accuracy of four early-warning scores and identify independent risk factors. A prospective cohort study of 207 adult patients transferred from ICUs to general wards at a tertiary university hospital over 20 months (March 2024-October 2025) was enrolled. Four early warning scores (PACS, MEWS, SWIFT, LACE) were calculated daily for 5 days post-transfer. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors. The total number Adverse events occurred in 52 patients (25.1%), most commonly ICU readmission (n = 46, 22.2%) and healthcare-associated infections (n = 29, 14.0%). Critically, 88% of events occurred within the first 48 h (day 1: 56.0%; day 2: 32.0%). SWIFT demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy at transfer (AUC 0.856). Mechanical ventilation was the strongest independent risk factor (OR 10.11), followed by prolonged ICU stay (OR 6.40), respiratory diagnosis (OR 4.99), > 3 invasive devices (OR 4.41) and comorbidities (OR 3.64). These five factors collectively explained 88.5% of adverse events. Adverse events affect one in four patients after ICU-to-ward transfer, with the vast majority occurring within the first 48 h. A simple set of readily identifiable risk factors can guide nursing surveillance and targeted interventions during this critical window. Bedside nurses should prioritize enhanced monitoring for patients with a history of mechanical ventilation, prolonged ICU stay, multiple invasive devices and significant comorbidities during the first 48 h post-transfer. Daily use of early-warning scores can inform monitoring frequency and rapid response activation.

articles.title: The Role of Emotional Intelligence in Intensive Care Nursing: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Emotional intelligence (EI) is critical in intensive care unit (ICU) nursing, where nurses face high stress, clinical instability and emotionally demanding situations. EI helps nurses manage emotions, improve communication and support clinical performance. It has also been linked to lower burnout and more adaptive coping among ICU nurses. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence on emotional intelligence among nurses working in ICUs, including its key dimensions, associated professional outcomes and current knowledge gaps. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and reported following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. A structured search was conducted in MEDLINE, CINAHL, PubMed and Scopus for studies published in the past 10 years in Portuguese, English or Spanish. In total, this review included nine studies. The evidence highlights the crucial role of EI in emotional regulation, communication and clinical performance among ICU nurses. Key dimensions of emotional intelligence, including empathy, emotional clarity and self-regulation, were consistently identified as important. Training programmes demonstrated significant improvements in EI and reduced burnout symptoms, and EI was also associated with more adaptive coping strategies and improved professional performance. Emotional intelligence is an important competency in ICU nursing and has been linked to improved communication, clinical decision-making and lower burnout among nurses. Despite these benefits, research still shows gaps, particularly in standardising EI assessment tools and in the need for longitudinal studies. Targeted emotional intelligence training programmes may strengthen ICU nurses' emotional resilience and enhance care quality. Integrating EI development into ICU nursing education and institutional policies can help reduce burnout, improve communication with patients and families, and enhance overall clinical performance, thereby supporting a healthier work environment and strengthening nurses' communication and professional performance in intensive care settings.

articles.title: Effect of Progressive Muscle Relaxation and Nature Sounds on Alarm Fatigue in Intensive Care Unit Nurses: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) nurses are exposed to numerous alarms, many of which are unnecessary and lead to alarm fatigue. This phenomenon, caused by desensitization to alarm sounds, reduces nurses' responsiveness to critical alerts and threatens both their well-being and patient safety. Alarm fatigue has been linked to elevated stress, burnout and errors in patient care, underscoring the need for effective interventions. Progressive muscle relaxation involves the gradual and systematic contraction and relaxation of different muscle groups throughout the body and nature sounds use for decrease stress and alarm fatigue. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) and exposure to nature sounds in reducing alarm fatigue among ICU nurses. A three-arm, parallel, single-blinded randomized controlled trial was conducted. Ninety-six ICU nurses from three hospitals in southern Iran, were randomly assigned to one of three groups: PMR (n = 32), nature sounds (n = 32) or control (n = 32). Alarm fatigue was assessed using a validated alarm fatigue scale at baseline, immediately after the intervention and 2 months post-intervention. Both PMR and nature sound interventions significantly reduced alarm fatigue among ICU nurses (p < 0.001). Between-group comparisons showed significant differences between the PMR and control groups (p < 0.001) and between the nature sound and control groups (p < 0.001). No significant difference was observed between the PMR and nature sound groups (p = 0.650). PMR and exposure to nature sounds significantly reduced alarm fatigue among ICU nurses, as reflected in lower fatigue scores. These interventions improved nurses' capacity to manage stress and fatigue, thereby supporting better job performance and enhanced patient safety. Given their simplicity and accessibility, both approaches represent promising strategies for addressing alarm fatigue in critical care settings. Progressive muscle relaxation and nature sounds may offer practical, non-pharmacological approaches to managing alarm fatigue among intensive care unit nurses. These interventions could be incorporated into nurses' work routines, although further research is needed to confirm their effectiveness and long-term benefits.

articles.title: Psychological Detachment Among Intensive Care Unit Nurses: A Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit nurses face sustained workload, vigilance and emotionally demanding care. Psychological detachment during non-work time is an important recovery experience, but evidence in this population remains limited. To describe psychological detachment among intensive care unit nurses and identify demographic, departmental psychological support resources availability, social support and burnout dimensions associated with it. A single-centre cross-sectional survey. Registered intensive care unit nurses from a tertiary grade A general hospital in eastern China were recruited by convenience sampling between June and July 2025. Participants completed demographic, psychological detachment, burnout and social support questionnaires. Descriptive analyses, univariate comparisons, correlation analyses and multivariable linear regression were performed. The study was reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology checklist. Of 220 questionnaires submitted, 199 valid responses were analysed (90.45%). The mean psychological detachment score was 11.68 ± 3.85. Mean emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and personal accomplishment scores were 37.75 ± 8.15, 16.93 ± 4.87 and 25.91 ± 6.25, respectively. Psychological detachment correlated negatively with emotional exhaustion (r = -0.230, p = 0.001) and positively with subjective support (r = 0.175, p = 0.013). Departmental psychological support resources availability (B = 1.674, β = 0.216, p = 0.001), head-nurse position (B = -4.776, β = -0.195, p = 0.004) and emotional exhaustion (B = -0.115, β = -0.243, p < 0.001) were independently associated with psychological detachment. In this single-centre sample of intensive care unit nurses, the reported availability of departmental psychological support resources was associated with higher psychological detachment, whereas head-nurse position and emotional exhaustion were associated with lower psychological detachment. These findings suggest that critical care nursing managers may consider departmental psychological support resources availability, nursing position and emotional exhaustion when assessing recovery needs among intensive care unit nurses.

articles.title: How Preceptors Can Cultivate Professional Identity Formation Through Meaningful Participation in Experiential Learning.
articles.journal: Journal of the American College of Clinical Pharmacy : JACCP
articles.abstract: When engaged in experiential learning, trainees enter a complex ecosystem where expertise relies on collaboration and the intentional use of environmental resources. To better explain this learning environment, this paper will define and describe concepts of educational theory related to situativity theory and the cognitive ecosystems perspective and offer ways to apply them to experiential learning design using an intensive care unit (ICU) as an example practice setting. By viewing the ICU as a cognitive ecosystem, we highlight how recognition and use of available resources and opportunities can support trainee growth and development of a contextualized, or situated, professional identity. Traditionally, experiential learning has emphasized internal mental processes, focusing on how trainees assess patients and recognize medication-related problems. However, expertise extends beyond individual knowledge and includes the ability to recognize and interact with the physical and social elements that exist within the clinical environment. Although the interconnected nature of clinical practice is widely recognized, limited guidance exists for applying situativity theory and cognitive ecosystems to experiential learning design. Viewing a practice setting as a cognitive ecosystem provides a lens for intentionally immersing trainees within the environment to promote meaningful participation in clinical practice. When viewed through this lens, microsystems within the practice setting emerge that support clinical reasoning, communication, and patient care. Across these microsystems, interactions with the resources and people within the environment may promote the development of clinical reasoning and situated professional identity. Intentional interactions within each microsystem can help trainees progress from an observational role to active participation in patient care, progressing beyond basic knowledge acquisition and recall. Using the ICU as an example, we argue that viewing the practice area as a cognitive ecosystem offers opportunities for experiential learning design for preceptors, along with enriching experiences for trainees that are critical for professional identity formation.

articles.title: Psychological Distress Among Black Surrogates of Intensive Care Unit Patients: A Cross-Sectional Survey Study.
articles.abstract: Anticipatory grief and Post-Intensive Care Syndrome-Family (PICS-F) are increasingly recognised as important sources of psychological distress among family members of critically ill patients. However, these experiences remain understudied among Black surrogate decision-makers. The aim of this study was to evaluate the association between anticipatory grief and PICS-F and to examine whether emotional closeness and positive religious coping were associated with anticipatory grief among Black family surrogates of intensive care unit (ICU) patients. In this cross-sectional survey study, 70 Black surrogate decision-makers of adult ICU patients were recruited from ICUs at a large metropolitan hospital in the Midwestern United States. Participants completed measures of emotional closeness, positive religious coping, anticipatory grief, anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress symptoms. Multivariable linear regression analyses examined associations among study variables. Emotional closeness and positive religious coping were not statistically significantly associated with anticipatory grief. Anticipatory grief was statistically significantly associated with higher PICS-F symptoms. Among Black ICU surrogate decision-makers, anticipatory grief was associated with greater psychological distress, suggesting it may represent an important target for future supportive interventions and research.

articles.title: Network Analysis of Factors Influencing ICU Patient Transfer Readiness: A Social-Ecological Model Approach.
articles.abstract: ICU transfer readiness is a multidimensional state influenced by informational, functional, emotional and support-related needs. Network analysis can clarify how readiness indicators and emotional distress co-occur as a system, rather than as independent factors. To (1) model conditional associations among ICU transfer-readiness indicators and anxiety/depressive symptoms and (2) identify highly connected and highly predictable targets that may be prioritised in transitional-care interventions. Transfer readiness was measured using the ICU Transfer Readiness Scale (15 items; 0-10) and emotional distress using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS; 14 items; 0-3). A regularised mixed graphical model (MGM) was estimated to accommodate mixed/ordinal data. Edge-weight accuracy, centrality robustness and node predictability (R2) were assessed using bootstrap procedures. Age and gender were included as background variables. A total of 276 ICU patients were included in the analysis. The estimated network showed a clear modular structure: transfer-readiness indicators clustered into personal status, disease knowledge, coping after transition and expected-support domains; HADS symptoms clustered into anxiety and depression domains. Within transfer readiness, the strongest association occurred between two expected-support indicators, suggesting perceived support is tightly interlinked. Within HADS, multiple strong within-subscale connections were observed for both anxiety and depression symptoms. Node predictability ranged from 0.224 to 0.633 (mean 0.434), with the highest predictability for key readiness indicators in the knowledge/coping domains (R2 ≈0.63). Bootstrap analyses supported acceptable stability of the main edge and centrality patterns. Demographic nodes showed comparatively weaker and more cautious-to-interpret associations. ICU transfer readiness and emotional symptoms form structured conditional interdependencies, indicating readiness should be conceptualised and addressed as a connected system rather than isolated determinants. Transitional-care strategies may be strengthened by prioritising highly connected/predictable readiness targets-particularly expected support and key knowledge/coping indicators-while concurrently screening for and addressing anxiety/depressive symptoms to improve transfer preparation and early post-transfer adjustment.

articles.title: Concept Analysis of Building Rapport in the ICU.
articles.abstract: Building rapport, understood as establishing a meaningful and trusting relationship through interpersonal interactions between healthcare professionals and patients or their family members, was described in research as early as the 1960s. Although studies highlight its importance in clinical relationships, the concept remains largely undefined, with limited research on experiences of rapport among family members of intensive care unit patients. This concept analysis can help to provide conceptual clarity for future practice and research. This paper aimed to analyse and define the concept of 'building rapport' with ICU family members. The concept analysis framework of Walker and Avant was used, following the systematic steps of identifying uses, attributes, antecedents, consequences and model cases. Data were obtained from Swedish and English dictionaries and peer-reviewed articles identified through a systematic literature search and screening. Titles and abstracts were reviewed, and six studies were selected based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. This analysis clarifies the previously undefined concept of building rapport from the perspective of ICU family members. Building rapport is characterized by empathy and mutual understanding. Key antecedents include communication, time and relationships, while consequences are increased trust and the development of a care partnership. An empirical referent is a shift from family members as passive recipients to active participants in care. Key features of building rapport with ICU family members are empathy and mutual understanding, supported by communication, time and relationships. The findings suggest that rapport may facilitate family participation and care partnerships in intensive care. However, the findings should be interpreted in light of the limited empirical basis and the absence of formal quality appraisal. Clarifying the concept of building rapport may support communication training, reflective practice and active listening strategies that strengthen partnerships with ICU family members.

articles.title: Nurse-Led Interventions to Mitigate High-Alert Medication Errors in Critical Care: A Systematic Review of Effectiveness and Implementation Strategies.
articles.abstract: Intensive care units (ICUs) are high-risk environments where nurses administer the majority of high-alert medications, making them the final checkpoint in the medication-use process. However, evidence on nurse-led interventions specifically targeting high-alert medication errors has not been systematically synthesized across all ICU populations. This systematic review evaluated the effectiveness of nurse-led interventions in reducing high-alert medication errors in neonatal, paediatric and adult intensive care units and examined implementation strategies that enhance patient safety. We followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus for studies published between January 2000 and June 2026. Inclusion criteria required nurse-led interventions, measurement of high-alert medication error rates and critical care settings. The risk of bias was assessed. A narrative synthesis was performed due to heterogeneity in study designs and outcome measures. Six studies met the inclusion criteria. Interventions included simulation-based training, staff education, smart pump integration, clinical decision support systems and standardization of medication orders and protocols. All studies reported improvements in medication safety outcomes, including reductions in medication error rates, improved compliance, enhanced accuracy and increased efficiency. Secondary outcomes included improved compliance with PRN orders (from 62.0% ± 9.2% to 77.7% ± 10.1%), reduced medication dispensing time (to < 1 min) and cost savings ($90 000-$130 000 per year). Risk of bias was moderate to low in five studies and high in one study. Nurse-led multicomponent interventions are associated with reductions in high-alert medication errors and improvements in safety outcomes in critical care settings. However, technology alone is insufficient without workflow integration and nursing education. Education and standardization require concurrent process redesign for sustained improvement. Nurses should advocate for multicomponent strategies combining training, technology and standardized protocols. Healthcare organizations must ensure workflow integration to maximize the benefits of smart pumps and clinical decision support systems. Future research should employ rigorous designs, include diverse ICU settings and low- to middle-income countries and evaluate long-term sustainability.

articles.title: Nursing Mechanisms of Intravenous Medication Loss in Adult Intensive Care: A Mixed-Methods Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Adult ICU medication loss is reported using non-equivalent forms and denominators, limiting interpretation and intervention design. To examine loss measurement, nursing mechanisms, intervention evidence and balancing outcomes. Convergent segregated mixed-methods systematic review. Three databases were searched to 1 July 2026, with citation searching, metadata checks and an uncapped rerun of two capped PubMed arms. Quantitative results remained in native units; qualitative findings were synthesised separately and integrated. MMAT 2018 was applied by design category; two reviewers checked screening, extraction and appraisal. Of 768 screened records (576 primary; 192 rerun), 79 reports were assessed with retained sources. Four reports could not be retrieved. Twenty-five reports from 21 independent studies were included; the rerun added none. Categories were prepared-unused medication (11), post-order or post-event loss (7), partial-container residual (8), delivery-system residual (3) and material-flow loss (4); categories were nonexclusive. Denominators were explicit in 10 studies, partial in 5 and absent in 6. No studies met pooling criteria. Two qualitative studies generated six low-confidence CERQual findings. Intervention evidence was uncontrolled, modelled or proposal-based; balancing outcomes were uncommon. Adult ICU loss comprised non-equivalent quantities, not one waste prevalence, and no study related it to a patient outcome. Studies would need to specify loss form, numerator, denominator, observation window, workflow node, result origin and balancing outcomes alongside resource use. Order review before non-urgent preparation, reconstitution and checking, storage and return pathways, and syringe, pump and line handling are candidate targets; no controlled adult ICU study has shown reduced loss without affecting access, dose delivery, sterility, compatibility or workload.

articles.title: Pilot Testing of the Teaching Engagement and Caregiving Help in the Intensive Care Unit (TEACH-ICU) Scale.
articles.journal: American journal of critical care : an official publication, American Association of Critical-Care Nurses
articles.abstract: Family members often assume caregiving responsibilities after a patient's discharge from the intensive care unit (ICU). Many family members are inadequately prepared due to limited training and support. Intensive care unit nurses can prepare family members to perform caregiving by proactively teaching family members in the ICU. However, no quantitative measure exists to examine nurses' willingness to teach caregiving skills to family members. To examine the Teaching Engagement and Caregiving Help in the ICU (TEACH-ICU) scale, adapted from the Family Willingness for Caregiving Scale. Refinements from cognitive interviews readied the TEACH-ICU scale for pilot testing to assess the broader survey process before examining the scale's validity and reliability in a larger-scale study. This was a descriptive, cross-sectional study of 30 adult ICU nurses recruited via convenience and snowball sampling through social media platforms and the American Association of Critical-Care Nurses Participate in Research website. Relationship testing was conducted between the TEACH-ICU scale, Hospital Ethical Climate Survey (HECS), and Marlowe-Crowne Social Desirability Scale-Short Form (MCSDS-Short Form). The TEACH-ICU scale showed high mean willingness scores across all items. The TEACH-ICU total scores significantly correlated with HECS total scores and 4 subscales: peers, managers, hospital, and physicians. No significant relationship was observed between TEACH-ICU scores and social desirability scores. The scale and survey process were modified based on this pilot study's results, in preparation for examining the validity and reliability of the TEACH-ICU scale.

articles.title: Female Representation and Quality Indicators in Anesthesiology and Critical Care Podcasts.
articles.abstract: Podcasts have emerged as prominent tools for asynchronous medical education, widely adopted across training levels and specialties. Diverse representation strengthens medical discourse, making an evaluation of speaker demographics essential for understanding equity and quality in digital knowledge dissemination. This study systematically evaluates female representation and quality assurance indicators in anesthesiology and critical care podcasts, including longitudinal publication trends. We systematically searched Apple Podcasts and Spotify using specialty-specific terms and manually reviewed the top twenty journals in the field for affiliated podcasts. Included were active, English-language, physician-hosted podcasts. Eighty-five podcasts (53.0% US-based) comprising 10,190 episodes were analyzed. Of 12,522 hosts, 31.5% (n = 3945) were female; of 10,822 guests, 35.9% (n = 3882) were female. Notably, among US-based podcasts, female guest representation exceeded the 26.5% female workforce proportion among US anesthesiologists. Episodes with exclusively male hosts had 2.13 times the odds of featuring only male guests (95% CI 1.88-2.41). A positive trend of increasing female participation was observed from 2010 to 2024. Content support was variable: using broad, inclusive definitions, 42.0% of episodes had show notes and 48.4% provided supplemental material. Analysis of quality-related structures showed that 40.0% (n = 34) of podcasts produced episodes linked to a publication, 50.6% featured some episodes with three or more speakers, 21.2% of podcasts were journal-affiliated, and 20.0% were university-affiliated. While a sex imbalance persists in anesthesiology and critical care podcasting, female participation among US-based podcasts exceeds local workforce demographic benchmarks, with a clear positive trend from 2010 to 2024. However, persistent sex similarity in speaker selection suggests ongoing biases. Quality assurance mechanisms remain highly variable, highlighting opportunities for incremental improvement. Future efforts could focus on structured guest selection and transparent quality indicators to accelerate progress toward equitable representation and educational quality in this influential medium. In modern times, many clinicians look for, and listen to, podcasts aimed at education in clinical specialties. This sampling of podcasts related to our specialty looked at how females and males contributed to podcast content generation and dissemination, as a marker for male versus female representation in speakership for continuing specialty education.

articles.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Creating Educational Material for Critical Care Clinicians: A Survey.
articles.abstract: One Minute Wonders (OMWs) are workplace-based microlearning resources that support continuing professional development in healthcare. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to create educational materials, but little is known about its application in OMWs development. To examine the use, experiences, opportunities and challenges related to AI-assisted generation of OMWs as perceived among healthcare professionals participating in the German-speaking OMW Network. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among members of the German-speaking OMW Network in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. A study-specific questionnaire assessed AI use, quality assurance practices, perceived benefits and risks and educational support needs. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively, and free-text responses underwent qualitative content analysis. A total of 136 healthcare professionals were included, predominantly nurses (n = 128, 94.1%). Overall, n = 63 (46.3%) reported using AI to create OMW. Among AI users, AI was most used for generating figures (n = 41, 65.1%), graphics (n = 35, 55.6%) and design elements (n = 33, 52.4%), with ChatGPT being the most frequently used tool (n = 60, 95.2%). Most AI users critically reviewed AI-generated content (n = 50, 79.4%). Inaccuracies requiring revision were reported by all AI users, most commonly ambiguous wording (n = 32, 50.8%), inappropriate images (n = 32, 50.8%) and incorrect content (n = 29, 46.0%). The content analysis identified a main theme for opportunities: AI as a facilitator of educational resource development and knowledge translation and a main theme for risks: AI as a potential threat to the trustworthiness and professional integrity of educational resources. The use of AI for developing educational materials such as OMWs seems to be established practice among participants of this study. AI offers benefits for efficiency and content creation but requires careful human oversight because inaccuracies and fabricated information are common. AI can support the rapid development of workplace-based educational resources. However, critical review and quality assurance are essential to ensure accuracy and safety.

articles.title: Inflammatory Biomarkers as Predictors of In-Hospital Mortality in Critically Ill COVID-19 Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Inflammatory biomarkers have been proposed as prognostic indicators in COVID-19; however, their prognostic associations within critically ill ICU-admitted patients remain of interest. This study aimed to evaluate the associations of selected inflammatory biomarkers with in-hospital mortality and their discriminatory performance among critically ill COVID-19 patients. In this retrospective cohort study, 244 adult patients with confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia admitted to the ICU between August 2020 and June 2021 were analyzed. Disease severity was assessed using the ISARIC 4 C Mortality Score. Associations between inflammatory biomarkers and mortality were evaluated using univariable and multivariable logistic regression, and discriminatory performance was assessed using ROC curve analysis. The in-hospital mortality rate was 90.6%. ESR and LDH levels were significantly higher in non-survivors. In a biomarker-restricted multivariable logistic regression model, ESR (OR 1.023 per 1 mm/h increase; 95% CI 1.004-1.042; p = 0.016) and LDH (OR 1.002 per 1 U/L increase; 95% CI 1.000-1.003; p = 0.009) remained significantly associated with in-hospital mortality after mutual adjustment for the other prespecified inflammatory biomarkers. LDH demonstrated good discriminatory performance (AUC 0.725; 95% CI 0.645-0.805). ESR showed modest discriminatory performance (AUC 0.646; 95% CI 0.559-0.732). ESR and LDH remained significantly associated with in-hospital mortality after adjustment for the other prespecified inflammatory biomarkers. These findings suggest that ESR and LDH may provide adjunctive prognostic information in critically ill ICU patients; however, they should be interpreted in the context of the biomarker-restricted model and the limited adjustment set. Confirmation in larger prospective studies incorporating established clinical prognostic factors is warranted.
