articles.title: Heat stroke presenting with choreiform dyskinesias: an unusual MRI pattern.
When Source Control Is Not Enough: Bilateral Adrenal Hemorrhage After Group A Streptococcal Necrotizing Soft Tissue Infection.
articles.abstract: Refractory septic shock following adequate surgical source control presents a major clinical challenge. While persistent vasopressor dependence in necrotizing soft tissue infections (NSTI) is frequently attributed to ongoing tissue necrosis or overwhelming cytokine release, acute primary adrenal failure due to Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome (WFS) represents an underrecognized, reversible etiology. We report a 41-year-old male who developed fulminant right upper extremity Group A Streptococcus (GAS) necrotizing fasciitis requiring emergent forequarter amputation. Despite definitive source control, targeted antitoxin antimicrobial therapy, and guideline-directed resuscitation, he experienced persistent vasopressor-dependent shock. On postoperative day 5, CT imaging revealed new-onset bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. The initiation of stress-dose hydrocortisone led to rapid hemodynamic stabilization and successful recovery. Surgeons must maintain a high index of suspicion for acute adrenal crisis in postoperative ICU patients with refractory shock despite source control, rather than solely driven by ongoing sepsis.

articles.title: Point-of-care ultrasound for confirming endotracheal tube placement in prehospital and critical care transport: a scoping review.
articles.abstract: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has demonstrated high pooled diagnostic accuracy for endotracheal tube (ETT) placement confirmation in adult Emergency Departments and Intensive Care Units,, but its translation to pre-hospital and Critical Care Transport (CCT) environments is unclear. We mapped the published evidence on POCUS-based ETT placement confirmation in transport, organized around six axes: clinical indication, transport modality, operator training, impact on management, technical barriers, and patient-oriented outcomes. Scoping review per the Joanna Briggs Institute 2020 framework, reported per PRISMA-ScR. Nine sources searched January 1st, 2015-May 12th, 2026: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, Europe PMC, Consensus.app, Google Scholar, ClinicalTrials.gov, and forward-citation tracking. Dual independent screening and charting were performed in Covidence with built-in conflict adjudication. From 2447 unique records, 51 met final inclusion. One primary study evaluated diagnostic performance in adult patients in an out-of-hospital setting. The remaining 50 records comprised contextual primary studies and secondary evidence, including cadaver and simulation studies, training evaluations, feasibility implementations, and reviews. Distribution by modality was skewed toward ground emergency medical services (EMS); rotor-wing helicopter EMS (HEMS) evidence was predominantly training-based; fixed-wing evidence was essentially absent. Operator profiles in transport-relevant studies were predominantly paramedic, flight medic, or flight nurse, mismatched against the physician-dominant pooled in-hospital meta-analytic estimates. No included study measured patient-oriented outcomes. Evidence supporting POCUS-based ETT confirmation in pre-hospital and critical care transport remains limited. Most studies addressed training, simulation, feasibility, or implementation rather than diagnostic performance in transported patients, and none demonstrated an effect on patient-oriented outcomes. Transport-specific prospective studies are needed before hospital-derived diagnostic-accuracy estimates can be generalized to transport practice.

articles.title: Management of dysglycemia in critically ill adults: current evidence, clinical practice and future directions.
articles.abstract: Hyperglycemia is among the most common metabolic disturbances in critically ill patients, affecting up to 50% of adults admitted to intensive care units (ICUs), regardless of pre-existing diabetes. Both diabetes and stress-induced hyperglycemia are associated with increased risk of organ dysfunction, healthcare-associated infections, prolonged mechanical ventilation, longer ICU and hospital length of stay, and mortality. Clinical guidelines recommend initiating intravenous insulin therapy when blood glucose remains ≥180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L) and targeting 140–180 mg/dL (7.8–10.0 mmol/L) for most critically ill adults. Recent advances in continuous glucose monitoring, computerized insulin dosing algorithms, automated insulin delivery systems and artificial intelligence-enabled clinical decision support are transforming glucose management in the ICU and have the potential to improve safety and efficiency. This review summarizes current understanding of the pathophysiology of stress hyperglycemia, the clinical consequences of dysglycemia, contemporary glucose targets, insulin therapy and glucose monitoring strategies. We also highlight emerging technologies, special patient populations and future directions expected to shape precision glycemic management for critically ill adults.

articles.title: Effect of interferon gamma as a treatment for post-aggressive immunosuppression in critically ill (INFINITY trial): study protocol for a randomised Bayesian double-blind controlled trial.
articles.abstract: Critically ill patients frequently develop a delayed immune dysfunction after the initial insult, commonly referred to as post-aggressive immunosuppression (PAIS). Persistently reduced monocytic human leucocyte antigen-DR (mHLA-DR) expression is a widely used biomarker of PAIS and has been associated with intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired infections, prolonged organ support and excess late morbidity and mortality. To date, no immunostimulatory strategy has proven efficacy in improving patient-centred outcomes in this population. Interferon gamma-1b (IFN-γ1b) can restore monocyte function and antigen presentation in experimental and clinical settings and has shown biological plausibility and acceptable tolerability in critically ill patients. The INFINITY trial aims to determine whether short-course IFN-γ1b, initiated in patients with biomarker-defined PAIS, increases ventilator-free days compared with placebo. INFINITY is a national, multicentre, phase II, Bayesian, superiority, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind, parallel-group trial with a 1:1 allocation ratio conducted in 6 ICUs in France. Adult ICU patients (≥18 years) with high initial severity (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) at ICU admission ≥6), receiving invasive mechanical ventilation at inclusion, and presenting with mHLA-DR <8000 AB/C measured between days 5 and 10 are eligible. Key non-inclusion criteria include pre-existing immunodeficiency, expected prolonged ventilation due to chronic conditions and contraindication to IFN-γ1b. Randomisation is centralised via a secure electronic system and stratified by centre. Participants receive either IFN-γ1b (Imukin) 2×106 IU (0.1 mg) subcutaneously every 24 hours for 3 consecutive days or matched placebo (0.9% sodium chloride), in addition to standard care. The primary endpoint is ventilator-free days alive at day 28. Secondary endpoints include mHLA-DR kinetics (day 0–7), lymphocyte count, ICU-acquired infections, antibiotic-free days, ICU-free days, SOFA kinetics and all-cause mortality at day 28 and day 90, alongside safety outcomes. A total of 170 participants (85 per group) are planned. Analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle using Bayesian models with pre-specified interim analyses and stopping guidelines. The study will be conducted in accordance with European regulations and was independently reviewed and approved by the French Ethics Committee Comité de Protection des Personnes Ile de France (EUCT number: 2023–5 06 725-11-00). The results will be reported in international peer-reviewed journals and presented at international and national conferences. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06694740; registered on 19 November 2024 (submitted 12 November 2024). Available at: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06694740.

articles.title: Phenotyping ARDS: A pragmatic path forward with the POLARIS international cohort.
European Society of Intensive Care Medicine consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit.
articles.abstract: A human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit (ICU) aims to integrate person-centred care, communication, emotional support, equity, and collaboration into ICU environments. The European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) developed a consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU following a systematic, multi-phase, evidence-informed methodology incorporating the views of ICU professionals, academics, and patient and family representatives. This international multidisciplinary panel of 46 members conducted rapid reviews addressing 20 Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes (PICO) questions across six domains: person-centred care; communication and transparency; emotional well-being; equity, diversity, and inclusion; ICU environment; technology and innovation. Based on the evidence synthesis, 53 draft statements were developed and evaluated through a two-round eDelphi study. The final set of statements was discussed and ratified at an expert consensus meeting with the initial panel of experts and with patients and family representatives. A total of 201 international stakeholders participated in round 1 and 149 in round 2. Members of the expert consensus meeting ultimately endorsed 43 consensus statements. Key recommendations supported flexible family visitation, structured interdisciplinary communication, empathy-based staff training, psychological support for patients and ICU professionals, culturally responsive care, environmental interventions to improve sleep and reduce delirium, and the integration of digital supported technologies. The consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU provides a comprehensive framework for clinicians with evidence-informed directions to deliver high-quality practice across diverse ICU settings. By prioritising person-centred care, communication, inclusivity, and well-being alongside responsible technological innovation, the experiences and outcomes of patients, families, and ICU professionals may improve.

articles.title: Safety and efficacy of volatile sedatives in critically ill patients receiving mechanical ventilation: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Volatile sedatives are increasingly utilised for sedation in critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. Despite numerous randomised controlled trials and observational studies comparing volatile sedation to intravenous sedation, questions regarding its safety and efficacy persist. A systematic search was performed in PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science databases for studies published up to July 2025. The analysis included randomised controlled trials and observational studies that compared the use of volatile sedation with intravenous sedation in patients admitted to the intensive care unit for mechanical ventilation. Eligible studies involved adults aged ⩾18 years, requiring mechanical ventilation, and utilising either volatile or intravenous sedatives. They also needed to report at least one outcome of interest: incidence of delirium, mortality, intensive care unit length of stay, or duration of mechanical ventilation. From 3182 identified publications, fifteen studies were included in the systematic review. Volatile sedation was not associated with a significant difference in the incidence of delirium compared to intravenous sedation (risk ratio 0.72; 95% confidence interval 0.38-1.34), mortality (risk ratio 0.97; 95% confidence interval 0.80-1.17), intensive care unit length of stay (mean difference 0.28 days; 95% confidence interval -1.74 to 2.30), or duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference -37.20 h; 95% confidence interval -78.60 to 4.20). Volatile sedation was not associated with significant differences in mechanical ventilation duration, delirium incidence, intensive care unit length of stay, or mortality compared to intravenous sedation. Further large-scale, high-quality randomised trials are needed to clarify its clinical benefit in critical care settings.

articles.title: Methadone to manage pain in pregnancy at Te Toka Tumai Auckland City Hospital: A retrospective observational analysis.
articles.abstract: Pain during pregnancy is common, yet evidence-based management remains limited. While non-pharmacological treatments are first-line, severe pain may necessitate pharmacological intervention. Methadone is well studied for opioid use disorder, but its role in acute pain management during pregnancy is less defined. This retrospective observational study examined pregnant patients prescribed low-dose methadone for pain management between January 2022 and December 2023 at a tertiary multidisciplinary pain service. Patients receiving opioid substitution therapy were excluded. Data on methadone dosing, pain scores, maternal side effects, and neonatal outcomes were analysed. Twenty-three patients were identified, with 22 included in the analysis. The mean gestation at methadone initiation was 29.7 weeks (standard deviation 5.1), and the median starting dose was 5 mg per day (interquartile range 2.5 to 5). Pain severity decreased significantly: the proportion reporting severe pain at rest fell from 82% to 14% at 48 hours (absolute risk reduction (ARR) 68%, number needed to treat (NNT) 2), and the proportion reporting severe pain with movement fell from 95% to 32% (ARR 64%, NNT 2), with sustained improvement at 4 weeks. Side-effects included sedation (14%) and nausea (23%) and were generally well tolerated. Among 19 neonates, no cases of neonatal abstinence syndrome were observed. Six required neonatal intensive care unit admission, but none for opioid withdrawal. These findings suggest that low-dose methadone, when used within a closely monitored multidisciplinary setting, may provide effective pain relief in the pregnant patient without significant neonatal harm. However, this high level of oversight may limit generalisability to other care settings. Further research is warranted to guide safe implementation and optimise dosing.

articles.title: Understanding Neurogenic Patient-Ventilator Discordance and its Management.
articles.abstract: Patients with an acutely injured brain may resist the mechanical physics of the ventilator. Neurogenic respiratory breathing patterns generated by the patient may result in the ventilator failing to synchronize with this abnormal drive. This asynchrony may be perceived as distress and with a high respiratory drive could also lead to global lung stress and diaphragmatic myoinjury, and affect liberation from the mechanical ventilator at a later point. Patient-ventilator synchrony concerns have rarely been prioritized in neurocritical care guidelines and are often inappropriately treated with escalating sedation. Starting with the essentials of waveform interpretation and moving towards more complex interpretations of these asynchronies, this review provides insight into the common themes of neurogenic synchrony concerns in mechanically ventilated patients. High respiratory drive, double-triggering/ breath-stacking, and reverse triggering are the most prevalent observations. Adjusting the ventilator can improve patient-ventilator interaction and a number of options to remediate these synchrony concerns are provided.

articles.title: Construction and External Validation of a Predictive Nomogram for Premature Unplanned Discontinuation in Elderly Patients Undergoing Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in the ICU.
articles.journal: Therapeutic apheresis and dialysis : official peer-reviewed journal of the International Society for Apheresis, the Japanese Society for Apheresis, the Japanese Society for Dialysis Therapy
articles.abstract: To develop and validate a 2-h early-warning nomogram for the risk of unplanned discontinuation of continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) in elderly intensive care unit (ICU) patients. This study retrospectively enrolled elderly CRRT patients from two tertiary hospitals (2022-2024) via convenience sampling for model development. Predictive performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration plots, and internal validation using 1000 bootstrap resamples, with goodness of fit assessed by the Hosmer-Lemeshow test; an external cohort (Jan-Aug 2025) was used for clinical applicability. The unplanned CRRT discontinuation rate reached 27.4% in the modeling cohort and 32.8% in an external temporal validation cohort (n = 247 sessions). Independent predictors included hypotension, therapeutic intervention scoring system (TISS) score, transmembrane pressure (TMP) at 2 h > 86 mmHg, and diagnosis. The model demonstrated robust predictive performance, with an AUC of 0.860 (training) and 0.865 (validation), good calibration (Brier scores: 0.107 internal, 0.127 external), and clinical net benefit across thresholds per decision curve analysis. The model demonstrates robust discrimination, calibration, and clinical net benefit, with readily available variables indicating substantial potential for valuable clinical applications.

articles.title: The secret life of dialysis catheters: A qualitative study of intensive care nurses' experiences of managing dialysis catheters.
articles.abstract: In Australian intensive care units (ICUs), approximately 9000 patients require renal replacement therapy annually for acute kidney injury. This requires a large-bore dialysis catheter to facilitate effective extracorporeal blood flow. However, these catheters have the highest failure rate of all central venous catheters used in ICU at 7-20%. While catheter insertion and renal replacement therapy guidance is evidence-based, there is limited guidance for post-insertion catheter care and troubleshooting. To explore ICU nurses' experiences managing dialysis catheters, and how existing policies and bedside practices influence nurses' decision-making. Qualitative, descriptive design. Registered nurses with experience caring for patients undergoing dialysis were recruited between November 2024 and January 2025. Data were collected through small group, semi-structured interviews and analysed using inductive content analysis. Eighteen clinicians participated across three focus groups, with a mean of 10.6 years' experience in dialysis catheter care. Two themes were identified: (1) Troubleshooting is complex, characterised by reliance on experiential knowledge, time sensitive decision-making, and balancing risk against benefit; and (2) The hidden cost, reflecting the stress, unrecognised labour and financial burden associated with troubleshooting catheter dysfunction. The absence of evidence-based guidance to manage troubleshooting and catheter dysfunction places substantial burden on ICU nurses. Evidence-based troubleshooting decision tools may have the potential to improve dialysis efficiency, reduce healthcare-associated risks and workforce stress. Effective post-insertion management of dialysis catheters requires clear, evidence-informed policy, particularly regarding safe, appropriate troubleshooting techniques. A structured hierarchy of interventions may enable efficient clinician response to catheter dysfunction and improve post-insertion care and reduce complications. Targeted education and skills training are essential to strengthen clinical judgement in time-critical situations. Improved interdisciplinary communication is also needed to ensure medical teams better understand the workload and clinical risks associated with managing dialysis catheters.

articles.title: Micronutrient deficiencies in continuous renal replacement therapy: A literature review and the emerging role of the pharmacist.
articles.journal: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
articles.abstract: Evaluating micronutrient deficiencies in the critically ill population is challenging given the complex clinical picture for many patients. Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is a risk factor for micronutrient deficiencies in this cohort, with deficiencies resulting from increased losses in dialysis effluent or adsorption to tubing or to the dialysis filter. The aim of this article is to summarize pertinent research literature regarding micronutrient supplementation and monitoring in CRRT and identify areas for pharmacists to improve patient outcomes from a nutrition standpoint. A computerized literature search was conducted of the PubMed electronic database, and articles were included if they discussed one of the prespecified micronutrients and renal replacement therapy. The micronutrients specifically addressed in this article are copper, selenium, zinc, L-carnitine, vitamin C, vitamin B1, vitamin B6, and vitamin B9. For each of these micronutrients, we summarize the evidence for deficiencies in CRRT and supplementation strategies. However, in many cases, literature is lacking to support supplementation and monitoring strategies specifically in CRRT. Current literature recognizes that standard supplementation may not be enough in the critically ill population on CRRT, but evidence is lacking for optimal micronutrient supplementation doses and monitoring parameters. Until future literature is available, pharmacists should be aware of these deficiencies and help guide recommendations for supplementation.

articles.title: Current nutrition practices and additional reimbursement of intensive care units in Japan: A cross-sectional survey study.
articles.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition
articles.abstract: A unique reimbursement for early nutrition intervention was introduced in Japan to promote guideline-adherent nutrition practices in intensive care units. However, the current status of nutrition therapy implementation across Japanese intensive care units remains unclear. This cross-sectional survey study investigated intensive care units nationwide, led by the Japanese Society of Intensive Care Medicine. Facility characteristics, nutrition management structure, nutrition practices (nutritional assessment, nutrition planning, therapy implementation, and monitoring), and dietitian involvement were assessed. We examined relationships between reimbursement claim status and nutrition practices. Among 337 intensive care units, most performed nutritional assessment using at least one standardized tool and planned nutrition targeting 25-30 kcal/kg/day for energy and 1.0-1.2 g/kg/day for protein. Enteral nutrition-related practices were widely implemented. Of these, 255 intensive care units (75.7%) claimed the reimbursement; incentivized units more frequently implemented written enteral nutrition protocols, dietitian-conducted nutritional assessments, dietitian-led enteral nutrition design, and enteral nutrition initiation within 48 h. However, Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition assessment, indirect calorimetry, written protocols for parenteral nutrition/diarrhea/constipation, dietitian-led parenteral nutrition design, and post-intensive care unit nutritional follow-up remained limited even in incentivized units. In Japan, reimbursement incentives were positively associated with higher implementation of nutritional assessment, enteral nutrition-related practices, and dietitian involvement. To further advance specialized nutritional care, simultaneous system development may be warranted.

articles.title: Beyond avoiding failure: the proactive and beneficial role of appropriate antimicrobial therapy in the ICU.
Prognostic significance of nucleated red blood cells in trauma patients.
articles.abstract: Nucleated red blood cells are early erythroid precursors typically confined to the bone marrow. Their appearance in peripheral blood reflects stress erythropoiesis and has been linked to hypoxia and systemic inflammation. While nucleated red blood cells have prognostic value in sepsis and critical illness, their significance in trauma remains poorly understood. This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of nucleated red blood cells during the first 10 days in the intensive care unit following severe trauma, and their association with 30-day mortality. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study including 1636 adult trauma patients admitted to the Reims Level-1 Trauma Center between January 2019 and March 2025, recorded in the TraumaBase© registry. Nucleated red blood cell counts were measured daily for the first 10 intensive care unit days. K-means clustering identified four nucleated red blood cell phenotypes based on temporal patterns. Outcomes included 10- and 30-day mortality, incidence of acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock, mechanical ventilation, and length of stay. Survival analyses used Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, Injury Severity Score, Simplified Acute Physiology Score II, and the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment, and propensity-weighted regression assessed dichotomised nucleated red blood cell status. Nucleated red blood cells were detected in 221 patients (13.5%). Phenotype classification revealed: transient early nucleated red blood cells (phenotype 1), single peak (phenotype 2), multiple intermittent peaks (phenotype 3), and persistent elevation (phenotype 4). Phenotype 2 was associated with reduced 10-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.06, 95% confidence intervals 0.01-0.46), while phenotype 4 exhibited markedly increased mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 9.6, 95% confidence intervals 2.23-41.4, P < 0.001). Nucleated red blood cell+ patients had higher risks of acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock, mechanical ventilation, and 30-day mortality. Kaplan-Meier curves confirmed significant differences in survival across phenotypes (log-rank P < 0.001). Nucleated red blood cell presence, particularly persistent elevation, identifies trauma patients at higher risk of adverse outcomes. Routine, daily nucleated red blood cell monitoring may serve as a simple, low-cost prognostic tool in intensive care unit trauma care. Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings and integrate nucleated red blood cell dynamics into risk stratification.

articles.title: Comparison of meropenem-based triple therapy vs minocycline-based triple therapy for carbapenem resistant Acinetobacter baumannii ventilator associated pneumonia - a prospective observational study.
articles.abstract: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) resulted from Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) poses serious treatment challenges. Our objective was to assess two triple medication combinations for VAP caused by CRAB. This prospective observational research was performed in the critical care unit of an academic medical center from January 2024 to March 2025. Two hundred adult patients with culture-proven CRAB-VAP were enrolled and treated with either minocycline-polymyxin-sulbactam or meropenem-polymyxin-sulbactam. Various outcomes assessed were clinical recovery, 7 and 28-day mortality, microbiological eradication, duration of ICU and hospital stay. The clinical recovery rates were comparable in both groups (54% minocycline vs. 47% meropenem, p = 0.322). The microbiological eradication rate was similar (39%) at day 28 in both groups. Patients treated with the minocycline regimen had significantly shorter ICU stay (16 vs. 18 days, p = 0.003) and hospital stays (24 vs. 28 days, p < 0.001) than the meropenem group. There was no significant difference between 7-day mortality (21% vs. 32%, p = 0.078) or 28-day mortality (46% vs. 53%, p = 0.322). Minocycline-based triple therapy was comparable to meropenem-based therapy in treating CRAB-VAP, with potential advantages in reducing duration of ICU and hospital stay. Minocycline may be a suitable alternative for CRAB-VAP in resource-limited settings.

articles.title: Doxycycline versus azithromycin in combination with beta-lactams for hospitalized community-acquired pneumonia: A propensity score-matched cohort study.
articles.abstract: Azithromycin plus a beta-lactam is a commonly used empiric regimen for hospitalized community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). Concerns about azithromycin resistance and patient-specific safety considerations have increased interest in doxycycline as an alternative; however, comparative effectiveness data for these two regimens remain scarce. Using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network (240 healthcare organizations; data accessed June 14, 2026), we conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults hospitalized with CAP between January 2016 and December 2023. Doxycycline plus beta-lactam recipients were compared with azithromycin plus beta-lactam recipients following 1:1 nearest-neighbor propensity score matching (11,906 patients per group). Thirty-day and 90-day all-cause mortality did not differ significantly between groups (HR: 1.03, 95% CI: 0.95-1.12; and HR: 1.06, 95% CI: 0.98-1.14, respectively), whereas 180-day mortality was modestly but significantly higher in the doxycycline cohort (HR: 1.08, 95% CI: 1.02-1.16; p = 0.014). Doxycycline-based therapy was associated with a consistently lower risk of antibiotic escalation at all time points assessed (RR: 0.59-0.65; p < 0.001). The 30-day risk of incident sepsis was significantly higher with doxycycline (RR: 1.29, 95% CI: 1.03-1.61; p = 0.024). ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor use, and Clostridioides difficile infection did not differ significantly between the two groups. No statistically significant difference in 30-day mortality was detected between doxycycline plus beta-lactams and azithromycin plus beta-lactams. This finding does not establish equivalence or noninferiority. Secondary findings, including 30-day sepsis and 180-day mortality, were exploratory and require confirmation in prospective randomized studies.

articles.title: Mitral annular plane systolic excursion as a prognostic marker in critical illness: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Cardiac dysfunction is common in critical illness, yet conventional indices such as left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) may fail to detect early impairment. Mitral annular plane systolic excursion (MAPSE), a marker of longitudinal function, may provide prognostic information, but its role in critical illness remains uncertain. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library were searched for studies evaluating MAPSE in critically ill adults. Studies were included if MAPSE could be dichotomized using prespecified cutoffs (10 or 12 mm). The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality; secondary outcomes included 28-30-day mortality and exploratory measures of cardiac function and organ support. Risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled. Risk of bias was assessed with QUIPS and certainty of evidence with GRADE. Ten observational studies including 1313 patients were analyzed; 414 (31.5%) had reduced MAPSE. Most patients had sepsis or septic shock. Reduced MAPSE was associated with higher in-hospital mortality (37.7% vs 11.7%; RR 4.81; 95% CI 1.28-18.04; p = 0.02; I2 = 70.6%), with consistent effects across both cutoffs (p = 0.111) and adequate information size on trial sequential analysis. Reduced MAPSE was also associated with lower LVEF (MD -13.0%; 95% CI -20.6 to -5.4; p < 0.01; I2 = 94.6%), but not with 28-30-day mortality or exploratory outcomes. Certainty of evidence was low for in-hospital mortality and very low for secondary and exploratory outcomes. Reduced MAPSE was associated with higher in-hospital mortality and may be a bedside marker of myocardial dysfunction. Given the limitations of the available evidence, MAPSE remains a hypothesis-generating marker requiring prospective validation.

articles.title: Thirteen years of environmental surveillance of ESKAPE organisms and Escherichia coli in an equine hospital: Informing infection control.
articles.abstract: Bacteria from the ESKAPE group (i.e., Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Enterobacter species) and Escherichia coli are frequently multidrug-resistant and can be associated with healthcare-associated infections, an increasing concern for veterinary settings. To determine the environmental prevalence of ESKAPE and E. coli on surfaces which can act as reservoirs of infection in clinical areas in equine hospitals. Observational study. Routine environmental sampling was performed in one busy equine hospital with Swiffer® wipes to screen surfaces from high-risk areas (e.g., surgical theatres, intensive care unit [ICU], isolation unit), equipment (e.g., endotracheal tubes) and high-touch areas (e.g., keyboards) following selective species-specific protocols for each target organism. Monitoring hand-hygiene of hospital staff and students was by hand-plate sampling. After a pilot phase E. faecium was excluded from routine screening. Nine hundred and ninety-five environmental and hand-plate samples were collected from April 2010 to February 2023. The overall E. coli-SKAPE (E. coli, methicillin-resistant S. aureus [MRSA], K. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, P. aeruginosa and Enterobacter spp.) prevalence was 37.9%, where E. coli was the most (and K. pneumoniae the least) common target organism identified (18.0% and 1.7% respectively). E. coli was most prevalent in general stables and yards (37.7%) and offices (25.7%). Enterobacter spp. was the main organism in the environmental samples from ICU (24.2%) and isolation unit (22.9%, along with E. coli). Concerningly, hand-plate sampling showed that MRSA was the most common organism detected on hands (8.4%), followed by A. baumannii (5.2%) and E. cloacae (3.9%); however, E. coli, P. aeruginosa and K. pneumoniae were not found in these samples. Inconsistent sampling limited longitudinal analysis. We generated baseline environmental contamination data and demonstrated high E. coli-SKAPE hospital surface and hand contamination, informing infection control to prevent environment-to-patient cross-transmission.

articles.title: Preliminary Exploration of the Hepatoprotective Effect of Nanocrystalline Curcumin Against Traumatic Hemorrhagic Shock-Induced Liver Injury in a Desert Dry-Heat Environment: A Network Pharmacology-Based Study.
articles.abstract: Traumatic hemorrhagic shock (THS) under desert dry-heat conditions can exacerbate secondary liver injury, highlighting the need for effective therapeutic interventions. This study investigated the protective effects of nanocrystalline curcumin (NC-Cur) against THS-induced liver injury in a desert dry-heat environment and explored its potential molecular mechanisms. Network pharmacology, Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment analyses, and protein-protein interaction network analysis were used to identify candidate targets. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations examined curcumin-protein interactions. Forty male Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly assigned to control, model, solvent, or NC-Cur treatment groups (n = 10 each). The model, solvent, and treatment groups underwent traumatic hemorrhagic shock under desert dry-heat conditions. Hepatic injury was assessed by histopathology, serum aminotransferases, inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress markers, and Western blotting. Network analysis identified 116 overlapping targets, with heat shock protein 90 alpha A1 (HSP90AA1), AKT serine/threonine kinase 1 (AKT1), and B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) prioritized as the core targets. Docking predicted favorable interactions with all three proteins, while molecular dynamics simulations supported stable binding between curcumin and HSP90AA1. Compared with untreated model rats, NC-Cur-treated rats showed attenuated hepatic histopathological injury, reduced alanine and aspartate aminotransferases, tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and malondialdehyde, and increased superoxide dismutase. Western blotting indicated reduced HSP90AA1 and increased phosphorylated AKT1 expression after NC-Cur treatment, with changes also observed in BCL-2 expression. These findings suggest that NC-Cur may alleviate liver injury associated with THS under desert dry-heat conditions in male rats, potentially involving HSP90AA1-AKT1-BCL-2-related signaling.

articles.title: From catheter to infection: Risk factors for central venous catheter-related infections in the intensive care unit.
articles.journal: The International journal of artificial organs
articles.abstract: A substantial proportion of critically ill patients require central venous catheterization, with infection being the most significant complication. Catheter-related infections may increase ICU length of stay, morbidity, and mortality. This study aimed to identify factors contributing to these infections. This retrospective observational study included 1985 central venous and hemodialysis catheters meeting predefined inclusion criteria. Catheters were classified by insertion site as femoral, internal jugular, or subclavian. Catheter-related infections were assessed as percentages and as incidence per 1000 catheter-days. Infection risks were compared using relative risk (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Catheter-related infection occurred in 309 catheters (15.6%). Infection rates did not differ significantly by insertion site when analyzed as percentages (femoral 16.7%, internal jugular 15.3%, subclavian 13.6%; p = 0.474). However, incidence analysis accounting for dwell time showed a higher infection incidence in femoral catheters (13.9 per 1000 catheter-days). Compared with subclavian catheters, femoral catheters had a significantly increased infection risk (RR 1.56; 95% CI 1.07-2.28). Central venous catheter-related infections are more frequent in femoral sites in a time-dependent manner. Early replacement of femoral catheters is important to reduce infection risk. In clinical practice, prevention strategies should consider not only the insertion site but also expected duration of use, frequency of access, catheter type, patient characteristics, and infection control measures.

articles.author: Elizabeth C Jury
articles.summary: Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a rare, life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome characterised by uncontrolled immune activation. Patients present with a sepsis-like syndrome, but management requires immune suppression. Comorbidities, demographics and postoperative sterile inflammation complicate this task, and proteins associated with them may be mistaken as sepsis-specific. articles.summary: This prospective, single-center, consecutive observational study evaluates clinical, metabolic, and endocrine factors influencing survival and clinical outcomes in adult patients undergoing temporary mechanical circulatory support at the Cardiovascular Intensive Care Unit of Gottsegen Gyorgy National Cardiovascular Institute. articles.title: Pilot Study of Anesthesiologists' Preoperative Prediction of Postoperative Intensive Care Unit Admission
articles.summary: This prospective observational pilot study will evaluate how accurately anesthesiologists can predict, before a procedure, whether an adult patient will require admission to an intensive care unit (İCU) after surgery or an endoscopic procedure. articles.title: Oral Care Apparatus for Intubated Patients
articles.summary: There are several practical challenges in providing oral care to intubated patients. The presence of an endotracheal tube often makes it difficult to thoroughly evaluate the oral cavity, and there is a risk of tube displacement or removal during oral care. articles.title: Capillary Leak Index Versus Conventional Biomarkers in Predicting Sepsis-Related Outcomes
articles.summary: This study aims to evaluate the prognostic significance of CLI in predicting 28-day mortality and other outcomes in critically ill patients who develop post-operative abdominal sepsis.

articles.title: Rhu-pGSN for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
articles.summary: BTI-203 is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter, Phase 2 proof-of-concept (POC) study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of rhu-pGSN plus standard of care (SOC) in subjects with moderate-to-severe ARDS (P/F ratio ≤150) due to pneumonia or other infections. articles.summary: The recommended volume resuscitation for patients with early sepsis-induced hypoperfusion is at least 30 ml/kg of crystalloid administered within the first three hours. articles.title: NMR Based Metabolomics Kinetics in ARDS Patients
articles.source: Sanjay Gandhi Postgraduate Institute of Medical Sciences
articles.summary: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a life-threatening condition requiring respiratory support to maintain oxygenation. Very few biomarkers about ARDS have been identified but none of them has a sufficient specificity or sensitivity to characterize by itself the severity of lung condition. articles.title: A Phase 3 Efficacy and Safety Study of Fosmanogepix for the Treatment of Adult Participants With Candidemia and/or Invasive Candidiasis.
articles.summary: The purpose of this clinical trial is to learn about the safety and effects of the study medicine (called Fosmanogepix) for the potential treatment of candidemia and/or invasive candidiasis, a life-threatening fungal infection caused by several species of yeast called Candida. The study is seeking patients who have a diagnosis of candidemia and/or invasive candidiasis. articles.title: A Communication Tool to Improve Communication in the ICU
articles.summary: The purpose of this study is to test the effectiveness of the Best Case/Worst Case-ICU communication tool on quality of communication, clinician moral distress, and ICU length of stay for older adults with serious traumatic injury. Investigators will follow an estimated 4500 patients aged 50 years and older who are in the ICU for 3 or more days and survey 1500 family members and up to 1600 clinicians from 8 sites nationwide.

articles.summary: This study will compare two commonly used methods of enteral feeding in critically ill adults: continuous feeding and intermittent feeding. The main purpose is to determine whether the amount of feeding fluid remaining in the stomach differs between the two methods. A total of 76 participants will be randomly assigned to receive either continuous gastric feeding or intermittent gastric feeding every 4 hours. articles.title: Mortality and Muscle Mass Loss in Critically Ill Patients.
articles.summary: The aim of the study is to monitor changes in muscle mass in critically ill patients and to verify whether a decrease in muscle mass of ≥10% during the first 7 days of hospitalization is associated with increased 28-day mortality. We will be used ultrasound for measurement the rectus femoris cross sectional area.

articles.title: An Observational Study in the United States to Learn How Venous Thromboembolism, Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation, and Sepsis Are Related
articles.summary: This is an observational study in which data already collected from people with venous thromboembolism (VTE) due to sepsis (blood poisoning) are studied. articles.summary: Researchers are looking for a better way to treat people who have sepsis induced coagulopathy. Sepsis happens when bacteria and their toxins spread in the blood, causing an infection. To overcome the infection the body responds activating the immune system, sometimes this immune response is too active and causes uncontrolled blood clot formation, also called sepsis-induced coagulopathy. articles.summary: This study aims to evaluate the effect of respiratory physiotherapy on diaphragm thickness in patients receiving mechanical ventilation support in the intensive care unit. articles.title: Comparison of Continuous Versus Intermittent Enteral Nutrition in Critically Ill Patients.
articles.summary: The purpose of the study is to compare continuous versus intermittent strategy for enteral nutrition. The study will examine if there is a difference in achieving nutritional delivery goals, tolerance and number of complications of enteral nutrition.

articles.summary: This study aims to evaluate the effect of ventilator hyperinflation combined with body positioning on arterial blood gases in patients with ventilator-associated pneumonia. articles.summary: Septic shock is the most common form of circulatory shock encountered in patients admitted in intensive care unit. articles.summary: This study aimed to compare between internal jugular vein and inferior vena cava collapsibility indices as a guidance of fluid responsiveness in septic shock cancer patients.

articles.summary: During assisted mechanical ventilation, breathing results from the interaction between the patient and the ventilator. Optimal titration of pressure support is essential to maintain a balance between over-assistance and under-assistance. Excessive respiratory may lead to dyspnea and cause respiratory muscle fatigue, whereas excessive assistance promotes muscle atrophy and delays weaning. articles.title: The Vancomycin Piperacillin/Tazobactam (VPT) Patient Safety Trial (VPS)
articles.summary: The VPT Safety Trial (VPS) compares two common antibiotic combinations to see how they affect the kidneys of patients in the hospital with serious infections. Both combinations are approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The goal is to help doctors know which combination is safer so they can make better choices for their patients.

articles.title: Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Propofol-Ketamine Combination Versus Propofol Monotherapy in Geriatric Patients Under Invasive Ventilation
articles.summary: The study is a prospective randomized controlled trial comparing the efficacy and safety of propofol-ketamine ("Ketofol") versus propofol monotherapy in geriatric ICU patients. articles.summary: To confirm feasibility and accessibility of the CCPC Platform (Oxymotion, Bridge Health Solutions medication adherence software, CloudDX home kit) in two different environments - in hospital and at-home, in patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery.

articles.summary: Intensive care units (ICUs) are specialized units where complex life-saving treatment and care activities are performed. Due to the treatment procedures performed in these specialized units, a large number of tools/equipment/devices/cables (endotracheal tubes, monitor cables, hemodialysis machines, mechanical ventilation, etc.) are placed on critically ill patients. The optimal ventilation strategy in this patient population remains uncertain. articles.title: Peripheral Perfusion Index Trajectory to Predict 28-Day Mortality in Patients With Sepsis in the Intensive Care Unit
articles.summary: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition caused by the body's overwhelming response to infection, and it remains a leading cause of death in intensive care units. Even when standard treatment targets such as blood pressure are met, blood flow to the small vessels of the skin and other tissues may remain impaired. articles.ai_summary: Researchers investigated whether the trajectory of peripheral perfusion index can predict 28-day mortality in ICU patients with sepsis. They found that the perfusion index trajectory may be linked to worse outcomes in these patients. The study aimed to identify a potential biomarker for sepsis severity.
articles.ai_significance: This study highlights the importance of monitoring peripheral perfusion in sepsis patients, as it may help identify those at higher risk of mortality. This could lead to more targeted and aggressive treatment.

articles.summary: Tracheostomy is a surgical procedure that involves creating an opening in the trachea and bringing it to the skin surface to form a stoma. It may be performed as an emergency or elective operation. The main indications include relief of upper airway obstruction, protection of the lower respiratory tract, and facilitation of assisted ventilation in critically ill patients. articles.title: Strategy to Avoid Excessive Oxygen Using an Autonomous Oxygen Titration Intervention
articles.summary: This study is a multicenter randomized controlled trial to determine the effectiveness of a closed loop/autonomous oxygen titration system (O2matic PRO100) to maintain normoxemia (goal range SpO2 90-96%, target 93%) during the first 72 hours of acute injury or illness, compared to standard provider-driven methods (manual titration with SpO2 target of 90-96%).

articles.source: Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology
articles.summary: Sepsis is defined as a life-threatening organ dysfunction that is caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Severe sepsis is the most common cause of death among critically ill patients in non-coronary intensive care units (ICU). Sustained excessive inflammation and immune dysfunction have been confirmed to play a key role in organ damage and early death of sepsis patients. articles.ai_summary: Researchers investigated the relationship between memory CD8+ T cells and sepsis severity and mortality in a single-center, observational study. articles.ai_significance: Understanding the correlation between memory CD8+ T cells and sepsis severity and mortality can help clinicians develop targeted interventions to reduce excessive inflammatory response and improve patient outcomes.

articles.summary: Traumatic brain injury is a leading cause of death and disability in trauma patients. articles.summary: Rapid diagnosis of sepsis is crucial for treatment and survival. Currently, blood culture takes 48 hours-5 days to complete. articles.summary: Intensive care unit (ICU) patients are frequently exposed to various stressors that contribute to severe sleep disruption and circadian rhythm disturbances. articles.summary: Patients who survive critical illness usually experience long-lasting physical and psychological impairments, which are often debilitating. articles.summary: The RUSH protocol has been used for several years for the rapid evaluation of a patient admitted to the emergency room with shock. articles.title: Serious Adverse Events in Adult ICU Patients: A Substudy of the PATIENCE Cohort.
articles.abstract: Prokinetic agents are used to enhance upper gastrointestinal motility, but adverse events related to these agents are poorly described. We aimed to provide detailed epidemiological data on predefined serious adverse events (SAEs) in a cohort of adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients with and without prokinetic treatment. We hypothesised that all predefined SAEs would occur in both patients treated and those not treated with prokinetic agents, and that a higher number of SAEs would occur among patients treated with prokinetic agents for more than three consecutive days. This substudy of the inception cohort study "Prokinetic agents in adult intensive care unit patients" included acutely admitted adult ICU patients. The prokinetic agents assessed (exposures) were erythromycin, metoclopramide, domperidone, and prucalopride. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients experiencing at least one episode of five pre-specified SAEs during ICU stay (cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, vomiting with aspiration, diarrhoea, extrapyramidal symptoms). Secondary outcomes were (1) proportion of patients experiencing each SAE, (2) the proportion of patients experiencing any of the SAEs after prokinetic treatment stratified by longest consecutive treatment duration, (3) time from index ICU admission to first SAE and (4) time from prokinetic initiation to first SAE. All analyses were descriptive, summarising SAE proportions and timing overall and according to prokinetic exposure. Among 1440 adult ICU patients, 710 SAEs occurred in 354 patients (24.6%), most commonly cardiac arrhythmias (199/1440, 13.8%). Across the exposure groups, the proportion of patients experiencing one or more SAEs ranged from 23.0% to 42.5%. Among patients treated with prokinetic agents for > 3 consecutive days, 14/59 (23.7%) experienced a SAE, which was similar to the proportion observed among patients not receiving prokinetic agents (291/1.253, 23.2%). Most SAEs occurred on median Day 2 after ICU admission and on median Day 3 after prokinetic initiation. One in four adult ICU patients experienced at least one SAE, with cardiac arrhythmias being the most frequent. Among patients receiving prokinetic agents, the proportion experiencing one or more SAEs ranged from 23.0% to 42.5% across treatment groups. The findings from this study may help inform the design of a future clinical trial. This analysis presents reported serious adverse event observed in an ICU trial cohort assessing gastrointestinal prokinetic drug effects. Serious adverse events were reported frequently in both the drug treatment groups and the comparison (no prokinetic drug) group. Types of serious adverse events reported are presented.

articles.title: Endpoint-specific mortality associated with malignancy among adults with sepsis or septic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a major global health challenge and increasingly affects patients with complex conditions such as malignancy. Prior studies suggest higher mortality in this population, but interpretation is limited by aggregation of heterogeneous endpoints. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to clarify endpoint-specific prognostic associations between malignancy and mortality in adults with sepsis or septic shock. This study was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251141216). PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library and Epistemonikos were searched through 16 September 2025, for studies comparing all-cause mortality between sepsis patients with and without malignancy. Mortality endpoints were grouped as ICU, in-hospital, early, intermediate and extended follow-up mortality. Crude odds ratios (ORs) were estimated using random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup, meta-regression and sensitivity analyses were performed to explore heterogeneity and assess consistency. Among 105 eligible studies comprising 20,089,138 participants, 85 studies contributing 101 endpoint estimates were included in the primary synthesis. Pooled estimates were elevated across endpoints: ICU (OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.94-1.56), in-hospital (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.69-2.13), early (OR 1.81, 95% CI 1.59-2.06), intermediate (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.72-3.03) and extended follow-up mortality (OR 2.41, 95% CI 1.70-3.42). Associations were sustained for haematologic malignancy, concentrated in in-hospital and early mortality for metastatic disease and more modest for solid tumours. Sensitivity analyses were directionally consistent, although risk ratio estimates were generally smaller than ORs. Exploratory meta-regression suggested that severity-related covariates may contribute to heterogeneity. Malignancy was associated with higher mortality among adults with sepsis or septic shock, with variation across mortality endpoints and clinical contexts. These findings support endpoint-specific prognostic assessment and highlight the need for future studies to incorporate more granular cancer characteristics. Because the primary estimates were unadjusted, results represent overall prognostic associations rather than independent causal effects.

articles.abstract: Cardiac arrest remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality, although contemporary care now enables potential survival with good neurologic outcome. The core acute management goals for survivors of cardiac arrest are to provide organ support, sustain adequate hemodynamics, and evaluate the underlying cause of the cardiac arrest. In this article, the authors review the current state of knowledge and clinical intensive care unit practice recommendations for patients after cardiac arrest, particularly focusing on important areas of uncertainty, such as targeted temperature management, neuroprognostication, coronary evaluation, and hemodynamic targets.

articles.title: Resting-State Functional MRI and Clinical Outcomes After Acute Disorders of Consciousness: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Accurate assessment and prognostication of patients with acute disorders of consciousness (DoC) after severe brain injury remain a substantial clinical challenge. Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) measures spontaneous, temporally correlated brain activity in the absence of external stimulation and provides objective insight into the integrity of large-scale neural networks that support brain function. Emerging evidence suggests that assessing neural integrity using rs-fMRI may improve outcome prediction in patients with acute DoC. This review summarizes the current evidence of rs-fMRI as an assessment tool during the acute phase of severe brain injury. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, we conducted a systematic literature search using MEDLINE and Embase databases from January 2006 to March 2026. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed empirical investigations of adult patients with acute DoC (<28 days postinjury) that examined associations between rs-fMRI measures and clinical outcomes. The systematic review protocol was registered in the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251085923). Of 396 studies screened, 30 met eligibility criteria. Across these studies, a total of 800 patients (mean age = 48, 69% male) were scanned at a weighted average of 9.31 days after intensive care unit admission. Ten studies included patients exclusively with traumatic brain injury, 8 with cardiac arrest, 2 with encephalopathy, and 10 included mixed etiologies. The most frequently assessed resting-state networks were the default mode (n = 20) and executive control networks (n = 11), followed by visual (n = 6), salience (n = 6), sensorimotor (n = 6), and auditory (n = 5) networks. Across studies, significant associations between rs-fMRI measures and outcome were consistently reported, despite heterogeneity in methodology. The most commonly reported patient outcomes were functional or neurologic status, assessed at hospital discharge or between 3 and 12 months postinjury. Current evidence consistently demonstrates that rs-fMRI acquired during the acute phase of brain injury is associated with neurologic and functional outcomes in patients with DoC. In addition, rs-fMRI may help identify patients more likely to recover consciousness and achieve favorable functional outcomes by characterizing the integrity of large-scale brain networks. However, substantial heterogeneity and small sample sizes limit comparability across studies. Standardized acquisition and analysis frameworks, along with larger prospective studies, are needed to validate the clinical utility of rs-fMRI and support translation into an assessment tool after brain injury.

articles.title: Development and validation of an interpretable machine learning model for early prediction of mortality in ICU patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and heart failure.
articles.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and heart failure frequently coexist, and the mortality risk for patients with these comorbidities is significantly elevated in the intensive care unit (ICU) setting. Therefore, developing an interpretable model for early mortality prediction is crucial to improving the prognosis and management of these patients. This study developed models based on the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database (3167 patients) and performed external validation using the eICU Collaborative Research Database (1781 patients). Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression combined with the Boruta algorithm was used to screen clinical features within the first 24 hours of ICU admission. Based on the selected features, 5 machine learning models (eXtreme Gradient Boosting, Categorical Boosting, Light Gradient Boosting Machine, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machine) were constructed and compared for their performance in predicting 28-day all-cause mortality. The optimal model was interpreted using the Shapley Additive Explanations framework. In internal validation, the Categorical Boosting model demonstrated the best overall performance, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.788, with a sensitivity of 0.482 and a specificity of 0.900. In independent external validation, the model's area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.739. Feature selection identified 14 key predictive variables. Shapley Additive Explanations analysis revealed that the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score, Simplified Acute Physiology Score II score, anion gap, vasopressor use, and respiratory rate were the top 5 features contributing most to the model's predictions. This study developed and validated an interpretable machine learning model based on multicenter data for the early prediction of 28-day mortality risk in ICU patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and heart failure. The model demonstrates good discriminative ability and reasonable generalizability, with its interpretability analysis clarifying core predictive factors to aid in clinical risk stratification and intervention.

articles.title: Brachial-to-Radial Pressure Gradient in Critically Ill Patients Treated With Vasoactive Agents: A Prospective Observational Study.
authors: Polish Perioperative and Critical Care Research Group (PERI-CRIT)
articles.abstract: To determine the incidence of a significant noninvasive brachial-to-radial arterial pressure gradient (NIBR-APG) and its clinical associations in critically ill patients receiving vasoactive agents. Prospective, multicenter, observational study. Thirteen ICUs in Poland. Adult ICU patients with radial arterial catheters receiving vasoactive agents hospitalized between April 2025 and July 2025. None. Invasive radial mean arterial pressure (MAP) and noninvasive brachial MAP were measured twice and averaged. A NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg was predefined as clinically significant. Baseline characteristics, hemodynamic variables, and outcomes were recorded. Among 303 patients, 49.5% were surgical admissions and 33.3% had septic shock. The median NIBR-APG was 4.5 mm Hg (interquartile range, 0.0-10.0 mm Hg). Fifty-six patients (18.4%) exhibited a NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg. Compared with patients without a significant gradient, these patients received higher norepinephrine-equivalent doses (0.23 vs. 0.10 µg/kg/min), had higher Sequential Organ Failure Assessment scores (11 vs. 10), prolonged capillary refill time (3.0 vs. 2.5 s), and higher lactate concentrations (2.7 vs. 1.3 mmol/L). In multivariable analysis, only vasoactive drug dose was independently associated with NIBR-APG greater than 11 mm Hg (odds ratio, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.12-2.52). ICU mortality was higher in patients with significant gradients (48.0% vs. 30.1%). Nearly one in five critically ill patients receiving vasoactive agents demonstrated a clinically significant NIBR-APG. The presence of this gradient was independently associated with higher vasoactive drug requirements and was accompanied by greater illness severity and higher ICU mortality.

articles.title: Patterns, and outcomes of airbag -related penetrating injuries: a retrospective analysis from a level 1 trauma center.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: The deployment of defective airbag inflators can generate high-velocity metallic fragments that cause face, neck or chest penetrating injuries with potentially lethal consequences. This study aimed to describe the injury patterns, management, and outcomes of suspected airbag-related penetrating injuries (ARPI) among patients in a Middle Eastern country. A retrospective observational study of patients presenting with penetrating injuries suspected of being related to defective airbag deployment. Data were obtained from the Qatar National Trauma Registry (QNTR), electronic medical records, emergency medical services (EMS), emergency department (ED), and Mortuary. Data were collected and analyzed descriptively. A total of 16 patients had suspected ARPIs between April 2019 and February 2026. The mean age was 33.1 ± 8.3 years, and 93.8% were male. Metallic foreign bodies (FBs) from airbag inflator fragmentation were documented in 11/16 (68.8%) patients by imaging, and surgical removal while in 4/16 patients there were only entry-exit wounds after deployment of airbags following car crash. In one case, airbag deployed while mechanic was repairing a car steering wheel. Penetrating neck (43.8%), thoracic (31.3%), and maxillofacial injuries (31.3%), predominantly mandibular fractures, were most common. Surgical intervention was required in 11 (68.8%) patients and 7/16 required intensive care unit admissions. Five patients died (31.3%), including one at the scene (transported directly by the EMS, no CPR, and moved to the hospital mortuary), two died at the ED after unsuccessful CPR and two died during the hospital course (one presented with cardiac arrest and died on the sixth day and the other one required prolonged ECMO for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and died after 4 months). Airbag inflator rupture can produce serious injury patterns resembling patterns of ballistic trauma, characterized by penetrating neck wounds, maxillofacial fractures and thoracic injuries. These injuries are potentially associated with high mortality, surgical intervention, and critical care utilization. The full extent of these injuries is undetermined as some victims may have simply died at the scene without the benefit of trauma center evaluation or post-mortem examination.

articles.title: Prognostic value of early point-of-care blood gas analysis in critically ill non-trauma patients.
articles.abstract: Critically ill non-trauma patients treated in the emergency department have a high risk of in-hospital mortality. While point-of-care diagnostics such as blood gas analysis are established tools for urgent management, data on their prognostic value in this specific patient cohort remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate whether initial blood gas parameters are independently associated with in-hospital mortality in critically ill non-trauma patients. This retrospective cohort study included adult critically ill non-trauma patients treated in the emergency department of a German university hospital. Initial blood gas parameters and clinical data were analyzed using univariate and multivariable logistic regression to assess their association with in-hospital mortality. Of 879 screened patients, 542 met the inclusion criteria. In-hospital mortality was 20% (n = 110). In addition to older age and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, anemia (hemoglobin < 12 g/dL; OR of 2.07, 95% CI 1.20-3.58; p = 0.009), acidosis (pH < 7.35; OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.09-4.95; p = 0.033) and hypobicarbonatemia (< 22 mmol/L; OR 2.79, 95% CI 1.42-5.69; p = 0.004) were independently associated with in-hospital mortality. The association for hyperlactatemia was borderline (> 2.2 mmol/L; OR 1.85, 95% CI 0.93-3.77; p = 0.08). Multivariate analysis did not reveal significant associations between other electrolyte imbalances and in-hospital mortality in this cohort. In this retrospective cohort, the presence of anemia, acidosis or hypobicarbonatemia on admission to the resuscitation room were independently associated with an elevated risk of in-hospital mortality in critically ill non-trauma patients. These readily available point-of-care parameters may support early risk stratification. Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.

articles.title: Prehospital point-of-care ultrasound as a decision-support tool: A structured narrative review.
articles.abstract: Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) may support focused bedside decisions, but prehospital implementation remains limited by operational constraints, heterogeneous protocols, variable training, and limited outcome-focused evidence. This narrative review examines prehospital POCUS as a clinical decision-support tool across cardiac, thoracic, trauma, pediatric, and obstetric applications. A structured narrative review was conducted in MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central from April 2017 to February 2026. Search terms combined the prehospital setting, ultrasound, and clinical applications. Of 464 records identified, 38 full-text articles were included, including nine systematic reviews on cardiac evaluation (n = 2), thoracic evaluation (n = 3), and trauma assessment (n = 4). Screening and full-text assessment were performed by a single reviewer. No formal risk-of-bias assessment, certainty grading, quantitative synthesis, or meta-analysis was performed. In cardiac arrest, prehospital POCUS may identify cardiac activity and selected reversible causes, guide interventions, confirm return of spontaneous circulation, and support prognostic assessment, provided that image acquisition does not interrupt resuscitation or delay defibrillation. In nontraumatic shock and cardiac dysfunction, focused cardiac, lung, and vascular ultrasound may help characterize shock mechanisms, guide fluid therapy, and identify actionable findings such as pulmonary congestion, pericardial effusion, right ventricular strain, or major aortic pathology. In acute dyspnea, lung ultrasound may improve diagnostic confidence, particularly for cardiogenic pulmonary edema. In trauma, E-FAST has high specificity and may support triage, destination choice, trauma pathway activation, and preparation for definitive care; however, limited sensitivity prevents its use as a rule-out test. Pediatric and obstetric applications are feasible but remain emerging. Prehospital POCUS is an adjunctive decision-support tool rather than a standalone diagnostic test. Its value lies in answering actionable questions that may influence treatment, triage, transport destination, hospital prealert, or pathway activation. Implementation requires protocols, training, quality assurance, and governance, and must not delay time-critical care or transport.

articles.title: Pitfalls in assessing graft outcomes from donors initially treated with ECPR for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

Impact of an early extended rehabilitation programme combining individually tailored nutrition and physical activity on patient outcomes after invasive mechanical ventilation and vasopressor therapy in the ICU: design and conduct of a multicentre, randomised, controlled, open-label, assessor-blinded trial (NUTRIREA-4).
articles.abstract: Survivors of severe critical illness often experience long-lasting physical, quality of life and psychological impairments. Intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired weakness develops early and is associated with prolonged mechanical ventilation, delayed functional recovery, impaired quality of life and greater healthcare utilisation. Nutritional support and early mobilisation are considered key components of ICU care. However, trials have evaluated either nutritional or physical rehabilitation strategies and have not consistently demonstrated long-term benefits. A strong physiological rationale exists for combining nutritional therapy and structured physical rehabilitation. Moreover, most interventions were limited to the ICU stay. The NUTRIREA-4 trial will assess whether an individualised, integrated rehabilitation strategy of nutritional support, physiotherapy and adapted physical activity initiated early in the ICU and continued throughout and after the hospital stay improves long-term physical performance and recovery. NUTRIREA-4 is the first large-scale multicentre randomised controlled trial evaluating such a comprehensive approach in survivors of severe critical illness. NUTRIREA-4 is a randomised controlled, multicentre, open-label trial comparing two parallel groups of patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation and vasopressor therapy for shock and randomised to either an individualised rehabilitation programme or usual care. The rehabilitation programme combines goal-directed nutritional support, physiotherapy and adapted physical activity delivered from ICU admission to 12 weeks after the return home. We will include 830 patients in 52 French ICUs. The primary endpoint is the 6-minute walk distance measured by blinded assessors 6 months after randomisation. Secondary outcomes include muscle strength, physical activity, nutritional intake, ICU-acquired infections, quality of life, mortality and psychological recovery. The NUTRIREA-4 trial has been approved by the appropriate ethics committee. Patients are included after informed consent according to French law. The results will be published in international peer-reviewed journals and presented at conferences. NCT06581939.

articles.title: Fatigue, anxiety and depression 12 months after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a population based cohort study.
articles.abstract: To determine the prevalence and factors associated with fatigue, anxiety, and depression 12 months after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA); examine their associations with health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and functional recovery; and compare symptom burden with population norms. This prospective, population-based cohort study included adults (≥18 years) who received EMS-attempted resuscitation and survived to hospital discharge following non-traumatic OHCA in Victoria, Australia, between July 2019 and June 2022. Survivors were identified from a statewide OHCA registry and completed a 12-month telephone interview. Primary outcomes were fatigue (Modified Fatigue Impact Scale), anxiety and depression (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale). Secondary outcomes included HRQoL (EQ-5D, SF-12), functional recovery (GOSE), living arrangement, and return to work. Of 1068 eligible 12-month survivors, 728 (68.2%) completed follow-up (median age 61 years; 555 [76.2%] male). Fatigue was reported by 35.8% (250/699), anxiety by 22.6% (162/716), and depression by 18.0% (129/716). Higher symptom burden was associated with lower EQ-5D and SF-12 scores, worse GOSE outcomes (all p < 0.001) and reduced return-to-work rates. Compared with population norms, survivors reported greater fatigue (SMD 0.64; 95%CI, 0.50-0.78; p < 0.001), and depression (SMD, 0.12; 95%CI, 0.02-0.21; p = 0.02) but lower anxiety (SMD, -0.27; 95%CI, -0.35 to -0.18; p < 0.001). In adjusted models, younger age, preexisting anxiety or depression, diabetes and initial non-shockable arrest were associated with higher symptom burden, whereas EMS-witnessed arrests were associated with lower symptom burden. Fatigue, anxiety, and depression were common at 12 months after OHCA and are associated with poorer recovery. Fatigue exceeded population norms and may be an under-recognised component of cardiac arrest survivorship.

articles.title: Regional implementation of a prehospital advanced life support program with video-assisted physician direction and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract: The smart advanced life support (SALS) program was introduced to provide prehospital advanced life support under real-time video-assisted physician direction for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). This study evaluated the association between regional SALS implementation and OHCA outcomes. This retrospective cohort study used difference-in-differences and event-study analyses with data from the OHCA surveillance system in South Korea and included adult OHCA cases (aged ≥19 years) from 2 years before through 4 years after SALS implementation in August 2015. The exposure was region-level implementation of SALS. Outcomes were the prehospital time interval, prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to discharge, and favorable neurological outcome. Pre- to post-implementation changes were compared between regions with and without SALS. A total of 129,207 cases were included. SALS regions had greater increases in the prehospital time interval (4.12 min; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.91-5.33) and prehospital ROSC (1.35 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.56-2.15) than regions without SALS. No significant additional improvements were observed in survival to discharge (-0.35 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.31 to 0.62) or favorable neurological outcome (-0.35 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.08 to 0.37). Event-study analyses suggested differential pre-intervention trends for prehospital time, but not for the other outcomes. SALS regions showed greater increases in prehospital time and prehospital ROSC without significant improvements in survival to discharge or favorable neurological outcome, but the finding for prehospital time should be interpreted cautiously because differential pre-intervention trends were observed.

articles.title: Association between capnographic changes during pulse checks of varying durations and clinical outcomes during cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a multicenter study from Türkiye (CaPTuRe).
articles.abstract: To investigate the association between capnographic changes during pulse checks of different durations and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) outcomes. This multicenter, prospective, controlled, quasi-randomized study categorized patients according to pulse check duration: Group A (≤5 s) and Group B (>5-≤10 s). Five measurements were obtained during the first six CPR cycles. Four capnographic parameters were evaluated for each measurement: Post-CPR end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2), Pre-CPR ETCO2, loss rate (percentage decrease between Post- and Pre-CPR ETCO2), and recovery time (time required to regain the previous cycle's Post-CPR ETCO2). The study included 252 cardiac arrest patients (Group A, n = 124; Group B, n = 128). In Group A, patients with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) had markedly lower loss rates and shorter recovery times than non-survivors, together with higher pre- and post-CPR ETCO2 values (all p < 0.001). Group A also had a higher ROSC rate than Group B (36.3% vs. 19.5%; p = 0.005). Logistic regression identified pulse check duration as an independent predictor of ROSC, with Group A having 2.39-fold higher odds of ROSC than Group B (odds ratio [OR] = 2.39, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.347-4.242; p = 0.003). Pre-CPR ETCO2 was strongly negatively correlated with loss rate (ρ = -0.770), whereas Pre- and Post-CPR ETCO2 values (ρ = 0.96) and loss rate and recovery time (ρ = 0.89) were strongly positively correlated. Pulse checks completed within 5 s were associated with more favorable capnographic dynamics and higher ROSC rates than those lasting 6-10 s. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant prospective validation.

articles.title: Identifying the operational bottleneck to shock delivery after automated external defibrillator activation.
articles.abstract: Cardiac arrest registries record automated external defibrillator (AED) use and shock delivery but not post-activation operational timing.
