We aimed to identify the largest measurable bottleneck and an exploratory pad-application target for shock delivery within 60 s of AED power-on. We retrospectively analyzed timestamps from remotely monitored Nihon Kohden AEDs between January 2018 and February 2026. After excluding inspection records, we grouped records into activation events and quantified intervals. Shock-timing and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were restricted to initially shock-advised events with recorded shock delivery. We analyzed 8115 activation events. Median times were 42 s (interquartile range [IQR], 30-56) from power-on to completion of pad application, nine seconds (IQR, 9-11) from pad application to the first analysis, and 52 s (IQR, 40-66) from power-on to the first analysis endpoint. The power-on-to-pad-application interval accounted for a median of 81% (IQR, 75-85) of the total power-on-to-first-analysis interval, increasing to 87% (IQR, 85-90) when first analysis occurred more than 60 s after power-on. Among 900 initially shock-advised events with recorded shock delivery, the median pad-application-to-shock interval was 15 s (IQR 13-17). Exploratory ROC analysis yielded a power-on to pad-application threshold of ≥51 s in relation to first recorded shock delivery occurring more than 60 s after AED power-on. The interval from AED power-on to electronically detected completion of pad application, encompassing all intervening actions, was the largest measurable post-activation bottleneck. Completion within 50 s may serve as an exploratory process target for first recorded shock delivery within 60 s among initially shock-advised events.

articles.title: Association between burst-suppression with identical bursts and multimodal measures of cerebral oxygenation after cardiac arrest.
authors: Pittsburgh Post Cardiac Arrest Service Investigators
articles.abstract: Burst-suppression with identical bursts (BSIB) is an electroencephalographic (EEG) pattern associated with severe post-cardiac arrest brain injury (PCABI). Whether modifiable mechanisms of brain injury underlie BSIB is unknown. We hypothesized BSIB is associated with impaired cerebral oxygen metabolism, reflected as pathologically elevated jugular bulb venous oxygen saturation (SjvO2), higher brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO2), normal jugular bulb venous-to-arterial carbon dioxide gradient (PbCO2 gap, and lower intracranial pressure (ICP) compared to other EEG patterns. This single-center retrospective study included patients resuscitated from cardiac arrest who underwent EEG and SjvO2 or PbtO2 monitoring. We categorized EEG patterns as BSIB, malignant without BSIB, and non-malignant. Using mixed effects linear regression, we examined associations between EEG and SjvO2, PbCO2 gap, PbtO2, and ICP. The SjvO2 and PbtO2 cohorts included 109 and 33 patients, respectively. SjvO2 did not differ between BSIB and malignant EEGs (β = 3; 95% CI, -0.6 to 7.0), but was higher with BSIB compared to non-malignant patterns (β = 12; 95% CI, 7.0 to 16.0). BSIB was associated with lower PbCO2 gap compared to malignant (β = -1.4; 95% CI, -2.6 to -0.3) and non-malignant (β = -2.6; 95% CI, -4.1 to -1.0) patterns. PbtO2 was highest with BSIB, but not significantly higher compared to malignant patterns in our adjusted model (β = 4.0; 95% CI, -4.7 to 13.0). ICP was lower in those with BSIB compared to malignant patterns (β = -19.0; 95% CI, -32.5 to -5.6). BSIB may represent a distinct subtype of PCABI characterized by impaired oxygen metabolism with preserved oxygen delivery and diffusion.

articles.title: Real-time feedback during bag-valve-mask ventilation for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a before-and-after study (VEntilation during Cardiac Arrest Resuscitation Study, VECARS-2).
authors: Paris Fire Brigade Cardiac Arrest Task Force
articles.abstract: This study compared bag-valve-mask ventilation quality and adherence to the guideline-recommended ventilation volume range during 30:2 cardiopulmonary resuscitation for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest before and after the implementation of real-time feedback. We conducted a before-and-after observational study of two sequential adult cohorts with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest managed by basic life support teams from the Paris Fire Brigade. A bidirectional sensor measured insufflated volume (Vi) and expiratory tidal volume (Vt). The display was masked during Period-1 and provided real-time feedback during Period-2. We assessed adherence to the guideline-recommended range using mixed-effects regression; we analyzed Vt and leak volume using gamma log-link generalized linear mixed models. We analyzed 4300 ventilations in 163 patients, 96 without feedback and 67 with feedback. Median Vi was lower with feedback (471 mL) than without (513 mL, p = 0.03 for the first ventilation of each cycle) but median Vt was unchanged (235 vs. 243 mL, p = 0.84). Vi dispersion was reduced by 35% (mean within-patient IQR ratio 0.65 [95%-CI, 0.53-0.77]). Vi was 400-600 mL in 68% of ventilations with feedback vs. 42% without feedback. In contrast, Vt was 400-600 mL in only 14% of ventilations with feedback vs. 15% without feedback. In multivariable analysis, leak volume was 12% lower with feedback (mean ratio, 0.88 [95%-CI, 0.77-0.99]). Real-time feedback was associated with improved adherence to the guideline-recommended range for Vi, less dispersed VI, and lower leak volume. Causal inference, clinical significance, and generalizability warrant further evaluation.

articles.title: Race, Gender, and Survival: a Scoping Review of Disparities in ICU Post-Resuscitation Care and Neurological Outcomes Following Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.journal: Journal of racial and ethnic health disparities
articles.abstract: Racial and ethnic disparities in healthcare are well documented, yet limited attention has been given to the intersection of race/ethnicity and gender in high-acuity critical care. Black women experience compounded inequities affecting access to and quality of intensive care unit (ICU) treatment following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Because outcomes after OHCA are influenced by each link in the chain of survival, disparities in early intervention and subsequent clinical decision-making may contribute to differences in survival and neurological recovery. This study synthesizes evidence on disparities in ICU treatment and outcomes among Black women in the United States while examining how inequities across the chain of survival may influence post-resuscitation care, neurocritical care, and outcomes following OHCA. We conducted a scoping review, guided by the Arksey and O'Malley framework, to analyze peer-reviewed studies identified through electronic databases (e.g., PubMed, CINAHL, and ScienceDirect). Fifteen studies met inclusion criteria and were analyzed using thematic synthesis. Findings indicate persistent disparities, including lower bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) rates, delayed emergency response, reduced access to ICU interventions, and higher rates of early do-not-resuscitate (DNR) orders and withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies (WLST). These inequities may contribute to poorer outcomes and likely reflect a combination of systemic, institutional, and social factors, although relatively few studies directly examined Black women from an intersectional perspective. Addressing these disparities requires improved data disaggregation, culturally responsive care, and interdisciplinary interventions to promote equitable post-resuscitation care and outcomes.

articles.title: Vasopressors Combination Therapy (Norepinephrine Plus Vasopressin Receptor Agonists) Improve Septic Shock Outcome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: BackgroundStudies showed different results of vasopressors combination therapy in septic shock patients. This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the outcomes of combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin receptor agonists in adult septic shock.MethodsCochrane Library, Embase, Web of Science, and PubMed databases were searched up to September 27, 2026, to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing the combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin receptor agonists versus norepinephrine alone in septic shock patients. Two reviewers independently extracted data on mortality, ICU length of stay, renal replacement therapy (RRT) and adverse events. Trial sequential analysis (TSA) was applied to assess random error.ResultsTwenty-one RCTs involving 3873 septic shock patients were included. The results showed that the combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin receptor agonists was associated with lower mortality at the longest complete follow-up compared with norepinephrine alone (RR = 0.90, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.99, P = .02), but with an increased risk of digital ischemia (RR = 2.21, 95% CI 1.15 to 4.27, P = .02). Subgroup analysis indicated that the combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin receptor agonists may provide survival benefits for more severe septic shock patients (RR = 0.90, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.00, P = .04). Moreover, compared with norepinephrine alone, the combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin showed a trend towards reducing the longest follow-up mortality (RR = 0.89, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.00, P = .05). TSA indicated lack of firm evidence for a beneficial effect.ConclusionsIn adults with septic shock, the combination of norepinephrine plus vasopressin receptor agonists may reduce mortality at the longest complete follow-up compared with norepinephrine alone (low quality of evidence), but may increase risk of digital ischemia (low quality of evidence). This benefit mainly appeared in more severe septic shock patients. Moreover, norepinephrine plus vasopressin may confer a survival advantage.

articles.title: Making blood work: Toward precision care after cardiac arrest.
In-Simulation Versus Post-Simulation Debriefing in Medical Training: A Scoping Review and Theoretical Framework for Military Application.
articles.abstract: Simulation-based medical training is important for readiness. Feedback and debriefing are important components of simulation that support learning. Debriefs for military training are traditionally conducted at the conclusion of training, but recent evidence in the civilian medical training literature suggests that in-simulation debriefing may provide benefits for skill acquisition. The purpose of this scoping review is to map the body of literature examining post-simulation and in-simulation debriefing, highlight trends in the literature, and identify research gaps. A scoping review of the literature was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute Scoping Review Methodology, searching PubMed, the Web of Science Core Collection, and gray literature. Studies were included if they evaluated simulation-based emergency medicine or critical care medical training with an in-simulation debriefing intervention compared to post-simulation debriefing, measured at least one learning or performance outcome, and included a randomization element. Studies were excluded if they lacked a comparison group, involved non-acute care, utilized solely device-generated feedback, or did not explicitly articulate in-simulation debriefing protocols. A total of 21 articles met inclusion criteria; none involved military populations. The majority of studies (90.5%) employed rapid cycle deliberate practice as the in-simulation debriefing method, and the most studied domain was cardiac arrest and resuscitation (57.1%). No studies reported performance or retention measures favoring post-simulation debriefing, and 77.8% of studies measuring time to intervention found significant improvements when in-simulation debriefing was utilized. Effect sizes were only reported in 14.3% of included studies. The majority of reviewed studies reported outcomes favoring in-simulation debriefing; no studies favored post-simulation debriefing for performance measures. Effective implementation of in-simulation debriefing in a military training context would require deliberate instructor development and standardized methods for aligning debriefing methods with the experience level of the target audience. Future research should examine the effects of in-simulation debriefing on tactical medical skill performance and the time to intervention in a military training context.

articles.title: Clinical characteristics and risk factors for intensive care unit admission and mortality in rapid response team-activated ward patients: a retrospective cohort study at a tertiary hospital in South Korea.
articles.abstract: Factors driving intensive care unit (ICU) transfer decisions and mortality after rapid response team (RRT) activation remain unclear. We identified independent predictors of ICU admission, 28-day mortality, and in-hospital mortality in RRT-activated ward patients. This retrospective cohort study included adults with first RRT activation from September 2023 to August 2025 at a Korean tertiary hospital (n=549). Multivariable logistic regression with backward elimination was used. Of 549 patients, 191 (34.8%) were transferred to the ICU. ICU admission was independently predicted by procalcitonin >0.5 ng/ml (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.833; P=0.021) and lower hemoglobin (aOR, 0.808 per g/dl; P=0.040), whereas solid tumor was associated with lower transfer likelihood (aOR, 0.142; P<0.001). Mortality did not differ significantly between ICU and ward groups at 28 days (27.7% vs. 27.7%, P=0.937) or during hospitalization (46.1% vs. 40.2%, P=0.162). Declining peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO₂)/fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO₂) ratio, rising lactate, and hyperkalemia predicted both mortality outcomes. Lower platelet count uniquely predicted 28-day mortality, whereas solid tumor, chronic kidney disease, and deep learning-based continuous cardiac arrest risk score (DeepCARS) additionally predicted in-hospital mortality. ICU admission itself was not independently associated with mortality. ICU transfer after RRT activation appears to reflect acute reversibility, clinical trajectory, and possible at/after-activation goals-of-care processes rather than severity alone. Mortality was more closely associated with oxygenation failure, hypoperfusion, and electrolyte instability than with disposition.

articles.title: Translating the R-EDByUS score into clinical decisions after cardiac arrest.
Microcirculatory Hemodynamic Changes on Full Support Microaxial Flow Pump in Cardiogenic Shock.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Impaired microcirculation predicts mortality in cardiogenic shock independent of systemic hemodynamics, yet current treatment strategies focus primarily on restoring macrocirculatory markers. We studied whether full-support microaxial flow pump (mAFP) therapy improves sublingual microcirculation in cardiogenic shock. A prospective, single-arm, observational study of serial sublingual microcirculation imaging via incident darkfield handheld videomicroscopy was performed in 18 cardiogenic shock patients undergoing Impella 5.5 (mAFP) placement. Microvascular flow index (MFI), microvascular heterogeneity index (MHI), proportion of perfused vessels (PPV), and perfused vessel density (PVD) were measured. Eighteen patients were enrolled. Microvascular flow index (p = 0.004), MHI (p = 0.055), PPV (p = 0.003), and PVD (p = 0.067) improved immediately on support, including when adjusted for vasoactive-inotropic score. Improvement in MFI, MHI, PPV, or PVD was most pronounced in those with impaired baseline microcirculatory hemodynamics (all p < 0.05), whereas those with preserved baseline values demonstrated no change. Improved agreement between systemic and microcirculatory hemodynamics was observed in association with mAFP support, and none experienced worsening microcirculatory function. These exploratory findings suggest full-support mAFPs may improve impaired microcirculation during cardiogenic shock, although device-specific effects cannot be isolated from overall clinical improvement; validation in larger studies is warranted. Although agreement between systemic and microcirculatory hemodynamic markers improved, no macrohemodynamic marker proved sufficient to ensure adequate microcirculatory perfusion.

articles.title: Toward very early vasopressin use in septic shock: observational data accumulate but trial evidence still lacking.
Hemoglobin trends and transfusion practices after cardiac arrest: a cohort study.
articles.abstract: Hemoglobin targets are absent from post-cardiac arrest guidelines. New trials suggest that patients with brain and myocardial injury, injuries common post-arrest, may benefit from higher hemoglobin targets. Trends in post-arrest hemoglobin and real-world practices remain poorly characterized. We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive adult cardiac arrests at three academic hospitals. We screened in-hospital and out-of-hospital arrests with resuscitation efforts ongoing at hospital arrival for inclusion. Patients who survived the initial resuscitation and had a hemoglobin value measured were included. All post-arrest hemoglobin values and red blood cell transfusions were collected through 30 days; descriptive statistics and graphical visualization were used to present hemoglobin trends and transfusion practices. Exploratory analyses evaluated the association between hemoglobin and in-hospital mortality. Of 2,634 cardiac arrests, 958 met inclusion criteria, with 152 (15.9%) out-of-hospital arrests and 806 (84.1%) in-hospital. The mean initial post-arrest hemoglobin was 9.75 g/dL (SD 2.60), with hemoglobin levels declining progressively over the first 20 days post-arrest. Red cell transfusions were delivered for 369 (38.5%) patients in the 30 days post-arrest, with 1,238 total transfusions. The mean pre-transfusion hemoglobin value was 6.96 g/dL (SD 1.06). Pre-transfusion hemoglobin levels were < 7 g/dL for 762 (61.6%) of transfusions, and ≥ 7 g/dL for 476 (38.4%) of transfusions. Over 30 days, the highest proportion of patients transfused was in the first 48 h. Patients with initial post-arrest hemoglobin ≥ 9 g/dL had lower in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.46-0.84, p<0.01). In time-varying analysis, post-arrest hemoglobin through 30 days demonstrated an L-shaped association with mortality, with 95% of the total reduction in mortality hazard captured below 9.20 g/dL. Anemia is common after cardiac arrest, worsening in initial survivors. There is substantial variation in pre-transfusion hemoglobin levels, reflecting clinical equipoise. Clinical trials are needed to disentangle anemia as a driver versus a marker of outcomes, and test whether the risk is modifiable.

articles.title: Leveraging High-Frequency Postoperative ICU Arterial Blood Pressure Data from Electronic Health Records for Research: A Brief Report.
articles.abstract: Postoperative blood pressure fluctuations after cardiac surgery are highly clinically relevant, yet analyzing high-frequency arterial pressure data remains challenging. In this study, we introduce a novel methodology for processing minute-by-minute postoperative intensive care unit (ICU) arterial pressure data. The pipeline implements a series of systematic data-cleaning steps to resolve artifacts and ensure physiological plausibility, and deploys a multi-stage imputation framework to address missing intervals. Our approach constructs longitudinal blood pressure profiles that quantify the time spent within predefined blood pressure ranges, minimizing assumptions and enhancing data utility for research. We detail a rigorous and reusable workflow for data extraction, cleaning, and imputation, which may address limitations of previous methods and offer a framework to build a robust exposure metric for future research utilizing postoperative arterial pressure data.

articles.title: Escalating Vasopressor Intensity and the Goals-of-Care Documentation Gap in Septic Shock: Relevance to the Proposed Refractory Shock Threshold.
articles.abstract: BackgroundThe 2026 joint SCCM/ESICM Delphi consensus identified vasopressor intensity as a defining feature of refractory septic shock, yet its relationship to real-world goals-of-care documentation remains unclear.ObjectivesWe assessed the association between escalating vasopressor intensity and documented surrogate goals-of-care markers among septic shock decedents.MethodsRetrospective cohort study of adult septic shock decedents in MIMIC-IV (2008-2022) requiring vasopressors ≥6 h and surviving ≥24 h after initiation. Vasopressor intensity was quantified by peak norepinephrine equivalent (NEE) dose during ICU stay and stratified as: 0.01-0.50 (stratum 1), >0.50-0.99 (stratum 2), and ≥1.00 µg/kg/min (stratum 3). The primary outcome was death without documented surrogate goals-of-care markers, defined as having neither a documented do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order nor documented palliative care involvement.ResultsThe final cohort included 2458 patients: stratum 1 (n = 1033), stratum 2 (n = 909), and stratum 3 (n = 516). Death without documented goals-of-care markers increased across strata (23.8%, 28.3%, 31.2%; p-for-trend=0.001). After multivariable adjustment, stratum 3 patients remained more likely than stratum 1 to die without documented goals-of-care markers (aOR 1.32; 95% CI 1.02-1.69; p = 0.03). Palliative care documentation declined progressively with increasing vasopressor intensity (59.2%, 52.0%, 46.9%; p-for-trend<0.001), accompanied by lower rates of integrated DNR/palliative care documentation (47.0%, 40.0%, 36.4%; p-for-trend<0.001). Patients exceeding the Delphi-proposed refractory shock threshold (NEE >0.50 µg/kg/min) were more likely to die without documented goals-of-care markers than those below the threshold (29.3% vs 23.8%; p = 0.002).ConclusionHigher vasopressor intensity was paradoxically associated with a greater likelihood of death without documented goals-of-care markers and with lower palliative care documentation. These findings suggest a disconnect between escalating physiologic severity and documentation of surrogate goals-of-care markers in refractory septic shock and warrant further evaluation.

articles.title: The use of capillary refill time In adult critically ill patients: a narrative review on potentials, pitfalls, and perspectives.
articles.journal: Journal of clinical monitoring and computing
articles.abstract: The evolution of Capillary refill time (CRT) use in clinical medicine is interesting, transforming a simple bedside observation into a reliable tool for assessing tissue perfusion in critically ill patients. When Henry Beecher and colleagues first systematized CRT measurement in 1947, they recognized its potential as a rapid method to evaluate circulatory status in trauma casualties, establishing a foundational framework that would influence intensive care practice for decades to come. However, clinicians soon discovered that relying on visual inspection alone introduced troubling variability between observers and even within the same observer's assessments, with expertise and training significantly influencing measurement accuracy. This recognition of CRT's limitations sparked a concerted effort to transform the measurement from a purely subjective exercise into a standardized, objective clinical tool. Researchers systematically refined protocols by establishing consistent pressure application techniques, standardized measurement sites, and defined normal thresholds (approximately 3 s for healthy adults). These methodological advances set the stage for rigorous clinical validation. Subsequent research revealed that CRT correlated powerfully with microvascular blood flow and independently predicted mortality and organ dysfunction in septic patients. Meta-analyses encompassing over 60,000 patients confirmed that abnormal CRT carried substantially elevated mortality risk, particularly when measured using standardized techniques. More recently, the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trials demonstrated that CRT could serve not merely as a prognostic marker but as an actionable resuscitation target. CRT is nowadays considered an adjunct bedside marker to guide fluid and vasopressor resuscitation in adults with sepsis and septic shock, supporting individualized hemodynamic strategies while reducing over-resuscitation risks.

articles.title: Diverging Trends in Treated In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Intensive Care Units and General Wards Using Location-Specific Patient-Days.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Hospital-level incidence estimates may obscure differences between intensive care units (ICUs) and general wards. We compared temporal trends in treated adult in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) using location-specific patient-days. Methods: This retrospective study covered January 2016 to June 2026 at a South Korean teaching hospital. Monthly treated IHCA counts were modeled using negative binomial regression with patient-days as an offset, a setting × time interaction, and adjustment for the COVID-19 period and seasonality. Calendar-month score-based HAC analyses assessed robustness to serial correlation. January-March 2022 was excluded because arrest location was unavailable. Results: The incidence cohort comprised 1712 events: 1373 in ICUs and 339 in general wards. The combined rate was 1.06 per 1000 patient-days. The setting × time interaction was significant (monthly IRR 0.9843, model-based 95% CI 0.9768-0.9918), corresponding to a 17.3% annual decrease in the ICU-to-ward rate ratio. Calendar-month score-based HAC confidence intervals also excluded 1. ICU incidence declined (monthly IRR 0.9875, 95% CI 0.9825-0.9925), whereas the general-ward model showed no statistically significant temporal trend (IRR 1.0033, 95% CI 0.9975-1.0090; p = 0.263). Conclusions: Location-specific patient-day denominators identified different temporal trajectories in treated IHCA. These findings describe observed treated events and do not establish changes in underlying arrest risk or resuscitation performance.

articles.title: Enhanced Early Risk Stratification in Cardiogenic Shock Using Machine Learning: A Hierarchical Clustering Analysis.
articles.abstract: Cardiogenic shock (CS) exhibits marked clinical heterogeneity, limiting the performance of conventional risk stratification tools like the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) staging system. Machine learning (ML) has identified reproducible CS phenotypes that improve risk prediction, but their temporal consistency across the progression of shock remains incompletely described. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the temporal evolution of ML-derived CS phenotypes across the first 3 intensive care unit (ICU) days and determine whether phenotype trajectories enhance mortality stratification beyond SCAI staging. In a multicenter retrospective registry of 2,906 adults with CS admitted to ICUs between 2016 and 2022, hierarchical agglomerative clustering was applied independently to clinical variables on ICU days 1, 2, and 3. On day 1, 3 phenotypes emerged: Cardiac (younger, acute myocardial infarction-predominant, preserved renal function; 15% mortality), Cardio-Renal (older, non-acute myocardial infarction-predominant, isolated renal extracardiac impairment, predominantly SCAI A and B on admission; 27% mortality), and Cardio-Metabolic (severe renal and tissue malperfusion, predominantly SCAI D and E on admission; 55% mortality). Similar phenotypes persisted on day 2 and day 3. These ML-derived phenotypes enhanced mortality stratification within each SCAI stage across days 1 to 3. Hierarchical clustering reproduced previously identified CS phenotypes that were consistent across the first 3 days of ICU stay, providing an enhanced framework for early risk stratification. Prospective validation is required for clinical implementation.

articles.title: Early versus deferred intravenous calcium in patients with sepsis and ionized hypocalcemia: a target-trial emulation.
articles.abstract: Intravenous calcium is frequently administered during sepsis, yet whether early treatment improves 24-h hemodynamic recovery remains uncertain. We compared 24-h hemodynamic recovery between calcium initiation within 2 h of a non-emergency low-ionized calcium (iCa) result and no calcium initiation during the first 6 h after the result. We conducted a retrospective target-trial emulation of 2016-2025 high-resolution electronic health records from Zigong Fourth People's Hospital. Adults with sepsis, final or corrected iCa of 0.90-1.10 mmol/L, and no emergency indication were eligible at result availability. Strategies were executed calcium within 2 h versus no calcium through 6 h; care after 6 h was unrestricted. Clone-censor weighting and overlap tilting addressed grace periods, measured time-varying confounding, and clinical equipoise. The primary outcome was being alive and vasopressor-free at 24 h. Estimates and two-sided 95% percentile intervals came from 2,000 patient-level bootstrap samples with model refitting. Of 5,993 patients, 1,538 initiated calcium within 2 h, 147 initiated at 2-6 h, and 4,308 received none through 6 h; none of the latter initiated calcium during 6-24 h. The standardized probability of 24-h hemodynamic recovery was 69.9% with early calcium and 61.1% with deferral, corresponding to a risk difference of + 8.69 percentage points (95% percentile interval, + 4.66 to + 12.84) and a risk ratio of 1.142 (1.074-1.214). The estimated association varied with baseline norepinephrine-equivalent dose (Holm-adjusted P = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶), whereas the iCa interaction did not remain statistically supported after adjustment (P = 0.097). Early calcium was associated with a 1.29-percentage-point higher observed risk of hypercalcemia (95% percentile interval, + 0.64 to + 2.05). Intervals for severe arrhythmia, new renal replacement therapy, and hospital mortality included the null. Early intravenous calcium was associated with a higher probability of 24-h hemodynamic recovery than the deferred strategy, whose observed pathway involved no calcium through 24 h. Estimated effects were larger at higher vasopressor doses. Early calcium was associated with a modestly higher observed risk of hypercalcemia. These findings support randomized evaluation in vasopressor-treated patients. Baseline iCa modification remains exploratory.

articles.title: Forty-Eight Hour Lactate Normalization Predicts Favorable Neurologic Recovery and Survival in Venoarterial ECMO for Cardiogenic Shock.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for cardiogenic shock (CS) is associated with high mortality and poor neurological outcomes. Dynamic assessment of metabolic recovery, reflected by lactate normalization, may offer additional prognostic value compared with static severity indices. We retrospectively analyzed 662 consecutive patients from the multicenter RESCUE II registry who remained on venoarterial ECMO for at least 48 hours. Patients were stratified by 48 hour lactate level: 48 hour lactate normalization group (< 2.0 mmol/L, n = 371) and persistent lactate elevation group (≥ 2.0 mmol/L, n = 291). The primary outcome was favorable neurologic discharge (FND), defined as discharge with a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 or 2. The persistent lactate elevation group had a higher SOFA score (9.8 ± 3.2 vs. 8.5 ± 3.4, p < 0.001) and initial serum lactate (7.9 ± 4.8 mmol/L vs. 6.0 ± 4.3 mmol/L, p < 0.001). Lactate normalization was associated with a higher rate of FND (71.4% vs. 41.9%, p < 0.001), remained an independent predictor of FND (odds ratio [OR]: 3.12, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.21-4.41, p < 0.001), and was associated with lower risks of all-cause death (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.49, 95% CI: 0.38-0.64, p < 0.001) at 12 months. In conclusion, lactate normalization within 48 hours of ECMO initiation is associated with favorable neurologic status and 12 month survival.

articles.title: Continuous glucose monitoring for diabetes mellitus in the perioperative and intensive care setting: a prospective observational validation study(✰).
articles.abstract: In-hospital diabetes mellitus management currently relies on intermittent glucose monitoring with point-of-care (POC) testing, rather than continuous glucose monitoring (CGM). Most studies on CGM have focused on its benefits and accuracy in the outpatient setting, in contrast to the hospital setting, where the accuracy may be different. In this prospective observational study (NCT06297850), we assessed the accuracy of CGM (Dexcom G7, Dexcom Inc.) compared with POC monitors in people with diabetes mellitus requiring glucose-lowering medication undergoing surgery or admission to the ICU. The primary outcome was agreement between CGM and POC measurements, defined as median absolute relative difference (MARD). Clarke error grid (CEG) and Bland-Altman analyses were used to quantify the accuracy. Secondary analyses assessed agreement during periods of hypoperfusion, defined as a mean arterial pressure of <65 mm Hg, infusions with vasopressors, or reduced peripheral perfusion index. In 58 participants (mean [standard deviation] age 71 [11]yr; 34% female), the median MARD was 10.9% (5.1-19.4%); 1186 of 1212 paired POC and CGM measurements (98%) were within clinically acceptable ranges (CEG zones A and B). MARD was 4.5% higher (95% confidence interval 2.3-6.7%) during periods of hypoperfusion. Given that hypoglycaemia (<4 mM) did not occur, no paired readings were obtained. Bland-Altman analysis showed similar CGM and POC measurements, with a mean difference of -1 mM (95% limits of agreement -5.6 to 3.4 mM). For the vast majority of interstitial glucose measurements, CGM was accurate in people with diabetes mellitus. Although overall performance was good, caution may be warranted when interpreting CGM data during periods of impaired peripheral perfusion. NCT06297850.

articles.title: Clinical Validation of the Nursing Diagnosis "Risk for Shock" in Patients with Acute Myocardial Infarction Admitted to the ICU.
articles.abstract: ObjectiveTo clinically validate the nursing diagnosis "Risk for shock" in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) admitted to an Intensive Care Unit (ICU).MethodA retrospective case-control study conducted at a high-complexity university hospital in Brazil. The sample consisted of 116 medical records of adult patients with AMI, equally distributed between the case group (with cardiogenic shock; n = 58) and the control group (without cardiogenic shock; n = 58). Diagnostic accuracy measures (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and likelihood ratios) were calculated, and multivariate binary logistic regression using the Stepwise Forward method was applied to identify independent predictors and control for confounders.ResultsIn the accuracy analysis, the indicator "Unstable blood pressure" showed the best clinical balance, with a sensitivity of 85.0% (95% CI: 76.2-93.8) and a specificity of 83.6% (95% CI: 74.4-92.8). "Hyperthermia" and "Inadequate fluid volume" showed the highest individual specificities (90.1% and 80.3%, respectively). After adjusting the logistic regression model (Nagelkerke R2 = 0.614; Hosmer-Lemeshow p = 0.782), only four factors remained significant as independent predictors of the outcome: unstable blood pressure (aOR = 7.80; 95% CI: 3.10-19.60; p < 0.001), hypoxia (aOR = 3.70; 95% CI: 1.50-9.20; p = 0.006), hypoxemia (aOR = 2.90; 95% CI: 1.40-6.10; p = 0.004), and inadequate fluid volume (aOR = 2.10; 95% CI: 1.00-4.50; p = 0.048). Thermal and hemorrhagic indicators lost significance after adjustment.ConclusionThe study clinically validated the diagnosis and confirmed a robust predictive model composed of four indicators. Prioritizing the monitoring of these risk factors enables critical care nurses to anticipate hemodynamic collapse, support targeted care protocols, and optimize multiprofessional decision-making at the bedside.

articles.title: Mechanical versus manual bag-valve ventilation during cardiopulmonary resuscitation in adults with cardiac arrest: a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Optimal ventilation delivery during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) remains uncertain. Current resuscitation guidelines do not recommend mechanical ventilation (MV) over manual bag-valve ventilation (BV). We evaluated the association between MV use during CPR and clinical outcomes in adults with cardiac arrest compared with manual BV. We searched 6 bibliographic databases from inception through May 31, 2026. Included studies compared MV and BV ventilation CPR in adult cardiac arrest patients. Patients receiving MV at any moment during CPR were classified as the MV group; those receiving only BV comprised the BV group. Primary outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to hospital admission, survival to hospital discharge, and good neurological outcome. Secondary outcomes included physiologic variables and pneumothorax. We calculated pooled risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences with 95% credible intervals (CrIs) using Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses. Eight studies involving 6847 patients were included. For the primary outcome, MV use during CPR was associated with a higher rate of ROSC than BV use (pooled RR, 1.20; 95% CrI, 1.04-1.42), with a 99% posterior probability of benefit. Posterior probabilities favoring MV for survival to admission, survival to discharge, and good neurological outcome were 92.3%, 93.6%, and 92.2%, respectively. Pneumothorax incidence was similar between groups. In adult cardiac arrest, MV use during CPR was associated with higher ROSC compared with manual BV. Evidence for improved survival and neurological outcomes remains imprecise and inconclusive.

articles.title: Acute Effects of Impella 5.5 on Biventricular Filling and Pressure-Volume Area in Patients With Heart Failure Associated Cardiogenic Shock.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Use of Impella 5.5 in patients with decompensated heart failure-associated cardiogenic shock (ADHF-CS) is increasing as a bridge to advanced therapies. The effects of maximal trans-valvular unloading on biventricular filling and pressure-volume area (PVA) in ADHF-CS are poorly understood. Nine patients with medically refractory ADHF-CS underwent Impella 5.5 placement with simultaneous invasive arterial, venous, and biventricular pressure-volume loop analysis. Acutely after Impella 5.5 activation, cardiac output (3.4 ± 0.5 vs. 5.0 ± 0.7 L/min, p = 0.0011), diastolic (67.2 ± 8.0 vs. 80.7 ± 9.7 mm Hg, p = 0.0044) and mean arterial pressures (77.9 ± 7.1 vs. 86.9 ± 10.4 mm Hg, p = 0.029) increased, compared to baseline. Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (24.1 ± 6.7 vs. 16.8 ± 5.4 mm Hg, p = 0.0027), volume (262.1 ± 103.9 vs. 231.5 ± 104.3 ml, p = 0.0036), and PVA (21,913 ± 7,055 vs. 18,357 ± 7,758 mmHg·ml, p = 0.013) decreased. Right ventricular end-diastolic (12.4 ± 4.6 vs. 9.1 ± 3.8 mm Hg, p = 3.8E-5) and end-systolic pressure (42.1 ± 11.9 vs. 34.4 ± 11.1 mm Hg, p = 0.030) and PVA (6,303 ± 3,851 vs. 4,437 ± 2,473 mm Hg·ml, p = 0.027) also decreased. These findings suggest that maximal left ventricular unloading can acutely reduce biventricular filling pressures and PVA in patients with ADHF-CS.

articles.title: Effect of vasopressin and its analogues on microcirculatory perfusion: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: Arginine vasopressin (AVP) is a non-adrenergic vasopressor increasingly used in the management of shock. While it restores arterial pressure, its effects on the microcirculation remain uncertain, with potential for reduced regional perfusion and tissue oxygenation. The aim of this systematic review is to evaluate the effects of intravenous AVP and its analogues on microcirculatory perfusion across different haemodynamic conditions and vascular beds. A systematic search of MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Web of Science was conducted. Animal and human publications evaluating the effects of intravenous AVP or analogues on microcirculatory perfusion assessed with in vivo microcirculatory imaging or flowmetry techniques were included. Publications were grouped by haemodynamic condition and vascular bed. Of 1693 records, 39 publications (31 animal, 7 human, 1 combined) were included, comprising 43 study-units and 152 individual measurements. Overall perfusion was decreased in 33%, unchanged in 48%, and increased in 19% of measurements, compared with baseline, saline, or other vasopressors. By haemodynamic condition, perfusion was decreased/unchanged/increased (n=study-units; % of measurements) in physiological conditions (n = 14: 57/38/4), vasodilatory or septic shock (n = 23: 24/55/21; versus baseline, fluid resuscitation or noradrenaline), haemorrhagic shock (n = 3: 17/17/67; versus baseline, saline or noradrenaline), cardiac dysfunction or arrest (n = 2: 0/67/33; versus adrenaline or noradrenaline) and cirrhosis-related portal hypertension (n = 1: 0/0/100). Across vascular beds: gastrointestinal tract (n = 18: 30/42/27), kidney (n = 9: medulla 77/23/0, cortex 27/64/9), sublingual bed (n = 7: 19/68/13), cerebral cortex (n = 2: 0/67/33), cutaneous bed (n = 6: 42/42/17), and conjunctiva (n = 1, 100/0/0). AVP and its analogues reduced microcirculatory perfusion most consistently under physiological conditions, whereas effects in vasodilatory or septic shock were more heterogeneous. Across vascular beds, the highest proportion of measurements showing reduced perfusion was in the renal medulla. These results highlight the divergent effects of vasopressin across vascular beds and clinical conditions.

articles.title: Immunonutritional status and survival after cardiac arrest: prognostic value of the prognostic nutritional index, the cholesterol-modified prognostic nutritional index, and the controlling nutritional status score in post-cardiopulmonary resuscitation intensive care patients.
articles.abstract: Patients achieving return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after cardiac arrest experience marked systemic inflammation, metabolic stress, and nutritional impairment, all of which contribute to high mortality. Practical prognostic indices reflecting immunonutritional status may facilitate early risk stratification in this population. To evaluate the prognostic value of immunonutritional indices for predicting mortality in patients with ROSC after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. This single-center, retrospective cohort study included adult patients admitted to the intensive care unit after ROSC following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest between January 2015 and January 2025. Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI), cholesterol-modified Prognostic Nutritional Index (CPNI), and Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) scores were calculated from laboratory parameters obtained within the first 24 h of ICU admission. Patients were classified as survivors or non-survivors based on ICU outcome. Associations with mortality were evaluated using univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses, and discriminatory performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. Among 444 post-ROSC patients, non-survivors had lower PNI (43.66 ± 15.47 vs. 55.06 ± 17.21) and higher CPNI (81.10 ± 13.70 vs. 66.90 ± 18.25) and CONUT scores (4.27 ± 3.04 vs. 2.43 ± 2.43; all p < 0.001). In separate stepwise multivariable models, PNI (aOR 0.64 per 10-point increase), CPNI (aOR 1.25 per 10-point increase), and CONUT (aOR 1.24 per 1-point increase) remained independently associated with mortality. AUCs were 0.689, 0.631, and 0.681, respectively; PNI showed the highest sensitivity (86.3%) at a cut-off of ≤ 59.90. PNI, CPNI, and CONUT were significantly associated with ICU mortality after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. These indices may reflect systemic inflammation, immune dysfunction, metabolic stress, and nutritional reserve rather than nutritional status alone. Their availability from routine laboratory parameters may support early risk stratification. Further prospective studies are needed to confirm their prognostic value and clinical applicability.

articles.title: Oral or Enteral Levothyroxine for Myxedema Coma When Intravenous Therapy Is Unavailable: A Systematic Review and Descriptive Evidence Synthesis.
articles.journal: Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists
articles.abstract: Intravenous levothyroxine is generally preferred for myxedema coma but may be unavailable in many healthcare settings. We summarized published treatment regimens and outcomes with oral or enteral levothyroxine when intravenous therapy was unavailable. Intravenous-only and mixed-route reports were included for clinical context. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from inception through March 2026. Studies reporting myxedema coma treated with oral, enteral, nasogastric, or intravenous levothyroxine and extractable clinical outcomes were included. Pooled proportions were calculated only as descriptive summaries of oral/enteral reports and were not interpreted as treatment-effect estimates. Intravenous-only and mixed-route studies were summarized narratively. Methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute tools, and certainty of evidence using GRADE. Nine studies comprising 70 patients were included: six oral/enteral, two intravenous-only, and one mixed-route study. Oral/enteral loading doses ranged from 300 to 1000 μg. Descriptively pooled proportions were 0.20 for mortality, 0.76 for intensive care unit admission, 0.54 for mechanical ventilation, and 0.62 for vasopressor requirement. These estimates are descriptive summaries of selected published reports and should not be interpreted as population-level event rates, treatment-effect estimates, route-specific risks, or expected outcome probabilities in routine clinical practice. Published reports document oral or enteral levothyroxine as a rescue approach when intravenous treatment is unavailable. However, evidence is insufficient to establish comparative efficacy, safety, equivalence, or an optimal dosing regimen. Intravenous levothyroxine should remain preferred when available, particularly in patients with shock, ileus, or unreliable gastrointestinal absorption.

articles.title: Hemodynamic trajectory phenotypes may modify associations between corticosteroid timing and outcomes in septic shock.
articles.journal: Journal of clinical monitoring and computing
articles.abstract: Corticosteroid trials in septic shock show conflicting results, with patient heterogeneity and treatment timing as likely contributors. We evaluated whether associations between corticosteroid timing and clinical outcomes differed by hemodynamic trajectory phenotype defined by dynamic time warping clustering of Blood Pressure-Vasopressor Index (BPRI) trajectories across three ICU cohorts. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using MIMIC-IV as the derivation cohort and eICU-CRD and PINES as validation cohorts. Adult patients with septic shock receiving vasopressors were included. Hemodynamic phenotypes were identified from 168-h BPRI trajectories. Corticosteroid timing was classified as early (≤ 6 h) or late (> 6 h) after sepsis onset. In MIMIC-IV, inverse probability of treatment weighting with cause-specific Cox regression was used to estimate associations between timing and 28-day mortality, hospital length of stay, and ventilation duration within each phenotype. Validation cohorts were analyzed using multivariable Cox regression, and cohort-specific estimates were summarized using random-effects meta-analysis with I2. Two phenotypes were identified in MIMIC-IV: Deteriorated (N=2,082, 38%), with declining hemodynamics and higher mortality, and Improved (N=3,361, 62%), with stable or rising trajectories. Similar trajectory patterns were observed in eICU-CRD and PINES. In the Deteriorated phenotype, late corticosteroids were associated with lower 28-day mortality in MIMIC-IV (HR 0.88 [0.78-0.98]) and shorter ventilation duration (HR 0.65 [0.58-0.73]) compared with early administration. The mortality association was not consistently replicated in validation cohorts, whereas the ventilation association was observed in PINES Deteriorated patients. In the Improved phenotype, late steroids showed no consistent mortality or hospital length-of-stay association. Exploratory hemodynamic response analysis showed a more favorable BPRI slope for late versus early steroids in the Deteriorated phenotype. Hemodynamic trajectory phenotypes identified clinically meaningful variation in the relationship between corticosteroid timing and outcomes in septic shock. In the Deteriorated phenotype, delayed corticosteroid initiation was associated with lower 28-day mortality and shorter recovery, whereas the Improved phenotype showed no mortality advantage from delayed treatment. These findings support incorporating dynamic hemodynamic trajectories into future studies of corticosteroid timing in septic shock.

articles.title: Pressure Points: A Scoping Review of Intracranial Pressure and Mean Arterial Pressure Measurement and Reporting Practices in Neurocritical Care.
articles.abstract: Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is a cornerstone of neurocritical care, but the literature shows substantial heterogeneity in how its components-intracranial pressure (ICP) and mean arterial pressure (MAP)-are reported. We conducted a scoping review following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR to map this variability. Structured searches in PubMed and Scopus (January 1997 to May 2026) identified 350 eligible original clinical studies. For each study, we extracted whether the ICP measurement method, ICP device, ICP zero reference, MAP measurement method, and arterial line zero reference were reported. Reporting completeness was analyzed overall and stratified by guideline era and primary diagnosis, using the χ2 tests, odds ratios with 95% CI, and the Cochran-Armitage test for trend. The ICP measurement method was reported in 84.0% of studies, and the ICP zero reference in 14.6%; the MAP method in 66.9%, and the arterial line zero reference in 28.6%. Only 6.6% of studies reported all 5 domains. After publication of the Brain Trauma Foundation fourth Edition, reporting improved across most domains-ICP method (79.0% vs. 96.1%, P<0.001) and arterial line zero reference (20.2% vs. 49.0%, P<0.001)-and the composite reporting score rose from 2.37 to 3.06 (P<0.001). ICP zero-reference reporting was similar between eras (16.5% vs. 9.8%, P=0.105) while showing a significant declining trend across the study period (Cochran-Armitage Z=-2.52, P=0.012). Traumatic brain injury and hemorrhagic conditions had the lowest ICP zero reference reporting (8.8% and 9.3%; OR=0.35 for TBI vs. non-TBI, 95% CI: 0.19-0.65). Improvements in reporting have not reached the level needed to determine whether CPP values are comparable across studies. We propose an 11-item Minimum Reporting Set for CPP-related studies.

articles.title: Early post-ROSC laboratory phenotypes and clinical outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a 10-year national cohort study.
articles.abstract: Prior phenotyping in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) relied predominantly on prehospital indicators, which neither describe nor grade the underlying ischemia-reperfusion injury. We aimed to derive laboratory-based phenotypes and describe their clinical characteristics and outcome associations. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult resuscitated OHCA patients of presumed cardiac etiology between 01/02/2011 and 01/01/2022, linking Singapore's national OHCA and cardiovascular databases. Unsupervised latent class analysis (LCA) was applied to 14 laboratory variables within six hours post-return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Stability was confirmed through split-sample validation. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards model, adjusted for age, sex and initial cardiac rhythm, assessed poor neurological recovery at hospital discharge, 30-day and 3-year mortality. Among 1514 eligible patients (median age 65.0 years, 73.6% males), LCA identified three distinct phenotypes: multi-organ dysfunction (MOD, N = 286), homeostatic (HOM, N = 967), and immune-dysregulated (IMD, N = 261), independently reproduced in derivation (entropy = 0.817) and replication (entropy = 0.892) subsamples. The most discriminative variables were creatinine, eosinophil and lymphocyte. Compared to MOD, both HOM (aOR: 0.50, 95% CI 0.30-0.78, p = 0.004) and IMD (aOR: 0.46, 95% CI 0.26-0.78, p = 0.005) phenotypes had significantly lower odds of poor neurological recovery. This pattern was consistent for 30-day mortality (HOM aHR: 0.71, 95% CI 0.61-0.83; IMD aHR: 0.78, 95% CI 0.64-0.94) and 3-year mortality (HOM aHR: 0.70, 95% CI 0.60-0.82; IMD aHR: 0.74, 95% CI 0.62-0.90), all p ≤ 0.01. Early post-ROSC laboratory data identified three prognostically distinct phenotypes among resuscitated OHCA patients. These exploratory findings support external validation and investigation of phenotype-guided therapies.

articles.title: Opioid-associated vs undifferentiated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: examining differences in outcomes and the relationship with Utstein variables.
articles.abstract: The pathophysiology of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) due to opioid toxicity is different from other OHCAs. Our aims were to determine: (1) whether opioid-toxicity is associated with OHCA outcomes; and, (2) whether the relationship between Utstein variables and outcomes differ between those with opioid-associated (OA) and other OHCA. We analysed adult emergency medical services (EMS)-treated OHCAs from the British Columbia Cardiac Arrest Registry. Using post-mortem toxicological investigations, death certificates, and hospital-based diagnoses, we classified as OA-OHCA or "undifferentiated OHCA". We fit a multivariable logistic regression model to assess the association between OA-OHCA (versus undifferentiated OHCA) and favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge. We then added pre-specified interaction terms to individual models for: sex, initial cardiac rhythm, bystander CPR, witnessed arrest, and location type. Of 10,786 OHCAs: 1349 (13%) were OA-OHCA, of whom 331 (25%) were female, and the median age was 40 years (IQR 31-50); 9437 (87%) were undifferentiated, of whom 2910 (31%) were female, and the median age was 70 years (IQR 58-81). We did not detect an association between OA-OHCA (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.77, 1.35) and survival with favourable neurological outcomes. Models adding interaction terms demonstrated statistically significant interactions for: sex (p = 0.032), initial cardiac rhythm (p = 0.024), and bystander-witnessed status (p ≤ 0.001). Overall, we did not detect an association between opioid toxicity and outcomes. In models with interaction terms, the relationship between Utstein and outcomes differed between opioid-associated and other OHCAs, highlighting the impact opioid-associated cases may have in observational OHCA analyses.

articles.title: IgM- and IgA-Enriched Polyclonal Intravenous Immunoglobulin Therapy in Sepsis: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Evidence for adjunctive intravenous immunoglobulin therapy in sepsis remains conflicting. This study evaluated the association of IgM- and IgA-enriched polyclonal intravenous immunoglobulin (IgGAM) therapy with clinical outcomes, including post hoc analyses according to initial empiric antibiotic therapy (IEAT) appropriateness. Methods: This single-center retrospective cohort study included 50 adults with sepsis or septic shock according to Sepsis-3 criteria, treated between November 2006 and March 2010. Twenty-five patients received adjunctive IgGAM plus standard sepsis management, and 25 received standard management alone. Primary outcomes were 28-day intensive care unit (ICU) mortality, overall ICU mortality, and in-hospital mortality. Results: Overall, 28-day ICU mortality was 28.0% with IgGAM and 32.0% with control (relative risk, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.37-2.05; p = 0.758); other mortality outcomes did not differ significantly. Kaplan-Meier survival distributions also did not differ significantly (log-rank p = 0.208). During the ICU stay, vasopressor therapy was required in 68% of the IgGAM group and 92% of the control group (p = 0.034); corresponding study day 1 requirements were 60% and 76% (p = 0.225). In the complete-case longitudinal analysis (IgGAM group, n = 20; control group, n = 25), SOFA scores decreased significantly over time within the IgGAM group (p = 0.017), whereas no significant within-group change was observed in the control group (p = 0.616). In the post hoc appropriate-IEAT subgroup, 28-day ICU mortality was 0.0% versus 36.8% (p = 0.026), in-hospital mortality was 25.0% versus 63.2% (p = 0.038), and Kaplan-Meier survival distributions differed significantly (log-rank p = 0.004). The 60-day restricted mean survival time was 58.1 versus 38.4 days, with a difference of 19.8 days (95% CI, 11.1-28.4). Conclusions: Adjunctive IgGAM therapy was not associated with significant differences in mortality overall. Findings in the post hoc appropriate-IEAT subgroup were hypothesis-generating and should be interpreted cautiously given potential selection bias, residual confounding, and multiple comparisons. Prospective evaluation within optimized sepsis care is warranted.

articles.title: Outcomes following impedance threshold device use during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract: Existing work is equivocal regarding the benefit of impedance threshold device (ITD) use among patients experiencing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). We examined the association of ITD use with prehospital outcomes and longer-term dispositions in a nationally representative sample of OHCA patients. We included adult, non-traumatic, OHCA scene runs from the 2024 ESO Data Collaborative. We compared patients treated with (a) ITD only; (b) ITD and active compression-decompression device (ITD + ACD); and (c) neither device (no ITD). Prehospital outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to hospital arrival (SHA); disposition outcomes included survival to hospital discharge and favorable neurologic outcome (i.e., discharge to home). We used multivariate logistic regression to examine the association of treatment group with outcomes, adjusting for demographics and several potential confounders. We included 97,439 patient records (85.3% no ITD; 13.1% ITD only; 1.6% ITD + ACD). Disposition outcomes were available for 13,026 patients (13.4%). ROSC was higher for patients treated with ITD only (26.7%) than those treated with no ITD (23.8%; aOR = 1.09 [1.04, 1.14]); a similar pattern emerged for SHA. Conversely, survival to discharge was lower for patients treated with ITD only (23.9%) than those treated with no ITD (32.0%; aOR = 0.68, [0.61, 0.76]); a similar pattern emerged for favorable neurologic outcome. The ITD + ACD group showed more extreme versions of the trends observed for ITD only. ITD use was associated with improved prehospital outcomes but worsened dispositional outcomes among patients experiencing OHCA, suggesting this device may prove beneficial early in resuscitation of OHCA patients.

articles.title: Spectral characteristics and parameters of pulse oximetry waveforms for assessing resuscitation status.
articles.abstract: Real-time assessment of physiological resuscitation status is critical for guiding personalised cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and avoiding unnecessary harm from prolonged chest compressions. Non-invasive, objectively trackable tools for this purpose remain limited. This multicentre retrospective study (2013-2018) included 451 adult patients with cardiac arrest (497 CPR episodes) from 14 Chinese tertiary hospitals, comprising 158 Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) episodes with prehospital SpO2/ECG monitoring continued upon ED arrival and full pulse oximetry plethysmography (POP)/ECG/end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) monitoring established in the ED, and 339 In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (IHCA) episodes occurring in the ED. We analysed POP waveforms across four statuses: compression-only (CC), chest compression with return of spontaneous circulation (CC + ROSC, spontaneous circulation during ongoing compressions), non-compression without ROSC, and spontaneous circulation-only (SC). Time-domain (area under the POP curve [POPAUC]) and frequency-domain spectral features were evaluated against clinically documented ROSC. A frequency-domain "hybrid" pattern during the CC + ROSC identified ROSC with 100% specificity (PPV 1.000). In CC status, POPAUC was higher in stable-ROSC than unstable-ROSC (3232.2 ± 1008.2 vs. 2769.6 ± 1013.0 PVPG, P = 0.007). The POPAUC was lower in CC + ROSC status than in SC status for stable-ROSC (2768.2 ± 997.8 vs. 3335.8 ± 842.4 PVPG, P = 0.001), but the reverse was observed for unstable-ROSC (2697.5 ± 941.0 vs. 1338.1 ± 952.6 PVPG, P < 0.001). POP waveforms disappearance with concurrent ECG presence identified pulseless electrical activity with 100% specificity. Pulse oximetry plethysmography waveform analysis-using signals already available on standard monitors-may provide a non-invasive, real-time approach that may help identify ROSC during ongoing compressions and distinguish between stable and unstable circulation.

articles.title: Predictors of High Self-Efficacy in Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Regression Model Analysis.
articles.abstract: Cardiac arrest remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Effective cardiopulmonary resuscitation relies not only on technical proficiency but also on contextual and psychological factors. Identifying determinants of high cardiopulmonary resuscitation self-efficacy among emergency nurses and physicians is therefore crucial to improving cardiopulmonary resuscitation performance and patient outcomes. A cross-sectional descriptive-correlational study was conducted with emergency nurses and physicians (N = 399) from emergency and critical care units in Spain. Data were collected in February 2025 using validated Spanish instruments, including the Spanish versions of the Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Motivation Scale and the cardiopulmonary resuscitation subscale of the Basic Resuscitation Skills Self-Efficacy Scale. Predictors of cardiopulmonary resuscitation self-efficacy were examined using multiple linear regression analysis. A 95% confidence level was established, and P values < .05 were considered statistically significant. Motivation (β = 0.31, P < .001), recent institutional cardiopulmonary resuscitation training (β = -0.23, P < .001), clinical experience in emergency and critical care (β = 0.12, P = .03), advanced postgraduate education (β = 0.11, P = .02), and age (β = 0.11, P = .049) were identified as significant independent predictors of cardiopulmonary resuscitation self-efficacy. Greater motivation, recent institutional cardiopulmonary resuscitation training, greater clinical experience in emergency and critical care settings, advanced postgraduate education, and age were associated with higher cardiopulmonary resuscitation self-efficacy among emergency nurses and physicians. These findings support implementing regular training, advanced educational pathways, and workforce strategies within emergency and critical care settings to strengthen cardiopulmonary resuscitation preparedness and improve the quality of care for patients who experience cardiac arrest.

articles.title: Incidence, Process of Care, and Outcomes of In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in China: A Multicenter Prospective Registry Study.
articles.abstract: In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is an acute event associated with high mortality. Although survival has improved in high-income countries, contemporary multicenter data from low- and middle-income countries remain scarce, limiting global benchmarking and the identification of system-level opportunities for improvement. This cohort study used data from the BASIC-IHCA (Baseline Investigation of In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest) registry. Adult patients (≥18 years) who experienced IHCA and received cardiopulmonary resuscitation between July 1, 2019, and December 31, 2020, at 37 hospitals across 29 provinces in China were included. The primary outcome was survival to 30 days or hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation, 6- and 12-month survival, and favorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category score 1-2). Process measures focused on the timeliness of resuscitation response and the implementation of postresuscitation interventions. Among 17 602 patients (median age, 66 years; 65.5% male), the annual incidence of adult IHCA was 4.1 per 1000 admissions. Cardiac etiology was identified in 6569 (37.3%) patients, and 2380 (13.5%) presented with initial shockable rhythm. Among all patients, 16 872 (95.9%) received cardiopulmonary resuscitation within 1 minute; timely defibrillation or epinephrine was achieved in 71.4% and 84.4% of patients with initial shockable and nonshockable rhythms, respectively. Sustained return of spontaneous circulation was achieved in 6200 (35.2%) patients, of whom 222 (3.6%) received temperature control therapy and 320 (5.2%) underwent coronary angiography. Overall, 1610 (9.1%) patients survived to 30 days or discharge, with 1241 (7.1%) having a favorable neurological outcome. At 12 months, 1075 (6.1%) patients remained alive, and 986 (5.6%) had a favorable neurological outcome. This multicenter registry highlights a substantial burden of IHCA in China, with markedly low survival rates. Despite prompt initial resuscitation, critical gaps persist in postresuscitation care. Systemic and cultural factors, including the infrequent use of do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation orders, may further contribute to survival disparities. These findings suggest several system-level opportunities to improve IHCA outcomes, including structured response systems, optimized critical care resource allocation, and greater integration of advanced care planning.

articles.title: Chronic posthypoxic myoclonus: Lance-Adams syndrome.
articles.abstract: Lance-Adams syndrome (LAS) is a rare condition described as chronic intentional myoclonus following prolonged hypoxia. With limited cases of the condition, no standardised diagnostic criteria, and features overlapping acute myoclonus status epilepticus (MSE), diagnosis and management are challenging.Our case is a man in his 20s, who was admitted to the intensive care unit following two in-hospital cardiac arrests. He consequently developed persistent generalised myoclonic seizures despite multiple antiepileptics and sedation. CT, MRI and electroencephalogram (EEG) ruled out a diagnosis of MSE, making LAS more likely. Ketamine was ultimately required to terminate the generalised myoclonic seizures after which antiepileptic drugs were optimised to reduce residual intention myoclonus.This report highlights key features prompting the clinical suspicion of LAS in a patient who has no significant evidence of brain injury, preserved consciousness with continued severe generalised myoclonus and outlines pharmacological and neurophysiological management.

articles.title: Amiodarone after conversion from a non-shockable to a shockable rhythm in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: A propensity score-matched analysis from the German resuscitation registry.
articles.abstract: Amiodarone should be administered after three shocks according the current ERC ALS guidelines. However, its effect in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with an initial non-shockable rhythm who subsequently convert to a shockable rhythm is not established. We performed a retrospective observational cohort study using data from the German Resuscitation Registry. Adult patients with non-traumatic OHCA, having an initial non-shockable rhythm and subsequently received at least two defibrillations were included. Propensity-score-matched patient pairs (1:1) were analysed to compare outcomes between patients who received amiodarone during resuscitation and those who did not. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included hospital admission with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), 24-h survival, survival to hospital discharge, and favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge. Of 5535 patients included 3181 received amiodarone and 2354 did not. After propensity-score matching, 1843 patients remained in each group. Amiodarone administration was associated with higher rates of hospital admission with ROSC (26.7% vs. 23.0%; OR 1.22, 95% confidence interval 1.05-1.42), 24-h survival (21.4% vs. 14.7%; OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.33-1.87), and survival to hospital discharge (6.5% vs. 4.2%; OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.18-2.12). Favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge was not statistically significant (3.7% vs. 2.9%; OR 1.31, 95% CI 0.91-1.89). In OHCA patients with an initial non-shockable rhythm who subsequently converted to a shockable rhythm, amiodarone administration was associated with improved short-term and long-term survival, but not with a statistically significant improved favourable neurological outcome. Future controlled studies might define the proper (earlier) time of amiodarone administration.

articles.title: Impact of cardiac rhythm dynamics during cardiopulmonary resuscitation on clinical outcomes in patients treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR): a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Although the initial presenting cardiac rhythm is an established prognostic factor for extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation, heart rhythm dynamics during conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation remain poorly studied. We evaluated how the evolution of rhythm affects neurological outcomes and survival among recipients of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation. We systematically searched PubMed and Embase for studies evaluating rhythm dynamics, focusing on Rhythm Improvement (from non-shockable to shockable) or Rhythm Decay (from shockable to non-shockable). The primary outcome was survival with a favorable neurological outcome at the longest follow-up; the secondary outcome was overall survival. A random-effects model analysis with the Hartung-Knapp adjustment was used. Ten observational studies evaluating 5183 subjects with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation were included. Rhythm improvement was associated with a higher probability of a favorable neurological outcome (RR 3.12, 95% CI 1.26-7.74; GRADE: Low) compared with refractory non-shockable rhythms. Conversely, rhythm decay reduced the likelihood of a favorable neurological outcome compared with a sustained shockable rhythm (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21-0.80; GRADE: Moderate). Notably, decay toward asystole showed a robust negative association with good neurological recovery (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.09-0.45; GRADE: Moderate), whereas decay toward pulseless electrical activity did not reach statistical significance (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.31-1.25; GRADE: Low). Rhythm dynamics provide valuable prognostic insights for candidates for extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Rhythm decay toward asystole may predict resuscitation failure and poor neurological survival, suggesting that it should prompt a critical re-evaluation of the appropriateness of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

articles.title: Non-enrolment and non-completion of cardiac rehabilitation among survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with ischaemic aetiology: a nationwide register-based cohort study.
articles.abstract: Survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) of ischaemic aetiology is increasing, yet access to and completion of cardiac rehabilitation remain uncertain. To investigate non-enrolment in and non-completion of cardiac rehabilitation among OHCA survivors of ischaemic aetiology including temporal trends, and to examine sociodemographic characteristics associated with non-participation and non-completion. This nationwide Danish register-based cohort study included adults surviving ≥30 days after a first-time OHCA between 2019 and 2023. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to examine the association between non-enrolment and non-completion, respectively, and sociodemographic parameters of age, sex, cohabitation, comorbidity, education, and employment. A total of 1684 OHCA survivors were included. Overall, 55% did not enrol in CR, and among those who enrolled, 50% did not complete the programme. Non-enrolment was highest in 2020-2022 (60-62%) and declined to 43% in 2023. Survivors who were retired had higher odds of non-enrolment (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.42-2.44), whereas higher education (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.55-0.98) and moderate/severe comorbidity (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.43-0.65) were associated with lower odds of non-enrolment. No sociodemographic characteristics were significantly associated with non-completion. A large proportion of OHCA survivors of ischaemic aetiology either did not enrol in or did not complete cardiac rehabilitation. The findings underscore the need for systematic referral to cardiac rehabilitation after OHCA and more tailored rehabilitation approaches.

articles.title: Time to return of spontaneous circulation and long-term outcomes in bystander-witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors.
articles.abstract: Immediate Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) survival is time-sensitive, however, evidence linking resuscitation time to recovery is limited. We examined time from emergency call to return of spontaneous circulation (time-to-ROSC) and survivor outcomes. From the Danish Cardiac Arrest Registry, we included adults with bystander-witnessed OHCA (2016-2023) surviving ≥30 days, without prior anoxic brain damage or nursing home admission. Time-to-event and multivariable regression analyses stratified by time-to-ROSC (A: 0-10, B: 11-18, C: >18 min) assessed 11-month anoxic brain damage and nursing home admission, plus long-term survival and return-to-work through December 2024. We included 2583 patients (n = 875, 869, 839; groups A-C, respectively), 78% male; median age 65; median time-to-ROSC 14 min. Anoxic brain damage increased with time-to-ROSC (A-C: 0.3%, 1.8%, 3.2%; p < 0.001). Adjusted analyses showed an overall association (p = 0.03); HRs: 5.58 (95% CI 1.58-19.64) for B and 9.98 (95% CI 2.93-33.96) for C versus A. Nursing home admission decreased with time-to-ROSC (A-C: 3.1%, 2.2%, 1.3%; p = 0.04), but adjustments attenuated the association (p = 0.3). Long-term survival was similar (5-year Kaplan-Meier estimate: 79%; 95% CI 77-81%; p = 0.80; adjusted p = 0.99). Among employed patients (n = 177, 168, 179), return-to-work was similar (5-year cumulative incidence: 60%; 95% CI 56-65%; p = 0.31; adjusted p = 0.29). In bystander-witnessed 30-day OHCA survivors, prolonged resuscitation does not preclude recovery, time-to-ROSC was associated with anoxic brain damage but not nursing home admission, return-to-work, or long-term survival.

articles.title: Automated external defibrillators for in-hospital cardiac arrest: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: Automated external defibrillators (AEDs) improve survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but their role in in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) remains uncertain. This systematic review evaluates whether ward-accessible AED capability prior to code blue team arrival improves survival and neurologic outcomes compared with standard resuscitation systems. Six databases were searched. Eligible studies compared AED use to manual defibrillation in IHCA outside specialized areas. Primary outcome was survival with favorable neurological status (CPC 1-2, mRS 0-3, or no deterioration from baseline). Secondary outcomes included ROSC, survival at 24 h, survival to discharge, 30-day survival, CPR quality, and timing metrics. Three independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. Due to substantial heterogeneity, results were synthesized descriptively. Six reports from five unique study cohorts met inclusion criteria (total screened = 5510). Neurologically favorable survival was inconsistent. One study reported improved outcomes following a combined AED-and-training intervention, whereas the largest multicentre cohort found no significant difference in neurological disability among survivors (adjusted relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.93-1.09). ROSC and survival to discharge were not consistently improved. Only one study directly quantified AED-associated compression pauses, and effects on time to defibrillation varied by setting. Available evidence is insufficient to determine whether routine ward-level AED deployment improves IHCA outcomes. Included studies were observational and heterogeneous and CPR quality and training were incompletely characterized. Potential benefit from earlier defibrillation in shockable rhythms must be weighed against possible compression interruptions. Contemporary comparative studies are needed.

articles.title: Prehospital prognostication after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in tertiary care centers: the R-EDByUS score in the JAAM-OHCA registry.
articles.abstract: The R-EDByUS score predicts unfavorable neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) using prehospital variables alone, with separate models based on return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) status at hospital arrival. However, whether the score remains valid in patients transported to tertiary care centers is uncertain. We therefore aimed to validate it externally in this setting. Using the JAAM-OHCA Registry, we analyzed adult patients with presumed cardiogenic OHCA transported to tertiary care centers. The regression-based R-EDByUS score was applied to predict unfavorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 3-5) at 1 month in the prehospital ROSC and ongoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) cohorts. Discrimination and calibration were assessed, and score performance was examined across in-hospital intervention subgroups (percutaneous coronary intervention, targeted temperature management, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation). We also assessed the proportion of patients with unfavorable outcomes among those with a predicted probability ≥99%. Of 29,345 patients, 3305 were classified into the prehospital ROSC cohort and 26,040 into the ongoing CPR cohort. The score showed good discrimination, with areas under the curve of 0.906 and 0.913, and good calibration in the prehospital ROSC cohort. Discrimination was lower among patients who received PCI, TTM, or ECMO in the ongoing CPR cohort. Among patients with a predicted probability ≥99%, 100% (112/112; prehospital ROSC) and 99.9% (20,560/20,588; ongoing CPR) had unfavorable outcomes. The R-EDByUS score showed good discrimination in the JAAM-OHCA Registry, supporting its use for early risk stratification in cardiogenic OHCA even in tertiary care centers.

articles.title: Extrapolation of MAP trends predicts hypotension and vasopressor up-titration in the ICU.
