articles.title: Assessing fluid responsiveness in mechanically ventilated patients with intra-abdominal hypertension: a two-center, prospective, observational study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) may reduce the diagnostic accuracy of the passive leg raising (PLR) test for predicting fluid responsiveness, with unclear mechanisms. The reliability of the end-expiratory occlusion (EEO) test and mini-fluid challenge in IAH remains unknown. This study explored the mechanisms underlying PLR impairment and assessed the accuracy of EEO and mini-fluid challenge in detecting fluid responsiveness in patients with and without IAH. METHODS: In this prospective study in two intensive care units (ICUs), we included ventilated patients with IAH ("IAH + "; intra-abdominal pressure [IAP] ≥ 12 mmHg) and without ("IAH-"), all monitored via transpulmonary thermodilution and receiving a 500-mL fluid challenge. Patients consecutively underwent a 1‑minute PLR, a 15‑second EEO, and a 1‑minute mini-fluid challenge of 100 mL, with cardiac index (CI) changes recorded during each maneuver. Following the mini-fluid challenge, the remaining 400 mL were infused over 14 min, and a ≥ 15% increase in CI was used to define fluid responders. The transmural pressure of the inferior vena cava was estimated by the central venous pressure (CVP) - IAP gradient. RESULTS: We included 88 patients, 44 IAH- (25 fluid responders and 19 non-responders) and 44 IAH + (22 responders and 22 non-responders). Baseline IAP was 9 ± 2 mmHg in IAH- and 17 ± 3 mmHg in IAH + (p < 0.001). In IAH- responders, CI increased by 19 ± 11% during PLR and 31 ± 17% after volume expansion, with PLR positive in 24/25 responders. In IAH + responders, CI increased by 6 ± 7% during PLR (p < 0.001 vs. IAH-) and 30 ± 18% after volume expansion (p = 0.907 vs. IAH-). The AUROC of the PLR for detecting fluid responsiveness was 0.96 (0.87-1.00) in IAH- and 0.71 (0.56-0.87) in IAH + (p = 0.009 vs. IAH-). Among IAH + , there were 16 false negatives and 6 true positives for PLR, both with negative baseline CVP-IAP gradients. During PLR, the gradient reversed in true-positives (from -2.4 ± 4.0 to + 2.2 ± 2.7 mmHg, p = 0.014), whereas it remained negative in false-negatives (from -6.3 ± 3.7 to -1.4 ± 3.4 mmHg, p < 0.001). AUROC between IAH- and IAH + was similar for either the EEO test (0.95 [0.87-1.00] vs. 0.89 [0.80-0.97], p = 0.332) or mini-fluid challenge (0.94 [0.87-1.00] vs. 0.90 [0.79-1.00], p = 0.514). CONCLUSION: In patients with IAH, the limited diagnostic value of PLR for fluid responsiveness may be related to persistently negative CVP-IAP gradients in false-negative cases, whereas EEO and mini-fluid challenge remain reliable alternatives.

articles.title: Echocardiographic assessment of left ventricular longitudinal function in critically ill patients.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: In the intensive care unit (ICU), conventional assessment of left ventricular systolic function relies on left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), but LVEF often has limited prognostic ability. Measures of longitudinal LV performance [global longitudinal strain (GLS), mitral annular plane systolic excursion (MAPSE), and tissue Doppler-derived systolic velocity (S')] are increasingly used in critical care echocardiography and may capture clinically relevant dysfunction better than LVEF. To date, the prognostic implications of GLS, MAPSE, and S' have been studied mainly in septic cohorts, while their feasibility and prognostic value in mixed ICU populations remain uncertain. We therefore aimed to evaluate the feasibility and prognostic value of these parameters in a mixed ICU cohort. METHODS: In this exploratory secondary analysis of a prospective observational ICU cohort, transthoracic echocardiography was performed within 24 hours of ICU admission. LVEF by Simpson biplane, GLS, MAPSE, and S' were analysed offline. Feasibility was quantified as the proportion of patients with analysable measurements. Associations between echocardiographic parameters were assessed using simple linear regression and are reported as coefficients of determination (R2). Associations with 90-day mortality were assessed using logistic regression, with adjustment for age, Simplified Acute Physiology Score 3, and cardiac index. RESULTS: Of 411 enrolled patients, 377 had at least one parameter available and were included. Feasibility was 71% for LVEF, 65% for GLS, 90% for MAPSE, and 83% for S'. GLS correlated most strongly with LVEF (R2=0.516), whereas correlations were weaker for MAPSE (R2=0.268) and S' (R2=0.195). Ninety-day mortality was 27% (101/377). After adjustment, GLS (odds ratio [OR] 1.08 per 1% less negative strain, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.00-1.16; p=0.048) and MAPSE (OR 1.17 per 1 mm decrease, 95% CI 1.06-1.30; p=0.002) remained associated with mortality, whereas LVEF and S' did not. MAPSE ≤10 mm was independently associated with mortality (adjusted OR 2.48, 95% CI 1.31-4.71; p=0.005). CONCLUSIONS: In a mixed ICU cohort, impaired MAPSE and GLS were associated with increased mortality, in contrast to LVEF and S'. MAPSE was also the most feasible measurement. Incorporation of MAPSE into routine ICU echocardiography may improve detection and risk stratification of LV dysfunction in critical illness. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Secondary analysis of data from a single-centre prospective observational study focused on systolic dysfunction in ICU patients (Clinical Trials ID: NCT03787810).
articles.ai_summary: This study evaluated the feasibility and prognostic value of echocardiographic parameters in a mixed ICU population. It found that impaired mitral annular plane systolic excursion (MAPSE) and global longitudinal strain (GLS) were associated with increased mortality. MAPSE was also the most feasible measurement.
articles.ai_significance: These findings suggest that incorporating MAPSE into routine ICU echocardiography may improve detection and risk stratification of left ventricular dysfunction in critical illness, potentially leading to better patient outcomes.

articles.title: Frequency-domain band-pass filtering enhanced pulsation method for pulmonary embolism diagnosis and risk stratification: a two-center retrospective study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pulmonary embolism (PE) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality in critical care, yet traditional diagnostic methods face limitations, especially in critically ill patients. This study introduces a novel frequency-domain band-pass filtering enhanced electrical impedance tomography (EIT) pulsation method for rapid, non-invasive PE diagnosis and risk stratification. METHODS: In a two-center retrospective study, 106 participants (53 PE patients, 53 healthy controls) were enrolled. A 16-electrode EIT system recorded pulmonary blood flow pulsation signals, and a heart rate-adaptive band-pass filter with its lower cutoff frequency set slightly below the estimated heart rate was applied to extract perfusion-related pulsatility while separating it from ventilation-related low-frequency components. Key parameters (Matching Index (MI), Dead space index (DI), Shunt Index (SI), Electrical Impedance VQ ratio(EIVQ)) were analyzed for PE diagnosis and risk stratification. RESULTS: Compared with healthy controls, PE patients had significantly lower MI (P < 0.001) and higher DI (P < 0.001) and SI (P = 0.005). For risk stratification, intermediate-high-risk PE patients showed lower MI and higher DI than lower-risk patients, with the strongest differences versus low-risk patients (both adjusted P < 0.001).Among the EIT-derived parameters, the combined MI + DI+SI model achieved the highest AUC (0.820, 95% CI: 0.741-0.899), although the improvement over MI alone was marginal; it outperformed DI and SI. EIVQ showed no significant discriminative value. CONCLUSIONS: The enhanced EIT pulsatility method shows promise for non-invasive bedside assessment of PE-related perfusion abnormalities. MI, DI, and SI differentiated PE patients from healthy controls, while MI and DI were associated with risk stratification. These findings support the diagnostic and risk-stratification potential of EIT-derived pulsatility parameters and warrant further validation in consecutive patients with suspected PE.
articles.ai_summary: Researchers developed a new method using electrical impedance tomography (EIT) to quickly and non-invasively diagnose pulmonary embolism (PE) in critically ill patients. The method uses a frequency-domain band-pass filter to extract perfusion-related pulsatility and separate it from ventilation-related low-frequency components. The study found that the method can accurately diagnose PE and risk-stratify patients based on three key parameters.
articles.ai_significance: This study has significant implications for ICU clinical practice as it provides a novel, non-invasive method for diagnosing and risk-stratifying patients with pulmonary embolism, which is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in critical care.

articles.title: How to optimize brain perfusion and prevent cerebral complications during extracorporeal life support.
articles.abstract: Extracorporeal life support (ECLS) is increasingly used to rescue patients with refractory respiratory failure, cardiogenic shock and/or cardiac arrest. Acute brain injury during ECLS is common and associated with a significant increase in mortality and long-term disability. Brain injury in ECLS patients can arise from either the underlying disease or pre-ECLS events, such as cardiac arrest, or from secondary mechanisms linked to ECLS-related complications, management strategies, and physiologic perturbations during support. In this review, we will focus on the modifiable factors and clinical management strategies to prevent or mitigate secondary brain injury during ECLS. Both veno-arterial membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) as well as veno-venous membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) will be discussed. First, we provide an overview of the interplay between patient and circuit related factors that determine brain perfusion and oxygen delivery in this critically ill patient population. Second, we highlight the importance of standardized multimodal neuromonitoring to detect evolving brain injury early and to guide individualized neurocritical care and ECLS management. Third, we identify modifiable ECLS factors and physiological targets which minimize secondary brain injury. We provide guidance on the titration of extracorporeal blood flow and blood pressure targets, the amount of sweep gas flow and oxygen fraction, temperature control and anticoagulation management. A comprehensive understanding of ECLS physiology and circuit-patient interactions, integrated with protocolized multimodal monitoring, enables individualized adjustment of modifiable ECLS settings to prevent or mitigate secondary brain injury.
articles.ai_summary: This review discusses how to prevent brain injury in patients on extracorporeal life support (ECLS) by optimizing brain perfusion and oxygen delivery. It highlights the importance of standardized multimodal neuromonitoring and individualized neurocritical care. The review provides guidance on adjusting ECLS settings to minimize secondary brain injury.
articles.ai_significance: Optimizing brain perfusion and preventing cerebral complications during ECLS is crucial for improving outcomes in critically ill patients, reducing mortality and long-term disability.

articles.title: Hyponatremia in septic shock: Pathophysiology, fluid resuscitation challenges, and neurological complications.
articles.journal: Journal of family medicine and primary care
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition characterized by organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated host response to infection, with septic shock representing its most severe form and carrying high mortality in intensive care units (ICUs). Among critically ill patients, hyponatremia (serum sodium) <135 mmol/L is a common electrolyte disturbance associated with worse outcomes. While prior studies have explored hypernatremia in septic shock, the pathophysiology, clinical implications, and management of hyponatremia in this context remain underexplored, creating uncertainty for clinicians regarding fluid resuscitation strategies and neurological safety. This narrative review aimed to synthesize current evidence on hyponatremia in septic shock, focusing on underlying mechanisms, resuscitation challenges, and neurological complications. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, EMBASE, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2017 and 2025, including clinical cohorts, case reports, and systematic reviews. The findings indicate that hyponatremia in septic shock arises from non-osmotic vasopressin release, systemic inflammation, acute kidney injury, and fluid shifts during aggressive resuscitation. Large-volume crystalloid administration may exacerbate sodium derangements, while rapid correction poses a risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), even under guideline-adherent practices. Case reports suggest plasma exchange may provide the most consistent benefit in severe neurological complications. In conclusion, hyponatremia in septic shock reflects complex neuroendocrine, inflammatory, and renal interactions. Optimized management requires individualized fluid strategies, cautious sodium correction, and prolonged neurological monitoring to mitigate complications and improve outcomes in critically ill patients.

articles.title: SvO₂ response to red blood cell transfusion in cardiovascular surgical icu patients: a retrospective observational study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Red blood cell (RBC) transfusion decisions after cardiovascular surgery require integration of hemoglobin (Hb), hemodynamics, bleeding status, and oxygen supply-demand balance. Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO₂) reflects the global relationship between oxygen delivery and oxygen consumption, but an increase in SvO₂ does not necessarily indicate improved tissue oxygenation or clinical benefit. We evaluated acute SvO₂ changes after RBC transfusion in cardiovascular surgical ICU patients. METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of adult cardiovascular surgical ICU patients who received one RBC-equivalent transfusion with pre-transfusion Hb ≥ 7.5 g/dL and paired pre- and post-transfusion SvO₂ measurements. The primary outcome was an individual-level SvO₂ response, defined a priori as ΔSvO₂ ≥5% points from baseline to approximately 60 min after transfusion initiation. Multivariable regression was used to evaluate predictors selected a priori based on physiologic relevance to oxygen delivery and consumption. Receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to evaluate the discriminative ability of pre-transfusion SvO₂. RESULTS: 1,352 unique patients met the final inclusion criteria. Mean Hb increased from 9.82 ± 0.92 to 10.24 ± 0.98 g/dL, corresponding to a paired mean difference of 0.42 g/dL (95% CI, 0.38 to 0.46; P < 0.001). Mean SvO₂ changed minimally at the cohort level, from 73.79 ± 9.91% to 73.86 ± 9.37%, corresponding to a paired mean difference of 0.08% points (95% CI, -0.28 to 0.43; P = 0.671). Lower pre-transfusion SvO₂ was associated with a higher probability of an individual-level SvO₂ response. In multivariable logistic regression, pre-transfusion SvO₂ was associated with SvO₂ response (adjusted odds ratio, 0.89 per 1% increase; 95% confidence interval, 0.86-0.91; P < 0.001). Pre-transfusion SvO₂ showed moderate discrimination for SvO₂ response, with an area under the curve of 0.778 (95% confidence interval, 0.740-0.816). The Youden-derived cutoff was 69%, which should be interpreted as an exploratory predictor of acute SvO₂ rise rather than a transfusion trigger. CONCLUSIONS: Lower pre-transfusion SvO₂ was associated with acute individual-level SvO₂ increase after transfusion, but mean SvO₂ change was minimal. The association did not establish tissue oxygenation or clinical benefit and does not support using SvO₂, including the 69% cutoff, as a transfusion indication or trigger.
articles.ai_summary: Researchers studied how mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) changes after red blood cell transfusions in cardiovascular surgery patients. They found that lower pre-transfusion SvO2 levels were associated with an increase in SvO2, but overall SvO2 levels didn't improve much. SvO2 is not a reliable indicator of tissue oxygenation or clinical benefit.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings suggest that SvO2 should not be used as a transfusion trigger or indicator of tissue oxygenation in cardiovascular surgery patients.

articles.title: Neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest due to aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: a multicenter cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) due to aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) is rare but associated with extremely poor prognosis. Data on neurological outcomes and prognostic factors are limited. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective multicenter cohort study across 12 French neuro-ICUs including all adult patients admitted alive after OHCA-aSAH between 2014 and 2024. Demographics, cardiac arrest characteristics, aSAH severity, ICU management, and 6-month neurological outcomes (modified Rankin Scale, mRS) were collected. Firth penalized logistic regression was applied to explore predictors of favorable outcome. RESULTS: Among 15,907 SAH admissions, 164 patients had OHCA-aSAH. Median age was 54 [43-62] years; 47.5% were male. Only 8 patients (4.9%) achieved favorable outcome (mRS ≤ 3) while 156 (95.1%) had poor outcome (mRS ≥ 4), including 154 deaths (mRS 6). Low-flow duration tended to be shorter, epinephrine use lower, and pupillary abnormalities less frequent among survivors, although no independent statistical association could be confirmed. All patients receiving pre-hospital antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy (n = 14, 8.7%) had poor outcome. External ventricular drainage, ICP monitoring, and endovascular aneurysm treatment were more frequent, and ICU and hospital length of stay were longer, in survivors. One hundred and eight patients (65.8%) progressed to brain death within 1 [1-2] day. Penalized regression did not identify independent predictors of good outcome, though pupillary abnormalities and epinephrine use were associated with progression toward brain death. CONCLUSIONS: OHCA-aSAH carries a dismal prognosis, with < 5% achieving favorable neurological recovery. Selected patients may benefit from aggressive neurocritical care, and the high rate of brain death emphasizes the importance of organ donation pathways.

articles.title: Hyperlactatemia in sepsis and shock: a renal metabolic perspective.
articles.abstract: Hyperlactatemia is a frequent finding in critically ill patients and is traditionally interpreted as a marker of tissue hypoxia and anaerobic metabolism. However, in sepsis, septic shock, and other states of circulatory failure - including post-cardiac arrest syndrome - elevated lactate concentrations often occur despite preserved arterial oxygenation and adequate oxygen delivery. Increasing evidence indicates that lactate is a central metabolic intermediate whose circulating concentration reflects the balance between stress-induced production, cellular utilization, and organ clearance. While hepatic metabolism has long been considered the dominant pathway for lactate disposal, the kidneys - particularly proximal tubular cells - play a major and often underappreciated role in lactate utilization and clearance. Acute kidney injury (AKI), a common complication of sepsis, directly alters systemic lactate homeostasis. In this narrative review, we synthesize current knowledge on lactate biology in critical illness and examine the contribution of renal metabolism to hyperlactatemia in patients with sepsis-induced AKI. We propose that lactate should be interpreted as an integrated metabolic signal reflecting systemic stress and impaired clearance - rather than as a surrogate for hypoxia alone - with important implications for the management of septic AKI. The potential of urinary lactate as a marker of proximal tubular metabolic dysfunction and the emerging role of protein lactylation in modulating the inflammatory-to-reparative phenotypic transition are also discussed.
articles.ai_summary: Critically ill patients with sepsis and shock often have high lactate levels, but this doesn't always mean they're not getting enough oxygen. Lactate is a key metabolic intermediate that reflects the balance between production, utilization, and clearance. The kidneys play a significant role in lactate utilization and clearance, especially in patients with acute kidney injury.
articles.ai_significance: Understanding lactate biology in critical illness can help clinicians interpret lactate levels more accurately and develop more effective management strategies for septic acute kidney injury.

articles.title: Triple M overlap syndrome in the intensive care unit: differential diagnosis and management.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are increasingly used as first-line therapy for various malignancies and are associated with a growing spectrum of immune-related adverse events. While many toxicities are managed in the outpatient setting, a clinically significant subset progresses to life-threatening multisystem disease requiring intensive care. Among these, the Triple M overlap syndrome, characterized by concurrent myasthenia gravis-like disease, inflammatory myositis, and myocarditis, represents the most severe and lethal phenotype encountered in critical care. MAIN TEXT: Triple M overlap syndrome presents unique diagnostic and management challenges in critically ill patients. Clinical features frequently overlap with sepsis, pneumonia, thromboembolism, and cardiopulmonary disease, creating significant diagnostic uncertainty. In addition, traditional diagnostic tools such as myasthenia gravis antibody testing and early cardiac imaging may be normal or nondiagnostic early in the disease course. This review focuses on the recognition and management of Triple M overlap syndrome in the intensive care unit. We highlight key diagnostic pitfalls, including the frequent under-recognition of occult myocarditis and the limitations of electrophysiologic and serologic testing. A structured ICU-oriented approach is proposed, emphasizing early multisystem evaluation with creatine kinase, serial troponins, electrocardiography, and cardiac imaging, alongside concurrent assessment for infection. Management strategies include prompt discontinuation of ICIs, early initiation of corticosteroids, and escalation to intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange for severe neuromuscular involvement. Cardiac complications require close monitoring and early immunosuppression. Targeted therapies such as abatacept are discussed in the context of myocarditis, with current evidence limited primarily to cardiac involvement. This review emphasizes a practical ICU-oriented framework incorporating parallel evaluation for immune-mediated toxicity and infection in critically ill patients. CONCLUSION: Triple M overlap syndrome represents a high-risk and often underrecognized manifestation of ICI toxicity in critically ill patients. Early recognition, parallel evaluation for infection and immune-mediated disease, and coordinated multisystem management are essential to improving outcomes. Greater awareness and structured diagnostic approaches may reduce delays in treatment and associated mortality.

articles.title: Red Cell Transfusion in Critically Ill and Noncritically Ill Patients With Acute Myocardial Infarction and Anemia-A Subanalysis of the Myocardial Ischemia and Transfusion (MINT) Trial.
authors: Myocardial Ischemia and Transfusion (MINT) Trial Investigators
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Anemia is common in critically ill patients. In prior trials, a restrictive transfusion strategy was at least as effective as, and possibly superior to, a liberal strategy in critically ill adult patients. However, the Transfusion Requirements in Critical Care (TRICC) trial suggested that a restrictive strategy might be harmful in critically ill patients with ischemic heart disease. Our objective was to compare outcomes for restrictive and liberal transfusion strategies in critically ill and noncritically ill patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and anemia. DESIGN: Subgroup analysis of a parallel, two-arm randomized, controlled trial. SETTING: One hundred forty-four sites in the United States, Canada, France, Brazil, New Zealand, and Australia. PATIENTS: Adult patients with AMI and anemia enrolled in the Myocardial Ischemia and Transfusion (MINT) trial. Patients being treated in an ICU at randomization were considered critically ill. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomly assigned to a restrictive (transfuse when hemoglobin < 7-8 g/dL) or liberal (transfuse when hemoglobin < 10 g/dL) transfusion strategy. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We determined the effect of transfusion strategy on death and the composite of death/myocardial infarction (MI) at 30 days among critically ill and noncritically ill patients. Of 3504 patients enrolled in MINT, 1679 (47.9%) were critically ill. At 30 days, death (11.9% vs. 6.5%) and death/MI (18.9% vs. 12.7%) occurred more frequently in critically ill patients compared with noncritically ill patients. A restrictive, compared with a liberal, transfusion strategy resulted in a nonsignificant increase in the risk of death by 9% (risk ratio [RR], 1.09; 95% CI, 0.77-1.54) and death/MI by 9% (RR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.85-1.38) in noncritically ill patients and a nonsignificant increase in the risk of death by 24% (RR, 1.24; 95% CI, 0.95-1.61; interaction p = 0.55) and death/MI by 21% (RR, 1.21; 95% CI, 0.99-1.47; interaction p = 0.52) in critically ill patients. CONCLUSIONS: There is no evidence that the overall MINT trial results, which generally favor a liberal transfusion strategy in AMI patients, apply differently to noncritically ill and critically ill patients.
articles.ai_summary: This study analyzed the effect of blood transfusion strategies in patients with acute myocardial infarction and anemia. It found that a restrictive transfusion strategy did not significantly reduce mortality in either critically ill or noncritically ill patients compared to a liberal strategy.
articles.ai_significance: Understanding the optimal blood transfusion strategy for critically ill patients with acute myocardial infarction and anemia is crucial for improving patient outcomes in the ICU.

articles.title: Comparative analysis of the hemodynamic and metabolic effects of alternative fluid resuscitation strategies in critically ill patients with combined chest trauma and hemorrhagic shock: impact on oxygen delivery-consumption balance and coagulation homeostasis.
articles.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effects of different fluid resuscitation strategies on clinical efficacy, oxygen metabolism, coagulation function, and inflammatory response in critically ill patients with chest trauma complicated by hemorrhagic shock, so as to provide evidence for optimizing emergency treatment strategies. A total of 107 patients with severe chest trauma and hemorrhagic shock who were admitted to our hospital between June 2023 and April 2025 were retrospectively enrolled. According to the type of treatment received, patients were divided into two groups. The control group (n = 55) received conventional fluid resuscitation, while the observation group (n = 52) received restrictive fluid resuscitation. The two groups were compared in terms of fluid resuscitation parameters, oxygen metabolism indicators [mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2), oxygen consumption (VO2), oxygen delivery (DO2)], coagulation indicators [activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), prothrombin time (PT), hematocrit (HCT)], inflammatory indicators [interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-10 (IL-10), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)], as well as mortality and complication rates during resuscitation. Compared with the control group, the observation group had significantly lower fluid input volume (P < 0.05); there were no significant differences in early resuscitation time or colloid use between the two groups (P > 0.05). After resuscitation, SvO2, VO2, DO2, and HCT levels were all significantly increased compared with before resuscitation, while APTT, PT, IL-6, IL-10, and TNF-α levels were significantly decreased in both groups. The magnitude of changes in the observation group was significantly greater than in the control group (P < 0.05). During the resuscitation period, the survival rate of the observation group was significantly higher than that of the control group, while the incidence of ARDS, DIC, and MODS was significantly lower (P < 0.05). Compared with conventional fluid resuscitation, restrictive fluid resuscitation shows more significant clinical advantages. Its application in patients with severe chest trauma complicated by hemorrhagic shock can reduce unnecessary fluid overload, more effectively improve oxygen metabolism, correct coagulation dysfunction, suppress inflammatory responses, thereby increasing survival rates and reducing the risk of complications.

articles.title: [Persistent inflammation, immunosuppression, and catabolism syndrome].
articles.abstract: Reduced early mortality in sepsis and severe injuries led to the formation of a cohort of patients with chronic critical conditions (diseases). One of the mechanisms of chronization of acute critical conditions is the development of persistent inflammation, immunosuppression and catabolism syndrome (PICS). Diagnosis of PICS is currently based on clinical and laboratory markers, whereas morphological changes insufficiently studied. Lack of pathogenesis and morphogenesis understanding makes it difficult to stratify patients with prolonged critical conditions and develop new treatment approaches, and also leads to the absence of PICS in clinical and anatomical diagnoses. The article systematized current understanding of PICS mechanisms of development and morphological manifestations. Examples of clinical cases are presented.

articles.title: Early-Phase Computed Tomography Bowel Diameter and Neurological Outcomes Post-Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation.
articles.abstract: We aimed to conduct an exploratory investigation on the association between bowel diameter on early-phase abdominal computed tomography (CT) and neurological outcomes in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). This observational study included patients who underwent ECPR for OHCA and abdominal CT before intensive care unit admission between January 2015 and December 2021 at a tertiary emergency medical center. Maximum bowel diameter was measured with a picture archiving and communication system by an investigator blinded to outcomes. The primary endpoint was unfavorable neurological outcomes at 1 month, defined as Cerebral Performance Category 3-5. The discriminatory ability of bowel diameter was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Data from 181 patients were analyzed (median age, 57 years; 84.5% male). Bowel diameter demonstrated a weak ability to predict unfavorable neurological outcomes, with an AUC of 0.58 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.47-0.70). However, higher discriminatory performance was observed in subgroups of patients aged ≥ 65 years (AUC, 0.83; 95% CI, 0.69-0.96) and those with initial nonshockable rhythms (AUC, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.47-0.91). The results of this exploratory investigation suggest that bowel diameter may represent a potential adjunctive marker associated with functional outcomes post-ECPR for OHCA.

articles.title: Interprofessional collaboration in emergency department nursing care for patients with diabetic ketoacidosis: a narrative review.
articles.abstract: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is an acute metabolic emergency requiring timely risk recognition, fluid resuscitation, insulin therapy, electrolyte correction, dynamic monitoring, and coordinated care transitions. These interdependent tasks pose substantial challenges to emergency nursing. This narrative review aimed to synthesise current evidence on interprofessional collaboration in emergency DKA nursing and propose a conceptual framework to support coordinated care. A structured narrative review was conducted using literature retrieved from PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and the Web of Science Core Collection from database inception to July 10, 2026. DKA-specific clinical and implementation evidence was integrated with broader literature on interprofessional collaboration, communication, and healthcare implementation. The evidence was synthesised using Donabedian's structure-process-outcome framework. Current collaborative approaches include nurse-led standardised pathways, risk-stratified subcutaneous insulin and non-intensive care unit management, collaborative medication management, laboratory and point-of-care monitoring, structured communication, digital decision support, and multidisciplinary discharge planning. Available evidence suggests that standardised collaborative pathways may improve the timeliness and consistency of care, shorten emergency department length of stay, and reduce intensive care resource use. However, evidence evaluating complete interprofessional nursing teams and nursing-sensitive outcomes remains limited. Based on the synthesis, a conceptual closed-loop collaboration framework comprising six interconnected stages was proposed: recognition and activation, shared risk stratification, coordinated monitoring and execution, escalation, care transition, and recurrence prevention. Effective interprofessional DKA nursing requires shared clinical information, explicit responsibility, timely feedback, and predefined escalation procedures, with emergency nurses serving as continuous information integrators and process coordinators. The proposed framework provides an evidence-informed approach to organising collaborative emergency care. However, it has not been prospectively validated, and further implementation research is required to evaluate its feasibility, safety, and effects on nursing-sensitive and patient outcomes.

articles.title: Post In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Simulation to Improve Medical Decision Making and Communication in Internal Medicine Residents.
articles.journal: MedEdPORTAL : the journal of teaching and learning resources
articles.abstract: Cardiac arrest is a common cause of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized patients, and is a critical event that hospital-based physicians must be prepared to manage. While cardiac arrest care follows established algorithms, management of patients after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is more dynamic and nuanced. Resident physicians therefore need structured training to provide high-quality post-ROSC care. We developed a 90-minute simulation session on postarrest care for internal medicine interns. The session included 2 simulation cases: one involving a patient with ventricular tachycardia arrest in the intensive care unit, and another featuring a patient with pulseless electrical activity arrest in an acute care setting. Interns alternated between roles as participants and observers to both practice and analyze communication and clinical skills. Between simulation cases, a brief teaching talk was delivered to review a framework for post-ROSC care. The curriculum was evaluated using pre- and postsession questionnaires to evaluate changes in knowledge and confidence. Thirty-four learners participated in our curriculum over 2 academic years. We observed a statistically significant increase in the percentage of learners who correctly answered knowledge-based questions about target blood pressure (50% to 100%) and oxygen saturation (22% to 74%) in the post-ROSC period. We also saw significant increases in learners' self-reported confidence in communication (28% to 74%) and ability to generate a differential diagnosis for a cardiac arrest (25% to 74%). Our simulation session increased intern knowledge and confidence in managing patients in the post-ROSC setting.

articles.title: Correlation of blood biomarkers with microstructural brain injury in survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
articles.abstract: In-hospital mortality among resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients remains high. Identifying patients who will benefit from intensive care while avoiding prolonged, potentially unnecessary treatments is essential. Blood-based biomarkers provide a novel method for evaluating brain injury. The ability of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain (NfL), neuron-specific enolase (NSE) and total-tau (t-tau) to measure white and grey matter injury is unestablished in comatose OHCA survivors treated with targeted temperature management (TTM) or xenon combined with TTM. We examined correlations between the biomarkers and white and grey matter injury assessed with diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). This was a randomized, single-blind, phase 2 clinical drug trial involving two multipurpose intensive care units in Finland. It was conducted between August 2009 and March 2015. One hundred and ten comatose OHCA patients aged 24 to 76 years were randomly assigned to either inhaled xenon treatment combined with 24-h TTM (33°C) (n = 55, xenon group) or TTM alone (n = 55, control group). MRI data were available from 96 patients, with a median imaging time of 53 h (interquartile range, 47-64 h) after OHCA. Biomarker data were obtained from 105 patients. In the control group of 48 patients, after adjusting for age, sex and site, a disruption of white matter microintegrity as measured by decreased fractional anisotropy (FA) of DTI, the primary endpoint of the trial, showed a significant negative correlation with NfL at 24, 48 and 72 h (ρ = -0.28 to -0.37; P < 0.05), NSE at 48 and 72 h (ρ = -0.30 to -0.35; P < 0.05) and t-tau only at 72 h (ρ = -0.30; P < 0.05). In the xenon group (n = 48), these correlations were absent at all timepoints. The NfL-FA partial correlations showed progressive divergence between the xenon and control groups, with a statistically significant between-group difference observed at 72 h (ρ = -0.37 versus ρ = 0.14; P = 0.016). Cortical or basal ganglia grey matter mean diffusivity did not have a consistent correlation with biomarker levels at different time points. No statistically significant differences were found between the xenon and control groups in the adjusted geometric mean levels of GFAP, NfL, NSE or t-tau at various time points following OHCA. In conclusion, NfL correlated with FA in controls but not in the xenon group. This between-group difference reached significance at 72 h, suggesting that xenon may modify the relationship between axonal injury and white matter microstructure after OHCA.

articles.title: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Knowledge Among Respiratory Therapy and Anesthesia Technology Students in Jordan: A Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.abstract: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) knowledge among future critical-care professionals is essential for improving survival after cardiac arrest. Evidence on CPR preparedness among respiratory therapy (RT) and anesthesia technology (AT) students in Jordan is limited. This study assessed CPR knowledge, willingness to perform CPR, and perceived motivators and barriers to CPR training. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among RT and AT students (n = 360) in Jordan. Eligible participants were second-year students and above. The questionnaire collected demographics, prior CPR training, a 10-item CPR knowledge test (score 0-10), and self-reported motivators and barriers. Descriptive statistics, χ2 tests, and t-tests were used. Of the 360 participants, 46.9% had received CPR training; the mean age was 20.4 years, and 69.7% were female. The overall mean knowledge score was 5.22 (SD 2.00). Knowledge did not differ by prior training (5.27 vs. 5.18; p = 0.696). Students with basic life support training scored higher than those with advanced training (5.27 vs. 3.50; p = 0.001). Recognition of the emergency number (90.6%) and chest-compression technique (66.9%) were the most correctly answered items, whereas compression depth (34.7%) and initial response steps (13.9%) showed the poorest knowledge. Almost all students (98.1%) were willing to attend CPR training. Key motivators were helping others (36.4%) and family cardiac disease (25.6%); barriers included lack of interest (34.2%), limited time (25.0%), and cost (19.4%). RT and AT students demonstrated moderate CPR knowledge but notable deficits in essential technical skills. High willingness to train supports integrating mandatory and recurrent CPR instruction into allied health curricula.

articles.title: Association Between Hour-by-Hour ICU Admission Timing and 24-h Mortality: A Single-Center Retrospective Observational Study.
articles.abstract: Prior studies of ICU admission timing often use broad categories (day vs. night), potentially masking hour-level effects. We examined hour-by-hour ICU admission timing and mortality, with attention to nighttime periods and routine handovers. We conducted a single-center retrospective observational study in a closed ICU with 24/7 on-site intensivist coverage, using prospectively registered data from the Japanese Intensive Care Patient Database. Adults (≥ 18 years) admitted to the E-ICU between April 2017 and July 2025 were included. Admission hour (0-23) was modeled as a continuous exposure using restricted cubic splines (reference 14:00). The primary outcome was 24-h mortality and the secondary outcome was ICU mortality. Multivariable logistic regression was adjusted for demographics, APACHE II, invasive mechanical ventilation at admission, comorbidities, diagnostic categories, admission source, and post-cardiac arrest status. Bootstrap resampling was used to estimate 95% confidence intervals. Additional analyses examined handover, nighttime, and 24-h periodic patterns. Among 5724 patients, 24-h and ICU mortality were 3.4% and 10.6%, respectively. Compared with 14:00, adjusted odds of 24-h mortality were higher in the early morning. The early-evening estimate was imprecise, with the 95% CI including unity. In contrast, ICU mortality showed no clear temporal pattern. Handover comparisons showed no clear mortality association; nighttime admission was not associated with higher mortality, and cosinor analysis was nonsignificant. Hour-by-hour analysis showed higher adjusted odds of 24-h mortality in the early morning, whereas evidence of an increase in the early evening was inconclusive. Direct comparisons of handover periods showed no clear association with mortality.

articles.title: Emergency department extracorporeal membrane oxygenation: Current concepts, systems-based implementation, and future directions.
articles.abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has emerged as a time-critical resuscitative strategy for carefully selected patients with refractory cardiac arrest and other reversible causes of circulatory or respiratory failure. As the role of emergency department ECMO (ED ECMO) continues to expand, emergency physicians have become integral members of multidisciplinary extracorporeal resuscitation teams. This review aims to summarize the current evidence on ED ECMO while highlighting practical considerations for program implementation, workflow optimization, and future directions. This invited narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence regarding the indications, patient selection, cannulation strategies, pericannulation management, and postcannulation physiological challenges of ED ECMO, with particular emphasis on extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation. In addition to published literature, practical aspects of ED ECMO implementation, including multidisciplinary team organization, operational governance, workflow optimization, quality metrics, and institutional experience, are discussed. Emerging concepts such as artificial intelligence-assisted decision support, digital twin-enabled system modeling, and regional implementation strategies are also reviewed. Current evidence indicates that successful ED ECMO depends not only on technical proficiency but also on timely patient selection, standardized protocols, efficient multidisciplinary coordination, and optimized operational systems. Contemporary implementation frameworks emphasize integrated governance, continuous quality improvement, and structured performance metrics to enhance clinical effectiveness. Emerging digital technologies, including artificial intelligence and systems modeling, may further improve patient selection, operational efficiency, and program scalability. ED ECMO should be regarded as a comprehensive, systems-based resuscitation strategy rather than a standalone rescue procedure. Future progress is likely to depend on the integration of evidence-based patient selection, standardized workflows, multidisciplinary collaboration, intelligent operational systems, and continuous quality improvement. The development of regional ED ECMO networks supported by robust emergency medical service infrastructure may improve timely access to extracorporeal resuscitation and optimize patient outcomes.

articles.title: Inferior vena cava peak velocity versus collapsibility index to predict volume status in patients with gastrointestinal bleeding: A pilot study.
articles.abstract: Patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with hemorrhagic shock secondary to acute gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding represent a substantial proportion of the critically ill population. Accurate evaluation of intravascular volume status in these patients is crucial for guiding fluid resuscitation. However, the limitations of invasive methods and inferior vena cava (IVC) diameter/collapsibility measurements in assessing intravascular volume have been widely discussed in the literature. Despite their validation, noninvasive hemodynamic monitoring techniques remain underutilized in the ED. Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the predictive value of IVC blood flow velocity measured by Doppler ultrasonography in intravascular volume assessment and to compare it with the IVC collapsibility index. Electrical velocity measurement was used as a surrogate marker of volume deficit. Eighteen patients presenting with a preliminary diagnosis of acute GI bleeding were included in the study. The study population consisted solely of patients with suspected hypovolemia; therefore, no normovolemic control group was included in the study. Demographic, vital, and laboratory data were recorded, along with IVC diameter, collapsibility, IVC peak velocity measured by continuous-wave Doppler, and noninvasive hemodynamic monitoring parameters at admission, at the 30th and 60th min, and immediately after completion of fluid replacement. All data were subjected to statistical analysis. A significant correlation was observed between initial IVC peak velocity and stroke volume variation at admission (P = 0.009). The measurement demonstrated a specificity of 100% and a sensitivity of 84%, although the confidence interval was wide due to the small number of patients without volume deficit. No statistically significant differences were detected at the other time points. This can be explained by the ongoing bleeding and the lack of a valid gold standard. Measurement of IVC peak velocity was found to be a significant predictor of hypovolemia, although it showed limited utility for volume monitoring. Furthermore, it demonstrated superior performance compared to IVC diameter and collapsibility measurements. However, the study does not evaluate its ability to distinguish hypovolemia from true normovolemia.

articles.title: Discussing Future Treatment and Care in the ICU: Perspectives From Patients.
articles.abstract: Treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) is usually predicated on curative treatment, but continuing all available treatment options may not always be beneficial for the patient or in line with their wishes. However, patients admitted to the ICU are often assessed as incapable of making decisions regarding their care; hence conversations about wishes for treatment are postponed. This study aimed to investigate the experiences of patients who participated in a conversation concerning treatment and care following ICU discharge based on the Danish version of the Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment (ReSPECT) form. Semi-structured telephone interviews were conducted with patients who had a conversation about future treatment and care with an intensivist using the ReSPECT form during an ICU admission between November 2024 and July 2025. Relatives who participated in the conversation and were present during the interviews were asked to elaborate on their experiences of the conversation's timing and how they felt about participating in the conversation. Data was analysed using content analysis. Nineteen patients were included in the study, of whom 15 patients (83%) participated in a telephone interview. Two themes were identified: Timing of the conversation and Clarifying goals of care and options. Based on these, four sub-themes were identified, two for each theme: Too soon, but not much later; Wishes in accordance; Hard, but necessary and Communicating in an understandable manner. Most patients were satisfied with having had a conversation about future treatment and care. Patients found the conversation relevant and necessary. The intensivists were praised for their communication skills and their ability to know and explain recommendations for future treatment and care. However, most patients believed that the conversation was conducted too soon after recovering from intensive care. They would have preferred to have had the conversation later during their admission. Most participating ICU patients found a conversation about future treatment and care relevant but preferred it to be held after ICU discharge. Future research should investigate the benefits of incorporating intensivists in these conversations in general wards. In this prospective study, former ICU patients were interviewed and asked about their experiences and opinions regarding a structured ReSPECT discussion that had been conducted in the end of their ICU stay. The goal of that interview was advance care planning, involving the patients and their family members. This study reports a qualitative analysis of interviews conducted at least 4 weeks later. Two main themes and four subthemes were identified. Almost all patients remembered having had the discussion, but the content was less clearly remembered. ICU physicians' communication skills were appreciated. The study assesses a function of our daily work from patient and family perspective, and discusses important issues such as optimal timing of the advance care planning.

articles.title: Low-intensity versus medium-intensity continuous renal replacement therapy for critically ill patients (LIMIT) trial: Protocol summary and statistical analysis plan of a randomised clinical trial.
articles.journal: Critical care and resuscitation : journal of the Australasian Academy of Critical Care Medicine
articles.abstract: Severe acute kidney injury in critically ill patients may require continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), yet mortality remains high. A standard CRRT intensity is 20-25 mL/kg/hr, because higher doses have not improved outcomes. Excessive treatment may cause harm by removing antibiotics and other essential substances and potentially impairing renal recovery. Observational data suggest that lower-intensity CRRT may be effective, warranting a clinical trial to compare low-versus standard-intensity therapy. The objective of this study was to describe the prespecified protocol and the statistical analysis plan of the low-intensity versus medium-intensity continuous renal replacement therapy for critically Ill patients (LIMIT) trial. The LIMIT trial is an investigator-initiated, multicentre, open-label, randomised clinical trial, with a target sample size of 400 participants. The trial compares low-intensity CRRT (12 mL/kg/hr) and medium-intensity CRRT (25 mL/kg/hr) in adult patients with acute kidney injury requiring CRRT in the participating intensive care units. The primary outcome is a hierarchical composite of survival and time to successful liberation from RRT through day 28 from randomisation, analysed using a win-ratio. Secondary outcomes include intensive care unit mortality, hospital mortality, dialysis dependence at hospital discharge among survivors, vasopressor-free days at day 28, and ventilator-free days at day 28. The LIMIT trial will evaluate the effect of low-intensity CRRT on mortality and time to successful liberation from RRT compared with medium-intensity CRRT in adults with acute kidney injury. Its findings may also inform future research on broader patient-centred and societal implications of CRRT intensity.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and continuous renal replacement therapy.
articles.abstract: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is an important intervention in the treatment of acute kidney injury (AKI) in intensive care, and its application scope continues to expand alongside technological advancements and an increasing patient population. However, in current clinical practice, several factors, including individual patient differences, dynamic treatment needs, and the rational allocation of medical resources, pose challenges to CRRT implementation. The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) offers new approaches to address some of these challenges, and its applications in developing decision-support models, refining workflows, and supporting patient communication and education may contribute to more precise and efficient CRRT management. In this article, we discuss the current evidence and potential applications of AI in CRRT, as well as the challenges and strategies for clinical implementation, aiming to provide a reference for future research and clinical translation of AI-assisted CRRT.

articles.title: Association of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Radiographic Findings Identified by Machine Learning and Outcomes of Patients Receiving Invasive Mechanical Ventilation.
articles.abstract: To determine whether predictions from a deep learning model that identifies acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) findings on chest radiographs (CXRs) can also predict clinical outcomes beyond traditional indicators of hypoxemia and illness severity. Retrospective cohort study. Single academic medical center. None. Adult patients with CXRs performed at the time of invasive mechanical ventilation initiation. We applied a deep learning model that was previously trained to identify bilateral airspace opacities consistent with ARDS to CXRs of 6591 patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. The resulting ARDS-CXR scores were evaluated for their ability to discriminate risk of 28-day mortality and their association with 28-day mortality and time to extubation after adjusting for a patient's Pao2/Fio2 or Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation-IV. The median ARDS-CXR score was -2.09, corresponding to an ARDS probability of 15%, and 1089 (17%) patients had a positive score, corresponding to an ARDS probability above 50%. Twenty-eight-day mortality was 35.1% among patients with a positive score and 13.5% among patients with a negative score. ARDS-CXR scores below the ARDS threshold also stratified risk, with mortality increasing from 12.8% at a score of -2 to 19.9% at -1 and 27.5% at 0. The ARDS-CXR score area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve was 0.68 (95% CI, 0.66-0.70) for predicting 28-day mortality, whereas the Pao2/Fio2 AUROC was 0.64 (95% CI, 0.62-0.66). After adjusting for either the patient's Pao2/Fio2 or Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation-IV, a 1-point increase in the ARDS-CXR score was significantly associated with higher 28-day mortality or prolonged time to extubation. A deep learning-derived ARDS-CXR score quantifying radiographic findings of ARDS independently predicted mortality and ventilator outcomes beyond hypoxemia and illness severity. Algorithmically derived markers of lung injury severity from chest imaging could be used to support clinical care decisions, predictive enrichment in research studies, or incorporated into a future ARDS definition.

articles.title: Clinical Outcomes and Complications of Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) in Adult Patients With COVID-19 in Central and Eastern Europe: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.journal: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a rescue therapy for severe COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). International datasets do not consistently report Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) separately. We aimed to assess mortality, clinical characteristics, and complications of ECMO-treated COVID-19 patients across the CEE region. MATERIAL AND METHODS We conducted a systematic review with single-arm meta-analyses of observational studies. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from January 2020 to August 2025 for studies reporting ECMO outcomes in adult (≥18 years) COVID-19 patients from CEE countries, with at least 10 ECMO-treated patients. Conference abstracts and overlapping cohorts were excluded. The study protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251077593). RESULTS Twelve studies included 802 patients from 6 countries. Pooled in-hospital mortality was 65% (95% CI 0.57-0.72; I²=70.6%; 10 studies; n=691), and ICU mortality was 61% (95% CI 0.47-0.74; I²=85.8%; 7 studies, n=526). Country-level in-hospital mortality estimates were 54% for the Czech Republic and 76% for Poland but were descriptive because of the small number of studies and wide CIs. Mean pre-ECMO mechanical ventilation duration was 4.8 days (95% CI 3.7-5.8; I²=4.4%), ECMO duration was 17.8 days (95% CI 12.8-22.9; I²=79.8%), and ICU length of stay was 23.6 days (95% CI 7.5-39.7; I²=92.6%). Serious bleeding occurred in 40% (95% CI 22-61%; I²=85.7%). Certainty was very low for all pooled outcomes. CONCLUSIONS These CEE-specific estimates provide regional benchmarks, but substantial heterogeneity and very low certainty limit international comparisons and country-level interpretation. Standardized regional registries, prospective multicenter data, harmonized complication reporting, and long-term outcome assessment are needed.

articles.title: Music Therapy During Weaning From Invasive Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The study examined the effect of daily music therapy on weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the ICU, with a primary focus on weaning duration. Secondary agitation, sedation, and analgesia doses, pain, delirium, and perceived stress after 90 days were assessed. Additionally, total IMV and ICU stay durations and tracheostomy rates were studied. Physiologic parameters were assessed in the music therapy group (MG). The study also aimed to promote the humanization of critical care through a biopsychosocial and creative music therapy approach. DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups: control group receiving standard care during weaning and MG receiving music therapy additionally. SETTING AND PATIENTS: Adult critically ill patients (n = 100) admitted to a general ICU who received IMV for at least 48 hours. INTERVENTIONS: MG received daily, individualized music therapy sessions averaging 25 minutes, based on patient needs and musical preferences, which included music relaxation, music listening, and clinical improvisation. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: No significant difference in weaning duration was observed between groups (p = 0.97). Patients in the MG group showed significant improvements in agitation and sedation levels (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) on days 1 and 3 (p = 0.048, 0.005, and 0.024) and a lower percentage required propofol (p = 0.028). No significant difference in perceived pain (Visual Analog Pain Scale). The MG obtained lower Perceived Stress Scale-14 scores (p = 0.24). Additionally, MG significantly reduced tracheostomy rates (14%; p = 0.025). Median total IMV and ICU stay duration were shorter in the MG group, but not significantly (p = 0.206 and 0.203). Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygenation showed no significant difference before and after music therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Music therapy may serve as a nonpharmacological complementary adjunct during weaning by reducing agitation, sedation, and tracheostomy rate. It may potentially decrease perceived stress and IMV and ICU stay durations. Further research is warranted.

articles.title: Ketamine as an Opioid-Sparing Adjunct During Mechanical Ventilation: Feasible and Ready for a Larger Trial.
Assessment of Tidal Volume in Patients Undergoing Noninvasive Ventilation: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) is widely used in acute respiratory failure (ARF), yet the association between high tidal volume (Vt) and clinical outcomes remains incompletely defined. We evaluated the association between Vt and NIV failure overall and by ARF type, and its relationship with respiratory and clinical outcomes. MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and Latin American and Caribbean Health Science Literature (1976 to September 2025). Observational studies of adults with ARF treated with NIV reporting Vt or Vt normalized to predicted body weight (Vt/PBW) in NIV success and failure groups. Three pairs of reviewers identified studies and extracted data independently. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using Risk of Bias In Nonrandomized Studies of Interventions and Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation. Eleven studies (1136 patients) were included. Vt/PBW was higher in NIV failure vs. success (mean difference [MD], 1.02 mL/kg [95% CI, 0.60-1.45 mL/kg]), whereas absolute Vt did not differ (MD, 1.30 [-33.31 to 35.91]). In hypoxemic ARF, Vt/PBW remained higher in NIV failure (MD, 0.89 mL/kg [95% CI, 0.04-1.73 mL/kg]); no data were available for hypercapnic ARF. Post hoc analyses showed that higher Vt/PBW was associated with increased mortality (odds ratio, 9.11; 95% CI, 3.88-21.37), higher respiratory rate (RR; MD, 3.14 breaths/min [95% CI, 1.36-4.92 breaths/min]), and lower Paco2 (MD, -2.38 mm Hg [95% CI, -4.16 to -0.5938 mm Hg]), but no with pressure support (PS) level (MD, 0.24 [95% CI, -0.81 to 1.29]). Certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate. In adults with ARF treated with NIV, higher Vt/PBW was associated with NIV failure and worse outcomes. These findings reflect prognostic associations rather than causality, and interventional studies with systematic Vt monitoring are needed. Importantly, elevated Vt/PBW, higher RR, lower Paco2, and increased mortality, without differences in PS, collectively implicate elevated respiratory drive as a driver of increased mortality (PROSPERO [CRD42024584977]).Findings: Higher Vt/PBW was associated with NIV failure, particularly in hypoxemic respiratory failure; post hoc analyses showed associations with increased mortality, higher respiratory rate, and lower Paco2.
