articles.title: ICU-specific virtual reality for mental health after critical illness: an international three-arm randomized clinical trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Survivors of critical illness frequently experience symptoms of post-intensive care syndrome (PICS), including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), anxiety, and depression, with downstream impact on health-related quality of life (HRQoL). We evaluated whether an intensive care unit-specific virtual reality (ICU-VR) video improves mental health outcomes and whether timing (early vs. late) matters. METHODS: We conducted an international, three-arm, multicentre randomized clinical trial across eleven hospitals. Adults (≥ 18 years) with ICU stay ≥ 72 h and mechanical ventilation ≥ 24 h were randomized 1:1:1 to (1) standard care, (2) early ICU-VR (within 7-15 days post-ICU), or (3) late ICU-VR (≈ 3 months, during aftercare). The primary endpoint was PTSD symptom severity at six months (T3) measured by the Impact of Event Scale-Revised (range 0-88). Secondary endpoints included anxiety/depression severity and prevalence, and HRQoL. RESULTS: We randomized 344 participants (median age 61 years; 62% male); follow-up among survivors at six months (T3) was 80%. At six months, PTSD symptom severity did not differ between early ICU-VR and control (β = 0.32; 95% CI -3.38 to 4.02; p = 0.87) nor late ICU-VR and control (-0.82; 95% CI -4.62 to 2.97; p = 0.67). No between-group differences were observed for anxiety, depression, or HRQoL (all adjusted p > 0.05). Patients rated ICU-VR highly for improving understanding of the ICU experience and overall satisfaction (median 8/10). CONCLUSIONS: In this multicentre randomized clinical trial, a single ICU-VR video did not improve PTSD, anxiety, depression, or HRQoL at six months versus standard care. Findings should not be generalized to multi-session, therapist-guided, or personalized VR interventions. Future trials should target high-risk patients, make multi-session mandatory, and personalize ICU-VR. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was prospectively registered Netherlands: Trial Register/International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, NL9812, October 21, 2021.

articles.title: Music-Based Intervention in Postoperative Lung Transplant Care: A Feasibility Study.
articles.abstract: Music-based interventions may support recovery in medical and surgical settings; however, their implementation during the immediate postoperative period following lung transplantation remains understudied. This single-center randomized feasibility study examined whether a structured music-based intervention delivered by board-certified music therapists could be implemented at clinically meaningful postoperative recovery milestones and explored preliminary trends in pain, anxiety, medication use, sleep, and length of stay. Twenty-nine adult lung transplant recipients (experimental n = 17, control n = 12) were enrolled between September 2021 and September 2023. Participants in the intervention group received music-based intervention sessions during spontaneous awakening trials, 24-48 hr following extubation, and within 72 hr of transfer from the intensive care unit to a step-down unit. Intervention components included patient-preferred live music, music-assisted relaxation, and optional receptive or active music engagement tailored to patient status. Intervention delivery was feasible across all three postoperative milestones, although challenges related to recruitment, retention, sleep measurement, and intervention standardization were identified. Exploratory analyses suggested lower observed pain scores and lower median acetaminophen use in the intervention group compared to standard care; however, no outcomes reached statistical significance. Anxiety outcomes did not differ between groups, and sleep measurement using consumer-grade wearable devices was not feasible. These findings support the feasibility of music-based interventions during postoperative lung transplant recovery and provide guidance for the design of future adequately powered trials using refined outcome measures, milestone-based intervention delivery, and improved implementation strategies.

articles.title: Remote Multicomponent Rehabilitation in Intensive Care Unit Survivors: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Evidence for remote multicomponent rehabilitation among critical care survivors is sparse. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effects of a 6-week, remote, multicomponent rehabilitation intervention in survivors of critical illness following discharge from the hospital after an intensive care unit (ICU) admission compared with standard care on health-related quality of life at 8 weeks. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Pragmatic, multicenter, assessor-blinded, randomized clinical trial conducted from December 2022 to November 2025 at 52 National Health Service hospitals in the UK. Participants were adults who had been discharged from the hospital within the last 12 weeks with an ICU admission (required mechanical ventilation for ≥48 hours during ICU stay). INTERVENTIONS: Individuals were randomized to a 6-week, remote, multicomponent, individualized, rehabilitation intervention incorporating weekly symptom management; targeted exercise; psychological support; and peer support and information commenced within 12 weeks of hospital discharge (n = 231) or standard care (n = 198). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was health-related quality of life at 8 weeks measured by the EuroQoL 5-dimension 5-level questionnaire (EQ-5D-5L) utility score (from -0.285 [worst/worse than dead] to 1 [best health]; minimum clinically important difference: 0.08) and analyzed using linear regression (adjusted for baseline covariates). The secondary outcomes included leg strength and exercise capacity; self-reported perception of fatigue, anxiety, or depression; illness perception; acceptability of the intervention; and any adverse events. RESULTS: Of the 3705 screened patients, 429 (12%) were randomized (mean age, 55.4 [SD, 13.9] years; 184 female [42.9%]; 245 male [57.1%]; and had median Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score of 18 [IQR, 14 to 22]). The mean EQ-5D-5L utility score at 8 weeks was 0.69 (SD, 0.26) in the intervention group compared with 0.67 (SD, 0.27) in the standard care group (adjusted mean difference, 0.04 [95% CI, -0.001 to 0.09]; P = .05). The intervention improved 4 of the 6 secondary outcomes, including leg strength and exercise capacity, fatigue, anxiety, and acceptability of the intervention; there was no change in perception of depression or illness. Four adverse events were related to the intervention; no serious events were attributed to the intervention. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: A 6-week, multicomponent, rehabilitation program did not improve health-related quality of life at 8 weeks after discharge in ICU survivors who required mechanical ventilation. TRIAL REGISTRATION: isrctn.org Identifier: ISRCTN11266403.

articles.title: Key principles for rehabilitation of critically ill patients with obesity.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Patients with obesity who are admitted to an ICU bring specific challenges for rehabilitation during and after critical illness. This narrative review explores impact of differences in body compositions and pathophysiology on outcomes to summarise interprofessional, patient-centred rehabilitation strategies across the trajectory of recovery. METHODS: The interprofessional expert panel reviewed major trials and guidelines, integrating their clinical expertise with the current evidence. RESULTS: Three distinct phenotypes potentially influence outcomes for survivors. Whilst patients with preserved muscle mass may have a survival advantage, the phenotypes characterised by ectopic visceral fat or sarcopenia are frequently complicated by multimorbidity and polypharmacy, likely increasing the risk of adverse effects such as suboptimal sedation, prolonged ventilation and immobilisation, malnutrition, and impaired recovery. Targeted respiratory interventions, including secretion-clearance techniques and appropriate patient positioning to prevent atelectasis, reduce the work of breathing. Optimisation of communication and swallowing function is an essential component for facilitating safe oral intake and promoting active patient participation in rehabilitation. Concurrently, targeted nutrition strategies combined with early, targeted, progressive mobilisation might mitigate ICU acquired weakness and support functional recovery. The availability of appropriate weight‑based equipment is fundamental to ensuring safe mobilisation for both patients and healthcare professionals. CONCLUSION: Interprofessional collaboration is central to optimising outcomes and should extend beyond the ICU to structured post-ICU follow-up to address persistent, worsening, or newly emerging health impairments. Early rehabilitation in critically ill patients with obesity should integrate physiological, logistical, and psychosocial considerations to support equitable and functional recovery.
articles.ai_summary: This study reviewed rehabilitation strategies for critically ill patients with obesity, identifying three distinct phenotypes that influence outcomes. Targeted interventions, including respiratory, nutrition, and mobilization strategies, can mitigate complications and support functional recovery.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings highlight the importance of interprofessional collaboration and early rehabilitation in critically ill patients with obesity, emphasizing the need to address physiological, logistical, and psychosocial considerations to support equitable and functional recovery.

articles.title: The ARDS, Pneumonia, and Sepsis Consortium: Rationale, Design, and Feasibility of a National Platform for Phenotyping Critical Illness Syndromes.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: To enhance biological understanding of ARDS, pneumonia, and sepsis and to accelerate therapeutic development in these areas, the National Institutes of Health developed the ARDS, Pneumonia, and Sepsis (APS) Consortium. RESEARCH QUESTION: Is the APS Consortium study rapidly generating data and biospecimens from a large cohort of critically ill adults with ARDS, pneumonia, and sepsis that will facilitate phenotyping of these syndromes? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: The APS Consortium Phenotyping Study is a multicenter, longitudinal, prospective, observational cohort study aimed at enrolling 4,000 critically ill adults with ARDS, pneumonia, sepsis, or a combination thereof over 4 years. Data and biospecimens are collected to characterize many aspects of each participant's chronic health, acute illness, and long-term recovery to facilitate phenotyping, that is, subclassifying ARDS, pneumonia, and sepsis into precise biologically based subsets with shared pathophysiologic characteristics. Feasibility of the study was assessed by evaluating the first 1,000 participants in terms of recruitment pace, participant characteristics, biospecimen collection, and proportion with confirmed ARDS, pneumonia, and sepsis based on expert adjudication. RESULTS: The first 1,000 participants were recruited ahead of schedule in < 13 months. Median age was 64 years, 75% received vasopressors, 50% received invasive mechanical ventilation, and 25% died in the hospital within 4 weeks of enrollment. Biospecimen collection rates were high, with 99% of participants with blood samples, 98% with upper respiratory swabs, 37% with lower respiratory samples, 80% with urine samples, and 65% with gastrointestinal samples. Expert adjudication resulted in 40% classified with ARDS, 52% classified with pneumonia, and 89% classified with sepsis. INTERPRETATION: The APS Consortium Phenotyping Study is producing a cohort of critically ill adults with ARDS, pneumonia, and sepsis with high severity of disease and a rich set of data and biospecimens. The study will continue to full enrollment of 4,000 participants. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov; No.: NCT06521502; URL: www. CLINICALTRIALS: gov.

articles.title: The molecular ICU: a primer on omics, informatics and the future of precision critical care.
articles.abstract: Critical care has produced hundreds of neutral randomized trials, in part because therapies have been tested in biologically incoherent populations that dilute meaningful treatment effects. Syndromic diagnoses such as sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and traumatic brain injury group distinct pathobiological states under a single label, limiting the ability to detect treatment-responsive subgroups. While high-dimensional omics technologies have revealed this biologic heterogeneity, the field lacks a practical framework to translate these insights into clinical trial design and bedside decision-making. This Review addresses the translational gap in precision critical care through a pathway-level framework. We synthesize advances in genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, highlighting their roles in capturing susceptibility, host response, effector function, and real-time physiology. We propose pathway-focused biomarkers as clinically translatable signatures that preserve biological mechanisms while enabling practical measurement. We outline how pathway enrichment, network analysis, and multi-omic integration can identify these programs, and how feature selection can derive parsimonious biomarker panels for clinical use. This approach also supports pathway-guided drug repurposing by linking dysregulated molecular programs to existing therapies. Together, these signatures provide a framework for predictive enrichment, aligning patient selection with therapeutic mechanisms and facilitating implementation within adaptive platform trials. This Review serves as a practical primer that outlines the concepts and methods needed to translate omics into clinically actionable tools. By shifting from syndromic classification to pathway-defined biology, it provides a framework for biomarker development, trial design, and precision critical care.
articles.ai_summary: This study reviews the current limitations in critical care research due to syndromic diagnoses and proposes a pathway-level framework to translate omics insights into clinical trial design and bedside decision-making.
articles.ai_significance: This framework has the potential to improve patient outcomes by enabling personalized treatment and more effective use of existing therapies in critical care settings.

articles.title: Effect of the orexin receptor antagonist, suvorexant, on sleep architecture in the early postoperative period following cardiac surgery: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients recovering from cardiac surgery in the intensive care unit (ICU) do not sleep well. Commonly used sedative-hypnotic medications can disrupt sleep architecture and increase the risk of delirium in critically ill patients after surgery. The orexin receptor antagonist suvorexant, improves sleep onset and duration in patients with chronic insomnia. We hypothesized that suvorexant improves sleep onset and duration while also reducing the incidence of delirium after cardiac surgery. METHODS: This multicentric, double-blind, randomized controlled trial was conducted at two university-based cardiac ICUs. One hundred adult patients were enrolled after admission to the ICU following cardiac surgery. Enrollment occurred between March 2020 and February 2025. Participants were randomized to receive either a once daily oral dose of suvorexant 20 mg or placebo. Treatment began on the first night after extubation and continued until hospital discharge or for a maximum of seven days, whichever occurred first. Sleep was recorded using an electroencephalography (EEG) monitor (SedLine, Masimo Corp., California, USA) on the first night after extubation and was scored blindly by an experienced registered polysomnographic technologist. The primary outcome was wakefulness after persistent sleep onset (WASO). Sleep onset was defined as the first 30-second epoch classified by rapid eye movement (REM) or non-REM stages 1, 2, 3 after lights off. Wakefulness was defined as an awake period of 30s or longer. Sleep questionnaires were administered and delirium screenings were conducted every morning until hospital discharge. RESULTS: One hundred patients were randomized to receive suvorexant (n = 49) or placebo (n = 51). EEG analysis indicated that neither the median [inter-quartile range] nighttime WASO (200.7 [112.1, 328.4] minutes vs. 184.2 [80.4, 304.2] minutes; p = 0.33) nor total sleep time (224.0 [112.0, 379.0] minutes vs. 253.0 [68.0, 420.0] minutes; p = 0.92) differed significantly between the groups. There was no significant difference in rescue medication (melatonin, dexmedetomidine, benzodiazepine) utilization between the groups. Subjective sleep quality, incidence of delirium, and delirium-free days did not differ between the two groups. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: Clinical Trials Registry no. NCT04092894, Registration Date 09/17/2019. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients recovering in the ICU who underwent cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, the suvorexant treatment did not affect wakefulness after sleep onset or post-operative delirium.
articles.ai_summary: This randomized controlled trial tested the sleep-promoting effects of suvorexant in patients recovering from cardiac surgery. Suvorexant did not improve sleep architecture or reduce delirium in these patients. The study found no significant differences in sleep quality, delirium incidence, or rescue medication use between suvorexant and placebo groups.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings are significant for ICU clinicians as they suggest that suvorexant may not be an effective treatment for improving sleep or reducing delirium in patients recovering from cardiac surgery.

articles.title: Body composition-guided protein dosing in critically ill patients: a before-and-after study (PROGRESS-ICU).
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: To compare whether fat-free mass (FFM)-adjusted protein dosing is associated with different clinical and metabolic outcomes compared with total body weight (TBW)-based dosing in critically ill patients in the intensive care unit (ICU). METHODS: Adult ICU patients (April 2020-October 2025) with serial bioelectrical impedance analysis were included in the PROGRESS-ICU observational cohort study. Patients received either TBW-based protein dosing (1.5 g/kg/day; April 2020-June 2023) or FFM-based dosing after protocol revision (1.85 g/kg/day dry FFM, corrected for fluid overload; July 2023 onward). The primary outcome was 90-day all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included 30-day mortality, ICU and hospital length of stay, invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) duration, and longitudinal changes in FFM and urea-to-creatinine ratio (UCR). Survival was analysed using multivariable Cox regression and inverse probability of treatment weighting; longitudinal outcomes were assessed using mixed-effects models. RESULTS: Among 620 patients (310 per cohort), median age was 69 years, and ~ 60% were male. Notable baseline differences included a higher proportion of COVID-19 admissions in the TBW cohort (40% vs. 1%), which may have influenced outcomes. Ninety-day mortality did not differ significantly between groups (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 0.78, 95% CI 0.56-1.09). FFM-based dosing was associated with shorter ICU stay (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69-0.91) and fewer IMV days (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65-0.96); hospital length of stay was similar (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.67-1.10). TBW-based dosing was associated with higher UCR trajectories and greater FFM loss. These associations should be interpreted cautiously due to the observational design, substantial baseline imbalances, and potential residual confounding. CONCLUSIONS: In this observational before-after study, FFM-based protein dosing was not associated with differences in mortality compared with TBW-based dosing. Associations with ICU stay, IMV duration, and metabolic markers were observed but may reflect residual confounding and temporal changes. The study was underpowered to detect modest differences in mortality, and confidence intervals include the possibility of clinically relevant benefit or harm. These findings are exploratory and require confirmation in adequately powered randomised controlled trials. TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was approved by the local ethics committee (protocol number 2403-017; 11 April 2024) and registered prior to data analysis on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07312708; 5 December 2025), the Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/3SU49; 4 December 2025), and the Dutch Central Committee on Research Involving Human Subjects (NL-010953; 26 October 2025). Patients admitted before ethics approval were retrospectively included under a waiver of informed consent, and from April 2024 an opt-out consent procedure was implemented for all new admissions. Data were collected as part of routine clinical care. The study protocol, including prespecified analyses, was finalised and registered before the research team accessed the data.
articles.ai_summary: Critically ill patients were given protein based on either their total body weight or fat-free mass. The study found that using fat-free mass-based dosing was associated with shorter ICU stays and fewer days on a ventilator, but not with a difference in mortality.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings suggest that adjusting protein dosing based on a patient's fat-free mass may be beneficial for critically ill patients, but further research is needed to confirm this.

articles.title: Implementation of the kidney protection strategy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury - a multi-center prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The international Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines recommend the implementation of a kidney protection strategy (KPS) in patients at high risk of and with Acute Kidney Injury (AKI). However, real-world implementation of this strategy in critically ill patients with AKI is unclear. We quantified timely and sustained adherence to KPS in critically ill adults with moderate-to-severe (KDIGO stage 2 or 3) AKI and explored associations with clinical outcomes. METHODS: This was a multicenter, prospective cohort study enrolling adult patients with moderate or severe AKI requiring vasopressors and/or mechanical ventilation across five centers in Europe. The primary endpoint was adherence to the KPS, which included hemodynamic monitoring, sustained optimization of mean arterial pressure (MAP) > 65 mmHg, monitoring of serum creatinine and urine output, and avoidance of hyperglycemia, radiocontrast agents and nephrotoxins when possible, within 12 h after AKI diagnosis for 48 h or until ICU discharge. Exploratory analyses examined associations between adherence and renal outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 258 patients were enrolled (median age 69 years [IQR 62-75]; 65% male; median SOFA 10 [IQR 8-13]). The complete KPS was implemented in 80 patients (31%; 95% CI, 25.5-37.2%). Adherence to individual components of the KPS varied widely with optimization of MAP showing the lowest implementation rate (33%). In exploratory analyses accounting for death as a competing risk, KPS adherence was associated with a lower incidence of AKD beyond day 7 (subdistribution hazard ratio [SHR] 0.64; 95% CI, 0.41-0.99; p = 0.046), a higher incidence of renal recovery at hospital discharge (SHR 6.02; 95% CI, 4.00-9.05; p < 0.0001), and a lower incidence of RRT within 30 days (SHR 0.12; 95% CI, 0.02-0.91; p = 0.04). After multivariable adjustment, the association with renal recovery remained robust (adjusted SHR 6.29; 95% CI, 3.08-12.85; p < 0.0001). A clear dose-response relationship was observed between the number of implemented KPS components and renal outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: In critically ill patients with moderate-to-severe AKI, the complete KDIGO-recommended kidney protection strategy was implemented in approximately one-third of patients, and full KPS adherence was associated with a higher rate of renal recovery at hospital discharge.
articles.ai_summary: This study looked at how well a kidney protection strategy was implemented in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury. They found that about a third of patients received the full strategy, and those who did had a higher rate of kidney recovery. The study also found a link between the number of strategy components implemented and better kidney outcomes.
articles.ai_significance: This study is important for ICU clinicians because it highlights the need to implement a kidney protection strategy in critically ill patients with acute kidney injury to improve kidney recovery rates.

articles.title: Extracorporeal life support in adult critically ill patients: mechanisms of benefit in respiratory and cardiac failure.
articles.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
authors: endorsing societies of Faculty of Intensive Care Medicine (FICM); Pulmonary Vascular Research Institute (PVRI); Protective Ventilation Network (PROVE Network); Association for Cardiothoracic Anaesthesia and Critical Care (ACTACC); Society of Mechanical Ventilation (SMV); Protecting the Right Ventricle Network (PRORVnet)
articles.abstract: Extracorporeal life support provides temporary cardiorespiratory support for patients with severe, potentially reversible cardiac and/or respiratory failure refractory to conventional measures. Its application has broadened across a wide spectrum of critical illness, yet the mechanistic basis of its physiological benefit remains incompletely defined.This review explores the mechanisms through which extracorporeal life support may confer benefit in respiratory and cardiac failure. These include restoration of gas exchange, optimization of circulatory dynamics, and mitigation of secondary organ injuries, creating conditions that facilitate tissue repair, enable adjunctive therapies, and in selected cases, provide a bridge to transplantation. In isolated respiratory failure, respiratory extracorporeal life support stabilizes gas exchange and modulates respiratory drive, enabling lung-protective ventilation and potentially attenuating ventilator- and patient self-inflicted lung injury. In cardiogenic shock, cardiac extracorporeal life support restores systemic perfusion and may reduce myocardial oxygen demand, while during cardiac arrest it may confer neuro-protective effects. In combined cardiorespiratory failure, advanced extracorporeal support modalities may augment both systemic and pulmonary circulation, supporting gas exchange and maintaining end-organ perfusion. Mechanistically, these interventions interrupt the cascade of hypoxemia- and/or hypercapnia- induced pulmonary vasoconstriction, right ventricular overload, and systemic hypoperfusion, facilitating multi-organ recovery. Optimizing patient selection, timing for extracorporeal life support initiation, and use of adjunctive therapies require a nuanced understanding of the interplay between these physiological pathways alongside careful considerations of key limitations including device-related complications, hematologic and inflammatory perturbations, and physiological trade-offs. This concise clinical review synthesizes the current literature on the mechanistic basis of extracorporeal life support in adults.

articles.title: Nurse-led family participatory support intervention on clinical outcomes in ICU patients: a prospective quasi-experimental study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Delirium is a common and serious complication in critically ill patients, and family-centered care has emerged as a promising non-pharmacological strategy. However, evidence on structured, nurse-led family participatory support (NFPS) intervention remains limited. AIM: To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of NFPS in critically ill adult patients. METHODS: Adult patients admitted to intensive care units (ICU) from three tertiary hospitals in Gansu Province were allocated to either the NFPS group or a usual care group without family participation (non-NFPS). In the NFPS group, trained family members participated in care under the guidance of ICU nurses. The primary outcome was the incidence of delirium. RESULTS: After 1:1 propensity score matching, 365 patients were included in each group. The NFPS group demonstrated significant reductions in incidence of delirium [26.85% vs. 34.25%, p = 0.03]. Compared with the control group, the NFPS group also had significantly shorter hospital length of stay (HLOS) (25 [17-34] vs. 30 [22-38] days, P < 0.001), ICU-LOS (13 [7-17] vs. 14 [10-18] days, P < 0.001), duration of mechanical ventilation (10 [6-15] vs. 11 [8-17] days, P < 0.001) and lower hospitalization cost (193,931.99 [117,616.64-294,201.02] vs. 199,330.72 [138,636.05-300,993.88] CNY, P = 0.032). No significant differences were observed in 6-month mortality (6.03% vs. 7.67%, P = 0.380), 1-year mortality (9.32% vs. 11.51%, P = 0.330), ICU-acquired weakness (26.58% vs. 29.59%, P = 0.270), ICU-acquired infection (19.45% vs. 19.73%, P = 0.930), or adverse events (2.19% vs. 3.84%, P = 0.190). CONCLUSION: The NFPS significantly reduced the incidence of delirium and was associated with shorter durations of mechanical ventilation, ICU-LOS, HLOS, lower hospitalization costs, without increasing the risks of ICU-AW, ICU-acquired infection, or adverse events. No significant differences were observed in long-term mortality between the two groups.
articles.ai_summary: This study evaluated a nurse-led family participatory support intervention in ICU patients. The intervention significantly reduced the incidence of delirium and was associated with shorter hospital and ICU stays, lower hospitalization costs, and shorter durations of mechanical ventilation.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings have significant implications for ICU clinical practice, as they suggest that a structured, nurse-led family participatory support intervention can improve patient outcomes and reduce costs without increasing risks.

articles.title: Carbocisteine or Hypertonic Saline for Acute Respiratory Failure.
articles.journal: The New England journal of medicine
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mucoactive agents are widely used in patients with acute respiratory failure despite limited evidence of their effectiveness or safety. METHODS: We conducted a multicenter, open-label, randomized trial with a 2-by-2 factorial design that involved critically ill, mechanically ventilated participants 16 years of age or older with acute respiratory failure and difficult-to-clear secretions. All participants received usual care along with carbocisteine (750 mg three times daily enterally), 6% or 7% nebulized hypertonic saline (HTS) (4 ml four times daily), both interventions, or usual care alone for up to 28 days. The primary outcome was duration of mechanical ventilation (from randomization to first successful unassisted breathing). The primary comparisons were between any carbocisteine and no carbocisteine and between any HTS and no HTS, with each comparison comprising two treatment groups. RESULTS: A total of 1956 participants underwent randomization: 486 were assigned to carbocisteine, 485 to HTS, 492 to both treatments, and 493 to usual care alone (472, 474, 479, and 478, respectively, were included in the primary analysis). No evidence of treatment interaction was found (hazard ratio, 1.01, 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.22; P = 0.91). The median duration of mechanical ventilation was 186.1 hours (95% CI, 168.3 to 196.6) with carbocisteine and 172.7 hours (95% CI, 165.2 to 190.4) with no carbocisteine (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.05; P = 0.34) and 184.5 hours (95% CI, 165.6 to 194.1) with HTS and 174.3 hours (95% CI, 166.9 to 192.7) with no HTS (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.91 to 1.10; P = 0.98). Clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding occurred significantly more often with carbocisteine than with no carbocisteine (13 of 965 [1.4%] vs. 2 of 966 [0.2%]; risk ratio, 6.51; 95% CI, 1.47 to 28.76; P = 0.01). Bronchoconstriction leading to bronchodilator use occurred significantly more often with HTS than with no HTS (23 of 967 [2.4%] vs. 4 of 964 [0.4%]; risk ratio, 5.73; 95% CI, 1.99 to 16.52; P = 0.001), as did hypoxemia during nebulization (40 of 967 [4.1%] vs. 3 of 964 [0.3%]; risk ratio, 13.29; 95% CI, 4.12 to 42.83; P<0.001). One serious adverse reaction was reported in the combination group. CONCLUSIONS: Among critically ill patients with acute respiratory failure, neither carbocisteine nor HTS significantly reduced the duration of mechanical ventilation, and each was associated with harm. (Funded by the NIHR Health Technology Assessment Programme and the Belfast Health and Social Care Trust Charitable Trust Fund; MARCH ISRCTN Registry number, ISRCTN17683568.).

articles.title: Restrictive vs Liberal Physical Restraint Strategies in Critically Ill Patients: The R2D2-ICU Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: The effect of wrist-strap physical restraints on outcomes in patients receiving mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit (ICU) remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effect of a low-use wrist-strap physical restraint strategy in critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Open-label randomized clinical trial conducted across 10 ICUs in France. Between January 5, 2021, and January 2, 2024, 405 adult patients who had initiated invasive mechanical ventilation within the previous 6 hours and were expected to require ventilation for at least 48 hours were enrolled. Follow-up was completed on May 17, 2024. Statistical analysis was conducted from June 1, 2025, to December 15, 2025. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomized to undergo either a restrictive, low-use physical restraint strategy (wrist straps avoided unless necessary because of severe agitation, defined as a Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale score of ≥3 [on a scale from -5 (unresponsive) to 4 (combative)]; n = 201) or a liberal, high-use strategy (wrist straps applied systematically and reassessed daily; n = 204). Discontinuation of restraints was allowed in patients who were awake or extubated without delirium (measured via the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was the number of days alive without coma or delirium during the first 14 days after randomization. Secondary outcomes included incidence of self-extubation and day-90 mortality. RESULTS: Among 396 patients with available primary outcome data, the median (IQR) age was 65 (56-73) years, 245 (62%) were male, and the median (IQR) Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score was 7 (4-10). The mean days alive without coma or delirium were 6.67 days (95% CI, 5.69-7.65) in the low-use strategy group and 6.30 days (95% CI, 5.35-7.24) in the high-use strategy group (adjusted mean difference, 0.37 days [95% CI, -0.71 to 1.46]; P = .51). Self-extubation occurred in 18 patients (9.2%) in the low-use strategy group and 17 (8.5%) in the high-use strategy group, and day-90 mortality was 37.2% and 41.0%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this randomized clinical trial, among adult patients receiving mechanical ventilation in the ICU, a low-use wrist-strap physical restraint strategy compared with a high-use strategy did not reduce days free of delirium or coma at 14 days. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04273360.

articles.title: Impact of early goal-directed mobilization on ICU-acquired weakness: a meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: ICU-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) significantly impairs muscle strength and physical function in critically ill patients. Early mobilization interventions have been increasingly adopted, yet the specific effects of a structured EGDM program on ICU-AW and functional outcomes have not been systematically quantified. This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of EGDM on ICU-AW, muscle strength, and functional outcomes. PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data, and Viper Information Products (VIP) databases were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) up to November 30, 2025. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2.0. RevMan 5.4 was used for meta-analysis. Subgroup analysis was prespecified by allocation concealment. Nine RCTs (907 patients) were included. EGDM reduced ICU-AW [RR = 0.57, 95%CI (0.33 ~ 0.97), p = 0.04 for the overall effect; I2 = 77%, p = 0.002 for heterogeneity], but sensitivity analysis of high-quality trials showed no significant effect [RR = 0.84, 95%CI (0.48 ~ 1.46), p = 0.54 for the overall effect]. EGDM improved muscle strength [MD = 4.94, 95%CI (3.39 ~ 6.50), I2 = 59%, p = 0.02 for heterogeneity], shortened the duration of mechanical ventilation [MD = -81.95 h, 95%CI (-115.45 ~ -48.46), p < 0.00001 for the overall effect; I2 = 85%, p < 0.00001 for heterogeneity], and reduced ICU stay[MD = -4.55 days, 95%CI (-6.22 ~ -2.89), p < 0.00001 for the overall effect; I2 = 74%, p = 0.0004 for heterogeneity], both with substantial heterogeneity. Although the primary Barthel Index analysis was not statistically significant, sensitivity analysis suggested improvement in patients with moderate baseline function [MD = 8.27, 95%CI (5.66 ~ 10.87), p < 0.00001 for the overall effect]. EGDM may improve muscle strength and physical function in ICU patients. The available evidence does not confirm a reduction in ICU-AW. The effects on ventilation duration and ICU stay varied substantially across studies, likely influenced by sedation protocols, weaning practices, and other context-specific factors. Further rigorous trials with detailed reporting of interventions and contextual factors are needed to guide precise clinical implementation. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261280603, CRD420261280603.

articles.title: Nurse Competencies, Patient Characteristics, and Pain Management Protocol Adherence in Intensive Care Units: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study Accounting for ICU Clustering.
articles.abstract: To examine the associations between nurse competencies (knowledge, self-efficacy, and attitude), patient characteristics, and pain management protocol adherence in adult intensive care units, while accounting for between-ICU clustering. Adherence to pain management protocols remains suboptimal despite available guidelines. Nurse competencies are essential for evidence-based practice, yet their translation into clinical performance may depend on contextual factors. ICU-level organizational context has been described in recent reviews, but empirical examination of these relationships remains limited. This multicenter cross-sectional study included 525 ICU nurses from seven hospitals in Tehran, Iran (July-October 2025). One index patient was assessed for each nurse. ICU-level organizational characteristics were assessed through unit observation and head nurse interviews. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for protocol adherence was computed from an empty mixed model. Multivariable linear regression with ICU entered as a fixed effect was used to identify individual-level factors associated with adherence. Organizational context was retained as a descriptive variable only. Protocol adherence was moderate (mean 8.5/12; 32.4% good adherence). The ICC for protocol adherence was 0.02 (95% CI: 0.001-0.15), indicating minimal clustering. In the multivariable model with ICU as a fixed effect (18 predictors), knowledge (β = 0.311), self-efficacy (β = 0.290), and attitude (β = 0.276) remained independently associated with adherence (all p < 0.001). Patient characteristics remained significantly associated: substance use history (β = -0.138, p = 0.016), inability to communicate (β = -0.148, p = 0.010), GCS < 9 (β = -0.160, p = 0.008), and mechanical ventilation (β = -0.121, p = 0.028). The full model explained 53.4% of the variance in adherence. Organizational support across the seven ICUs ranged from 1 to 5 (weighted mean 3.42 ± 1.15). Nurse competencies and patient characteristics are independently associated with pain management protocol adherence in this multicenter ICU sample. Between-ICU clustering was minimal (ICC = 0.02), suggesting that individual-level factors are the primary correlates of adherence in this sample. Given the small number of ICU clusters (n = 7), organizational findings are descriptive only and require confirmation in larger multilevel studies. Nurse managers may consider competency-based pain management education and regular audits with feedback. Given the small number of ICU clusters (n = 7), these recommendations are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multilevel studies.

articles.title: Effects of higher versus lower protein intake in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: The optimal protein dose for critically ill patients remains uncertain, and emerging evidence suggests that the effects of higher protein intake may differ across clinically relevant subgroups. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating protein delivery in critical illness adults (up to July 2026). Higher and lower protein groups were defined according to each trial's original allocation. Primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included mechanical ventilation (MV) duration, Intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay (LOS), muscle outcomes, health-related quality of life (HRQoL), biochemical outcomes, and adverse events. Results were reported as risk ratios (RRs) or mean difference (MD) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) was performed to control for random error, and the certainty of evidence was rated using the GRADE framework. Thirty three RCTs involving 11,622 participants were included. No significant differences were observed between higher and lower protein groups for all-cause mortality (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.08), MV duration (MD -0.48, 95% CI -1.08 to 0.13), or ICU LOS (MD -0.18, 95% CI -0.86 to 0.51), with TSA confirming these null findings. Some muscle metrics favored the higher protein group; however, there was a trend towards poorer HRQoL (SMD -0.12, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.00). The higher protein group showed improved nitrogen balance (MD 5.58, 95% CI 2.89 to 8.27) and higher serum albumin levels (SMD 0.18, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.29), but increased urea (MD 2.06, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.64) and blood urea nitrogen concentrations (MD 2.94, 95% CI 1.32 to 4.56). Sensitivity analyses restricted to 27 isocaloric-design trials yielded consistent results. Subgroup analyses revealed that higher protein intake was linked to increased mortality in patients with acute kidney injury (RR 1.46, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.87); however, higher protein intake combined with rehabilitation interventions was associated with reduced mortality (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.93), shorter MV duration (MD -1.45, 95% CI -2.61 to -0.29), and beneficial muscle effects. Higher protein intake was not associated with better clinical outcomes. While it may increase mortality in patients with AKI, combining it with physical rehabilitation yields survival and clinical benefits, warranting confirmation in future factorial RCTs. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251109618, identifier [CRD420251109618].

articles.title: Stress hyperglycemia ratio and short-term mortality in critically ill patients with respiratory diseases: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: To systematically evaluate the association between the HbA1c-adjusted stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) and short-term mortality in patients with severe respiratory diseases and characterize its linear and nonlinear dose-response relationships. PubMed, Embase, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang, VIP, and the Chinese Biomedical Literature Database were searched for observational studies evaluating SHR and short-term mortality, including in-hospital, intensive care unit (ICU), 28-day, or 30-day mortality. Odds ratios (ORs) and hazard ratios (HRs) were pooled separately using random-effects models. Sensitivity analyses, linear dose-response analyses, restricted cubic spline analyses, and exploratory analyses of low and high SHR were performed. Eleven studies were included. Four studies contributed to the OR-based primary meta-analysis. Short-term mortality tended to be higher in the highest SHR category than in the study-specific reference category, but the association was not statistically significant (OR = 2.72, 95% CI: 0.74-9.93, P = 0.091; I 2 = 86.4%). Three studies contributed to the HR-based primary meta-analysis, which showed a significant association between higher SHR and increased short-term mortality risk (HR = 1.87, 95% CI: 1.71-2.05, P = 0.001; I 2 = 0%). In HR studies, each 0.1-unit increase in SHR was associated with an approximately 5% increase in short-term mortality risk (HR = 1.05, 95% CI: 1.02-1.08, P = 0.023). OR studies showed a similar direction of association but did not reach statistical significance. Restricted cubic spline analyses found no clear evidence of nonlinearity. Exploratory analyses suggested higher risks at both low and high SHR levels, but the estimates were imprecise. Current evidence suggests that higher SHR is associated with increased short-term mortality risk in patients with severe respiratory diseases. HR-based evidence was more consistent and supported a positive linear dose-response relationship. OR-based findings pointed in the same direction but showed substantial heterogeneity and did not reach statistical significance. The available evidence is insufficient to confirm a clear nonlinear pattern. Given the limited number of studies and wide confidence intervals, the apparent increase in risk at both low and high SHR levels should be interpreted as exploratory and does not yet support a stable U-shaped or J-shaped dose-response pattern. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261418259, PROSPERO CRD420261418259.

articles.title: Comprehensive Echocardiographic Assessment of Right Ventricular Afterload and Right Ventricular-Pulmonary Arterial Coupling in the Intensive Care Unit.
articles.abstract: Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is common in critical illness, yet RV afterload cannot be adequately characterized by pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) alone. Bedside echocardiography can estimate right atrial and pulmonary artery pressures, suggest increased pulmonary vascular resistance, and assess RV-pulmonary arterial coupling while simultaneously evaluating RV size, systolic function, septal interaction, and forward flow. Peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity combined with right atrial pressure estimates RV systolic pressure and, in the absence of outflow obstruction, approximates PASP. Pulmonary regurgitation velocities provide complementary estimates of mean and end-diastolic pulmonary artery pressure, whereas pulmonary artery acceleration time, RV outflow tract velocity-time integral, and systolic notching provide information regarding pulmonary vascular load and forward flow. A multiparametric assessment of RV systolic performance is essential because tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion, tissue Doppler systolic velocity, fractional area change, RV free-wall strain, and three-dimensional RV ejection fraction assess different aspects of contraction. The tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion/PASP ratio relates longitudinal systolic performance to pulmonary pressure but remains a surrogate of coupling, without a universal intensive care threshold. These measurements depend on image quality, loading conditions, and ventilatory support and may differ substantially from invasive hemodynamics in individual patients. Their greatest value lies in integrated physiologic assessment and serial reassessment after treatment. Echocardiography complements right heart catheterization, which remains necessary when precise hemodynamic classification or measurement of pulmonary artery wedge pressure, cardiac output, or pulmonary vascular resistance will change management.

articles.title: Long-Term Impact of Timing on Spinal Implantation for Lumbar Fractures in Polytrauma Patients: A Systematic Review.
articles.journal: Journal of long-term effects of medical implants
articles.abstract: The timing of osteosynthesis in polytrauma patients with lumbar spine fractures may influence key clinical outcomes, including hospital length of stay (HLOS), ICU length of stay (ICULOS), and mechanical ventilation duration (VENT DAYS). This systematic review aimed to evaluate how surgical timing affects these outcomes. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, and CENTRAL was completed in February 2025. Inclusion criteria involved studies on adult polytrauma patients (> 18 years) with lumbar spine fractures from blunt trauma, requiring surgical fixation, comparing early ( 72 h) surgery. Studies had to report Injury Severity Scores (ISS), outcomes of interest (HLOS, ICULOS, and VENT DAYS), include statistical comparisons between groups, and meet a minimum of "moderate" risk of bias based on the ROBINS-I tool. Out of 588 studies initially identified, three fulfilled the inclusion criteria, involving 1,111 patients-759 underwent early fixation and 352 late. The weighted average age was 39.1 years in the early group and 41.2 years in the late group. The weighted average ISS was 27.3 (early) and 29.2 (late). The weighted average VENT DAYS was 4.9 in the early group and 7.8 in the late group. The weighted average ICULOS was 10.9 d (early) and 13.7 d (late). The weighted average HLOS was 37.9 d (early) and 36.8 d (late). The impact of osteosynthesis on VENT DAYS and ICULOS remains uncertain, while HLOS shows no clinically relevant difference. ISS significantly influences outcomes.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of early mobilization in patients with ARDS: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the effect of early mobilization in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Computerized searches were conducted in PubMed, EMbase, The Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang Data, CBM, and VIP databases for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on early mobilization in ARDS patients. The retrieval period was from the establishment of each database to September 30, 2025. Two reviewers independently assessed the quality of included literature and extracted data in accordance with Cochrane systematic review methodology. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.4.1 software for eligible studies. A total of 7 RCTs were included, consisting of 4 English and 3 Chinese articles. Meta-analysis showed that compared with conventional treatment, early mobilization significantly reduced the incidence of intensive care unit-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) [OR = 0.35, 95% CI (0.19,0.64), P = 0.0006] and delirium [OR = 0.51, 95% CI (0.28,0.91), P = 0.02], shortened the duration of mechanical ventilation [MD = -2.40,95% CI (-2.96,-1.84), P < 0.00001], length of ICU stay [MD = -3.36, 95% CI (-4.21,-2.52), P < 0.00001] and total hospital stay [MD = -2.74,95% CI (-3.49,-1.98), P < 0.00001]. Meanwhile, it improved patients'functional independence score (Barthel Index) [MD = 17.27, 95% CI (11.18, 23.35), P < 0.00001] and decreased the incidence of complications [OR = 0.39, 95% CI (0.17, 0.86), P = 0.02]. All pooled effects were statistically significant. Early mobilization yields significant clinical benefits for ARDS patients, improving short-term clinical outcomes and functional recovery. It is worthy of clinical promotion and application. However, multicenter, large-sample, and methodologically standardized RCTs are still needed to further verify its long-term effects and optimal implementation protocols.

articles.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the timing of rehabilitation training intervention for recipients of extracorporeal membrane oxygenators.
articles.abstract: To systematically evaluate the effects of early versus delayed rehabilitation training interventions (RTI) on clinical outcomes in patients receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled studies, and observational cohort studies comparing early and delayed RTI in patients receiving ECMO. We searched databases including Embase, PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, China Science and Technology Journal Database, and China Biology Medicine disc from inception to 1 April 2025. Study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers. Outcomes included complications, intensive care unit (ICU) and hospital length of stay (LOS), duration of mechanical ventilation, ECMO duration, and in-hospital mortality. Twelve studies (five RCTs, four non-RCTs, and three cohort studies) were included. Compared with delayed RTI, early RTI significantly reduced the risk of complications [risk ratio (RR) = 0.43, 95% CI: 0.26-0.69, P < 0.001], shortened ICU LOS [mean difference (MD) = -1.12 days, 95% CI: -1.30 to -0.94, P < 0.001], and reduced hospital LOS (MD = -4.69 days, 95% CI: -8.11 to -1.27, P = 0.007). No significant differences were found in mechanical ventilation duration (MD = 0.14 days, P = 0.914), ECMO duration (MD = -1.77 days, P = 0.136), or in-hospital mortality (RR = 0.72, P = 0.097). Sensitivity analysis excluding one study demonstrated a greater reduction in hospital LOS significant (MD = -5.82 days, 95% CI: -9.34 to -2.30, P = 0.001), while other outcomes remained unchanged. Early RTI is associated with reduced complications and improved recovery outcomes (ICU/hospital stay) in ECMO patients compared with delayed RTI. However, due to the limited number and moderate quality of included studies, these findings should be interpreted with caution. High-quality RCTs are needed to confirm these results. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?ID=CRD420251025533, PROSPERO CRD420251025533.

articles.title: Associated factors for stress ulcers and gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with sepsis or septic shock: A systematic review.
articles.abstract: Sepsis continues to be a major contributor to death among critically ill individuals and places a heavy strain on healthcare resources. In addition to causing systemic inflammation and affecting hemodynamics, sepsis has a significant effect on the gastrointestinal system, leading to complications like stress ulcers and notable gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB), which worsen patient outcomes. While stress ulcer prophylaxis (SUP) has traditionally been included in sepsis treatment protocols, the concept of applying it universally is being increasingly scrutinized due to the absence of definitive mortality advantages and the risk of adverse effects, such as hospital-acquired pneumonia. Nevertheless, there is a notable gap in synthesized research that specifically addresses the independent risk factors for stress ulcers in sepsis patients. We carried out a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA standards, exploring eight databases (CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, Sinomed, PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library) from their inception until September 1, 2026. We included observational analytical studies (either cohort or case-control) that examined factors linked to stress ulcers or significant gastrointestinal bleeding in adult patients with sepsis. Two researchers independently handled the selection of studies, extraction of data, and evaluation of quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Due to the limited number of studies for each association between associated factors and outcomes, a narrative synthesis was utilized. A total of six studies encompassing 131,568 individuals suffering from sepsis or septic shock were analyzed. The incidence rates of stress ulcers or gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB) varied between 2.0% and 32.3%. The identified associated factors were divided into three categories: patient-related (older age, history of GIB, cirrhosis, HIV, cancer/immunosuppression), disease-related (coagulopathy, kidney impairment, high BUN levels, severity of illness scores, source of infection), and treatment-related (mechanical ventilation, use of anticoagulants, corticosteroid therapy, duration of ICU stay). Specifically for stress ulcer, factors such as respiratory failure, high BUN levels, shock, and increased HMGB1/TLR2/TLR4 levels were found to be independently linked to a higher odds. In summary, the likelihood of developing stress ulcers and gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with sepsis is shaped by a variety of factors related to the patient, their illness, and the treatments they receive. Key indicators that consistently emerge include issues with blood coagulation, the presence of shock, the need for mechanical ventilation, liver and kidney dysfunction, the severity of the disease, and any previous occurrences of gastrointestinal bleeding. These results advocate for tailored strategies for stress ulcer prophylaxis based on individual risk rather than a one-size-fits-all approach, offering crucial insights for precise clinical decision-making. Additional high-quality research is essential to confirm and enhance the understanding of these associated factors. PROSPERO (CRD420251242849).

articles.title: Impact of Proportional Assist Ventilation Versus Pressure Support Ventilation on Adult Liberation From Mechanical Ventilation: A Revised Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of RCTs.
articles.abstract: Pressure assist ventilation (PAV) is considered superior to pressure support ventilation (PSV). We performed an updated systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate comparative effectiveness in terms of weaning outcomes. We searched PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane for eligible randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published before October 2025 that directly compared clinical outcomes of PAV and PSV in mechanically ventilated adults. R program was used to calculate risk ratio (RR) and mean difference (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). After screening the titles, abstracts, and full texts, we included eight RCTs consisting of 1057 patients in our systematic review and meta-analysis. PAV was associated with a higher rate of weaning success as compared to PSV (RR: 1.09; 95% CI, 1.01-1.18; p = 0.03; I 2 = 23%). PAV was associated with a lesser duration of ventilation (MD: -1.06; 95% CI, -1.82 to -0.29, p = 0.006; I 2 = 0%) and intensive care unit (ICU) stay (MD: -1.49; 95% CI: -2.43 to -0.54, p = 0.002; I 2 = 25%) as compared to PSV. However, no statistically significant benefit was observed for PAV over PSV with regard to rate of reintubation (RR: 0.82; 95%, CI: 0.58-1.16, p = 0.21, I 2 = 0%) and mortality (RR: 0.89; 95% CI: 0.63-1.25 p = 0.4I 2 = 30%). PAV is superior to PSV for weaning, showing increased success and shorter duration of ventilation and ICU stays, though reintubation and mortality rates were similar.

articles.title: Protocol and Statistical Analysis Plan for the Pragmatic Trial Examining Oxygenation Prior to Intubation of Preoxygenation With Noninvasive Ventilation vs Oxygen Mask in Critically Ill Adults.
articles.abstract: Hypoxemia is a common and life-threatening complication during emergency tracheal intubation of critically ill adults. The administration of supplemental oxygen before the procedure (ie, preoxygenation) decreases the risk of hypoxemia during intubation. Does preoxygenation with noninvasive ventilation prevent hypoxemia during tracheal intubation of critically ill adults compared with preoxygenation with an oxygen mask? The Pragmatic Trial Examining Oxygenation Prior to Intubation (PREOXI) is a prospective, multicenter, nonmasked randomized comparative effectiveness trial being conducted in seven EDs and 17 ICUs across the United States. The trial compares preoxygenation with noninvasive ventilation vs oxygen mask among 1,300 critically ill adults undergoing emergency tracheal intubation. Eligible patients are randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either noninvasive ventilation or an oxygen mask before induction. The primary outcome is the incidence of hypoxemia, defined as a peripheral oxygen saturation of < 85% between induction and 2 min after intubation. The secondary outcome is the lowest oxygen saturation between induction and 2 min after intubation. Enrollment began on March 10, 2022, and is expected to conclude in 2023. The PREOXI investigation will provide important data on the comparative effectiveness of preoxygenation with noninvasive ventilation vs oxygen mask for the prevention of hypoxemia during emergency tracheal intubation. Specifying the protocol and statistical analysis plan before the conclusion of enrollment increases the rigor, reproducibility, and interpretability of the trial. ClinicalTrials.gov; No.: NCT05267652; URL: www.clinicaltrials.gov.

articles.title: Variation in capability, organisational structure, and treatment processes for critically ill adults with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury in Australia and New Zealand.
articles.journal: Critical care and resuscitation : journal of the Australasian Academy of Critical Care Medicine
articles.abstract: To characterise between-centre variation in capability, organisational structure, and treatment processes for adults with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury (msTBI) admitted to intensive care (ICU) in Australia and New Zealand (ANZ). Cross-sectional questionnaire supplemented by linked Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society CORE Critical Care Resources Registry descriptors. ANZ ICUs treating adults with msTBI, October-December 2025. Variation in organisational structure and capability, ICU treatment processes, neuroprognostication, withholding or withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy, and fulfilment of selected Australian TBI Quality Indicator Set elements. Heterogeneity was assessed using the index of qualitative variation (IQV) for nominal items and Leik's dispersion for ordinal items; values <0.3 were considered low, 0.3-0.7 moderate, and >0.7 substantial. Moderate or substantial heterogeneity was observed in 39 of 74 measured items (53%). Substantial heterogeneity included neurocritical care subspecialty expertise (IQV 1.00), perceived devastating traumatic brain injury management (IQV 0.99), cerebrospinal fluid drainage timing (IQV 0.93), withholding or withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy decision-making processes (IQV 0.86), arterial transducer zero level for cerebral perfusion pressure calculation (IQV 0.82), haemoglobin targets (Leik's dispersion 0.81), and post-ICU follow-up interval (IQV 0.81). Low heterogeneity in several advanced neuromonitoring and neuroprognostication modalities reflected consistent non-use or unavailability. Fulfilment of the six measured Australian TBI Quality Indicator Set indicators ranged from 2/6 to 5/6 across centres. Among ANZ ICUs providing care for adults with msTBI, moderate or substantial variation was evident in over half of measured organisational and clinical aspects of care. These findings identify targets for research and quality improvement and highlight centre variation as a potential modifier of patient outcomes.

articles.title: Resting-State Functional MRI and Clinical Outcomes After Acute Disorders of Consciousness: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Accurate assessment and prognostication of patients with acute disorders of consciousness (DoC) after severe brain injury remain a substantial clinical challenge. Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) measures spontaneous, temporally correlated brain activity in the absence of external stimulation and provides objective insight into the integrity of large-scale neural networks that support brain function. Emerging evidence suggests that assessing neural integrity using rs-fMRI may improve outcome prediction in patients with acute DoC. This review summarizes the current evidence of rs-fMRI as an assessment tool during the acute phase of severe brain injury. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, we conducted a systematic literature search using MEDLINE and Embase databases from January 2006 to March 2026. Eligible studies included peer-reviewed empirical investigations of adult patients with acute DoC (<28 days postinjury) that examined associations between rs-fMRI measures and clinical outcomes. The systematic review protocol was registered in the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251085923). Of 396 studies screened, 30 met eligibility criteria. Across these studies, a total of 800 patients (mean age = 48, 69% male) were scanned at a weighted average of 9.31 days after intensive care unit admission. Ten studies included patients exclusively with traumatic brain injury, 8 with cardiac arrest, 2 with encephalopathy, and 10 included mixed etiologies. The most frequently assessed resting-state networks were the default mode (n = 20) and executive control networks (n = 11), followed by visual (n = 6), salience (n = 6), sensorimotor (n = 6), and auditory (n = 5) networks. Across studies, significant associations between rs-fMRI measures and outcome were consistently reported, despite heterogeneity in methodology. The most commonly reported patient outcomes were functional or neurologic status, assessed at hospital discharge or between 3 and 12 months postinjury. Current evidence consistently demonstrates that rs-fMRI acquired during the acute phase of brain injury is associated with neurologic and functional outcomes in patients with DoC. In addition, rs-fMRI may help identify patients more likely to recover consciousness and achieve favorable functional outcomes by characterizing the integrity of large-scale brain networks. However, substantial heterogeneity and small sample sizes limit comparability across studies. Standardized acquisition and analysis frameworks, along with larger prospective studies, are needed to validate the clinical utility of rs-fMRI and support translation into an assessment tool after brain injury.

articles.title: Effect of circadian-oriented goal-directed sedation on sleep quality and clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients.
articles.journal: Journal of clinical neuroscience : official journal of the Neurosurgical Society of Australasia
articles.abstract: Sleep disruption and circadian rhythm disturbances are common in mechanically ventilated intensive care unit (ICU) patients and are associated with delirium, prolonged ventilation, and poor clinical outcomes. Conventional sedation strategies may further impair sleep architecture and circadian regulation. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effects of circadian-oriented, goal-directed sedation on sleep quality and clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. This study enrolled 65 mechanically ventilated patients admitted to ICU at Suzhou Ninth People's Hospital between March 2024 and December 2024. Using convenience sampling, 33 patients admitted between March and July 2024 were allocated to the control group and received routine sedation and nursing care, while 32 patients admitted between August and December 2024 were formed the intervention group and received sedation management individualized according to circadian sleep-wake patterns. Sleep quality was assessed on days 1, 3, 5, and 7 after intervention using the Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire (RCSQ) and a portable sleep monitor. Delirium was evaluated by Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU). Sedative dosage, duration of mechanical ventilation, length of ICU and hospital stay, , clinical improvement rate, complications, and hospitalization costs were compared between groups. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the two groups. Sleep quality improved over time in both groups; however, Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire scores were significantly higher in the intervention group at all assessment points (p < 0.05). Patients receiving circadian-oriented sedation experienced shorter durations of mechanical ventilation, reduced ICU and total hospital stays, higher rates of clinical improvement, and lower hospitalization costs compared with the control group (p < 0.05). The incidence of complications, including delirium, was also significantly lower in the intervention group. Sedation management aligned with circadian sleep-wake patterns significantly improves sleep quality, reduces sedative requirements, lowers delirium incidence, and shortens mechanical ventilation duration, demonstrating a favorable safety profile in mechanically ventilated patients.

articles.title: Antidepressant use in invasively ventilated patients in intensive care: Frequency of withholding and association with delirium-An observational study.
articles.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
articles.abstract: The aim of this study was to explore antidepressant use in invasively ventilated patients in intensive care who were able to be given medicines enterally (i.e. via feeding tube). As a secondary observation, we examined whether withholding an antidepressant was associated with positive Confusion Assessment Method - Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) scores. A 12-month (1st Jan 2020 to 31st Dec 2020) retrospective cohort study was conducted in the ICU of a 484-bed tertiary referral hospital. Invasively ventilated patients capable of receiving enteral medicines were included. Of invasively ventilated ICU patients prescribed antidepressants prior to admission, 93% had their antidepressants withheld (for part, or all) of their ICU stay and antidepressant withholding was associated with higher odds of a positive CAM-ICU score. Invasively ventilated patients who had an antidepressant withheld were over five times more likely to have had a positive CAM-ICU score during their ICU stay. Availability of a buccal dosage form or a dosage form that could be given enterally did not impact prescribing or administration of pre-existing antidepressants or facilitate swapping to an alternative antidepressant. Antidepressant withholding is frequent in invasively ventilated patients in intensive care who were able to be given medicines enterally. An association was identified between antidepressant withholding and positive CAM-ICU scores, warranting further investigation. Given the observed association between antidepressant withholding and positive CAM-ICU scores, review of antidepressants management may be reasonable when managing invasively ventilated patients with positive CAM-ICU scores.

articles.title: Monitoring the incidence of hypotension and hypoxemia as systemic secondary insults in patients with catastrophic brain injury evolving to brain death. A prospective observational pilot study.
articles.abstract: Maintenance of systemic homeostasis and prevention of secondary injury are a cornerstone of treatment in neurocritical care to prevent organ dysfunction and adverse clinical outcome. This is a pilot descriptive and hypothesis generating study aiming to measure and characterize the incidence of systemic hypotension and hypoxemia occurring during the intensive care unit (ICU) stay in patients with catastrophic brain injury potentially evolving to brain death. Adult patients admitted to ICU with catastrophic brain injury and Glasgow coma scale ≤5 have been enrolled. Arterial blood pressure and SpO2 were collected minute by minute from a central station connected to patients' bedside monitors. We report on 24 patients recruited prospectively from the University Hospital of Messina, Italy as a part of a larger ongoing multi-centre study. Patient monitoring data ranged from 8-3000 hours (0.3-125 days). Admission diagnoses were intracerebral haemorrhage (N= 13), TBI (N=4), SAH (N=3), ischaemic stroke (N=3) and hypoxic encephalopathy (N=1). The proportion of valid monitoring time spent with secondary insults and the pressure time index (PTI) are presented and discussed. Day 3 and 4 demonstrated the largest number of secondary insults which were mainly hypotension. Patients who progressed to brain death (n = 9) or who died in ICU from cardiac complications (n = 7) exhibited a more severe and sustained hypotensive burden compared with patients alive at discharge (n = 8). This descriptive study proved useful for identifying an optimal window for tracking insults as well as piloting several key summary measures and visualisations which will be utilized in a larger multi-centre study. In patients with catastrophic brain injury, the incidence of hypotension remains the highest among systemic secondary insults in patients progressing to brain death and cardiac death.

articles.title: The overall effects of virtual reality interventions on ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients frequently experience psychological distress, pain, sleep disruption, and motor impairments. Virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising nonpharmacological adjunct to improve these outcomes, yet existing evidence remains fragmented and inconsistent. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized recent clinical trials to evaluate the effectiveness of VR on mental health, pain, sleep, functional outcomes, and delirium in adult ICU patients. This review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (2020) guidance and was registered in International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42023482529). Eight databases were searched for randomized controlled trials published between January 2000 and September 2025. Eligible studies included adult ICU patients receiving immersive or non-immersive VR interventions. Primary outcomes were anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD); secondary outcomes included pain, sleep quality, lower-limb function, and bedside balance. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB tool, and certainty of evidence was graded using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation. Twenty randomized controlled trials were identified, involving a total of 1551 patients. This meta-analysis showed that VR intervention helped improve anxiety (standardized mean difference [SMD] = -0.67, 95% confidence interval [CI: -1.00 to -0.35], P < .0001), depression (SMD = -0.46, 95% CI [-0.72 to -0.21], P = .0004), PTSD [mean difference = -5.48, 95% CI (-9.36 to -1.59), P = .006], lower-limb function score [mean difference = 2.83, 95% CI (1.99 to 3.67), P < .001] and sleep quality (SMD = 0.70, 95% CI [0.47 to 0.92], P < .0001), but had no significant effect on pain score (SMD = -0.57, 95% CI [-1.49 to 0.36], P = .23) and bedside balance score (SMD = 0.61, 95% CI [-0.44 to 1.66], P = .25). Most studies were assessed as having varying degrees of risk of bias. All evidence was rated from very low to moderate. VR interventions may confer meaningful benefits for anxiety, depression, PTSD, and sleep quality in adult ICU patients, and may improve lower-limb function in selected populations. However, evidence for analgesic effects and bedside balance remains inconclusive. Standardized VR protocols, objective outcome assessment, and adequately powered multicenter trials are needed to clarify the clinical value of VR in ICU care.

articles.title: Acute Pain Management in the Intensive Care Unit.
articles.abstract: This review summarizes current approaches to pain assessment and pharmacologic therapy in the intensive care unit (ICU) and evaluates the expanding role of regional anesthesia (RA). Contemporary ICU analgesia emphasizes systematic pain assessment and multimodal therapy while avoiding unnecessary deep sedation. RA provides targeted, opioid-sparing analgesia for localized pain but is limited by coagulopathy, infection, altered anatomy, and practical considerations. Fascial-plane blocks may provide useful alternatives in selected patients. Thoracic epidural and paravertebral techniques remain options for selected patients but may cause hypotension and clinically significant bleeding. Ultrasound-guided techniques, including erector spinae, serratus anterior, parasternal, rectus sheath, and transversus abdominis plane blocks, expand analgesic options. Continuous catheter techniques may extend analgesia when prolonged pain is anticipated. However, evidence in heterogeneous ICU populations remains limited, and much of the current evidence is derived from perioperative or trauma populations rather than general medical ICU cohorts. Further ICU-specific comparative trials are needed to define patient selection and clinically meaningful outcomes.

articles.title: Dexmedetomidine Suspected Fever and Clinical Escalation: A Pilot Study Evaluating the Impact in the Intensive Care Unit.
articles.journal: The Journal of pharmacy technology : jPT : official publication of the Association of Pharmacy Technicians
articles.abstract: Dexmedetomidine, an alpha-2 agonist commonly used as a sedative agent in mechanically ventilated patients, has been associated with drug-induced fever. Concern for fever may prompt diagnostic evaluation and empiric antimicrobial therapy, potentially leading to unnecessary health care utilization. This pilot study aimed to evaluate if dexmedetomidine use in mechanically ventilated medical intensive care unit (ICU) patients was associated with increased escalation of care compared with alternate sedative agents. This single-center, retrospective, matched cohort study included patients 18 years or older who were admitted to the medical ICU and required a sedative agent to facilitate mechanical ventilation. Patients receiving dexmedetomidine were matched 1:1 with patients receiving alternate sedative agents. The primary outcome was the composite outcome of initiation of diagnostic evaluation and/or antimicrobial escalation (IDEA). A total of 150 patients were included (75 per group). Most patients were male (68%), and 45% had a primary diagnosis of respiratory failure. The primary outcome, IDEA, occurred in 53 patients (71%) receiving dexmedetomidine and 51 patients (68%) receiving alternate sedatives (P = .723). Fever occurred in 24 patients (32%) receiving dexmedetomidine compared with 17 patients (23%) receiving alternate sedatives. Median ICU length of stay was longer in the dexmedetomidine group (5 [interquartile range, IQR 1-8] vs 4 [IQR 1-5] days; [P = .002]). In-hospital mortality occurred in 14 patients (19%) receiving dexmedetomidine and 24 patients (32%) receiving alternate sedative (P = .060). There was no statistically significant difference between escalation of care in the use of dexmedetomidine versus other sedatives in ICU patients.

articles.title: Inhaled sedation versus intravenous sedation in critically ill patients (IS-CRITIC): protocol for a multicentre, randomised, controlled clinical trial in Spain.
