articles.abstract: Intravenous sedatives are widely used in the intensive care unit (ICU) and are part of routine clinical practice. However, these agents and their active metabolites may be associated with adverse events. Volatile anaesthetics have recently emerged as an attractive alternative for ICU sedation, and isoflurane has been approved by regulatory agencies in several European countries for use in critically ill patients. Although isoflurane has been shown to be non-inferior to propofol-based sedation during short-term sedation periods, it remains unclear whether inhaled sedation with isoflurane offers advantages over intravenous sedation in patients requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation and, consequently, prolonged sedation. This is a phase IV, low-intervention, open-label, multicentre randomised clinical trial conducted on an intention-to-treat basis. A total of 620 patients will be randomised in a 1:1 ratio to receive either inhaled sedation with isoflurane administered using the Sedaconda ACD-S device or intravenous sedation with propofol. Adult patients expected to require more than 48 hours of mechanical ventilation will be included. The primary outcome is ventilator-free days through day 28 post-randomisation. The key secondary outcome is ICU-free days through day 28 post-randomisation. Patient recruitment began in December 2025 and is expected to conclude in December 2027. Final analysis is planned for 2028. The study protocol was approved by the ethics committee of Hospital Universitario La Paz, Madrid, Spain (#6844) and the European Medicines Agency on 13 March 2025. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations. NCT07000526. This clinical trial is registered in the European Union (EU) Clinical Trials Information System (CTIS), under the EU Clinical Trials Regulation (Regulation 536/2014). CTIS ID: (2024–5 18 521-14-00).

articles.title: Virtual Reality for Delirium Prevention in Intensive Care Unit Nurses and Mechanically Ventilated Patients: Descriptive Qualitative Study.
articles.abstract: Patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) who are on mechanical ventilation are at high risk of developing delirium. Virtual reality (VR) technology, as an emerging intervention method, shows promising application prospects in delirium prevention, but its specific experience in clinical practice still requires in-depth exploration. This study aims to explore the real experiences of ICU nurses and mechanically ventilated patients in participating in VR delirium prevention, with the aim of providing practical evidence for the optimization and application of this technology in clinical practice. A descriptive qualitative research design was adopted. From March to June 2025, using purposive sampling, participants were selected from the internal medicine, surgery, central, and respiratory ICU departments of a tertiary hospital in Zhengzhou. A total of 73 patients on mechanical ventilation were screened. Among them, 49 were excluded due to not meeting the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) or Barthel Index (BI) score criteria, 5 had delirium at the time of enrollment, 1 was excluded due to visual impairment, and 2 voluntarily withdrew during the study. Finally, 16 patients on mechanical ventilation and 16 nurses were included for semistructured interviews. Data analysis was conducted using the inductive content analysis method. Through the analysis of the interview data, a total of 3 main themes and 14 subthemes were extracted. In terms of perceived benefits, patients experienced an immersive environment and a sense of empowerment driven by tasks, while nurses felt the convenience of resource integration, the intimacy of the nurse-patient relationship, and a sense of professional significance. In terms of perceived challenges, patients faced difficulties with the interaction interface and physical and mental obstacles, while nurses encountered difficulties in communication assessment and responsibility definition. In terms of perceived needs, patients expected personalized content design and continuity of nursing services, while nurses suggested differentiated content adjustment, comprehensive functional integration, and standardized safety management. The participants expressed a positive attitude towards the prevention of delirium based on VR and reported various perceived benefits, challenges, and needs. Future research should prioritize content personalization, functional integration, and safety management. Meanwhile, it is necessary to recognize the limitations of this technology in specific target populations. For those who do not meet the inclusion criteria, adaptive alternative intervention measures should be developed to promote the precise and sustainable application of VR-based delirium prevention.

articles.title: Retrospective evaluation of predictors and clinical impact of postoperative delirium in liver transplant recipients.
articles.abstract: This study aimed to analyze the epidemiology, predictors, and clinical outcomes of postoperative delirium (POD) in liver transplant (LT) recipients. Clinical data from 427 LT recipients from the Third Xiangya Hospital were retrospectively reviewed. The epidemiology (incidence, onset, and duration), predictors, and associated clinical outcomes of POD were analyzed using standardized delirium assessment tools and multivariate regression. POD occurred in 19.0% of recipients, with a median onset at 26.0 hours posttransplant. Multivariate analysis identified 4 independent pre and postoperative predictors, including a higher model for end-stage liver disease score and hepatic encephalopathy within 24 hours before LT, infection within 2 months prior to LT, and abnormal sodium within 1 hour after LT (all P < .05). In a sensitivity analysis treating early death or persistent coma as a composite outcome with POD (n = 436), the same 4 independent predictors were identified, with consistent effect estimates. Regarding clinical outcomes, POD was significantly associated with prolonged intensive care unit stays, extended mechanical ventilation requirements, and increased use of renal replacement therapy (all P < .01). Although recipients with POD showed higher 1- and 6-month all-cause mortality in unadjusted analyses, POD was not an independent predictor of mortality after adjustment for confounding factors. POD occurs frequently and early after LT, with identifiable pre and postoperative risk factors. While POD markedly increases perioperative morbidity and resource utilization, it does not independently predict short-term all-cause mortality in this cohort.

articles.title: Differences in donation after circulatory determination of death (DCD) liver donor management. An international survey initiated by the international liver transplantation society (ILTS), society for the advancement of transplant anesthesia (SATA), and liver intensive care group of europe (LICAGE).
articles.journal: Liver transplantation : official publication of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and the International Liver Transplantation Society
articles.abstract: We conducted a survey to evaluate variability in determination of death and management of Donation after Circulatory Determination of Death (DCD) liver donors across different countries. 153 centers from 17 countries were included (48.4% US, 51.6% non-US). Most reported using onset of hemodynamic instability, rather than withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy (WLST), as the beginning of the waiting time for decision making related to organ acceptance (76.1% US vs. 47.1% non-US). Actual and maximum acceptable waiting times were comparable between groups (43.7 vs. 50.2 and 50.8 vs. 60.3 min, respectively), frequently exceeding limits defined by national policies. Onset of hemodynamic instability was most commonly defined using systolic blood pressure (SBP) alone (51.4% US vs. 31.6% non-US) or a combination of SBP and oxygen saturation (SpO2) (41.6% US vs. 56.6% non-US). Less commonly, centers used SpO2 (4.2% vs. 3.9%) or arrythmia alone (1.4% US vs. 0.0% non-US). Thresholds for SBP and SpO2 were similar between US and non-US centers (SBP 80 mmHg; and 80% for both). Sedation and analgesia for donor comfort was used less frequently in US centers compared to non-US centers (27.8% vs. 48.1%, p=0.02). Decision-making regarding waiting time was more commonly performed by a multidisciplinary team outside the US (26.1% vs. 52.0%). Over half of US and non-US centers reported using machine perfusion in over 50% of DCD grafts (64.9% vs. 51.9%). When used, normothermic regional perfusion cannulation was more commonly initiated after declaration of death (71.6% US vs. 62.0% non-US). These findings demonstrate substantial variability in DCD donor management. Standardization of definitions and practices, particularly with regard to exclusion of hemodynamic stability period from Warm Ischemic Time (WIT), may improve consistency in decision-making related to organ acceptance.

articles.title: Retrospective review of traumatic brain injury: is skull X-ray still clinically relevant?
articles.abstract: Head computed tomography (CT) is the gold standard imaging modality for the evaluation of head injury. Skull radiography is no longer recommended in current guidelines due to its limited diagnostic value. Despite this, skull X-ray continues to be used in clinical practice. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of skull X-ray and its association with intracranial injury. We conducted a retrospective study of 12,392 patient encounters with head injury at a single centre between 2018 and 2023. We analysed imaging utilization and findings. Diagnostic performance of skull X-ray was assessed in 759 cases where both X-ray and CT were performed. CT served as the reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and associations with intracranial haemorrhage were calculated. Most X-rays were without a fracture (97.0 %). Skull X-ray demonstrated low sensitivity (43.6 %) and high specificity (91.4 %) for detecting skull fractures. Intracranial haemorrhage was present in 13.3 % of cases and occurred in 11.2 % of patients without a fracture on X-ray. Notably, 14.2 % of all CT scans (441 of 3,103) showed haemorrhage without fracture. Fracture on X-ray was associated with increased risk of intracranial haemorrhage (Odds Ratio [OR] 2.85, 95 % Confidence Interval [CI] 1.74-4.68). Clinically significant traumatic brain injury (csTBI) occurred in 17 of 759 encounters (2.2 %), with 12 admissions to intensive care unit, 10 neurosurgical interventions and 8 deaths after head injury. However, the association was not statistically significant (OR 2.64, 95 % CI 0.91-7.67, p = 0.075). Skull radiography has limited diagnostic value, fails to detect intracranial injury and may provide false reassurance in a clinical setting. CT remains the preferred imaging modality, and routine use of skull X-ray should be reconsidered.

articles.title: Intracranial EEG for Detecting Epileptic Activity in Acute Brain Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) has been increasingly explored as part of multimodal neuromonitoring in acute brain injury, yet its diagnostic benefit compared with continuous surface EEG (suEEG) remains uncertain. We have performed a meta-analysis to quantify seizure and rhythmic and periodic pattern detection rates and concordance with suEEG. Secondary objectives were the assessment of correlations with brain injury, safety, and techniques. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched for studies reporting iEEG monitoring in adults with acute brain injury. Epileptic patterns were harmonized to the American Clinical Neurophysiology Society Standardized EEG Nomenclature for Critically Ill Patients (ACNS) 2021 terminology, classifying events as seizures/status epilepticus (SZ/SE) or rhythmic and periodic/ictal-interictal continuum patterns (RPP/IIC). Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa scale and custom bias domains. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted for (i) pooled proportions and (ii) pooled paired within-patient comparisons. Twelve cohorts (n = 864 participants) with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (n = 343), traumatic brain injury (n = 351), and mixed etiologies (n = 170) were included. Six studies provided paired iEEG-suEEG data (n = 273). Techniques were based on a strip or depth electrode. No severe adverse events were reported. Pooled iEEG versus suEEG incidence rates were respectively: 26% vs. 15% for SZ/SE, 47% vs. 34% for RPP/IIC, and 57% vs. 37% for clinically relevant epileptic activity. Pooled paired analysis demonstrated that iEEG additionally detected SZ/SE in 16.5% of patients [pooled McNemar odds ratio (OR) 3.46 (0.51-23.6); I2 = 63%; p = 0.158] and RPP/IIC in 26% [pooled OR 4.25 (0.19-96.1); I2 = 73%; p = 0.236], while suEEG was negative. Sensitivity analyses for high-risk studies or cohort overlap did not alter the results. Invasive EEG monitoring substantially increased the detection of seizures and RPP/IIC patterns compared with suEEG alone in patients with acute brain injury, serving as a promising monitoring adjunct.

articles.title: Association of Altered Anteriorization of Electroencephalographic Alpha Oscillation During Transition to Unconsciousness With Postoperative Delirium: A Prospective Observational Study.
articles.abstract: During sevoflurane-induced anesthesia, electroencephalography analysis demonstrates alpha oscillations shifting from the occipital to the frontal regions, with further characteristic changes during maintenance and emergence. We aimed to exploratorily investigate whether alterations in alpha anteriorization and functional network efficiency are associated with postoperative delirium. This prospective, exploratory observational study enrolled 100 patients from a single tertiary university hospital. Patients were classified into nondelirium (n = 81) and delirium (n = 19) groups based on delirium assessments. After excluding 17 patients due to artifacts on electroencephalography, 19-channel electroencephalography data were collected from 83 elderly patients under sevoflurane-induced anesthesia. Artifact-free epochs were extracted during the induction, maintenance, emergence, and postanesthesia care unit phases. Spectral, topographical, and network analyses were conducted. Postoperative delirium was assessed using confusion assessment method for intensive care unit and a chart review. Significant group differences emerged just before the loss of responsiveness, with the nondelirium group exhibiting robust alpha power amplification across all brain regions (median [interquartile range {IQR}] in dB; frontal: 4.24 [1.86-6.57] vs -0.88 [-1.59-3.38], P = .007; parietal: 3.71 [0.51-5.55] vs -0.95 [-2.33-1.11], P = .046; occipital: 2.81 [0.49-5.71] vs -0.04 [-2.06-1.27], P = .048), whereas the delirium group showed minimal changes. During the maintenance phase, spectral analysis revealed higher alpha power in the nondelirium group across all 19 channels (frontal: 5.42 [2.90-8.16] vs 2.89 [-0.03-5.09], P = .007; 18 of 19 channels significant by false-discovery-rate (FDR)-corrected permutation test). Network analysis demonstrated longer averaged characteristic path lengths in the delirium group (mean ± standard deviation [SD], 4.49 ± 0.62 vs 3.57 ± 0.16, P = .026, FDR-corrected), consistently in the frontal, parietal, and occipital regions, suggesting reduced network efficiency. Delirium was associated with early disruption of alpha anteriorization during induction and globally reduced functional network efficiency during maintenance. Perioperative electroencephalogram (EEG) transition features may serve as early markers of delirium susceptibility.

articles.title: Pneumothorax rates following cardiac surgery with versus without continuous serratus anterior plane catheters: a secondary analysis of trial data with propensity score matching to a historic cohort.
articles.journal: Canadian journal of anaesthesia = Journal canadien d'anesthesie
articles.abstract: Moderate to severe pain is common after cardiac surgery, especially in the first two postoperative days. Inadequate pain control may prolong intensive care unit (ICU) stay, may increase cost, and contributes to chronic pain. Enhanced Recovery After Cardiac Surgery (ERACS) protocols prioritize multimodal analgesia, including regional anesthesia techniques. In a recent randomized trial with continuous serratus anterior plane (SAP) catheters, we found unexpectedly high pneumothorax rates. To address this, we aimed to design a propensity-score-matched comparison using patients from the same institution to control for institutional practice patterns, surgical techniques, and patient demographics that could confound comparisons with published literature rates from other centres. We conducted a secondary analysis of RCT data with propensity score matching to a historic cohort. We compared the pneumothorax rates in patients receiving continuous SAP catheters in our previous Cardiac-Serratus Anterior Plane (Cardiac-SAP) trial with those in a retrospective institutional database cohort of patients receiving standard care undergoing cardiac surgery via sternotomy. The two groups were propensity score matched in a 1:20 ratio based on age, sex, smoking status, surgery type, and pre-existing respiratory disease. We analyzed univariate comparisons using Fisher's exact test or the percentile bootstrapping method. We matched 50 patients from the Cardiac-SAP trial to 989 retrospective cohort patients. After matching, the SAP catheter group was associated with a significantly higher risk of pneumothorax (12% vs 3%; odds ratio, 5.3; 95% confidence interval, 2.1 to 13.6; P < 0.001). There were no significant differences for other outcomes, including ICU readmissions, length of ventilation, and length of ICU or hospital stay. Patients who developed a pneumothorax had longer ventilation time and longer hospital stays. Our data suggest that SAP catheter use as a part of a randomized trial for cardiac surgery was associated with a higher rate of pneumothorax in trial participants than in a historic cohort of a similar population, though causality is unclear. Differences in monitoring within the trial and the inherent risks in this population may have contributed.

articles.title: Clinical safety, tolerability, and efficacy of fospropofol disodium for sedation: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: Fospropofol disodium (fospropofol) is a water-soluble prodrug of propofol with a distinct pharmacological and tolerability profile. However, evidence regarding the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of fospropofol across broader sedation contexts and different comparators remains insufficiently synthesized. This systematic review summarized current research findings on fospropofol to clarify its clinical role and guide future research. This systematic review was registered prior to initiation (PROSPERO CRD42023477740). Comprehensive searches were performed in PubMed, Web of Science, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via Ovid, Embase via Ovid, ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to 26 August 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating fospropofol for sedation and reporting extractable efficacy or safety outcomes were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated according to the GRADE approach. Meta-analysis was performed for clinically comparable evidence groups, with other findings synthesized according to SWiM principles. This systematic review included 10 original studies, comprising six procedural-sedation trials and four trials for ICU sedation. Quantitative synthesis was conducted for two comparable evidence groups, whereas the remaining outcomes were synthesized narratively. In three endoscopic procedural-sedation trials, fospropofol 6.5 mg/kg achieved a higher sedation success than 2 mg/kg (RR 3.27, 95% CI 2.62-4.08). In mechanically ventilated ICU patients, hypotension risk did not clearly differ between fospropofol and propofol (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.67-1.28). Procedural studies showed a dose-dependent pattern in sedation efficacy, whereas ICU studies generally reported comparable target-sedation attainment between fospropofol and comparator sedatives. Paresthesia/pruritus was commonly reported, while rates of cardiorespiratory adverse events varied across settings and doses and showed no consistent comparative advantage for fospropofol. Evidence for injection pain and satisfaction was limited. Certainty of evidence ranged from high to very low, mainly because of risk of bias and imprecision. Fospropofol can provide effective sedation across procedural and ICU settings, but its efficacy and safety profiles vary according to dose, comparator, and clinical setting. Higher doses may improve procedural-sedation efficacy but may also increase adverse effects in some settings. Current evidence does not establish a consistent cardiorespiratory safety advantage for fospropofol over other sedatives, and further adequately powered randomized trials are needed to clarify its comparative safety and optimal clinical role.

articles.title: Music Therapy During Weaning From Invasive Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The study examined the effect of daily music therapy on weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the ICU, with a primary focus on weaning duration. Secondary agitation, sedation, and analgesia doses, pain, delirium, and perceived stress after 90 days were assessed. Additionally, total IMV and ICU stay durations and tracheostomy rates were studied. Physiologic parameters were assessed in the music therapy group (MG). The study also aimed to promote the humanization of critical care through a biopsychosocial and creative music therapy approach. DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups: control group receiving standard care during weaning and MG receiving music therapy additionally. SETTING AND PATIENTS: Adult critically ill patients (n = 100) admitted to a general ICU who received IMV for at least 48 hours. INTERVENTIONS: MG received daily, individualized music therapy sessions averaging 25 minutes, based on patient needs and musical preferences, which included music relaxation, music listening, and clinical improvisation. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: No significant difference in weaning duration was observed between groups (p = 0.97). Patients in the MG group showed significant improvements in agitation and sedation levels (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) on days 1 and 3 (p = 0.048, 0.005, and 0.024) and a lower percentage required propofol (p = 0.028). No significant difference in perceived pain (Visual Analog Pain Scale). The MG obtained lower Perceived Stress Scale-14 scores (p = 0.24). Additionally, MG significantly reduced tracheostomy rates (14%; p = 0.025). Median total IMV and ICU stay duration were shorter in the MG group, but not significantly (p = 0.206 and 0.203). Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygenation showed no significant difference before and after music therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Music therapy may serve as a nonpharmacological complementary adjunct during weaning by reducing agitation, sedation, and tracheostomy rate. It may potentially decrease perceived stress and IMV and ICU stay durations. Further research is warranted.

articles.title: Physiology-Guided Management of Acute Right Ventricular Failure and Pulmonary Hypertension in Critically Ill Patients: Hemodynamic Phenotypes, Ventilator Interactions, and Rescue Strategies.
articles.abstract: Patients with acute right heart failure or pulmonary hypertension require cautious resuscitation because the right ventricle is highly preload-sensitive and has a narrow therapeutic window; both hypovolemia and volume overload may worsen hemodynamics. Echocardiographic guidance can help optimize fluid administration. The management of right heart failure also includes increasing contractility and reducing systemic afterload with inodilators such as dobutamine and milrinone. In cases of high pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) contributing to right heart failure, the use of selective pulmonary dilators can decrease the right ventricular afterload, while largely avoiding the systemic hypotension associated with intravenous vasodilators. Hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis may increase PVR, while sedation, intubation, and positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) may reduce preload, precipitating hemodynamic collapse. When possible, noninvasive respiratory support may be cautiously used to optimize oxygenation and ventilation and avoid intubation. With either form of PPV, airway pressures should be minimized to reduce the risk of hemodynamic compromise. Additionally, preload should be carefully optimized; hypotension-inducing sedatives, such as propofol, should be minimized; vasopressors should be readily available. In ARDS complicated by acute cor pulmonale, a right ventricular-protective ventilation strategy should be considered alongside conventional lung-protective ventilation. This approach emphasizes limiting excessive plateau and driving pressures, avoiding severe hypercapnia and hypoxemia, and carefully titrating positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to prevent excessive increases in PVR and right ventricular afterload. In patients with right-to-left intracardiac shunting, elevated right-sided pressures may worsen shunt flow and cause refractory hypoxemia that responds poorly to increasing FiO2 and ventilation pressures. Management should therefore focus on reducing PVR, optimizing right ventricular function, and limiting factors that increase right-sided pressures.

articles.title: Veno-arterial ECMO for the management of propofol infusion syndrome following cardiac surgery.
articles.journal: Revista espanola de anestesiologia y reanimacion
articles.abstract: Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS) has been described in patients requiring prolonged sedation with this drug, as may occur in some cases after cardiac surgery. Its treatment is based on discontinuation of the drug and supportive management of organ dysfunction until resolution. In the postoperative period of cardiac surgery, diagnosing PRIS poses a challenge, since it must be differentiated from other, more common complications such as postcardiotomy shock. In these patients, PRIS may fatally worsen the prognosis. Veno-arterial ECMO therapy may help maintain cardiac output. Both the diagnosis of PRIS after cardiac surgery and its treatment with ECMO have been scarcely reported. We present a case of PRIS after cardiac surgery successfully managed with ECMO.

articles.title: Postoperative delirium and 1-year functional decline, institutionalization and mortality.
articles.abstract: Postoperative delirium is a common and serious complication in older surgical patients and has been associated with increased morbidity, healthcare costs, long-term functional decline and mortality. To determine whether postoperative delirium is associated with functional status, quality of life, institutionalisation and mortality at 1 year after surgery in a large multicentre surgical cohort. Prospective multicentre observational study. Forty-three hospitals in Spain. Surgical patients were recruited in November 2023 and assessed for delirium 48 h after surgery, with follow-up at 1 year. A total of 2442 adult surgical patients undergoing elective or urgent procedures requiring hospital admission. Postoperative delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), CAM for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the telephone-administered 4AT according to clinical setting. None. Functional status and quality of life at 1 year assessed using the 12-item World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS 2.0). Secondary outcomes included institutionalisation and mortality. After excluding 81 deaths and 462 nonresponders, the 1-year telephone follow-up was completed for 1899 patients. Postoperative delirium within the first 48 h was independently associated with a 4.6-point higher WHODAS score at 1 year: adjusted mean difference = 4.60 [95% confidence interval (CI), 1.57 to 7.64, P = 0.003]. Delirium was also associated with increased institutionalisation and higher mortality: odds ratio (OR) 2.5 (95% CI, 1.07 to 5.84, P = 0.03), and (16.7 vs. 3.1%; P < 0.001), including 30-day, 60-day, and 365-day mortality (all P < 0.001), respectively. Postoperative delirium is independently associated with long-term functional decline, loss of independence, institutionalisation and increased 1-year mortality. These findings highlight delirium as a key perioperative complication and support prevention strategies and structured long-term follow-up after surgery. ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NC-T06127901).

articles.title: Association between burst-suppression with identical bursts and multimodal measures of cerebral oxygenation after cardiac arrest.
authors: Pittsburgh Post Cardiac Arrest Service Investigators
articles.abstract: Burst-suppression with identical bursts (BSIB) is an electroencephalographic (EEG) pattern associated with severe post-cardiac arrest brain injury (PCABI). Whether modifiable mechanisms of brain injury underlie BSIB is unknown. We hypothesized BSIB is associated with impaired cerebral oxygen metabolism, reflected as pathologically elevated jugular bulb venous oxygen saturation (SjvO2), higher brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO2), normal jugular bulb venous-to-arterial carbon dioxide gradient (PbCO2 gap, and lower intracranial pressure (ICP) compared to other EEG patterns. This single-center retrospective study included patients resuscitated from cardiac arrest who underwent EEG and SjvO2 or PbtO2 monitoring. We categorized EEG patterns as BSIB, malignant without BSIB, and non-malignant. Using mixed effects linear regression, we examined associations between EEG and SjvO2, PbCO2 gap, PbtO2, and ICP. The SjvO2 and PbtO2 cohorts included 109 and 33 patients, respectively. SjvO2 did not differ between BSIB and malignant EEGs (β = 3; 95% CI, -0.6 to 7.0), but was higher with BSIB compared to non-malignant patterns (β = 12; 95% CI, 7.0 to 16.0). BSIB was associated with lower PbCO2 gap compared to malignant (β = -1.4; 95% CI, -2.6 to -0.3) and non-malignant (β = -2.6; 95% CI, -4.1 to -1.0) patterns. PbtO2 was highest with BSIB, but not significantly higher compared to malignant patterns in our adjusted model (β = 4.0; 95% CI, -4.7 to 13.0). ICP was lower in those with BSIB compared to malignant patterns (β = -19.0; 95% CI, -32.5 to -5.6). BSIB may represent a distinct subtype of PCABI characterized by impaired oxygen metabolism with preserved oxygen delivery and diffusion.

articles.title: Race, Gender, and Survival: a Scoping Review of Disparities in ICU Post-Resuscitation Care and Neurological Outcomes Following Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest.
articles.journal: Journal of racial and ethnic health disparities
articles.abstract: Racial and ethnic disparities in healthcare are well documented, yet limited attention has been given to the intersection of race/ethnicity and gender in high-acuity critical care. Black women experience compounded inequities affecting access to and quality of intensive care unit (ICU) treatment following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Because outcomes after OHCA are influenced by each link in the chain of survival, disparities in early intervention and subsequent clinical decision-making may contribute to differences in survival and neurological recovery. This study synthesizes evidence on disparities in ICU treatment and outcomes among Black women in the United States while examining how inequities across the chain of survival may influence post-resuscitation care, neurocritical care, and outcomes following OHCA. We conducted a scoping review, guided by the Arksey and O'Malley framework, to analyze peer-reviewed studies identified through electronic databases (e.g., PubMed, CINAHL, and ScienceDirect). Fifteen studies met inclusion criteria and were analyzed using thematic synthesis. Findings indicate persistent disparities, including lower bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) rates, delayed emergency response, reduced access to ICU interventions, and higher rates of early do-not-resuscitate (DNR) orders and withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies (WLST). These inequities may contribute to poorer outcomes and likely reflect a combination of systemic, institutional, and social factors, although relatively few studies directly examined Black women from an intersectional perspective. Addressing these disparities requires improved data disaggregation, culturally responsive care, and interdisciplinary interventions to promote equitable post-resuscitation care and outcomes.

articles.title: Iatrogenic withdrawal syndrome in adult intensive care unit patients: An alternative perspective to design sedation protocols.
articles.journal: Revista espanola de anestesiologia y reanimacion

articles.title: Weathering the storm: Predictors and resource burden of paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity after severe traumatic brain injury.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Reported incidence of paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (PSH) after severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) approaches one-third, largely from cohorts that excluded early deaths. Predictors and resource consequences remain unclear. We identified predictors of PSH development and associations between diagnosis, PSH Assessment Measure (PSH-AM) subscores [clinical features scale (CFS) and diagnosis likelihood tool (DLT)], and resource utilization. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with severe TBI admitted to a tertiary care center intensive care unit (ICU) (October 2020-September 2025), stratified by PSH diagnosis. Two reviewers assigned PSH-AM scores. PSH cannot be diagnosed until the syndrome declares itself over days, so exposure is conditioned on survival; mortality is reported descriptively. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of PSH diagnosis. Log-transformed linear regressions estimated associations of PSH diagnosis and subscores with hospital length of stay (LOS), ICU LOS, and ventilator days. Thirty-day composite outcomes, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and landmark analysis evaluated robustness. Of 509 patients with severe TBI, 86 (17%) developed PSH. Younger age [odds ratio (OR): 0.97 (95% CI: 0.96-0.98); P<0.001) and higher ISS [1.05 (1.02-1.07); P<0.001] independently predicted PSH. PSH was associated with longer hospital LOS (372.9%), ICU LOS (278.3%), and more ventilator days (266.4%; all P<0.001). Mortality was 11.6% (PSH) versus 35.9% (non-PSH). IPTW demonstrated PSH had fewer days alive and out of hospital (-46.8%; P<0.001) and landmark analysis highlighted fewer ventilator-free days (-40.2%; P=0.0097) and ICU-free days (-46.9%; P<0.001). Higher DLT subscores were associated with longer hospital (36.3%; P=0.001) and ICU (23.3%; P=0.005) stays, whereas the CFS subscore showed no associations. The PSH diagnosis is contingent on survival. Younger patients with severe TBI who survive their initial injuries are more likely to develop PSH and occupy hospital beds meaningfully longer. The diagnosis likelihood tool, not the clinical features scale, tracks with that burden. Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

articles.title: Sedation strategy and the search for a better patient experience in ICU.
Early Nocturnal Care Disruption and the Hazard of Incident ICU Delirium in Critically Ill Adults: A Target-Trial Emulation in MIMIC-IV.
articles.abstract: Nighttime care contacts fragment sleep and are often invoked as a contributor to intensive care delirium. Whether a higher intensity of those contacts early in the stay is associated with later incident delirium is unclear. Sicker, more sedated patients are monitored more often overnight and are also more likely to become delirious. We emulated a target trial in MIMIC-IV version 3.1. Adults were eligible if the first intensive care stay lasted at least 48 hours and the delirium screen was negative at that landmark. High exposure was a nocturnal contact rate above the cohort median, built from vital-sign charting, laboratory draws, and bedside medication administrations between 22:00 and 05:59 and divided by 16 nocturnal hours. Follow-up for incident delirium began at the landmark. We estimated the hazard ratio with stabilized inverse-probability weights and a pooled-logistic survival model. Of 12,922 eligible stays, 2,862 developed incident delirium. High nocturnal care-contact intensity was associated with a higher hazard (adjusted hazard ratio 1.43, 95% confidence interval 1.27 to 1.60). The hazard rose across tertiles of the contact rate and was higher for vital-sign charting and phlebotomy than for medication administration. A higher intensity of early nocturnal care contacts was associated with a moderately higher hazard of incident delirium. Residual confounding remains possible, including reverse causation if prodromal delirium itself increases overnight contacts before the first positive screen.

articles.title: Swanson's theory of caring applied to mechanical ventilation weaning in the ICU: Humanizing care.
articles.abstract: To analyze the scientific evidence on the application of Swanson's Theory of Caring in the process of invasive mechanical ventilation weaning in Intensive Care Units (ICU), identifying nursing interventions that correspond to Swanson's five theoretical processes (knowing, being with, doing for, enabling, and maintaining belief) and assessing their implications for clinical practice. Scoping review conducted according to the methodological framework of Arksey and O'Malley (2005), enhanced by Levac et al. (2010), and the updated JBI guidance for scoping reviews (Peters et al., 2020). Reporting followed the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). A search of scientific literature published between January 2020 and January 2026 was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, SciELO, CUIDEN, Cochrane Library and CINAHL, complemented by backward citation tracking. Forty-five articles were included after applying rigorous selection criteria, through independent screening by two reviewers with discrepancies resolved by consensus. Data were analyzed through structured extraction and narrative synthesis, organizing interventions according to Swanson's five caring processes. The review identified multiple nursing interventions during ventilator weaning that showed conceptual correspondence with Swanson's theory. Only 8 of the 45 articles (18%) explicitly used Swanson's framework, and a single study directly linked it to ventilator weaning, identifying a significant knowledge gap. The "knowing" process includes individualized assessment using validated scales and continuous monitoring. "Being with" is manifested through therapeutic presence, effective communication, and facilitation of family contact. "Doing for" encompasses sedation titration, ventilation management, and respiratory physiotherapy techniques. "Enabling" comprises health education, use of augmentative communication systems, and support in decision-making. "Maintaining belief" is materialized through positive reinforcement, management of realistic expectations, and emotional accompaniment. Swanson's Theory of Caring provides a relevant and potentially operational theoretical framework to structure and humanize nursing care during ventilator weaning in the ICU. The conceptual correspondence identified suggests that its systematic application could contribute to improving patient experience, reducing psychological complications, and optimizing weaning outcomes. Implementation gaps are evident due to the absence of prospective studies, scarcity of data to quantify the impact of relational care on the weaning process, and the absence of specific protocols that merge the NANDA-NIC-NOC taxonomy and the Swanson theoretical framework. Prospective studies applying Swanson's framework from the design phase are required to evaluate the specific impact of interventions based on this theory through controlled clinical trials.

articles.title: Association of Admission Serum Homocysteine with Discharge Neurocognitive Dysfunction after Acute Cerebrovascular Disease in a High-Altitude Setting.
articles.abstract: Discharge-phase neurocognitive abnormalities may affect rehabilitation participation, self-management, and discharge safety after acute cerebrovascular disease, but early clinically accessible correlates remain incompletely defined. We examined the association between admission serum homocysteine and clinically adjudicated discharge neurocognitive dysfunction in a high-altitude clinical setting. This single-center retrospective cohort included 227 adults admitted for acute ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, or transient ischemic attack. The first available serum homocysteine measurement within 24 h of hospital arrival was analyzed continuously and by cohort-derived tertiles. The primary outcome was neurocognitive dysfunction documented within 24-48 h before discharge and adjudicated independently by two reviewers blinded to homocysteine levels; standardized cognitive instruments were not systematically available. Logistic regression was sequentially adjusted for demographic, renal, neurological, neuroimaging, and cerebrovascular phenotype-related factors. Among 227 patients, 98 (43.2%) had discharge neurocognitive dysfunction. Admission homocysteine was higher in patients with dysfunction than in those without dysfunction (18.3 ± 6.2 vs. 12.4 ± 4.7 µmol/L, P < 0.001), and dysfunction prevalence increased from 22.4% in T1 to 38.5% in T2 and 69.9% in T3 (P for trend < 0.001). In the primary fully adjusted model, each 1 µmol/L increase in homocysteine was associated with higher odds of dysfunction (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.07-1.21, P < 0.001), and T3 versus T1 remained associated with the outcome (OR 4.36, 95% CI 2.00-9.51, P < 0.001). Estimates were similar in prespecified sensitivity analyses, including exclusion of delirium or positive confusion assessment method for the intensive care unit (CAM-ICU) screening and restriction to acute ischemic stroke. Higher admission homocysteine was associated with discharge-phase neurocognitive dysfunction, supporting prospective evaluation of homocysteine as a potential marker of short-term neurocognitive vulnerability rather than a validated predictor of persistent post-stroke cognitive impairment.

articles.title: Prevalence and Associated Factors of Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome in Adults Admitted to an Intensive Care Unit: A Retrospective Observational Descriptive Study.
articles.abstract: Prolonged opioid administration for pain control and to facilitate tolerance of mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit (ICU) may lead to tolerance and physical dependence. Following opioid discontinuation, opioid withdrawal syndrome (OWS) may occur. Although this condition has been well described in pediatric populations, its incidence and associated factors in critically ill adults remain uncertain because of diagnostic heterogeneity and the frequent clinical overlap with delirium. The aim of this study was to assess the prevalence of OWS and to identify factors associated with its development in adult patients. We conducted a retrospective, descriptive, observational study including patients evaluated at the post-ICU follow-up clinic of Lozano Blesa University Clinical Hospital (Zaragoza, Spain) over a 12-month period. This study investigated the association between multiple opioid medications and adjunctive medications and the occurrence of OWS. Eligible patients had an ICU stay of >7 days, received mechanical ventilation for >48 hours, and had been exposed to opioids. Demographic, clinical, and pharmacological variables were collected, including types of opioids, weight-adjusted cumulative dose, and use of adjuvant medications. OWS was diagnosed during the first 48 hours after opioid discontinuation using a combination of the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) and Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed to evaluate the impact of morphine exposure. A total of 66 patients were included (mean age 59.9 ± 13.6 years; predominantly male). The leading cause of ICU admission was respiratory disease (48.5%). Mean Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) score at admission was 17.0 ± 6.1, and median ICU length of stay was 19 days. Twenty-two patients (33.3%) developed OWS, which was mild in 90.9% and moderate in 9.1% according to the COWS. No significant differences were observed between groups in baseline characteristics or delirium occurrence. Patients who developed OWS were more likely to have received morphine (100% vs. 75%; p = 0.010) and had a higher weight-adjusted cumulative morphine dose (3.15 ± 2.33 vs. 2.21 ± 2.50 mg/kg; p = 0.047), whereas no differences were found for fentanyl exposure. In addition, they more frequently required benzodiazepines (68.2% vs. 18.2%), neuroleptics (68.2% vs. 6.8%), and dexmedetomidine (31.8% vs. 4.5%) (p < 0.01 for all comparisons). Cumulative morphine dose showed modest discriminatory performance for OWS (area under the curve (AUC) 0.653; p = 0.048). OWS is a common complication among adult ICU survivors, although it is predominantly mild in severity. A higher cumulative dose of morphine was associated with its onset, although no association was found with the total duration of exposure. Clinical overlap with delirium and the reactive use of psychoactive medications may contribute to under-recognition of this condition, underscoring the need for structured OWS screening during ICU stay and in post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) follow-up.

articles.title: Failed quality improvement project to improve adherence to CAM-ICU and RASS documentation in a tertiary intensive care unit: a cautionary tale.
articles.abstract: In a four-unit tertiary intensive care service in central London, baseline audit revealed poor compliance with documentation of the Richmond Agitation Sedation Scale (RASS) and the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU). To improve documentation compliance with RASS and CAM-ICU and to reflect on the determinants of success and failure of such interventions. A multifaceted intervention was designed comprising quarterly multidisciplinary education, an updated sedation and delirium guideline, proposed optimisation of the electronic health record (EHR) and a family information pack. Compliance was measured retrospectively from EHR data on day 2 of admission for patients staying ≥3 days. The audit ran from August to October 2023; the re-audit from January to March 2024. RASS documentation compliance fell from 17% to 5%, and CAM-ICU compliance fell from 42% to 36%. The intervention did not improve documentation and on the most stringent measure appeared to worsen it. Several planned components, including EHR optimisation and a delirium smartphrase, had not been implemented at the time of re-audit. A known EHR defect that auto-populated CAM-ICU as positive in deeply sedated patients also remained live throughout. This report sets out, honestly, why a multidisciplinary intervention did not work. We identified five interacting factors, namely incomplete bundle delivery; reliance on low-intensity didactic education without engaging content or visible bedside champions; a baseline unit culture in which the target assessments were de-prioritised; persistent EHR defects that disincentivised documentation; and a frequency-based outcome measure that did not capture clinical fidelity. These findings echo an implementation-science literature showing that passive education alone rarely changes clinician behaviour. ICU teams contemplating similar work should sequence system fixes before behavioural interventions, invest in local champions, and choose outcomes that reflect clinical care rather than the act of charting.

articles.title: Dexmedetomidine Use and Short-Term All-Cause Mortality in Intensive Care Unit Patients with Ischemic Stroke and Atrial Fibrillation: A Propensity-Matched Analysis from MIMIC-IV.
articles.abstract: Preclinical studies have demonstrated that dexmedetomidine (DEX), a sedative widely used in intensive care units (ICU), exerts neuroprotective effects. However, its potential protective role and underlying mechanisms in ischemic stroke patients with atrial fibrillation (IS-AF) remain unclear. The study's objective was to assess the connection between the early administration of DEX and short-term mortality from all causes in patients with IS-AF. From the MIMIC-IV database, patients with IS-AF were identified, including those who were administered DEX and those who were not. The primary endpoint was 7-day all-cause mortality, and the secondary endpoint was 90-day all-cause mortality. Propensity score matching (PSM) was utilized to ensure baseline covariates were balanced. Cox proportional hazards models and Kaplan-Meier survival curves and were utilized to evaluate the association between DEX use and mortality, with subgroup analyses conducted to ensure the findings' robustness. In total, 1,355 patients with IS-AF participated, with 253 (18.7%) receiving DEX. After PSM, 208 pairs were matched. In the fully adjusted model, DEX administration was significantly associated with lower all-cause mortality compared with the control group at both 7 days (before PSM, HR = 0.36, 95% CI: 0.19-0.68, p = 0.002; after PSM, HR = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.12-0.54, p < 0.001) and 90 days (before PSM, HR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.66-1.07, p = 0.162; after PSM, HR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.53-0.97, p = 0.031). The subgroup analyses revealed that DEX's protective effect was stronger in patients aged 70 and above, females, those with hypertension, and those without heart failure or chronic kidney disease. Kaplan-Meier survival curves consistently illustrated that DEX users had greater survival probabilities both before and after matching. In patients with IS-AF, DEX administration is connected to decreased all-cause mortality mortality, underlining the possible importance of DEX in ICU settings.

articles.title: Harm reduction opportunities following ICU admission for prescription opioid overdose: An 8-year comparative audit at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) admission following prescription opioid overdose represents an important opportunity for multidisciplinary intervention and harm reduction, yet Australian data describing inpatient management are limited. A retrospective audit was conducted of 70 adults admitted to the ICU at the Royal Melbourne Hospital with prescription opioid overdose between 2021 and 2024. The primary outcome was provision of take-home naloxone (THN) before discharge among patients meeting institutional eligibility criteria. Secondary outcomes included opioid education, multidisciplinary involvement and discharge opioid management, with comparison with the previous institutional audit where comparable data were available. Only five patients (7.5%, 95% confidence interval 3.2-16.3) were supplied with THN despite all meeting institutional eligibility criteria. Polypharmacy overdose was common (77%). Most patients received at least one specialist referral (83%), although 15% received no inpatient specialist referral. Opioid education was documented in 58 patients (87%) compared with 17% previously (P <0.001), although content and documentation were inconsistent. These findings demonstrate persistent gaps in THN provision, structured opioid education and coordinated discharge planning, highlighting ICU admission as an important opportunity for prescription opioid harm reduction. Strengthening guideline-based multidisciplinary interventions during admission may improve patient outcomes and inform harm reduction strategies nationally.

articles.title: Open Visiting Policy and Delirium in Adult Patients in ICUs: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
authors: and the Padova Intensive Care Unit (PADUA-ICU) Group
articles.abstract: To critically evaluate the comparative effects of open or flexible family presence policies vs. restricted or traditional family presence policies on the occurrence of delirium and other major outcomes among adult patients admitted to ICUs. We conducted a comprehensive electronic search of MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from inception to November 21, 2025. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing open or flexible vs. restricted ICU visiting policies in adult patients. The primary outcome extracted was delirium occurrence. Secondary outcomes included the duration of invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), ICU length of stay, hospital-acquired infections, and ICU mortality. Thirteen RCTs comprising 3861 patients were included. Random-effects models showed that compared with restricted policies, open/flexible family presence reduced delirium occurrence (risk ratio [RR], 0.48; 95% CI, 0.29-0.81; low certainty) and IMV duration (mean difference [MD], -0.36 d; 95% CI, -0.46 to -0.26 d; low certainty). The intervention did not affect the ICU length of stay (MD, 4.21 d; 95% CI, -4.65 to 13.07 d; very low certainty), the rates of hospital-acquired infections (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.81-1.23; low certainty), or ICU mortality (RR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.72-1.08; very low certainty). Open/flexible ICU family presence may reduce delirium and shorten the duration of IMV slightly, without increasing infections or ICU mortality, although the certainty of evidence is low and heterogeneity remains substantial.

articles.title: Ventilatory Management in Neurocritical Versus Non-Neurocritical Care Patients: A Pooled Analysis From the PRIME Database.
authors: PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS (PRoVENT), PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries (PRoVENT-iMiC), and Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes (ENIO) investigators
articles.abstract: To describe ventilatory management in neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients and determine whether specific ventilator settings are associated with development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and mortality in neurocritical care patients. The primary endpoint was a diagnosis of ARDS after initiation of invasive ventilation; one secondary endpoint was ICU mortality. Post hoc pooled analysis of harmonized individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies combined into the PRIME database. PRIME is a harmonized pooled database comprising individual patient data from three recent prospective observational studies on ventilatory management in critically ill patients: "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients without ARDS" (PRoVENT), "PRactice of VENTilation in critically ill patients in Middle-income Countries" (PRoVENT-iMiC), and "Extubation strategies in Neuro-ICU patients and associations with Outcomes" (ENIO). We excluded patients with ARDS at the start of ventilation. Demographic and clinical characteristics, ventilator settings, respiratory variables, arterial blood gas values, and clinical outcomes were extracted from the harmonized PRIME database. Derived ventilation parameters included tidal volume normalized to predicted body weight, driving pressure, respiratory system compliance, mechanical power, ventilatory ratio, and Pao2/Fio2 ratio. This analysis included 3848 patients, including 1702 neurocritical care and 1920 non-neurocritical care patients. Based on recorded ventilatory variables, neurocritical care patients received lower median tidal volumes (Vts), positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. They had lower median driving pressure (ΔP), mechanical power (MP) of ventilation, and ventilatory ratio, as well as higher respiratory system compliance compared with non-neurocritical care patients. These differences were consistently observed at both assessed time points. ARDS was diagnosed more frequently in neurocritical care patients than in non-neurocritical care patients (8.7% vs. 3.9%; p < 0.001), while ICU mortality was lower (14.3% vs. 22.8%; p < 0.001). Among neurocritical care patients, those who developed ARDS were ventilated with lower median Vt and higher Fio2 and had higher median ΔP and MP. Vt normalized for predicted body weight in neurocritical care patients was independently associated with the development of ARDS. In this cohort, ventilatory management at the initial and 48-hour assessments differed between neurocritical care and non-neurocritical care patients, particularly with respect to key ventilator settings like Vt, positive end-expiratory pressure, and Fio2. In neurocritical care patients, ARDS was more often diagnosed than in non-neurocritical care patients.

articles.title: Global Neurointensive Care: A Field Yet to Be Born.
articles.abstract: Neurological conditions represent the leading cause of disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) and the second leading cause of death globally, with more than 11 million deaths annually, 87% of which occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). While global neurosurgery has emerged as a recognized field with dedicated frameworks for advocacy and action, the critical care continuum of neurological disease has been persistently overlooked. Global neurointensive care (GNIC) does not yet exist as a formally defined discipline, yet its need is urgent and measurable: ICU bed density in LMICs ranges from 0.1 to 2.5 per 100,000 inhabitants compared with 5 to 30 per 100,000 in high-income countries (HICs); a cross-sectional survey of 408 providers from 42 LMICs found that only 36.8% had access to a dedicated neurointensive care unit; and traumatic brain injury (TBI) mortality at 6 months exceeds 37% in Latin American LMICs. This viewpoint defines GNIC, characterizes the epidemiological and structural dimensions of the unmet need with granular supporting evidence, reviews existing initiatives and their limitations, and proposes a 6-domain strategic agenda for its development. GNIC must be established as a field parallel and complementary to global neurosurgery, ensuring the critical care continuum of neurological disease is not abandoned in the global effort towards universal health coverage.

articles.title: Diagnostic and Prognostic Value of Sonographic Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter in Patients with Ischemic Stroke or Hypertensive Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
articles.abstract: Elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) is a critical complication in nontraumatic brain injury, yet invasive monitoring carries significant risks, and noninvasive alternatives remain undervalidated. Optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) ultrasonography represents a promising bedside technique, but data in nontraumatic populations are limited. This study evaluated the diagnostic and prognostic value of ONSD in neurocritical patients with ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage. This prospective observational cohort study enrolled 100 neurocritical intensive care unit (ICU) patients with acute nontraumatic brain injury [ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage; Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) < 9] who underwent admission computed tomography (CT) and bedside ONSD ultrasonography. Sixty age- and sex-matched healthy volunteers were enrolled exclusively to provide descriptive reference values for physiological ONSD and were not included in the primary diagnostic or prognostic analyses. CT-based radiologic ICP surrogates were the reference standard. Exploratory analyses evaluated inter-eye variability, adjusted models, and in-hospital survival. ONSD increased stepwise across healthy controls, patients with negative CT, and patients with positive CT (4.62 ± 0.33, 5.52 ± 0.51, and 6.50 ± 0.51 mm, respectively). Among neurocritical patients, a cohort-derived cutoff of ≥ 6.00 mm yielded 86.7% sensitivity, 85.0% specificity, 89.7% positive predictive value, 81.0% negative predictive value, 86.0% accuracy, and 0.901 area under the curve (AUC). Above-threshold ONSD remained independently associated with CT-positive elevated ICP after adjustment for age, body mass index (BMI), GCS, and systolic blood pressure (SBP) in exploratory multivariable analysis. Exploratory survival analysis showed significantly higher in-hospital mortality in patients with ONSD above the cohort-derived threshold (log-rank p = 4.77 × 10-13). Bedside ultrasonographic ONSD measurement appears clinically useful for early triage and longitudinal bedside surveillance in neurocritical patients with ischemic stroke or hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage, particularly when invasive monitoring is unavailable or delayed.

articles.title: Isoflurane-Based Inhaled Sedation in Mechanically Ventilated Adults With Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: The SAVE-ICU Randomized Clinical Trial.
authors: SAVE-ICU Investigators and the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group
articles.abstract: Rigorous evidence for inhaled sedation using isoflurane in mechanically ventilated patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) is limited. To evaluate whether an inhaled sedation strategy lowers hospital mortality compared with usual care intravenous sedation strategy in mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF. Pragmatic, effectiveness, open-label, superiority, randomized clinical trial in 14 intensive care units (ICUs) in Canada. Adults (≥18 years) receiving sedation for less than 72 hours and receiving mechanical ventilation for AHRF from non-COVID respiratory failure (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen [Pao2] to fraction of inspired oxygen [Fio2] <300 mm Hg) or COVID-19 were enrolled between September 2020 and March 2025 with follow-up through June 2025. Patients were randomized to an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed or to a usual intravenous sedation care strategy. Sedatives were titrated to achieve the desired target sedation score guided by clinical teams and continued until extubation or death. Primary outcome was all-cause hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU- and ventilator-free days at day 30; hospital-free days at day 60; use of refractory hypoxemia adjunctive therapies; delirium- and coma-free days at day 14; and quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months. Of 786 patients randomized, 780 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 61.1 years; 34.0% female; 73.7% non-COVID AHRF, mean Pao2:Fio2 ratio, 152.6 mm Hg); 385 in the inhaled sedation and 395 in the intravenous sedation groups. In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization. At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled sedation group had died, compared with 171 of 390 patients (43.8%) in the intravenous sedation group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.84 to 1.14]; P = .85). There was no effect modification in prespecified subgroup analyses for age, sex, and COVID-19 status. ICU-, ventilator-, and hospital-free days were similar between groups. The inhaled sedation group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; between-group difference, 8.89% [95% CI, 1.95% to 15.83%]) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (between-group difference, -0.95 [95% CI, -1.69 to -0.22]). There was no difference in quality-of-life and disability scores between groups. In mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF, an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed did not reduce hospital mortality compared with an intravenous sedation strategy. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04415060.

articles.title: Characteristics and outcomes of haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury and combined injuries from a South African Trauma Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: To describe and compare injury severity, clinical management and mortality among haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury (TBI) and combined haemorrhage+TBI cohorts in a South African trauma population. Secondary analysis of data from the Epidemiology and Outcomes of Prolonged Trauma Care (EpiC) multicentre observational cohort study, April 2021 to December 2024. Six government health facilities and affiliated government ambulances across the Western Cape, South Africa. 18 840 adult patients with blunt and/or penetrating traumatic injuries enrolled in the EpiC registry were eligible for this secondary analysis. Patients <18 years of age and prisoners are excluded from EpiC. Burn injuries, non-haemorrhage and non-TBI injuries were excluded from this analysis. Patients were assigned to one of three mutually exclusive cohorts (haemorrhage, TBI or haemorrhage+TBI) using anatomic and physiologic criteria. The primary outcome was crude, all-cause prehospital or in-hospital mortality. Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios (RRs) for mortality were adjusted for injury severity, injury force type and mode of prehospital transportation. Secondary outcomes included critical interventions, hospital admission, length of stay and time from injury to death. A total of 7614 patients met inclusion: 5146 (67.6%) haemorrhage, 1556 (20.4%) TBI and 912 (12.0%) haemorrhage+TBI. The majority were male (85.1%) with a median age of 31 years. Patients with haemorrhage+TBI received more intensive care, including airway interventions (38%), transfusions (41%) and intensive care unit admissions (36%). Crude mortality was highest in haemorrhage+TBI (31.3%), followed by TBI (7.7%) and haemorrhage (5.4%). After injury-pattern specific severity adjustment, mortality risk remained significantly higher in haemorrhage+TBI than in TBI (RR 1.87, 95% CI 1.60 to 2.19) and haemorrhage (RR 3.38, 95% CI 2.96 to 3.85). Estimates were similar after additional adjustment for injury force and prehospital transportation (RR 1.84 and 2.98). In this South African population, haemorrhage+TBI was the least prevalent but most high-risk cohort with greater morbidity and mortality compared with haemorrhage or TBI alone, even after adjusting for injury severity. These findings may inform system level planning and resource allocation particularly in resource-limited settings.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence for Early Prediction of Intracranial Hypertension: From Single-Centre Development to Multicentre Validation.
authors: CENTER-TBI High-Resolution ICU (HR ICU) Sub-Study Participants and Investigators
articles.abstract: Raised intracranial pressure is one of the most severe secondary insults after traumatic brain injury. Recognising physiological patterns before they progress to dangerous intracranial pressure elevations could enable preventive rather than reactive interventions. In our previous Uppsala single-centre study, an XGBoost machine learning model showed high discriminative performance for prediction of imminent intracranial pressure insults. The model identifies short-term physiological trajectories associated with imminent threshold crossing rather than predicting independent future clinical events. Whether these results are generalisable across centres is unknown. The aim was therefore to evaluate whether the XGBoost model trained on an Uppsala dataset maintains similar performance when applied to a multicentre TBI cohort - The CENTER-TBI High-Resolution ICU cohort. The XGBoost model trained on the Uppsala high frequency traumatic brain injury cohort was externally validated using data from the multicentre CENTER-TBI cohort. Minute-level averages of intracranial pressure and invasive arterial blood pressure were used to predict the onset of an intracranial pressure insult within 30 min on the basis of a 4h historical window. A bidirectional validation design was applied and performance was assessed using multiple metrics. The cohorts comprised 602 patients from Uppsala and 255 patients from the CENTER-TBI database. When trained on the Uppsala cohort and tested on CENTER-TBI, the model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 97.4%, sensitivity of 93.8%, and specificity of 98.6%. Training on CENTER-TBI and testing on the Uppsala dataset yielded an AUROC of 96.1%, sensitivity of 81.2%, and specificity of 98.7%. Balanced accuracy exceeded 88% in both validation directions. The XGBoost model retained high performance under external multicentre validation, indicating that pre-insult physiological patterns preceding increased intracranial pressure are shared across cohorts. Differences in sensitivity between validation directions were observed and may reflect cohort characteristics or dataset size. These findings support the need for local evaluation before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Incidence of severe mountain bike-related injuries and mortality: A 15-year statewide analysis.
articles.abstract: Mountain biking has grown in popularity and has seen widespread trail development but carries risk for severe trauma. No studies have analysed severe injuries in the context of contemporary mountain biking to understand trends and modifiable risk factors. To describe the incidence and longitudinal characteristics of severe injuries related to mountain biking in Tasmania, Australia. Retrospective analysis of all patients admitted to Tasmanian public hospitals with severe mountain bike (MTB)-related injuries from 1st January 2010-31 st December 2024. Incidence of severe MTB-related injuries (including mortality) as defined by hospital admission to an intensive care unit or neurosurgery high dependency unit; for emergency surgery (in <4 h); or transfer intra- or interstate for definitive treatment. Secondary outcomes were annual injury trends in mechanism of injury, body regions, injury profiles, and incident location. For the total period there were 85 severe injuries (including 4 mortalities) from 6643 MTB-related emergency department (ED) presentations. Annual severe MTB-related cases increased over the 15 years from 0.8 cases/year before 2015, to 8.1 cases/year in later years. Severe injury cases accounted for only 1.3% of all MTB-related ED presentations. Most severely injured riders were male (97%); the mean age was 36 years (SD 16.9) for the total period, but this increased from 18.5 years (SD 5.8) pre-2015-36.9 years (SD 16.8) post-2015. Executing a jump was the dominant mechanism of injury (44%), followed by fall over handlebars (14%), obstacle collision (11%) and adverse trail conditions (9%). The most injured body regions were abdomen (31%), neck (23%) and thorax/chest (20%). The most common types of injuries were fracture/dislocation (44%), abdominal organ injury (24%) and thoracic organ injury (15%). Spinal cord injury occurred in 6% of cases and traumatic brain injury in 7%. Over 50% of severe injury incidents occurred on purpose-built MTB trails. Severe MTB-related injuries increased proportionally to all MTB-related injuries suggesting the increase was largely driven by rider exposure. Targeted injury prevention strategies, safe trail design, and understanding risk factors are needed to ensure safe progression of this popular sport.

articles.title: Risk factors and preventive strategies for pressure injury and medical device-related pressure injury in ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation: A scoping review.
articles.abstract: Adult ICU patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) are at risk of pressure injury (PI) and medical device-related pressure injury (MDRPI) due to immobility, impaired perfusion, and device contact. This scoping review synthesized evidence on PI and MDRPI risk factors and preventive strategies. This scoping review followed the Arksey and O'Malley framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Five databases (PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, MEDLINE, ScienceDirect) were searched from inception to April 2026. Studies of adult ICU patients receiving IMV reporting PI, MDRPI, risk factors, or preventive strategies were eligible. Forty-two studies from 14 countries (2009-2026) were included. PI incidence ranged from 10.3 to 36.3% (up to 88.7% when prone-positioned); MDRPI (oral mucosal injury) ranged from 25.9 to 43.1% (80.1% with a broader erythema criterion). Cutaneous PI mainly affected the sacrum, heels, occiput, face, and thorax (generally Stage 1-2); oral mucosal MDRPI, assessed using heterogeneous severity criteria, was typically mild-to-moderate. Onset was commonly reported on days 3-9. PI risk factors included immobility, impaired perfusion, vasopressor therapy, and poor nutrition; MDRPI risk factors involved prolonged intubation and device exposure. Preventive strategies included device repositioning, securement adjustment, device-contact protection, and oral care. Prolonged mechanical loading and reduced tissue tolerance are intensified by immobility, sedation, hemodynamic instability, impaired perfusion, vasopressor use, and device exposure. Early-stage cutaneous PI and mild-to-moderate mucosal MDRPI were more commonly reported than severe cutaneous and mucosal injuries; given the descriptive, non-comparative evidence, this cannot be attributed to preventive effectiveness. Early monitoring may be important for detecting early-stage injury and identifying progression toward more severe injury. Prevention should combine pressure redistribution with tolerance-based repositioning, skin monitoring, device securement, device-contact protection, and oral mucosal care. An exploratory, hypothesis-generating observation is that the first 10 days of ICU stay may be a high-risk period, requiring prospective validation.

articles.title: Changes in clinical management related to continuous versus routine EEG in critically ill adults: analysis of a randomized trial.
articles.abstract: Continuous electroencephalogram (cEEG) is increasingly utilized in the intensive care unit for consciousness-impaired patients with various conditions. It is, however, costly in terms of technical and human resources, and its impact on prognosis compared with routine EEG (rEEG) remains debated. We aimed to characterize the effect of cEEG vs rEEG on clinical management modifications, and to determine if these correlated with a better outcome. This is an ancillary analysis using data of CERTA (NCT03129438), a randomized trial comparing cEEG versus repeated rEEG in critically ill adults with altered consciousness. Clinical management modifications due to the EEG intervention, pre-defined as performed within 60 hours of EEG start, were prospectively recorded (anti-seizure medication -ASM, sedation, new radiological examination, new surgical intervention, withdrawal of life sustaining therapy). Correlation with the EEG type were analyzed by 2x2 tables; Mantel-Haenszel tests explored the impact on mortality and functional outcome at 6 months. The trial included 364 patients completing follow-up (182 each in the cEEG and rEEG groups). While 58.2% of cEEG and 45.6% of rEEG patients had any management change (p= 0.018), ASM were modified in 22.0% (cEEG) and 12.1% (rEEG) (p = 0.012)); other clinical interventions were comparable across EEG groups. Adjusting for ASM modifications, mortality (p=0.845) and functional outcome (p=0.619) remained similar between the EEG groups. In critically ill adults, cEEG is associated with more clinical management modifications compared to repeated rEEG, particularly regarding ASM, but this does not seem to translate into improved patients' outcomes.

articles.title: Development and external validation of a nomogram for predicting in-hospital mortality in status epilepticus patients in the intensive care unit: A MIMIC-IV and eICU-CRD study.
articles.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape
articles.abstract: To develop and externally validate a nomogram for predicting in-hospital mortality in ICU patients with SE, using readily available clinical data collected within the first 24 h of ICU admission. We identified adult SE patients from MIMIC-IV (training cohort, 2008-2019) using ICD-9/ICD-10 codes. Twenty-seven candidate predictors were screened by LASSO logistic regression with 10-fold cross-validation. The final model was constructed with multivariable logistic regression and presented as a nomogram. Internal validation used 1000 bootstrap resamples with optimism correction. External validation was performed in an independent SE cohort from the eICU-CRD database (2014-2015). The training cohort comprised 299 patients (69 deaths, 23.1% mortality). LASSO selected nine predictors: age, first ICU care unit, Glasgow Coma Scale, temperature, SpO2, white blood cell count, glucose, bicarbonate, and the Elixhauser comorbidity index. The optimism-corrected AUC was .807 (95% CI, .754-.860) with a Brier score of .124. External validation in 597 eICU patients yielded an AUC of .750 (95% CI, .685-.815). In sensitivity analyses, a reduced model without the comorbidity score achieved an optimism-corrected AUC of .786 and an external AUC of .730, and a model without the ICU care-unit type achieved .817 and .764, respectively. This nine-variable nomogram provides a validated, bedside-applicable tool for mortality risk stratification in ICU SE patients, enabling manual risk calculation without electronic computation.

articles.title: Impact of clinical frailty on mortality after elective surgery in patients aged ≥ 90 years admitted to critical care: a binational intensive care registry analysis.
articles.abstract: Increasing numbers of patients aged ≥ 90 years require elective surgery. Frailty is increasingly recognised as a key determinant of peri-operative risk, but high-quality evidence to understand the impact on outcomes in this age group is limited. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Adult Patient Database. Patients aged ≥ 90 years admitted to ICU following elective surgery were included, encompassing planned and unplanned ICU admissions. Frailty was assessed at ICU admission using the Clinical Frailty Scale and patients categorised as non-frail or frail. Propensity score matching was performed to balance age; sex; acute illness severity; and comorbidities. Primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU mortality; in-hospital mortality; return to pre-admission residence; and ICU and duration of hospital stay. The matched cohort comprised 5398 patients (2699 without frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 1-4) and 2699 living with frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 5-8)), with good post-matching covariate balance. Mortality in ICU was low and not significantly different between patients who were frail and non-frail. Frailty was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (matched hazard ratio (HR) 1.66, 95%CI 1.22-2.27, p = 0.001) and higher 1-year mortality (matched HR 1.66, 95%CI 1.47-1.87, p < 0.001).
