articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Patients with obesity who are admitted to an ICU bring specific challenges for rehabilitation during and after critical illness. This narrative review explores impact of differences in body compositions and pathophysiology on outcomes to summarise interprofessional, patient-centred rehabilitation strategies across the trajectory of recovery. METHODS: The interprofessional expert panel reviewed major trials and guidelines, integrating their clinical expertise with the current evidence. RESULTS: Three distinct phenotypes potentially influence outcomes for survivors. Whilst patients with preserved muscle mass may have a survival advantage, the phenotypes characterised by ectopic visceral fat or sarcopenia are frequently complicated by multimorbidity and polypharmacy, likely increasing the risk of adverse effects such as suboptimal sedation, prolonged ventilation and immobilisation, malnutrition, and impaired recovery. Targeted respiratory interventions, including secretion-clearance techniques and appropriate patient positioning to prevent atelectasis, reduce the work of breathing. Optimisation of communication and swallowing function is an essential component for facilitating safe oral intake and promoting active patient participation in rehabilitation. Concurrently, targeted nutrition strategies combined with early, targeted, progressive mobilisation might mitigate ICU acquired weakness and support functional recovery. The availability of appropriate weight‑based equipment is fundamental to ensuring safe mobilisation for both patients and healthcare professionals. CONCLUSION: Interprofessional collaboration is central to optimising outcomes and should extend beyond the ICU to structured post-ICU follow-up to address persistent, worsening, or newly emerging health impairments. Early rehabilitation in critically ill patients with obesity should integrate physiological, logistical, and psychosocial considerations to support equitable and functional recovery.
articles.ai_summary: This study reviewed rehabilitation strategies for critically ill patients with obesity, identifying three distinct phenotypes that influence outcomes. Targeted interventions, including respiratory, nutrition, and mobilization strategies, can mitigate complications and support functional recovery.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings highlight the importance of interprofessional collaboration and early rehabilitation in critically ill patients with obesity, emphasizing the need to address physiological, logistical, and psychosocial considerations to support equitable and functional recovery.

articles.title: Echocardiographic assessment of left ventricular longitudinal function in critically ill patients.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: In the intensive care unit (ICU), conventional assessment of left ventricular systolic function relies on left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), but LVEF often has limited prognostic ability. Measures of longitudinal LV performance [global longitudinal strain (GLS), mitral annular plane systolic excursion (MAPSE), and tissue Doppler-derived systolic velocity (S')] are increasingly used in critical care echocardiography and may capture clinically relevant dysfunction better than LVEF. To date, the prognostic implications of GLS, MAPSE, and S' have been studied mainly in septic cohorts, while their feasibility and prognostic value in mixed ICU populations remain uncertain. We therefore aimed to evaluate the feasibility and prognostic value of these parameters in a mixed ICU cohort. METHODS: In this exploratory secondary analysis of a prospective observational ICU cohort, transthoracic echocardiography was performed within 24 hours of ICU admission. LVEF by Simpson biplane, GLS, MAPSE, and S' were analysed offline. Feasibility was quantified as the proportion of patients with analysable measurements. Associations between echocardiographic parameters were assessed using simple linear regression and are reported as coefficients of determination (R2). Associations with 90-day mortality were assessed using logistic regression, with adjustment for age, Simplified Acute Physiology Score 3, and cardiac index. RESULTS: Of 411 enrolled patients, 377 had at least one parameter available and were included. Feasibility was 71% for LVEF, 65% for GLS, 90% for MAPSE, and 83% for S'. GLS correlated most strongly with LVEF (R2=0.516), whereas correlations were weaker for MAPSE (R2=0.268) and S' (R2=0.195). Ninety-day mortality was 27% (101/377). After adjustment, GLS (odds ratio [OR] 1.08 per 1% less negative strain, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.00-1.16; p=0.048) and MAPSE (OR 1.17 per 1 mm decrease, 95% CI 1.06-1.30; p=0.002) remained associated with mortality, whereas LVEF and S' did not. MAPSE ≤10 mm was independently associated with mortality (adjusted OR 2.48, 95% CI 1.31-4.71; p=0.005). CONCLUSIONS: In a mixed ICU cohort, impaired MAPSE and GLS were associated with increased mortality, in contrast to LVEF and S'. MAPSE was also the most feasible measurement. Incorporation of MAPSE into routine ICU echocardiography may improve detection and risk stratification of LV dysfunction in critical illness. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Secondary analysis of data from a single-centre prospective observational study focused on systolic dysfunction in ICU patients (Clinical Trials ID: NCT03787810).
articles.ai_summary: This study evaluated the feasibility and prognostic value of echocardiographic parameters in a mixed ICU population. It found that impaired mitral annular plane systolic excursion (MAPSE) and global longitudinal strain (GLS) were associated with increased mortality. MAPSE was also the most feasible measurement.
articles.ai_significance: These findings suggest that incorporating MAPSE into routine ICU echocardiography may improve detection and risk stratification of left ventricular dysfunction in critical illness, potentially leading to better patient outcomes.

articles.title: The molecular ICU: a primer on omics, informatics and the future of precision critical care.
articles.abstract: Critical care has produced hundreds of neutral randomized trials, in part because therapies have been tested in biologically incoherent populations that dilute meaningful treatment effects. Syndromic diagnoses such as sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and traumatic brain injury group distinct pathobiological states under a single label, limiting the ability to detect treatment-responsive subgroups. While high-dimensional omics technologies have revealed this biologic heterogeneity, the field lacks a practical framework to translate these insights into clinical trial design and bedside decision-making. This Review addresses the translational gap in precision critical care through a pathway-level framework. We synthesize advances in genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, highlighting their roles in capturing susceptibility, host response, effector function, and real-time physiology. We propose pathway-focused biomarkers as clinically translatable signatures that preserve biological mechanisms while enabling practical measurement. We outline how pathway enrichment, network analysis, and multi-omic integration can identify these programs, and how feature selection can derive parsimonious biomarker panels for clinical use. This approach also supports pathway-guided drug repurposing by linking dysregulated molecular programs to existing therapies. Together, these signatures provide a framework for predictive enrichment, aligning patient selection with therapeutic mechanisms and facilitating implementation within adaptive platform trials. This Review serves as a practical primer that outlines the concepts and methods needed to translate omics into clinically actionable tools. By shifting from syndromic classification to pathway-defined biology, it provides a framework for biomarker development, trial design, and precision critical care.
articles.ai_summary: This study reviews the current limitations in critical care research due to syndromic diagnoses and proposes a pathway-level framework to translate omics insights into clinical trial design and bedside decision-making.
articles.ai_significance: This framework has the potential to improve patient outcomes by enabling personalized treatment and more effective use of existing therapies in critical care settings.

articles.title: High-resolution monitoring reveals fragmented 24-hour light exposure in intensive care units.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Light is a key regulator of circadian rhythms, sleep, and neuroendocrine function. Abnormal light exposure has been associated with delirium and adverse outcomes in critically ill patients. While previous ICU studies have generally reported low daytime illuminance and intermittent nocturnal light exposure, most relied on averaged measurements or low temporal resolution monitoring, potentially obscuring clinically relevant exposure patterns. In routine ICU care, light exposure often occurs as brief but frequent events related to necessary interventions, yet the extent and temporal structure of such light fragmentation remain poorly characterized. This study therefore aimed to characterize high-resolution 24-hour light exposure patterns and nocturnal fragmentation in ICU patients. METHODS: In this observational study, ambient illuminance was continuously recorded every 5 s in adult ICU patients over a one-year period. A total of 222 patients were monitored for up to 7 consecutive days, yielding more than 14 million individual measurements. Light exposure was analysed across complete 24-hour cycles and stratified into daytime (07:00-20:59) and nighttime (21:00-06:59) periods. Outcomes included median illuminance, frequency of light events, extreme illuminance (99th percentile), and duration of uninterrupted nocturnal darkness. Mixed-effects models and negative binomial regression were used to account for repeated measurements and to assess associations with room configuration. RESULTS: Across the 24-hour cycle, median illuminance demonstrated a flattened diurnal pattern, with daytime light levels remaining markedly below those typically encountered in indoor working environments and limited sustained darkness at night. Nighttime exposure was dominated by frequent short-duration light events, resulting in pronounced fragmentation of nocturnal darkness. Fragmentation patterns were largely independent of room configuration and treatment intensity, as ambient illuminance did not differ according to organ support modality once time of day was considered. Extreme illuminance values occurred intermittently, predominantly during daytime, and varied according to room type. CONCLUSIONS: ICU light exposure is characterized primarily by temporal fragmentation rather than sustained brightness. Repeated interruptions of darkness may represent a plausible environmental mechanism contributing to circadian dysregulation. These findings highlight care processes as a key target for interventions and support the use of fragmentation-based metrics in future circadian research in critical care.

articles.title: How to optimize brain perfusion and prevent cerebral complications during extracorporeal life support.
articles.abstract: Extracorporeal life support (ECLS) is increasingly used to rescue patients with refractory respiratory failure, cardiogenic shock and/or cardiac arrest. Acute brain injury during ECLS is common and associated with a significant increase in mortality and long-term disability. Brain injury in ECLS patients can arise from either the underlying disease or pre-ECLS events, such as cardiac arrest, or from secondary mechanisms linked to ECLS-related complications, management strategies, and physiologic perturbations during support. In this review, we will focus on the modifiable factors and clinical management strategies to prevent or mitigate secondary brain injury during ECLS. Both veno-arterial membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) as well as veno-venous membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) will be discussed. First, we provide an overview of the interplay between patient and circuit related factors that determine brain perfusion and oxygen delivery in this critically ill patient population. Second, we highlight the importance of standardized multimodal neuromonitoring to detect evolving brain injury early and to guide individualized neurocritical care and ECLS management. Third, we identify modifiable ECLS factors and physiological targets which minimize secondary brain injury. We provide guidance on the titration of extracorporeal blood flow and blood pressure targets, the amount of sweep gas flow and oxygen fraction, temperature control and anticoagulation management. A comprehensive understanding of ECLS physiology and circuit-patient interactions, integrated with protocolized multimodal monitoring, enables individualized adjustment of modifiable ECLS settings to prevent or mitigate secondary brain injury.
articles.ai_summary: This review discusses how to prevent brain injury in patients on extracorporeal life support (ECLS) by optimizing brain perfusion and oxygen delivery. It highlights the importance of standardized multimodal neuromonitoring and individualized neurocritical care. The review provides guidance on adjusting ECLS settings to minimize secondary brain injury.
articles.ai_significance: Optimizing brain perfusion and preventing cerebral complications during ECLS is crucial for improving outcomes in critically ill patients, reducing mortality and long-term disability.

articles.title: Effect of the orexin receptor antagonist, suvorexant, on sleep architecture in the early postoperative period following cardiac surgery: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients recovering from cardiac surgery in the intensive care unit (ICU) do not sleep well. Commonly used sedative-hypnotic medications can disrupt sleep architecture and increase the risk of delirium in critically ill patients after surgery. The orexin receptor antagonist suvorexant, improves sleep onset and duration in patients with chronic insomnia. We hypothesized that suvorexant improves sleep onset and duration while also reducing the incidence of delirium after cardiac surgery. METHODS: This multicentric, double-blind, randomized controlled trial was conducted at two university-based cardiac ICUs. One hundred adult patients were enrolled after admission to the ICU following cardiac surgery. Enrollment occurred between March 2020 and February 2025. Participants were randomized to receive either a once daily oral dose of suvorexant 20 mg or placebo. Treatment began on the first night after extubation and continued until hospital discharge or for a maximum of seven days, whichever occurred first. Sleep was recorded using an electroencephalography (EEG) monitor (SedLine, Masimo Corp., California, USA) on the first night after extubation and was scored blindly by an experienced registered polysomnographic technologist. The primary outcome was wakefulness after persistent sleep onset (WASO). Sleep onset was defined as the first 30-second epoch classified by rapid eye movement (REM) or non-REM stages 1, 2, 3 after lights off. Wakefulness was defined as an awake period of 30s or longer. Sleep questionnaires were administered and delirium screenings were conducted every morning until hospital discharge. RESULTS: One hundred patients were randomized to receive suvorexant (n = 49) or placebo (n = 51). EEG analysis indicated that neither the median [inter-quartile range] nighttime WASO (200.7 [112.1, 328.4] minutes vs. 184.2 [80.4, 304.2] minutes; p = 0.33) nor total sleep time (224.0 [112.0, 379.0] minutes vs. 253.0 [68.0, 420.0] minutes; p = 0.92) differed significantly between the groups. There was no significant difference in rescue medication (melatonin, dexmedetomidine, benzodiazepine) utilization between the groups. Subjective sleep quality, incidence of delirium, and delirium-free days did not differ between the two groups. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: Clinical Trials Registry no. NCT04092894, Registration Date 09/17/2019. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients recovering in the ICU who underwent cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, the suvorexant treatment did not affect wakefulness after sleep onset or post-operative delirium.
articles.ai_summary: This randomized controlled trial tested the sleep-promoting effects of suvorexant in patients recovering from cardiac surgery. Suvorexant did not improve sleep architecture or reduce delirium in these patients. The study found no significant differences in sleep quality, delirium incidence, or rescue medication use between suvorexant and placebo groups.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings are significant for ICU clinicians as they suggest that suvorexant may not be an effective treatment for improving sleep or reducing delirium in patients recovering from cardiac surgery.

articles.title: Nurse-led family participatory support intervention on clinical outcomes in ICU patients: a prospective quasi-experimental study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Delirium is a common and serious complication in critically ill patients, and family-centered care has emerged as a promising non-pharmacological strategy. However, evidence on structured, nurse-led family participatory support (NFPS) intervention remains limited. AIM: To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of NFPS in critically ill adult patients. METHODS: Adult patients admitted to intensive care units (ICU) from three tertiary hospitals in Gansu Province were allocated to either the NFPS group or a usual care group without family participation (non-NFPS). In the NFPS group, trained family members participated in care under the guidance of ICU nurses. The primary outcome was the incidence of delirium. RESULTS: After 1:1 propensity score matching, 365 patients were included in each group. The NFPS group demonstrated significant reductions in incidence of delirium [26.85% vs. 34.25%, p = 0.03]. Compared with the control group, the NFPS group also had significantly shorter hospital length of stay (HLOS) (25 [17-34] vs. 30 [22-38] days, P < 0.001), ICU-LOS (13 [7-17] vs. 14 [10-18] days, P < 0.001), duration of mechanical ventilation (10 [6-15] vs. 11 [8-17] days, P < 0.001) and lower hospitalization cost (193,931.99 [117,616.64-294,201.02] vs. 199,330.72 [138,636.05-300,993.88] CNY, P = 0.032). No significant differences were observed in 6-month mortality (6.03% vs. 7.67%, P = 0.380), 1-year mortality (9.32% vs. 11.51%, P = 0.330), ICU-acquired weakness (26.58% vs. 29.59%, P = 0.270), ICU-acquired infection (19.45% vs. 19.73%, P = 0.930), or adverse events (2.19% vs. 3.84%, P = 0.190). CONCLUSION: The NFPS significantly reduced the incidence of delirium and was associated with shorter durations of mechanical ventilation, ICU-LOS, HLOS, lower hospitalization costs, without increasing the risks of ICU-AW, ICU-acquired infection, or adverse events. No significant differences were observed in long-term mortality between the two groups.
articles.ai_summary: This study evaluated a nurse-led family participatory support intervention in ICU patients. The intervention significantly reduced the incidence of delirium and was associated with shorter hospital and ICU stays, lower hospitalization costs, and shorter durations of mechanical ventilation.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings have significant implications for ICU clinical practice, as they suggest that a structured, nurse-led family participatory support intervention can improve patient outcomes and reduce costs without increasing risks.

articles.title: Restrictive vs Liberal Physical Restraint Strategies in Critically Ill Patients: The R2D2-ICU Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: The effect of wrist-strap physical restraints on outcomes in patients receiving mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit (ICU) remains uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effect of a low-use wrist-strap physical restraint strategy in critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Open-label randomized clinical trial conducted across 10 ICUs in France. Between January 5, 2021, and January 2, 2024, 405 adult patients who had initiated invasive mechanical ventilation within the previous 6 hours and were expected to require ventilation for at least 48 hours were enrolled. Follow-up was completed on May 17, 2024. Statistical analysis was conducted from June 1, 2025, to December 15, 2025. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomized to undergo either a restrictive, low-use physical restraint strategy (wrist straps avoided unless necessary because of severe agitation, defined as a Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale score of ≥3 [on a scale from -5 (unresponsive) to 4 (combative)]; n = 201) or a liberal, high-use strategy (wrist straps applied systematically and reassessed daily; n = 204). Discontinuation of restraints was allowed in patients who were awake or extubated without delirium (measured via the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was the number of days alive without coma or delirium during the first 14 days after randomization. Secondary outcomes included incidence of self-extubation and day-90 mortality. RESULTS: Among 396 patients with available primary outcome data, the median (IQR) age was 65 (56-73) years, 245 (62%) were male, and the median (IQR) Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score was 7 (4-10). The mean days alive without coma or delirium were 6.67 days (95% CI, 5.69-7.65) in the low-use strategy group and 6.30 days (95% CI, 5.35-7.24) in the high-use strategy group (adjusted mean difference, 0.37 days [95% CI, -0.71 to 1.46]; P = .51). Self-extubation occurred in 18 patients (9.2%) in the low-use strategy group and 17 (8.5%) in the high-use strategy group, and day-90 mortality was 37.2% and 41.0%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this randomized clinical trial, among adult patients receiving mechanical ventilation in the ICU, a low-use wrist-strap physical restraint strategy compared with a high-use strategy did not reduce days free of delirium or coma at 14 days. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04273360.

articles.title: Impact of early goal-directed mobilization on ICU-acquired weakness: a meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: ICU-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) significantly impairs muscle strength and physical function in critically ill patients. Early mobilization interventions have been increasingly adopted, yet the specific effects of a structured EGDM program on ICU-AW and functional outcomes have not been systematically quantified. This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of EGDM on ICU-AW, muscle strength, and functional outcomes. PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data, and Viper Information Products (VIP) databases were searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) up to November 30, 2025. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2.0. RevMan 5.4 was used for meta-analysis. Subgroup analysis was prespecified by allocation concealment. Nine RCTs (907 patients) were included. EGDM reduced ICU-AW [RR = 0.57, 95%CI (0.33 ~ 0.97), p = 0.04 for the overall effect; I2 = 77%, p = 0.002 for heterogeneity], but sensitivity analysis of high-quality trials showed no significant effect [RR = 0.84, 95%CI (0.48 ~ 1.46), p = 0.54 for the overall effect]. EGDM improved muscle strength [MD = 4.94, 95%CI (3.39 ~ 6.50), I2 = 59%, p = 0.02 for heterogeneity], shortened the duration of mechanical ventilation [MD = -81.95 h, 95%CI (-115.45 ~ -48.46), p < 0.00001 for the overall effect; I2 = 85%, p < 0.00001 for heterogeneity], and reduced ICU stay[MD = -4.55 days, 95%CI (-6.22 ~ -2.89), p < 0.00001 for the overall effect; I2 = 74%, p = 0.0004 for heterogeneity], both with substantial heterogeneity. Although the primary Barthel Index analysis was not statistically significant, sensitivity analysis suggested improvement in patients with moderate baseline function [MD = 8.27, 95%CI (5.66 ~ 10.87), p < 0.00001 for the overall effect]. EGDM may improve muscle strength and physical function in ICU patients. The available evidence does not confirm a reduction in ICU-AW. The effects on ventilation duration and ICU stay varied substantially across studies, likely influenced by sedation protocols, weaning practices, and other context-specific factors. Further rigorous trials with detailed reporting of interventions and contextual factors are needed to guide precise clinical implementation. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261280603, CRD420261280603.

articles.title: Nurse Competencies, Patient Characteristics, and Pain Management Protocol Adherence in Intensive Care Units: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study Accounting for ICU Clustering.
articles.abstract: To examine the associations between nurse competencies (knowledge, self-efficacy, and attitude), patient characteristics, and pain management protocol adherence in adult intensive care units, while accounting for between-ICU clustering. Adherence to pain management protocols remains suboptimal despite available guidelines. Nurse competencies are essential for evidence-based practice, yet their translation into clinical performance may depend on contextual factors. ICU-level organizational context has been described in recent reviews, but empirical examination of these relationships remains limited. This multicenter cross-sectional study included 525 ICU nurses from seven hospitals in Tehran, Iran (July-October 2025). One index patient was assessed for each nurse. ICU-level organizational characteristics were assessed through unit observation and head nurse interviews. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for protocol adherence was computed from an empty mixed model. Multivariable linear regression with ICU entered as a fixed effect was used to identify individual-level factors associated with adherence. Organizational context was retained as a descriptive variable only. Protocol adherence was moderate (mean 8.5/12; 32.4% good adherence). The ICC for protocol adherence was 0.02 (95% CI: 0.001-0.15), indicating minimal clustering. In the multivariable model with ICU as a fixed effect (18 predictors), knowledge (β = 0.311), self-efficacy (β = 0.290), and attitude (β = 0.276) remained independently associated with adherence (all p < 0.001). Patient characteristics remained significantly associated: substance use history (β = -0.138, p = 0.016), inability to communicate (β = -0.148, p = 0.010), GCS < 9 (β = -0.160, p = 0.008), and mechanical ventilation (β = -0.121, p = 0.028). The full model explained 53.4% of the variance in adherence. Organizational support across the seven ICUs ranged from 1 to 5 (weighted mean 3.42 ± 1.15). Nurse competencies and patient characteristics are independently associated with pain management protocol adherence in this multicenter ICU sample. Between-ICU clustering was minimal (ICC = 0.02), suggesting that individual-level factors are the primary correlates of adherence in this sample. Given the small number of ICU clusters (n = 7), organizational findings are descriptive only and require confirmation in larger multilevel studies. Nurse managers may consider competency-based pain management education and regular audits with feedback. Given the small number of ICU clusters (n = 7), these recommendations are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multilevel studies.

articles.title: Statistical analysis plan for a stepped-wedge cluster randomized clinical trial for the evaluation of the clinical impact of different telemedicine practices in intensive care units - TELESCOPE 2 trial.
articles.abstract: The optimal model for delivering Tele-ICU is still to be determined. In the TELE-critical Care verSus usual Care on ICU Performance (TELESCOPE) trial, implementing medical-led daily multidisciplinary rounds did not show evidence of improved clinical outcomes. The TELESCOPE 2 trial was therefore designed to evaluate whether expanding this model to include a structured multidisciplinary care bundle, along with a formalized quality and safety management framework, would translate process improvements into measurable patient-centered outcome benefits. To evaluate whether a structured Tele-ICU intervention, comprising intensivist-led daily multidisciplinary rounds, a multidisciplinary care bundle (nursing, physical therapy, pharmacy), and a quality and safety management package, can reduce intensive care unit length of stay in Brazilian public intensive care units. TELESCOPE 2 is a multicenter, open-label, stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial including 25 intensive care units in Brazil from January 2024 to January 2026. Intensive care units are randomized to five sequences, receiving the intervention at staggered times. All adult patients admitted to participating units are eligible, except those admitted for non-medical reasons or those previously included in the study. The multifaceted telemedicine intervention comprises: i) daily multidisciplinary rounds led by board-certified intensivists; ii) coordinated care by a multidisciplinary team; and iii) a management strategy focused on quality improvement and patient safety. The primary outcome is intensive care unit length of stay. Secondary outcomes include clinical endpoints (mortality, ventilator-free days at 28 days, and ventilator-associated events), process-of-care indicators (mobilization, head-of-bed elevation, and sedation management), and unit-level organizational outcomes. We describe the statistical analysis plan for the TELESCOPE 2 trial, finalized prior to database lock. This pre-specified approach mitigates analysis bias and ensures the transparency and robustness of the reported results.

articles.title: Multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions for preventing delirium in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract: It is necessary to evaluate the efficacy of multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions in preventing and managing intensive care unit (ICU) delirium and identify the most effective intervention combinations. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses A&I databases from inception to July 3, 2026, supplemented by a hand search of prior meta-analyses. Only randomized trials were included. Meta-analysis was performed using risk ratios (RR) or mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and modified Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals were used. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized controlled trials. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. The search identified 13 randomized controlled trials encompassing 5,525 patients. Multicomponent interventions significantly reduced delirium incidence (RR 0.53, 95% CI [0.36, 0.76], I2 = 72.5%, low-certainty evidence). The effect remained significant after excluding the two cluster-randomized trials (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.30-0.67; I2 = 55.7%), the active-control trial (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.38-0.79; I2 = 73.0%), and all three trials simultaneously (RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.31-0.70; I2 = 57.0%). In exploratory subgroup analysis, the within-subgroup pooled estimate for component pattern B, comprising cognitive assessment and stimulation, reorientation, sleep and environmental management, family or community support, and physical activity, showed a reduced incidence of delirium (RR 0.43, 95% CI [0.23, 0.82]); however, the formal test for subgroup differences was not significant (p = 0.604). No statistically significant effects were found for delirium duration, ICU or hospital length of stay, delirium-free days, or mortality. This study demonstrated that multi-component interventions effectively reduce delirium incidence in critically ill patients. The evidence did not establish that one component combination was superior to another. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42024592821.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of early mobilization in patients with ARDS: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the effect of early mobilization in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Computerized searches were conducted in PubMed, EMbase, The Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang Data, CBM, and VIP databases for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on early mobilization in ARDS patients. The retrieval period was from the establishment of each database to September 30, 2025. Two reviewers independently assessed the quality of included literature and extracted data in accordance with Cochrane systematic review methodology. Meta-analysis was performed using RevMan 5.4.1 software for eligible studies. A total of 7 RCTs were included, consisting of 4 English and 3 Chinese articles. Meta-analysis showed that compared with conventional treatment, early mobilization significantly reduced the incidence of intensive care unit-acquired weakness (ICU-AW) [OR = 0.35, 95% CI (0.19,0.64), P = 0.0006] and delirium [OR = 0.51, 95% CI (0.28,0.91), P = 0.02], shortened the duration of mechanical ventilation [MD = -2.40,95% CI (-2.96,-1.84), P < 0.00001], length of ICU stay [MD = -3.36, 95% CI (-4.21,-2.52), P < 0.00001] and total hospital stay [MD = -2.74,95% CI (-3.49,-1.98), P < 0.00001]. Meanwhile, it improved patients'functional independence score (Barthel Index) [MD = 17.27, 95% CI (11.18, 23.35), P < 0.00001] and decreased the incidence of complications [OR = 0.39, 95% CI (0.17, 0.86), P = 0.02]. All pooled effects were statistically significant. Early mobilization yields significant clinical benefits for ARDS patients, improving short-term clinical outcomes and functional recovery. It is worthy of clinical promotion and application. However, multicenter, large-sample, and methodologically standardized RCTs are still needed to further verify its long-term effects and optimal implementation protocols.

articles.title: Refractory Status Epilepticus Following Erroneous Intrathecal Injection of Tranexamic Acid: A Case Report and Long-Term Follow-Up and Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Accidental intrathecal injection of tranexamic acid (TXA) is a rare but catastrophic preventable adverse event associated with high mortality and severe neurological consequences. It represents a major neurological emergency that requires immediate specialized management. A 32-year-old man erroneously received an intrathecal injection of 300 mg of TXA instead of bupivacaine during a saphenous vein stripping procedure. He rapidly developed refractory myoclonic status epilepticus, sympathetic hyperactivity, and rhabdomyolysis. Management included multiple antiseizure medications, continuous EEG-guided sedation, and targeted use of neuromuscular blockade. The patient recovered without immediate neurological deficit but developed persistent cognitive impairment and posttraumatic stress disorder at follow-up. This case highlights the severe neurotoxicity of intrathecal TXA and the importance of early and aggressive intensive care management. It also underscores the need for long-term multidisciplinary follow-up for the assessment of anesthetic procedure-related complications.

articles.title: Ketamine use in the refractory and super refractory status epilepticus: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: Refractory status epilepticus (RSE) and super-refractory status epilepticus (SRSE) are associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and intensive care requirements. Ketamine has emerged as a potential adjunct because of its N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonism and relatively favourable haemodynamic profile. To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of ketamine in RSE and SRSE resolution. This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024625516). PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Biblioteca Virtual en Salud were searched from inception to 20 November 2025. Two independent reviewers screened studies, extracted clinical, therapeutic, electroencephalographic, haemodynamic, and survival data, and assessed risk of bias using National Institutes of Health quality assessment tools. Meta-analysis was not performed because of substantial heterogeneity. Twelve studies comprising 491 patients were included. Ketamine was generally administered as part of multimodal therapy after failure of several antiseizure medications and intravenous anaesthetics. Infusion rates ranged from 0.05 mg/kg/h to 10.5 mg/kg/h, and treatment duration ranged from 6 h to 29 days. Study-defined response rates following ketamine initiation ranged from 43.3% for complete electrographic seizure cessation to 100% for overall RSE/SRSE resolution; however, the highest estimates often reflected combined treatment rather than ketamine alone. Short-term or hospital survival ranged from 45.8% to 81.8%. Immediate haemodynamic deterioration appeared uncommon, although attribution was limited by baseline instability and concomitant therapy. Ketamine-containing regimens were associated with clinically relevant seizure reduction or cessation in RSE/SRSE, without a consistent signal of acute haemodynamic harm. However, the independent effect of ketamine on sustained seizure control, survival, and functional recovery remains uncertain. Prospective comparative studies using standardised dosing, timing, and outcome definitions are required. PROSPERO identifier CRD42024625516.

articles.title: Cenobamate in super-refractory status epilepticus: current evidence from a patient-level synthesis.
articles.abstract: Super-refractory status epilepticus (SRSE) represents a challenging neurological emergency, with limited therapeutic options after conventional intravenous antiseizure medications (ASMs) and continuous anesthetic therapy have failed. Cenobamate has shown remarkable efficacy in drug-resistant focal epilepsy, but its role in SRSE is currently supported only by isolated case reports. We performed a patient-level synthesis of published cases of cenobamate-treated SRSE, focusing on treatment latency, titration strategy, electroclinical response, concomitant therapies, safety, and functional outcomes. Three publications reporting six patients were identified. Cenobamate was introduced between 13 and 103 days after SRSE onset, following failure of multiple intravenous and oral ASMs, anesthetic agents, and, in most cases, immunomodulatory therapies. Although the timing of treatment initiation varied substantially, electroencephalographic improvement generally occurred within two weeks after cenobamate initiation and was usually accompanied by clinical recovery, successful withdrawal of anesthetic therapy, and liberation from the intensive care unit. Most patients initiated cenobamate at the recommended dose of 12.5 mg/day but underwent individualized dose-escalation schedules compared with the approved outpatient regimen. No cases of drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, severe cardiac adverse events, or treatment discontinuation attributable to cenobamate were reported. Although the available evidence remains limited to a small number of observational reports, this patient-level synthesis identified consistent clinical patterns that support further investigation of cenobamate as an adjunctive therapy for SRSE. At present, no conclusions regarding treatment efficacy can be drawn. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to clarify cenobamate optimal timing, titration strategy, safety, and potential role within SRSE treatment algorithms.

articles.title: Cardiac troponin T and 28-day mortality in traumatic brain injury: a retrospective cohort study and machine learning prediction model.
articles.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) frequently induces cardiac dysfunction via the brain-heart axis, yet the prognostic value of cardiac troponin T (cTnT) in TBI remains incompletely characterized. This study investigated thye association between cTnT levels and 28-day all-cause mortality in TBI patients and developed a machine learning-based prediction model. This retrospective cohort study included 837 adult TBI patients from the MIMIC-III/IV databases (development cohort) and 121 patients from a single Chinese center (external validation cohort). The first cTnT measurement within 24 h of ICU admission was analyzed. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) regression was used to explore nonlinear relationships. cTnT was categorized into quartiles (Q1 ≤ 0.03, Q2 0.03-0.06, Q3 0.06-0.17, Q4 > 0.17 ng/mL). A two-step Boruta plus LASSO feature selection identified 13 robust predictors. Five machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, BART, GBM, CTREE, SVM) were trained. The primary outcome was 28-day all-cause mortality. Among 837 patients, 217 (25.9%) died within 28 days. RCS revealed a significant nonlinear association (P for nonlinearity < 0.001). In multivariable Cox regression adjusted for the 12 LASSO-selected covariates (excluding cTnT quartile itself), patients in Q3 and Q4 had nearly twofold higher mortality risks compared with Q1 (HR = 2.01, 95% CI: 1.37-2.95, p < 0.001; and HR = 1.96, 95% CI: 1.31-2.93, p = 0.001, respectively). Random Forest achieved the best discriminative performance, with an internal AUC of 0.783 and an external validation AUC of 0.706 (95% CI: 0.584-0.828). The model also demonstrated good calibration (Brier score = 0.155) and favorable clinical utility across clinically relevant threshold probabilities as shown by decision curve analysis. Elevated cTnT is independently associated with 28-day mortality in TBI patients, with a potential risk threshold of ≥0.06 ng/mL. The Random Forest model integrating cTnT with clinical variables provides moderate mortality prediction. cTnT may serve as an integrative marker of systemic stress and multi-organ dysfunction in TBI.

articles.title: Intraoperative Dexmedetomidine and Postoperative Delirium After Head and Neck Cancer Surgery with Free-Flap Reconstruction: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: Postoperative delirium is common after major head and neck cancer surgery. We investigated whether intraoperative dexmedetomidine infusion was associated with a lower incidence of postoperative delirium in patients undergoing head and neck cancer surgery requiring free-flap reconstruction. This was a delirium-focused secondary analysis of a single-centre, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Adult patients with head and neck cancer scheduled for elective surgery requiring free-flap reconstruction under general anaesthesia were randomly assigned to receive intraoperative dexmedetomidine infusion at 0.3 μg kg-1h-1 until 1 h before the end of surgery; subjects in the placebo group were given comparable volumes of normal saline. The primary outcome was the incidence of delirium during the first 5 postoperative days, assessed once daily using the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). There was less delirium during the initial 5 postoperative days in patients assigned to dexmedetomidine (14.9%, 7 of 47 patients) than in those given placebo (34.7%, 17 of 49 patients). Dexmedetomidine was associated with lower odds of postoperative delirium after adjustment for age, preoperative Mini-Mental State Examination score, and operative time (adjusted odds ratio 0.31, 95% confidence interval 0.10-0.92; p = 0.036). Postoperative pain and early sleep outcomes were improved by dexmedetomidine. Haemodynamic adverse events and postoperative complications did not differ significantly between groups. In patients undergoing head and neck cancer surgery with free-flap reconstruction, intraoperative dexmedetomidine infusion was associated with a lower incidence of postoperative delirium during the first 5 postoperative days, without an apparent increase in perioperative adverse events. ChiCTR2300067376.

articles.title: Association between Early Postoperative Sodium Change and Postoperative Delirium after General Anesthesia.
articles.journal: Journal of Nippon Medical School = Nippon Ika Daigaku zasshi
articles.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a frequent neuropsychiatric complication after surgery under general anesthesia and is associated with adverse outcomes. Although perioperative dysnatremia has been linked to POD, most studies relied on static sodium measurements and failed to capture early postoperative dynamics. We investigated whether early postoperative sodium change is associated with late-onset POD. This retrospective single-center cohort study included adults undergoing surgery under general anesthesia between July 2021 and December 2025. A Day-3 landmark design ensured temporal precedence between exposure and outcome. Perioperative sodium change (ΔNa) was defined as the difference between preoperative baseline sodium and the most recent sodium value within 48 hours after surgery and was categorized as decrease (≤-3 mmol/L), stable (-3 to +3 mmol/L), or increase (≥+3 mmol/L). Late-onset POD occurring on postoperative days 3 through 7 was identified using the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist and antipsychotic prescriptions. Multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline models were applied. Among 18,424 patients, both perioperative sodium increase and decrease were independently associated with higher odds of late-onset POD, as compared with stable sodium levels. Baseline preoperative sodium was not associated with POD. Spline analyses showed a U-shaped association between ΔNa and POD, with the lowest risk was near ΔNa = 0 mmol/L. Findings were consistent across sensitivity and subgroup analyses. Early postoperative sodium fluctuations were associated with increased risk of late-onset POD. Monitoring of perioperative sodium trajectories may aid in stratifying early postoperative risk.

articles.title: Relationship Between Blood Urea Nitrogen to Albumin Ratio and Risks of Mortality and Delirium in Pancreatitis Patients: A Retrospective Analysis of the MIMIC-IV Database.
articles.abstract: This study is aimed at evaluating the predictive value of the blood urea nitrogen-to-albumin ratio (BAR) for both mortality and delirium risk in patients with pancreatitis. Pancreatitis carries a substantial mortality risk and significant long-term sequelae, with delirium being a severe neurological complication, underscoring the clinical need for effective prognostic markers. A retrospective cohort study was performed using the MIMIC-IV v3.0 database. A total of 1748 ICU patients meeting diagnostic criteria for pancreatitis (ICD-9/10 codes: 577.0, 577.1, K85) with documented baseline blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and albumin levels were included. BAR was calculated (BUN[mg/dL]/Albumin[g/dL]) and patients were stratified into quartiles (Q1: BAR < 3.0; Q2: BAR 3.0-5.0; Q3: BAR 5.0-9.2; Q4: BAR ≥ 9.2). The primary endpoints were all-cause mortality and delirium occurrence (identified using ICD-9 codes 293.0, 293.1, and ICD-10 codes F05, F05.9). Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression (mortality) and logistic regression (delirium) were employed, adjusting for demographics, illness severity scores (GCS, SAPS II, OASIS, and Charlson Comorbidity Index), and comorbidities. Restricted cubic splines (RCS) were used to explore nonlinear associations. Higher BAR levels significantly correlated with greater disease severity: compared with Q1, Q4 exhibited a higher Charlson Comorbidity Index and mortality rate. BAR was an independent predictor of delirium; each 1-unit increase in BAR was associated with a 2.7% increased risk of delirium (adjusted OR = 1.027, 95% CI: 1.009-1.044), and patients in Q4 had a significantly higher risk compared with those in Q1 (adjusted OR = 1.882, 95% CI: 1.157-3.108). After multivariable adjustment, BAR was not significantly independently associated with mortality (Q4 adjusted HR = 1.022, p = 0.8). RCS analysis revealed BAR > 9.0 as a high-risk threshold, characterized by delirium OR > 1.78 and mortality HR > 1.97. The BAR quartile model yielded AUCs of 0.635 and 0.599 for predicting mortality and delirium, respectively, indicating modest predictive ability. BAR independently predicts delirium risk and reflects disease severity in pancreatitis patients, but does not demonstrate significant independent predictive value for mortality after accounting for confounders. The identified threshold (BAR > 9.0) supports the utility of BAR as a supplementary biomarker for delirium risk stratification in this population.

articles.title: External validation and comparative performance of four risk scores for acute kidney injury in critically ill adults.
articles.abstract: Several parsimonious scores predict acute kidney injury (AKI), but their comparative performance in critically ill adults is uncertain. We hypothesized that the ICU-derived UCSD-Mayo score would show higher discrimination than three scores developed in broader acute-care populations. This single-center retrospective validation study included 1,723 emergency ICU patients admitted from 2014 to 2021. We compared the UCSD-Mayo, AKI-RiSc, Bell, and APS scores for in-hospital AKI, AKI within 7 days, and stages 2 and 3 AKI. Analyses included AUROC with paired DeLong comparisons, cross-validated local recalibration, calibration plots, IDI, categorical NRI at the event rate, decision-curve analysis, and prespecified sensitivity analyses. In-hospital AKI occurred in 406 patients (23.6%), 281 (16.3%) developed AKI within 7 days, and 169 (9.8%) developed stages 2 and 3 AKI. UCSD-Mayo had the highest observed AUROC for in-hospital AKI (0.713, 95%CI 0.685-0.740), 7-day AKI (0.690, 0.658-0.723), and stages 2 and 3 AKI (0.706, 0.665-0.746). Its 7-day AUROC did not differ significantly from AKI-RiSc (difference 0.029, 95%CI -0.006 to 0.064; p = 0.103). Reclassification and net benefit varied by outcome and threshold; sensitivity analyses did not materially change the overall pattern. In this single-center Chinese emergency ICU cohort, UCSD-Mayo showed the highest observed discrimination, but improvements were modest and were not uniform across all outcomes, metrics, or decision thresholds. These scores may support risk awareness and monitoring but should not be used as stand-alone treatment rules.

articles.title: Low-intensity versus medium-intensity continuous renal replacement therapy for critically ill patients (LIMIT) trial: Protocol summary and statistical analysis plan of a randomised clinical trial.
articles.journal: Critical care and resuscitation : journal of the Australasian Academy of Critical Care Medicine
articles.abstract: Severe acute kidney injury in critically ill patients may require continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), yet mortality remains high. A standard CRRT intensity is 20-25 mL/kg/hr, because higher doses have not improved outcomes. Excessive treatment may cause harm by removing antibiotics and other essential substances and potentially impairing renal recovery. Observational data suggest that lower-intensity CRRT may be effective, warranting a clinical trial to compare low-versus standard-intensity therapy. The objective of this study was to describe the prespecified protocol and the statistical analysis plan of the low-intensity versus medium-intensity continuous renal replacement therapy for critically Ill patients (LIMIT) trial. The LIMIT trial is an investigator-initiated, multicentre, open-label, randomised clinical trial, with a target sample size of 400 participants. The trial compares low-intensity CRRT (12 mL/kg/hr) and medium-intensity CRRT (25 mL/kg/hr) in adult patients with acute kidney injury requiring CRRT in the participating intensive care units. The primary outcome is a hierarchical composite of survival and time to successful liberation from RRT through day 28 from randomisation, analysed using a win-ratio. Secondary outcomes include intensive care unit mortality, hospital mortality, dialysis dependence at hospital discharge among survivors, vasopressor-free days at day 28, and ventilator-free days at day 28. The LIMIT trial will evaluate the effect of low-intensity CRRT on mortality and time to successful liberation from RRT compared with medium-intensity CRRT in adults with acute kidney injury. Its findings may also inform future research on broader patient-centred and societal implications of CRRT intensity.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and continuous renal replacement therapy.
articles.abstract: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is an important intervention in the treatment of acute kidney injury (AKI) in intensive care, and its application scope continues to expand alongside technological advancements and an increasing patient population. However, in current clinical practice, several factors, including individual patient differences, dynamic treatment needs, and the rational allocation of medical resources, pose challenges to CRRT implementation. The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) offers new approaches to address some of these challenges, and its applications in developing decision-support models, refining workflows, and supporting patient communication and education may contribute to more precise and efficient CRRT management. In this article, we discuss the current evidence and potential applications of AI in CRRT, as well as the challenges and strategies for clinical implementation, aiming to provide a reference for future research and clinical translation of AI-assisted CRRT.

articles.title: Serum ammonia improves early risk stratification beyond West Haven criteria in acute liver failure.
articles.journal: Liver transplantation : official publication of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and the International Liver Transplantation Society
authors: US Acute Liver Failure Study Group
articles.abstract: The prognosis of patients with acute liver failure (ALF) presenting with low grade hepatic encephalopathy (HE) defined by the West Haven criteria (WHC) is difficult to establish. We studied the association between HE severity, assessed by WHC and serum ammonia, with outcomes across different age groups. Retrospective analysis of the prospective multicentre United States ALF Study Group registry (2000-2016). Exposures were WHC and serum ammonia on day 1 post inclusion. Endpoints were transplant-free survival (TFS) and mortality due to cerebral events on day 21. Findings were validated in a different and more recent (2010-2023) European cohort. Among 1092 patients, median age was 39 years and 526 (48.2%) had acetaminophen toxicity. On day 1, 968 (88.6%) patients were in the intensive care unit and 669 (61.3%) were receiving any specific organ support (ventilation vasopressors, or renal replacement therapy). TFS and cerebral mortality on day 21 were 45.2% and 6.3%, respectively. Patients with hyperammonemia (≥50 µmol/L) on day 1 had lower TFS on day 21 than others, both for WHC grades 1-2 (53.0% vs. 65.2%) and 3-4 (31.8% vs. 60.9%). Higher ammonia on day 1 was independently associated with lower TFS on day 21, irrespective of WHC grade (odds ratio of 0.958 per each 10 µmol/L increment). Ammonia on day 1 of ≥100 µmol/L showed a significant threshold effect for TFS or cerebral mortality on day 21. Patients with <40 years had the highest probability of cerebral mortality on day 21. In ALF, serum ammonia may help to define HE and assess prognosis earlier, irrespective of WHC grade. Patients with early serum ammonia of ≥100 µmol/L require optimized monitoring and treatment.

articles.title: Rethinking Oliguria in the ICU: From Threshold to Trajectory.

Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Major Postoperative Complications After Noncardiac Surgery Under General Anesthesia Using Routinely Available Electronic Health Record Data: Retrospective Multicenter Development and Validation Study.
articles.abstract: Postoperative complications after noncardiac surgery under general anesthesia remain a major cause of morbidity, mortality, and resource-intensive care. Conventional risk assessment tools rely mainly on preoperative information and may not capture perioperative physiological and procedural factors associated with postoperative risk. This retrospective multicenter observational study aimed to develop and validate electronic health record (EHR)-based machine learning (ML) models for predicting major postoperative complications and to evaluate their discrimination, overall probabilistic performance, calibration, and potential clinical utility. We analyzed 35,702 adults who underwent noncardiac surgery under general anesthesia at 3 tertiary hospitals between January 2021 and March 2025. Preoperative, intraoperative, and early postoperative variables were extracted from diagnosis procedure combination (DPC) claims, EHRs, and anesthesia information systems. The primary outcome was a 30-day composite of in-hospital death, unplanned reoperation, prolonged mechanical ventilation, new initiation of renal replacement therapy, and postoperative infection. Logistic regression (LR), extreme gradient boosting (XGB), and light gradient boosting machine (LGBM) models were developed using preoperative variables alone or with 7 additional intraoperative and early postoperative variables. Leave-one-facility-out internal-external cross-validation (IECV) was the primary validation framework, with a stratified random 80:20 hold-out analysis as secondary validation. Performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC), Brier score, scaled Brier score, calibration measures, and decision curve analysis. The primary composite outcome occurred in 3884 of 35,702 patients (10.9%). In pooled IECV, perioperative models consistently outperformed the corresponding preoperative models. AUROC increased from 0.784-0.791 to 0.810-0.817, PR-AUC increased from 0.356-0.361 to 0.405-0.413, Brier scores decreased from 0.082-0.083 to 0.078-0.080, and scaled Brier scores increased from 0.144-0.151 to 0.175-0.191. Calibration varied across facilities; pooled calibration slopes for the perioperative models ranged from 0.875 to 0.902, and calibration intercepts ranged from -0.367 to -0.222, indicating overly extreme predictions and overall risk overestimation. Exploratory decision curve analysis generally showed greater net benefit for perioperative models across threshold probabilities of 0.01-0.30, although the curves overlapped substantially. Secondary and sensitivity analyses were consistent with the primary findings. Adding routinely available intraoperative and early postoperative variables produced modest but consistent improvements in postoperative risk prediction compared with preoperative variables alone. However, facility-specific variation in calibration limits direct transportability of absolute risk estimates. The models may support prioritization for postoperative clinical reassessment, but exploratory decision curve analysis did not establish a specific intervention or triage threshold. Local recalibration and prospective workflow evaluation are required before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Ex Vivo Assessment of Lamotrigine Clearance During Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy.
articles.abstract: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) provides renal support for unstable ICU patients but significantly alters drug concentrations. For patients on long-term antiepileptics such as lamotrigine, CRRT may increase risk for breakthrough seizures due to subtherapeutic levels. Conversely, CRRT may aid in lamotrigine overdose. While partial clearance of lamotrigine by intermittent hemodialysis has been reported, CRRT clearance is not well studied. This study determined lamotrigine extraction by CRRT in an ex vivo system. Medication was administered at two concentrations: one therapeutic and one supratherapeutic to closed-loop, blood-primed, ex vivo CRRT circuits. Drug concentrations were measured in plasma, hemofiltrate (effluent), and matching control samples at specific time points. For each time point, percent recovery of lamotrigine was calculated, and differences between CRRT circuits and controls were analyzed using two-sample t-tests. Plasma lamotrigine concentrations decreased rapidly, with 10% (n = 3, SD = 4%) and 17% (n = 2, SD = 3%) recovery at four hours for therapeutic and supratherapeutic doses, respectively. Although lower starting concentrations trended toward greater clearance, differences were not statistically significant (P = .13). Control concentrations remained stable, with approximately 100% recovery. Lamotrigine concentrations were significantly affected by CRRT circuits. Patients receiving lamotrigine who require CRRT may need dosing adjustments to maintain clinical efficacy. Additionally, CRRT effectively clears lamotrigine, suggesting potential utility in overdose management.

articles.title: Refractory Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Supported by Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation due to Leptospirosis at Réunion Island and a Literature Review.
articles.journal: The American journal of tropical medicine and hygiene
articles.abstract: Leptospirosis is a zoonosis prevalent on Réunion Island. Severe forms with acute respiratory failure can lead to refractory hypoxemia, requiring the use of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). The aim for the present study was to describe all cases of leptospirosis complicated by refractory acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) requiring veno-venous ECMO on Réunion Island and to conduct a literature review. This retrospective observational study was conducted in a multidisciplinary intensive care unit of the University Hospital of Réunion Island. The aim was to describe the clinical, biological, and prognostic characteristics of patients who developed leptospirosis complicated by refractory ARDS requiring ECMO between January 2011 and December 2024. A total of 14 patients with a median age of 38 years and few comorbidities were included. The organ failure most commonly associated with respiratory involvement was acute kidney injury (93%). The median delay between mechanical ventilation and ECMO support was 0 (0-1) days. The median duration of ECMO support was short (7 [4-12] days). The mortality rate in this population was 29%. A systematic literature review revealed 50 cases of patients with leptospirosis requiring ECMO, with a median age of 34 years and a mortality rate of 20%. The favorable prognosis of patients with refractory ARDS due to leptospirosis justifies the use of ECMO. Early referral to a center equipped with ECMO is essential, given the rapid decline in respiratory function.

articles.title: Stress hyperglycemia ratio as a marker of major postoperative complications after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass.
articles.abstract: This study examined whether the stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) at intensive care unit (ICU) admission is associated with major postoperative complications after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass and whether this association differs from that of absolute ICU admission glucose. This single-center retrospective study included 731 surgical episodes from 709 adults who underwent cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. SHR was calculated as the first ICU glucose divided by HbA1c-derived estimated average glucose. The primary outcome was an unweighted composite of 30-day mortality, stroke, Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes stage 3 acute kidney injury, reoperation for bleeding, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and deep sternal wound infection. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for clinically relevant covariates. The composite outcome occurred in 90 surgical episodes (12.3%). SHR was associated with the composite outcome after adjustment (odds ratio [OR], 1.103 per 0.1 increase; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.008-1.208; P = 0.033), whereas ICU admission glucose was not significantly associated (OR, 1.019 per 10 mg/dL increase; 95% CI 0.946-1.096; P = 0.626). SHR at ICU admission was associated with major postoperative complications in the primary analysis, whereas absolute ICU admission glucose was not significantly associated after multivariable adjustment. Confidence intervals for SHR included 1.0 in several sensitivity analyses. SHR warrants prospective evaluation as an early postoperative risk marker after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass.

articles.title: When Insulin Must Wait: The Role of Renal Replacement Therapy in Refractory Hypokalemia During Severe Diabetic Ketoacidosis.
articles.journal: The American journal of case reports
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a common life-threatening metabolic emergency characterized by hyperglycemia, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and ketosis. Severe hypokalemia before insulin therapy is uncommon but may complicate management and delay treatment. CASE REPORT A 37-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of generalized abdominal pain and progressive shortness of breath. He was drowsy and tachypneic, with Kussmaul respirations. Laboratory evaluation revealed severe DKA, acute kidney injury, and severe hypokalemia. Insulin therapy was initially withheld according to the DKA protocol. Intravenous potassium supplementation failed to achieve sustained correction, resulting in repeated interruptions of insulin therapy. Due to refractory hypokalemia, an emergency 2-hour session of intermittent hemodialysis was performed, followed by continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). During CRRT, serum potassium increased, serum creatinine decreased, metabolic acidosis improved, and the anion gap closed. Insulin therapy was resumed without further interruption. However, the clinical course was complicated by severe septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and catastrophic intracerebral hemorrhage, ultimately resulting in death. CONCLUSIONS Severe hypokalemia at presentation in DKA poses a critical therapeutic challenge because insulin therapy must be withheld until the electrolyte abnormality is corrected. In rare cases of refractory hypokalemia, CRRT may serve as an adjunctive strategy to facilitate metabolic stabilization and safe DKA management. This case adds to the limited literature and highlights the need for further studies to clarify the role and effectiveness of this approach. Biochemical resolution of DKA may not correspond to clinical recovery, and critically ill patients warrant continuous monitoring.

articles.title: Association Between the Modified Renal Angina Index and Major Adverse Kidney Events at 90 Days in Critically Ill Adults: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Adult modified Renal Angina Index (mRAI) formulations predict acute kidney injury, but their association with major adverse kidney events at 90 days (MAKE90) remains unclear. We examined the association in critically ill adults without established chronic kidney disease (CKD). Methods: This retrospective cohort included 250 adults admitted to a tertiary intensive care unit (ICU) between December 2023 and April 2025. mRAI was calculated from data available at ICU admission. MAKE90 was defined as death, renal replacement therapy, or persistent renal dysfunction within 90 days. We used logistic regression, receiver operating characteristic analysis, and nested-model comparisons. Results: Admission mRAI was higher in patients with MAKE90 than in those without MAKE90 (median 10 [IQR 5-20] vs. 3 [IQR 1-6]; p < 0.001). After adjustment for SOFA score and sepsis, mRAI remained associated with MAKE90 (adjusted OR per point from the linear model, 1.073; 95% CI, 1.032-1.116). Spline analysis demonstrated a significant nonlinear association (p = 0.004), indicating that the per-point OR should be interpreted as a summary estimate rather than a constant effect across the score range. The AUC of mRAI was 0.752 (95% CI, 0.691-0.814), higher than that of admission AKI stage (0.653) and not significantly different from APACHE II (0.702) or SOFA (0.718). Adding mRAI to SOFA and sepsis raised the AUC from 0.735 to 0.782. Conclusions: In critically ill adults without established CKD, higher admission mRAI remained associated with MAKE90 after adjustment for SOFA score and sepsis and showed moderate discrimination. External validation in larger, independent cohorts is needed to confirm these findings.

articles.title: Meropenem Exposure, Target Attainment, and Therapeutic Drug Monitoring Practices in Critically Ill Adults Receiving Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: To critically evaluate meropenem pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) target attainment, therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM), infusion strategies, and clinical outcomes during continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Ovid MEDLINE, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to August 15, 2026, using meropenem, TDM, β-lactam, and CRRT terms, with adult, human, and English-language limits. Thirteen reports representing 12 unique studies (2 randomized, 10 non-randomized) reporting meropenem concentration data during CRRT were included. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2 or ROBINS-I. Total clearance ranged from 3.60 to 6.6 L/h. Lower or primary PK/PD target non-attainment ranged from 0% to 26.7%, while aggressive-target non-attainment ranged from 0% to 53.3% in most analyses and reached 93% in 1 study when a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 8 mg/L was assumed. Continuous or prolonged infusion may facilitate sustained exposure, but comparative evidence was limited. Four used routine TDM; only 2 implemented protocolized TDM-guided dose adjustment. Low exposure was associated with higher mortality in 1 adjusted observational analysis, but evidence for clinical outcomes was of very low certainty. Standardized meropenem regimens cannot be assumed to provide consistent exposure during CRRT. Optimized infusion and timely, protocolized TDM may support individualized dosing when multidisciplinary expertise is available. Available evidence supports a shift from standardized empirical dosing toward individualized, measurement-guided meropenem therapy in patients receiving CRRT.

articles.title: Association Between Albumin-Bilirubin Index and Clinical Outcomes in Septic Acute Kidney Injury Patients.
articles.abstract: BackgroundThe albumin-bilirubin index (ALBI) has been reported as a prognostic marker in various clinical conditions; however, its value in patients with septic acute kidney injury (AKI) has not been clearly evaluated. This study aimed to investigate the association between ALBI and clinical outcomes in this population.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study used data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database. ALBI was analyzed as both a continuous variable in the primary analysis and a categorical variable according to tertiles in sensitivity analysis. The primary outcomes were 28-day, 60-day, 90-day, and 1-year all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included intensive care unit (ICU) transfer, septic shock, and disease severity. Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate the association between ALBI and mortality, and restricted cubic spline analyses were performed to assess potential nonlinearity. Subgroup analyses were further conducted to examine the consistency across different sub-group populations.ResultsOverall, 6700 patients with septic AKI were included. In adjusted Cox models, each 1-standard deviation increase in ALBI was associated with higher risks of 28-day mortality (HR 1.16, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.10-1.22), 60-day mortality (HR 1.14, 95% CI 1.10-1.19), 90-day mortality (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.08-1.18), and 1-year mortality (HR 1.10, 95% CI 1.06-1.14). The association between ALBI and mortality was generally consistent across most prespecified subgroups. Higher ALBI was also linked with septic shock (odds ratio [OR] 1.15, 95%CI 1.08-1.21, P < .001), ICU transfer (OR 1.09, 95%CI 1.02-1.16), and greater disease severity. RCS curves showed a nonlinear increase in mortality risk with ascending ALBI. Sensitivity analyses based on ALBI tertiles yielded broadly consistent findings.ConclusionHigher ALBI was independently associated with increased short- and long-term mortality and adverse clinical outcomes in septic AKI patients.

articles.title: Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation in Dextrocardia: Lessons From a Complex Redo Case.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Dextrocardia with situs solitus poses significant surgical challenges for left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation, particularly in patients with prior sternotomy and complex valvular disease. We report on a 60 year old man with dextrocardia, advanced heart failure, prior mechanical mitral valve replacement, and bicuspid aortic valve disease who underwent successful Corheart 6 LVAD implantation during redo sternotomy with concomitant bioprosthetic aortic and mitral valve replacement. Intraoperative findings included extensive pannus/thrombus on the mechanical mitral prosthesis (causing relative stenosis) and an unsuspected 10 g left atrial thrombus, both of which were removed. Total cardiopulmonary bypass time was 330 minutes, and aortic cross‑clamp time was 233 minutes. Postoperative acute kidney injury requiring dialysis resolved, and the patient was discharged after 137 days. At 1 year follow-up, the left ventricular end-diastolic diameter decreased from 69 to 66 mm, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) remained stable (28-25%), New York Heart Association (NYHA) class improved from IIIb‑IV to II, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) recovered from 32 ml/min at 9 months to 51 ml/min at 1 year.

articles.title: [Correlation between acute kidney injury diagnosed by serum creatinine and urine output criteria and short-term prognosis in critically ill patients following non-cardiac surgery].
articles.journal: Beijing da xue xue bao. Yi xue ban = Journal of Peking University. Health sciences
articles.abstract: To analyze the correlation between acute kidney injury (AKI) diagnosed by elevated serum creatinine (Scr) versus only meeting the urine output (UO) reduction criteria and short-term adverse outcomes in critically ill patients following non-cardiac surgery, and to evaluate the association between even mild elevations in Scr and clinical outcomes furthermore. This study was a secondary analysis of data from a prospective cohort study. A total of 1020 non-cardiac surgery adults admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) of Peking University First Hospital from May 20, 2019 to March 7, 2022 were included. According to Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guideline, AKI patients were classified into two groups: the AKI-Scr group (those meeting the Scr elevation criteria) and the AKI-UO group (those fulfilling only the UO reduction criteria). The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality in patients with AKI, and the secondary outcomes were major renal adverse events, post-operative renal replacement therapy (RRT), postoperative complications, postoperative mechanical ventilation time, ICU stay, postoperative hospital stay, total hospital stay, and total medical costs. Multivariate Logistic regression analysis was used to identify risk factors of hospitalized death in critically ill patients with AKI following non-cardiac surgery. A total of 1020 non-cardiac surgical patients admitted to the ICU were enrolled, among whom 429 were diagnosed with AKI. There were 91 cases in the AKI-Scr group and 338 cases in the AKI-UO group. The primary study endpoint: no statistically significant difference in in-hospital mortality was observed between the AKI-Scr and AKI-UO groups (5.5% vs. 2.1%, P>0.05). The secondary study endpoints: compared with the AKI-UO group, the patients in the AKI-Scr group had a higher incidence of major renal adverse events (9.8% vs. 4.4%), postoperative RRT (4.4% vs. 0.3%) and postoperative complications (50.5% vs. 24.0%, all P < 0.05), a significantly longer duration of postoperative mechanical ventilation (12.0 d vs. 7.5 d), ICU stay (2 d vs. 1 d), postoperative hospital stay (14 d vs. 9 d) and total hospital stay (21 d vs.17 d, all P < 0.05), and a significantly higher total medical expenditure (112000 yuan vs. 89000 yuan, P<0.001). Multivariate Logistic regression analysis showed that postoperative RRT (OR=33.164, 95%CI: 1.305-842.794, P=0.034) and sepsis during hospitalization (OR=23.096, 95%CI: 4.242-125.175, P < 0.001) were independent risk factors for hospitalized death in the critically ill patients with postoperative AKI. Compared with the ΔScr≤24% patients (Scr increased by less than 24% from baseline within 7 d), even in the patients with only a minor elevation in Scr (ΔScr increase of 25%-49% from baseline but < 26.5μmol/L), the incidence of postoperative complications was significantly higher (48.6% vs. 19.2%, P < 0.001), along with prolonged ICU stay [1(1, 3) d vs. 1(1, 2) d], postoperative hospital stay (13 d vs. 9 d), and total hospital stay (23 d vs. 16 d, all P < 0.05). Compared with the non-AKI group, the incidence of in-hospital mortality (2.1% vs. 0.3%, P < 0.05) and postoperative complications (24.0% vs. 18.3%, P < 0.05) was higher in the AKI-UO group, and the ICU stay [1(1, 3) d vs. 1(1, 2) d, P < 0.001] was longer. In critically ill patients with AKI following non-cardiac surgery, the short-term prognosis of patients with AKI whose diagnosis was mainly based on increased Scr was worse than patients who only met the diagnostic criteria of oliguria. Even a mild elevation in serum creatinine was associated with adverse patient outcomes.

articles.title: Drug Dosing During Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in Critically Ill Patients: A Practical Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Drug dosing during continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is difficult in critically ill patients because drug exposure is influenced by both the patient and the extracorporeal treatment. This narrative review provides a practical overview of drug dosing during CRRT, while intermittent hemodialysis and sustained low-efficiency dialysis are discussed only where they provide relevant contextual or comparative information. It summarizes the main drug-related, patient-related, and treatment-related factors that influence extracorporeal drug clearance and discusses their clinical implications for commonly used drug classes. Loading and maintenance doses should be considered separately: loading doses depend mainly on volume of distribution and the need for early therapeutic exposure, whereas maintenance dosing depends on total clearance, including residual renal, extracorporeal, and non-renal clearance.
