Multiple clinical factors jointly affect vancomycin steady-state trough concentrations in patients undergoing combined CABG and valve surgery, including dosing regimen, age, renal biomarkers, and critical-care supportive interventions such as IABP, CRRT and prolonged mechanical ventilation. IABP support represents an intriguing observational signal; this finding remains hypothesis-generating and requires prospective external validation before it can guide formal dose-adjustment strategies. Individualized vancomycin management for this population should comprehensively integrate hemodynamic support measures and laboratory indices rather than depend merely on renal-function markers. This study focuses on clinically accessible trough concentration monitoring rather than constructing complex pharmacokinetic models, which is more in line with real-world clinical practice.

articles.title: Case Report: mNGS-negative Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome with small bowel obstruction as the initial manifestation in a glucocorticoid-exposed COPD patient: a fatal case.
articles.abstract: Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome (SHS) is a life-threatening condition in immunocompromised hosts with an extremely high mortality rate. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) demonstrates limited sensitivity for parasitic detection, and its clinical value remains to be fully elucidated. The conventional microscopy remains an indispensable tool for the diagnosis of parasitic infections. A 73-year-old male patient with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and cerebral infarction presented with abdominal pain and distension for 7 days and no bowel movement for 3 days. He was diagnosed with incomplete small bowel obstruction at an outside hospital and treated with fasting, enemas, meropenem, and methylprednisolone. He was subsequently transferred to our hospital due to acute lower respiratory tract infection. Chest radiography revealed bilateral diffuse infiltrates, and his condition rapidly deteriorated, requiring admission to the intensive care unit (ICU), endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Stool smear and retrospective sputum examination both identified larvae of Strongyloides stercoralis. However, mNGS of sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) obtained upon admission failed to detect any parasitic sequences. The patient was treated sequentially with albendazole and ivermectin, in combination with broad-spectrum antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral therapy. He ultimately died on February 11, 2025, due to severe pneumonia, sepsis, and bone marrow suppression. For immunocompromised hosts with multiple risk factors, particularly those exposed to glucocorticoids, active parasitic microscopic examination of stool and respiratory secretions should be pursued when unexplained pulmonary infiltrates coexist with gastrointestinal symptoms, even in the setting of negative mNGS results, to avoid missed diagnosis.

articles.title: Phenotypic characterization of patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage: a data-driven analysis of a multicentre, retrospective, nationwide cohort.
articles.abstract: Severe diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) is a potentially fatal complication of ANCA-associated vasculitides (AAV). This study aimed to identify distinct clinical phenotypes among patients to the ICU, and to examine their association with mortality. We conducted an ancillary analysis of the national multicenter retrospective PLEXHIA cohort, including 197 patients with severe AAV-related DAH, defined by respiratory symptoms with new infiltrates consistent with alveolar hemorrhage, along with oxygen saturation ≤85%, high-flow oxygen or mechanical ventilation requirement. Kohonen self-organizing maps were applied to predefined clinical variables at ICU admission, excluding treatment and outcomes. Clusters were interpreted and compared regarding organ involvement, severity, management, and mortality at 30 and 90 days. Between 2012 and 2024, 197 patients (66 years old, 52% female) were included, revealing marked clinical heterogeneity. Three phenotypes emerged: The MPO pulmonary-renal (MPO-PR) cluster included patients with anti-MPO ANCA, renal involvement and high oxygen requirements. The mild-respiratory (Mild-R) cluster included predominantly female patients with less severe respiratory compromise and mild renal involvement. The PR3 multi-organ (PR3-MO) cluster involved younger patients with anti-PR3 ANCA, severe acute respiratory failure and multiorgan failure. Renal replacement therapy was most frequent in the MPO-PR group (73%), while invasive mechanical ventilation was most common in the MPO-PR and PR3-MO groups (71% and 68%). Thirty-day mortality differed significantly: 23% (MPO-PR), 4% (mild-R cluster), and 14% (PR3-MO cluster). This large ICU cohort highlights three clinically relevant phenotypes of AAV-related DAH, which could inform the development of phenotype-driven immunosuppressive strategies.

articles.title: Landmark-specific phenotypic heterogeneity in CRRT discontinuation timing: a multi-landmark target trial emulation using MIMIC-IV.
articles.abstract: The optimal timing for discontinuing continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) in critically ill patients remains uncertain. Observational studies commonly simplify discontinuation timing into "early" vs. "delayed" categories, yet the same label may correspond to different clinical states at different stages of illness. We evaluated whether the clinical meaning of the early-discontinuation label and its association with 30-day mortality varied across landmarks and analytic frameworks. Using MIMIC-IV (2008-2019), we emulated a target trial among adults who were alive and still receiving CRRT 48 h after initiation. Early discontinuation was defined as stopping CRRT within 24 h after the 48-hour landmark, whereas delayed discontinuation was defined as continuing CRRT beyond 24 h. The primary outcome was 30-day all-cause mortality. Analyses included crude Cox regression, baseline IPTW-Cox, multi-landmark analyses at 48, 72, 96, and 120 h, a marginal structural model (MSM) using time-varying IPTW, and clone-censor-weighting (CCW) with stabilized censoring weights under a 24-hour grace period. Phenotype decomposition was also performed to assess the clinical composition of patients classified as having early discontinuation at different landmarks. A total of 1,432 patients were included, of whom 369 (25.8%) met the definition of early discontinuation. Baseline IPTW-Cox suggested that early discontinuation was associated with higher 30-day mortality (HR 1.36, 95% CI 1.13-1.64; P = 0.001). Multi-landmark HRs ranged from 1.13 to 1.35 without a monotonic pattern; precision decreased at later landmarks, and the landmark-by-exposure interaction was not statistically significant. The MSM estimate was OR 1.16 (95% CI 0.82-1.63; P = 0.40), and the revised CCW estimate was HR 1.08 (95% CI 0.91-1.28; P = 0.38). Phenotype decomposition showed that sepsis prevalence increased from 55.6% at 48 h to 69.1% at 120 h, baseline vasopressor exposure increased from 55.8% to 71.9%, and urine output decreased from 818 mL to 524 mL. Baseline IPTW generated a significant signal suggesting harm from early CRRT discontinuation, but this was not reproduced in multi-landmark, MSM, or CCW analyses. Phenotype decomposition indicated that "early weaning" captures different clinical profiles at different time points rather than a stable, homogeneous exposure. Observational CRRT weaning studies should consider dynamic treatment strategies, time-varying causal methods, and clinically grounded outcome definitions.

articles.title: SIRT5 deficiency exacerbates sepsis acute renal injury by activating ACSL4/FTH1 axis dependent ferroptosis.
articles.abstract: Sepsis‑associated acute kidney injury (S‑AKI) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients, yet effective targeted therapies remain lacking due to an incomplete understanding of its pathogenesis. Ferroptosis, an iron‑dependent form of regulated cell death driven by lipid peroxidation, has recently been implicated in AKI, but the upstream regulators of this process in sepsis remain undefined. Here, we identify SIRT5, a mitochondrial NAD ⁺ ‑dependent desuccinylase, as a critical endogenous suppressor of ferroptosis in S‑AKI. Using a cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) murine model and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)‑stimulated HK‑2 proximal tubular cells, we show that SIRT5 expression is significantly downregulated in septic kidney injury. Renal tubular‑specific ablation of Sirt5 exacerbated CLP‑induced renal dysfunction, structural damage, and tubular cell death, whereas AAV9‑mediated SIRT5 overexpression attenuated these pathological changes. Mechanistically, SIRT5 deficiency tipped the balance of the ACSL4/FTH1 axis toward ferroptosis: it increased ACSL4‑dependent membrane lipid remodeling and reduced FTH1‑mediated iron sequestration, accompanied by suppression of the antioxidant enzyme GPX4. Consequently, lipid peroxidation, iron overload, and mitochondrial damage were markedly amplified. Notably, knockdown of ACSL4 in SIRT5‑deficient HK‑2 cells effectively reversed lipid peroxidation, iron accumulation, and cell death, establishing ACSL4 as a key downstream effector of SIRT5‑mediated ferroptosis suppression. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized SIRT5-ACSL4/FTH1 regulatory axis that governs ferroptotic susceptibility in renal tubular cells during sepsis, and suggest that pharmacological restoration of SIRT5 activity or blockade of ACSL4‑driven ferroptosis may offer novel therapeutic avenues for S‑AKI.

articles.title: Factors Associated with Early Sepsis-Associated Liver Injury and Predictors of 30-Day Mortality: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Sepsis-associated liver injury (SALI) is associated with higher mortality, but the factors associated with early SALI and the determinants of mortality in patients with SALI remain incompletely understood. This retrospective cohort study included 524 consecutive patients with sepsis (Sepsis-3) in a tertiary intensive care unit (ICU). SALI was defined as total bilirubin ≥2 mg/dL with international normalized ratio ≥1.5, or alanine aminotransferase ≥68 U/L (twice the local upper limit of normal), within 24 hours of ICU admission. Factors independently associated with SALI and with 30-day mortality in SALI were identified by logistic regression after multiple imputation and elastic-net selection, with bootstrap internal validation. Of 523 evaluable patients, 135 (25.8%) met the SALI definition, and their 30-day mortality was higher (63.4% vs 50.0%, p=0.010). Factors independently associated with SALI were macrophage activation-like syndrome (MALS) (aOR: 5.33), an abdominal focus (aOR: 4.03), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) score ≥5 (aOR: 3.07), acute kidney injury on admission (aOR: 2.29) and log-ferritin (aOR: 1.31; 1.48 without MALS and DIC) (all p<0.05; optimism-corrected area under the curve [AUC]: 0.770). Among patients with SALI, immunosuppressive therapy (OR: 8.13), a thoracic focus (OR: 8.62), log-ferritin (OR: 2.04) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) (OR: 1.08 per second) were independently associated with 30-day mortality (all p<0.05); appropriate antibiotic therapy showed a non-significant protective trend (p=0.076). The mortality model showed good discrimination (optimism-corrected AUC: 0.857) but limited calibration (slope: 0.562). SALI was associated with higher 30-day mortality in sepsis. Because the factors associated with SALI were assessed concurrently with liver injury, they describe its clinical profile rather than predict its development. Immunosuppressive therapy, a thoracic focus, higher ferritin levels and prolonged aPTT were associated with 30-day mortality in SALI. These findings should be interpreted with caution and require external validation.

articles.title: Precision fluid therapy in sepsis: fluid responsiveness vs. fluid tolerance.
articles.abstract: Intravenous fluid is the most frequently administered drug in septic shock and one of the least precisely dosed. Two decades of trials have progressively dismantled the assumption that more fluid is better: protocolized early goal-directed therapy failed to improve on contemporary usual care, high-volume bolus protocols caused frank harm where organ support was limited, and restrictive strategies applied after an initial resuscitation have proven neutral rather than superior. What has replaced a universal volume prescription is a pair of questions that must be asked separately for each patient and repeated over time: will this patient's cardiac output actually rise with more fluid (fluid responsiveness), and can the lungs, kidneys, and venous system absorb that volume without harm (fluid tolerance)? This narrative review examines how to answer both questions in the modern intensive care unit. We ground the discussion in Guytonian venous return physiology and in the revised Starling model, in which sepsis-induced glycocalyx degradation makes infused crystalloid a short-acting drug with a cumulative side-effect profile. Using an index case of a mechanically ventilated patient with pneumococcal septic shock, atrial fibrillation, lung-protective tidal volumes, obesity, and acute kidney injury, we show why the two most widely used bedside indices, respiratory variation in inferior vena cava diameter and pulse pressure variation, are physiologically invalid in precisely the patients in whom the fluid decision is hardest, and why maintenance infusions and fluid creep deserve the same scrutiny as boluses. We make the case for direct stroke volume measurement paired with a reversible dynamic challenge, most commonly a passive leg raise, as the one approach that remains interpretable across arrhythmia, low tidal volume, spontaneous respiratory effort, and elevated intra-abdominal pressure, and we discuss dynamic arterial elastance as a complementary tool for predicting whether arterial pressure will follow flow. We review the outcome evidence, including the FRESH trial and supporting meta-analyses, the emerging literature on sepsis endotypes and subphenotypes, and the 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommendations. Finally, we address fluid tolerance and de-resuscitation, where venous congestion assessment and lung ultrasound are increasingly used, and outline where the evidence remains thin.

articles.title: Dynamic lactate clearance within the first 48 hours predicts pressure injury during ECMO support: a longitudinal cohort study.
articles.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the association between dynamic lactate clearance and the development of pressure injuries in adult patients undergoing extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support and to evaluate its incremental value for early risk prediction. This was a retrospective longitudinal cohort study. A total of 317 adult patients receiving ECMO support were enrolled. Lactate concentrations were measured at ECMO initiation and at 6, 24, and 48 h thereafter. Lactate clearance rates were calculated for each corresponding time point. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent risk factors for pressure injury development. The predictive performance of lactate clearance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, five-fold cross-validation, net reclassification improvement (NRI), and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). Pressure injuries occurred in 95 patients (30.0%). Compared with those without pressure injuries, affected patients exhibited significantly lower lactate clearance rates throughout the first 48 h post-ECMO initiation (all P < 0.001). Independent predictors of pressure injury included higher body mass index, elevated vasoactive-inotropic score, VA-ECMO mode, and concomitant renal replacement therapy. The baseline clinical model yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.710. Incorporating lactate clearance significantly improved model discrimination, with AUCs increasing to 0.796, 0.825, and 0.899 for the 6-hour, 24-hour, and 48-hour models, respectively. Consistent enhancements in predictive accuracy were confirmed by cross-validation, NRI, and IDI analyses. Impaired lactate clearance is independently associated with pressure injury development in critically ill adults supported by ECMO. Dynamic monitoring of lactate clearance substantially enhances risk stratification beyond traditional clinical parameters.

articles.title: Use of intraoperative right ventricular strain as a predictor of outcomes in adult heart transplant patients.
articles.abstract: Right ventricle (RV) evaluation in the perioperative period is challenging for anesthesiologists, given the limited objective assessment methods available for transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). Speckle-tracking strain imaging may offer a more objective evaluation of RV function. This study evaluated the predictive value of intraoperative RV free wall strain (RVFWS) for early outcomes following orthotopic heart transplantation (OHT). This was a single-center retrospective cohort study of 147 adults who underwent isolated OHT between January 2025 and December 2025. Patients with multiorgan transplant, congenital cases, and those without measurable intraoperative RVFWS were excluded. Post-bypass RVFWS was measured using TEE at a single time point with speckle-tracking analysis. The primary outcome was 90-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included severe primary graft dysfunction, 30-day mortality, need for postoperative venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), vasoactive-inotropic score, and cardiac index at 24 and 72 h, and intensive care unit length of stay. Multivariable Firth-penalized logistic and median quantile regressions were used, adjusted for a priori pre-transplant weighted risk score. The median post-bypass RVFWS was -13.9% IQR (interquartile range) -19.3 to -9.6. Fourteen recipients (9.5%) died within 90 days of transplantation. After adjusting for the pre-transplant risk score, RVFWS was independently associated with higher 90-day mortality [odds ratio (OR) 2.84 per 5% decrease in magnitude, 95% confidence interval 1.65-5.58; p < 0.001]. Among the secondary outcomes, the associations with severe primary graft dysfunction (OR 2.70; raw p = 0.001), CRRT (OR 1.58; raw p = 0.001), and 30-day mortality (OR 2.94; raw p = 0.002) remained statistically significant after Bonferroni adjustment for eleven secondary comparisons (adjusted p = 0.011, 0.011, and 0.022, respectively). RVFWS demonstrated higher discrimination for 90-day mortality [area under the curve (AUC) 0.83] than qualitative intraoperative RV grading (AUC 0.68), although this difference in AUC did not reach statistical significance. RVFWS retained independent prognostic value in a combined model. Intraoperative post-bypass RVFWS is a feasible and objective intraoperative measure that is independently associated with early adverse outcomes after adult OHT. RVFWS shows promise as a signal of early allograft dysfunction that is not fully explained by pre-transplant risk factors.

articles.title: Beginning Kidney Replacement Therapy Before or After Liver Transplantation: Does the Timing of Dialysis Matter? A Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) in liver transplant patients is associated with increased morbidity, mortality, and reduced graft survival. However, the impact of the timing of dialysis initiation-before versus after transplantation-remains unclear. To characterize liver transplant recipients with Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Stage 3 AKI-requiring dialysis (AKI-D) according to the timing of kidney replacement therapy (KRT) initiation (pre- versus posttransplant) and to evaluate 90-day mortality. Secondary objectives included identifying independent predictors of dialysis dependence and assessing liver graft function at 90 days. This retrospective, single-center cohort study included all consecutive adult liver transplant recipients who received dialysis in a Brazilian intensive care unit (ICU) between 1999 and 2015. The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Federal University of Sao Paulo (UNIFESP), with a waiver of informed consent. Patients were grouped according to the timing of dialysis initiation: pre- or postliver transplantation. Multiple logistic regression was used to identify predictors of 90-day mortality and dialysis dependence. Ninety-day liver graft survival was analyzed using a multivariate Cox model. A total of 356 liver transplant patients with AKI-D were included. Of these, 109 (30.6%) initiated dialysis within 4 weeks before transplantation and 247 (69.4%) within 4 weeks after transplantation. The timing of dialysis initiation was not associated with 90-day mortality or dialysis dependence. Independent predictors of 90-day mortality included graft dysfunction and use of continuous KRT as the initial modality. Impaired pretransplant renal function and a history of diabetes mellitus were predictors of 90-day dialysis dependence. Posttransplant dialysis was associated with a twofold increased risk of liver graft failure. The timing of dialysis initiation (pre- versus posttransplantation) was not associated with 90-day mortality or dialysis dependence. However, initiation of dialysis after transplantation was associated with an increased risk of liver graft dysfunction.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of nafamostat mesilate for anticoagulation during ECMO/CRRT: insight from the integrated meta-analysis and FAERS pharmacovigilance study.
articles.abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) require a balance between maintaining circuit patency and minimizing bleeding risk. Nafamostat mesilate (NM) is a short-acting anticoagulant with distinctive pharmacokinetic properties, including rapid metabolism and a short half-life, which may reduce prolonged systemic anticoagulant exposure. These characteristics make NM a potential alternative to conventional anticoagulation strategies, particularly for patients at high risk of bleeding. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of NM as an anticoagulant for ECMO/CRRT. PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang Data were systematically searched for randomized controlled trials and cohort studies comparing NM with sodium citrate, unfractionated heparin (UFH), or no anticoagulation. A meta-analysis was conducted to evaluate filter lifespan, bleeding events, thromboembolic events, and 28-day/intensive care unit (ICU) mortality. Reporting characteristics and potential safety signals for the three anticoagulants were also compared using data from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). The meta-analysis included 17 studies involving 1,893 patients. Filter lifespan did not differ significantly between the NM and control groups (mean difference [MD] = 1.29 h; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.09-3.66), whereas the risk of bleeding events was significantly lower in the NM group (odds ratio [OR] = 0.61; 95% CI, 0.43-0.86). Subgroup analyses showed that NM was associated with a significantly lower risk of bleeding than sodium citrate (OR = 0.53; 95% CI, 0.31-0.90) and no anticoagulation (OR = 0.41; 95% CI, 0.19-0.90); sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of this finding. The FAERS analysis included 24,238 reports, comprising 233 for NM, 1,612 for sodium citrate, and 22,393 for UFH, with distinct reporting profiles observed among the three anticoagulants. Representative signals for NM included disseminated intravascular coagulation (n = 17; ROR = 112.68, 95% CI: 69.69-182.19), gastrointestinal hemorrhage (n = 12; ROR = 15.44, 95% CI: 8.74-27.29), and decreased platelet count (n = 13; ROR = 7.52, 95% CI: 4.35-13.00). NM may reduce bleeding risk while maintaining a filter lifespan comparable to that achieved with other anticoagulation strategies, potentially providing an individualized anticoagulation option for patients at high risk of bleeding. In clinical practice, coagulation abnormalities, changes in platelet counts, and bleeding-related events should be closely monitored.

articles.title: A secondary analysis of the SODa-BIC randomized clinical trial using multiple hierarchical composite outcomes.
articles.abstract: The Sodium Bicarbonate for Metabolic Acidosis in the ICU (SODa-BIC) trial assessed the effect of sodium bicarbonate on Major Adverse Kidney Events at 30 days (MAKE30) in critically ill patients with metabolic acidosis. Although the trial demonstrated no significant difference in the primary outcome, the individual components showed differing magnitudes and directions of effect; we undertook an exploratory analysis of the SODa-BIC trial using different hierarchical outcomes to better understand potential treatment effects of sodium bicarbonate. Post-hoc analysis of the SODa-BIC trial. All patients included in the SODa-BIC trial were eligible. The primary outcome was a win ratio analysis with a hierarchy consisting of death, requirement for renal replacement therapy, persistent renal dysfunction, and hospital length of stay. Several sensitivity and subgroup analyses were conducted. The primary analysis resulted in 59,250 pairs from 488 patients. Consistent with the SODa-BIC analysis, there was no overall evidence of a treatment effect of sodium bicarbonate, with a win ratio of 0.97 (95%CI 0.79 - 1.19) and a Desirability of Outcome Ranking probability of 0.49 (95%CI 0.45 - 0.54). A majority of pairwise comparisons were resolved by mortality and hospital length of stay. Evidence of significant treatment effect modification was observed across subgroups defined by acute kidney injury and severity of acidemia. In this post-hoc analysis of the SODa-BIC trial, the use of hierarchical composite outcomes did not alter the neutral overall interpretation of the original trial. However, this analysis provides additional insight into the relative contribution of individual components of the primary outcome.

articles.title: Renal Dose-Adjustment Concordance in Critically Ill Patients with AKI and CKD: A Cross-sectional Study.
articles.journal: Iranian journal of pharmaceutical research : IJPR
articles.abstract: Kidney dysfunction complicates drug dosing in the intensive care unit (ICU). Guidance is well established for stable chronic kidney disease (CKD) but is less certain in acute kidney injury (AKI), in which renal function can change rapidly. To assess concordance between prescribed maintenance regimens and reference-based renal dose-adjustment recommendations for adults with AKI, CKD, or AKI superimposed on CKD. This cross-sectional study included 80 adults admitted to four ICUs in 2024. Acute kidney injury was classified according to the Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, and end-stage renal disease (RIFLE) criteria using serial creatinine measurements and/or urine output, whereas CKD required documented chronicity. Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance (CrCl) was used to match patients to dosing-reference categories. Each patient-medication pair was classified once according to maintenance-dose amount and dosing interval, using UpToDate as the primary reference and the Sanford Guide as a supplementary source. Among 414 patient-medication pairs, 211 (51.0%; patient-level cluster-bootstrap 95% CI, 46.2%-55.8%) were discordant: 125 were lower and 86 were higher than recommended. Vancomycin (41.4%), ciprofloxacin (40.0%), and levofloxacin (40.0%) had the highest drug-specific discordance proportions. Nephrology and pulmonology had the highest patient-level service proportions (62.5% and 61.5%, respectively). Reference discordance was frequent, particularly for antimicrobials. Because measured exposure and clinical outcomes were unavailable, these findings identify regimens requiring review rather than confirming prescribing errors.

articles.title: Incidence and mortality of invasive fungal infections among patients admitted in intensive care units in India: findings from a multicentric registry-based study (2023-25).
articles.journal: The Lancet regional health. Southeast Asia
articles.abstract: Invasive fungal infections (IFIs) are challenging to treat in critical care, particularly among patients treated in Intensive care units (ICUs). The existing evidence on IFIs from India remains fragmented. This study characterises IFI incidence, risk factors, resistance pattern, treatment and outcome among patients admitted to ICUs. This multicentre observational study leveraged registry data on IFIs among patients admitted to 63 ICUs in eight Advanced Mycology Diagnostic and Research centres in India between January 2023 and November 2025. Patients with proven and probable IFI according to European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer/Mycoses Study Group Education and Research Consortium (EORTC/MSGERC) 2020 and the modified Aspergillus intensive care unit (AspICU) 2020 criteria were included. IFI incidence to hospital admission, all-cause in-hospital mortality, pathogen distribution and antifungal susceptibility were recorded. Mortality-associated factors were estimated using multivariable logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards analysis. Among 178,417 ICU admissions, 2500 IFI patients were identified with an incidence of 14/1000 admissions (95% CI 13.5-14.6) and all-cause mortality of 53.6% (95% CI 51.7-55.6%). Invasive candidiasis was the most frequently reported (57.1%), followed by invasive aspergillosis (37%), mucormycosis (3.4%), trichosporonosis (1.8%), pneumocystis pneumonia (1.1%), and cryptococcosis (1.2%). Median age of the patients was 45 years (IQR: 26-60), with 61.9% males and 38.1% females. Among candidiasis, Candida tropicalis predominated (35.6%), while Candida auris exhibited high fluconazole resistance (61.7%) and elevated amphotericin B minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) (40.7%). Aspergillus fumigatus (50.8%) and Aspergillus flavus (38.7%) predominated among culture-positive aspergillosis, with generally low MICs. Exploratory multivariable analyses showed that sepsis, chronic liver disease, immunosuppression, corticosteroid exposure, and total parenteral nutrition were associated with higher mortality in invasive candidiasis, whereas mechanical ventilation, corticosteroid exposure, and immunosuppression were associated with higher mortality in invasive aspergillosis. The study findings highlight a high IFI burden and mortality among patients admitted in ICUs of India, with mortality exceeding 50%, underscoring the need for continuous surveillance, rapid diagnostics, infection control and antifungal stewardship. This study was funded by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Delhi (Grant ID: 157401).

articles.title: Deimplementation of Tradition-Based Enteral Feeding Practices to Improve Clinical Outcomes.
articles.journal: Critical care nursing clinics of North America
articles.abstract: Enteral feeding is common in acute and critical care but there are many elements to this practice that are steeped in confusion and lack evidence. This article will focus on verification of feeding tube (FT) placement methods and timing, medication administration by FTs, unnecessary holding or stopping of enteral formula, gastric residual volumes, and volume-based feeding. Supporting evidence for these practices will be reviewed and recommendations made for evidence-based alternatives and possible deimplementation.

articles.title: Preserved anabolic skeletal muscle capacity in response to exercise and protein intake after critical illness.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Low muscle mass and persistent weakness are common after critical illness, but the mechanisms behind impaired recovery are incompletely understood. The aim of this study was to investigate the skeletal muscle anabolic response to combined resistance exercise and protein intake in intensive care unit (ICU) survivors, compared to matched controls without a history of critical illness. We hypothesised that residual anabolic resistance limits muscle regeneration after ICU stay. METHODS: Former patients were enrolled within 3 to 6 months of intensive care unit discharge. Muscle biopsies were obtained before and after resistance exercise using a flywheel leg extension ergometer, combined with ingestion of 24 g hydrolysed protein. Muscle protein fractional synthetic rate was determined from the incorporation of [ring-²H₅]phenylalanine into mixed-muscle protein during a primed continuous intravenous infusion. Anabolic and proteolytic pathways were measured using standard assays. Group-by-time differences were analysed using linear mixed models. The primary comparison was the between-group difference in pre-to-post change in muscle protein synthesis. RESULTS: Twenty ICU survivors (60 ± 12 years, 30% female, BMI 26.9 (IQR 22.9-28.7), SAPS 3 62.3 ± 15.8) and 20 age- and sex-matched controls were included. ICU survivors had significantly lower quadriceps muscle thickness (p = 0.02) and handgrip strength (p = 0.04) than controls. In ICU survivors, muscle protein synthesis from plasma precursor amino acids was higher at baseline than in controls (0.041%/hour vs. 0.030%/hour, p = 0.009), but increased less (Δ 0.031 vs. Δ 0.040%/hour, p = 0.04). Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis was similar between groups (0.071%/hour vs. 0.070%/hour, p = 0.70). At baseline, ICU survivors showed lower activation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway. In both groups, the intervention increased anabolic signalling, decreased initiation of autophagy and increased parts of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. CONCLUSIONS: In ICU survivors with persistent muscle loss and weakness, the increase in muscle protein synthesis after combined resistance exercise and protein intake was smaller than in controls, in the context of a higher baseline fractional synthetic rate. Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis rates were similar between groups. These findings provide the first mechanistic support for structured exercise-nutrition rehabilitation to promote muscle recovery after critical illness. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05261984), 2022-02-20.

articles.title: Clinical nutrition for critically ill patients: A practical appraisal of guideline gaps and perspectives for future research.
articles.abstract: Malnutrition and accelerated muscle wasting are frequent during critical illness and make nutritional support a central component of ICU care. Nutritional support is therefore central to ICU care, but its optimal timing, route, dose, and composition remain debated. Recent randomized trials have challenged the traditional objective of early full feeding and shifted practice toward progressive, phase-adapted, and tolerance-based nutrition. This narrative review compares current international guidelines for nutritional support in critically ill adults. Guidelines broadly agree that nutrition should be initiated early after clinical stabilization, acute-phase overfeeding should be avoided, energy and protein delivery should be increased progressively, and refeeding syndrome should be anticipated. However, important differences remain regarding acute-phase energy targets, protein dosing, enteral versus parenteral nutrition, supplemental parenteral nutrition, indirect calorimetry, and enriched enteral formulas. These discrepancies reflect differences in methodology, healthcare context, and interpretation of evidence largely derived from mechanically ventilated patients during the first ICU week. Several clinically important situations remain insufficiently addressed, including prolonged critical illness, obesity, sarcopenia, post-extubation nutrition, post-ICU rehabilitation, and nutrition after major surgery. Future research should move toward individualized strategies based on illness phase, metabolic trajectory, nutritional phenotype, tolerance, and recovery-oriented outcomes.

articles.title: Association between augmented enteral protein and muscle mass attenuation in critically ill patients: A sub-study of a cluster randomized crossover trial.
articles.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition
articles.abstract: Critically ill patients experience muscle wasting, impacting recovery. The associations between augmented enteral protein and muscle mass, strength, physical function, and quality of life are uncertain. We performed a sub-study in adult TARGET Protein participants from two sites between 23/11/2022-23/05/2023. Our exposure of interest was enteral formula with augmented protein (100 g protein/L) and comparator usual protein formula (63 g protein/L), which were isocaloric. Our primary outcome was the change in quadriceps muscle layer thickness from Days 1 to 7, determined by ultrasonography and compared between groups. Our secondary outcomes were group differences in handgrip strength, change in physical function, and quality of life. Data are numbers (%), mean (standard deviation), and differences with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Seventy-two patients were included (augmented protein n = 46, 61 (16)y, 65% male; usual protein n = 26, 56 (16)y, 46% male), 56 had primary outcome data (augmented protein n = 35; usual protein n = 21). Delivered protein was higher with augmented protein (1.2 (0.4) vs 0.8 (0.3) g/kg/day). Quadriceps muscle layer thickness decreased in both groups, with change from Days 1 to 7 similar (0.01 cm; 95% CI, -0.27, 0.28; P = 0.970). Left handgrip strength at ICU discharge and quality of life at Day 90 were similar. Augmented protein was associated with greater right handgrip strength at ICU discharge (6.23; 95% CI, 0.67, 11.79) and was associated with greater decline in physical function at ICU discharge (-15.00; 95% CI, -19.75, -10.25), but not at Day 90. No clear difference was detected in quadriceps muscle layer attenuation over 7 days between augmented enteral protein and usual protein. Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry identifier: ACTRN12622001465741.

articles.title: Clinical Course and Prognosis of the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition-Defined Malnutrition in Critically Ill Patients with Sepsis: A Multicenter Prospective Observational Study.
articles.abstract: Sepsis is a critical condition with a high nutritional risk and mortality. Although the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) criteria have been proposed for diagnosing malnutrition, their clinical relevance in sepsis remains unclear. Therefore, we conducted a descriptive study on GLIM-defined malnutrition in intensive care unit (ICU) patients with sepsis to investigate its clinical course and prognosis. This was a multicenter prospective study conducted at 15 centers. Malnutrition was identified at ICU admission when both phenotypic and etiologic criteria were present. The primary outcome was a composite of in-hospital mortality or a decline in activities of daily living (Barthel Index <90) at discharge. Secondary outcomes included ICU length of stay, use of parenteral nutrition, and days to achievement of each ICU Mobility Scale level. Among 254 patients, 106 (41.7%) had malnutrition. The malnutrition group showed a significantly higher occurrence of the composite of in-hospital mortality and Barthel index <90 (76.4% vs. 64.2%, p = 0.04) and had significantly longer ICU stays (7 vs. 5, p = 0.001). Total nutrition delivery did not significantly differ between groups, while a higher percentage of patients in the malnutrition group received parenteral nutrition (57.6% vs. 43.2%, p = 0.02). Significant delays in achieving higher mobility levels were observed in the malnutrition group. GLIM-defined malnutrition in patients with sepsis was significantly associated with the composite outcome of in-hospital mortality or Barthel index <90 at discharge. These results suggest the clinical importance of an early GLIM assessment after ICU admission.

articles.title: The effects of intravenous glutamine supplementation in critically ill patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: Studies evaluating intravenous (IV) glutamine supplementation in critically ill patients have shown inconsistent results. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of IV glutamine on mortality, infectious complications, length of stay, and duration of mechanical ventilation. A systematic search of Ovid Medline, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and KoreaMed was conducted from inception through October 2023 and updated in April 2025. Randomized controlled trials comparing IV glutamine supplementation with standard care in critically ill adults were included. Pooled estimates were calculated using random-effects models. A total of 10 randomized trials involving 1,593 critically ill patients were included in the analysis. IV glutamine supplementation was not associated with reduced overall mortality (risk ratio [RR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.77-1.13) or overall infection rates (RR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.63-1.18). No mortality benefit was observed in either non-surgical or surgical/trauma subgroups. Glutamine supplementation was associated with reduced pneumonia incidence (RR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.49-0.87) and shorter mechanical ventilation duration (mean difference, -0.97 days; 95% CI, -1.62 to -0.32); however, these findings were based on a limited number of small studies. Intensive care unit and hospital length of stay were longer in the glutamine group. IV glutamine supplementation was not associated with improved survival or overall infection rates in critically ill adults. Current evidence does not support routine IV glutamine supplementation in unselected critically ill patients.

articles.title: Evaluation of Chromium Picolinate Supplementation and Insulin Requirements in Critically Ill Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
articles.journal: The Journal of pharmacy technology : jPT : official publication of the Association of Pharmacy Technicians
articles.abstract: Chromium picolinate has been studied as an adjunct to improve glycemic indices in ambulatory type 2 diabetes mellitus, but its role in critically ill patients is unknown. To evaluate whether chromium picolinate supplementation was associated with reduced insulin requirements without worsening glycemic control in critically ill adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus. We conducted a single-center retrospective pre-post cohort study of adult intensive care unit patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus or hemoglobin A1c ≥6.5% who received insulin and at least 4 consecutive chromium picolinate doses between July 2022 and January 2023. Patients served as their own controls during 24-hour pre- and post-chromium periods. The primary outcome was change in total daily insulin dose. Secondary outcomes included proportion of measured glucose values within 140 to 180 mg/dL, acute kidney injury, hypoglycemia, and exploratory Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-2 change. Among 91 screened patients, 45 met the inclusion criteria. Median total daily insulin dose decreased from 76.3 U/d (interquartile range [IQR], 40.1-96.9) before chromium to 40.0 U/d (IQR, 20.5-65.6) after chromium; the Hodges-Lehmann paired difference was -23.0 U/d (95% CI, -33.25 to -14.25; P < .0001). Proportion of measured glucose values within target did not differ significantly. No post-intervention hypoglycemia was observed, and 2 patients met the study-defined acute kidney injury criterion. Interpretation is limited by the retrospective design and absence of a concurrent control group. Chromium picolinate supplementation was associated with lower insulin requirements without worsening glycemic control. These hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in prospective controlled studies.

articles.title: Plasma amino acid profiles reveal metabolic signatures of mortality and infection in critically ill surgical patients requiring parenteral nutrition: A longitudinal analysis.
articles.abstract: Surgical intensive care unit (SICU) patients experience high rates of adverse outcomes, underscoring the need for insights into pathophysiology. We aimed to evaluate associations between plasma amino acids (AAs), post-surgical mortality, and hospital-acquired infections in SICU patients requiring parenteral nutrition (PN). Secondary analysis of a multicenter trial including 148 adults receiving glutamine-supplemented or standard PN after major surgery. Levels of plasma AAs were quantified at baseline, Day 3, and Day 7. Mortality and infections were monitored through day 28. Associations between AAs and outcomes were assessed via generalized linear models adjusted for clinical covariates. Machine learning models evaluated the classification performance of AAs. At baseline, a four AA signature (plasma aspartate, histidine, leucine, and methionine concentrations) showed similar discrimination of 28-day mortality as the APACHE II score (AUC 0.88 vs. 0.78, DeLong test P = 0.28). Increased concentrations of these AA suggest impaired uptake and utilization. At baseline, BSI was best classified by a model that included decreased concentrations of alanine, cystine, glutamate, glutamine, and lysine (AUC 0.79), with glutamate elevated in cases. The best classification model for pneumonia at Day 7 included decreased cystine, lysine, ornithine, threonine, tyrosine, and valine concentrations (AUC 0.86). At baseline and Day 7, for any infections, the classification model included decreased glutamine, glycine, lysine, ornithine, proline, serine, threonine, and valine concentrations (AUC >0.79). Elevated essential AA concentrations were associated with SICU mortality, while lower levels of both essential and non-essential AAs were linked to hospital-acquired infections.

articles.title: Association of enteral nutrition reduction or discontinuation with diarrhea volume and caloric delivery in critically ill adults with diarrhea: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.journal: Nutrition in clinical practice : official publication of the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition
articles.abstract: When critically ill patients receiving enteral nutrition (EN) develop diarrhea, clinicians often reduce or discontinue EN, although evidence supporting this practice is limited. We examined the association between EN management after diarrhea and diarrhea volume in critical care patients. This single-center retrospective cohort study included adult intensive care unit patients who developed new-onset diarrhea (Bristol Stool Form Scale ≥6 on 2 consecutive days) during EN. Based on Day 1 EN management, patients were classified as continuation (infusion rate decrease <10 mL/h) or reduction/discontinuation (decrease ≥10 mL/h or complete discontinuation). The primary outcome was cumulative diarrhea volume (grams) on Days 1-2. Cumulative EN calories (kcal) on Days 1-2 was a key secondary outcome. Inverse probability of treatment weighting with regression adjustment accounted for 8 pre-specified confounders. Sensitivity analyses included alternative exposure thresholds and propensity score models. Of 135 patients analyzed (median age, 74 years; 32% female), 96 (71.1%) continued EN and 39 (28.9%) underwent EN reduction/discontinuation. After adjustment, the reduction/discontinuation group had lower cumulative diarrhea volume on Days 1-2 (adjusted mean difference, -183.4 g; 95% confidence interval [CI], -350.1 to -16.7; p = 0.033) but received substantially fewer calories (-1260.1 kcal; 95% CI, -1464.4 to -1055.9; p < 0.001). The direction of the reduction in diarrhea volume was consistent across sensitivity analyses. Reducing or discontinuing EN after diarrhea was associated with a modest reduction in diarrhea volume but a substantial caloric deficit. This trade-off should be considered when reducing EN for diarrhea.

articles.title: Evaluation of a device for insertion of a small intestinal feeding tube in the critically ill: A prospective multicentre international cohort study.
articles.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
articles.abstract: Critically ill patients sometimes require insertion of a feeding tube into the small intestine. This study evaluated the ease of placement of a proprietary small intestinal feeding tube incorporating a distal tip camera. investigator-initiated, industry-funded, prospective cohort study was conducted at four intensive care units across two countries. Patients were eligible if the treating clinician requested small intestinal feeding tube insertion. Operators were physicians or senior dietitians, and attempts were categorised as "inexperienced" (≤4 attempts) or "experienced" (≥5 attempts). The primary outcome was the overall probability of successful small intestinal placement. Secondary outcomes included procedural time and the posterior probabilities of success according to operator classification and experience, estimated using Bayesian hierarchical regression models incorporating minimally informative priors and random intercepts for clustering within operators. The device was used by 11 operators in 68 patients. Prior 24-h cumulative gastric residual volumes were 454 (standard deviation: 453) millilitres. The overall probability of success was 75% (95% credible interval: 61-86%). Experienced users and inexperienced users were successful in 30 of 38 (79%) and 21 of 30 (70%) attempts, respectively. Overall median (interquartile range) procedural times for successful versus unsuccessful placement were 23 (10-35) and 30 (20-42) minutes, respectively. In a multivariable analysis, the posterior probabilities of improved success (odds ratio >1) were 83% (gastrokinetic drug prescription), 82% (operative versus nonoperative admission), and 65% (device experience). The probability of successful small intestinal placement of feeding tubes by motivated clinicians in a critical care environment approximated the prespecified threshold of 80%, without the need for extensive specific device experience.

articles.title: Clinical applications of gastric point-of-care ultrasound in adult emergency and critical care: a scoping review.
articles.abstract: Point-of-care ultrasound (PoCUS) is a cornerstone of bedside assessment in emergency and critical care, providing rapid, radiation-free visualization of anatomy and pathology. Gastric PoCUS offers a non-invasive method to assess gastric content, volume, and motility, informing management of aspiration risk, airway interventions, and enteral feeding. Despite supporting evidence, its use remains limited and poorly standardized. The objective of this scoping review is to map the clinical applications of gastric PoCUS in adult emergency department (ED) and intensive care unit (ICU) patients. A scoping review was conducted according to PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Medline, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane, CINAHL, were searched from 1950 to May 2025 for studies evaluating gastric ultrasound in adult ED or ICU populations. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted, and charted data. Thirty-five studies met inclusion criteria. Clinical applications of gastric PoCUS among ED and ICU were clustered under three domains: aspiration risk assessment and airway management (n = 5); enteral nutrition and gastric residual volume monitoring (n = 12); and diagnostic evaluation or therapeutic monitoring (n = 18). Across studies, gastric PoCUS reliably differentiated gastric content types, estimated gastric volume, and informed airway and feeding decisions. In diagnostic contexts, gastric PoCUS enabled rapid bedside identification of gastric outlet obstruction, volvulus, intramural hematoma, and perforated viscus. No studies reported complications or harm caused by performing gastric PoCUS. Gastric PoCUS is a versatile bedside tool bridging diagnostic and therapeutic domains in emergency and critical care. It enhances patient safety, optimizes nutritional management, and reduces radiographic dependence. Standardization of scanning protocols, structured training, and multicenter outcome-based validation studies are needed to support routine integration in acute care.

articles.title: Effect of enteral nutrition nursing combined with gastrointestinal function monitoring on gastric retention and abdominal distension in neurosurgical patients.
articles.abstract: This study evaluated the clinical effects of enteral nutrition nursing combined with gastrointestinal function monitoring in neurosurgical patients receiving enteral nutrition. This single-center retrospective cohort study included 120 neurosurgical patients who received enteral nutritional support from June 2023 to June 2025. Sixty patients received routine enteral nutrition nursing (control group), and 60 received routine care plus dynamic gastrointestinal function monitoring (combined nursing group). Outcomes included gastric retention, abdominal distension, nausea and vomiting, overall gastrointestinal intolerance, enteral nutrition interruption, aspiration/reflux, nutritional delivery, gastrointestinal recovery, hospital and intensive care unit (ICU) stay, nutritional tolerance, and nursing satisfaction. Logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with gastric retention. Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups (all P > .05). Gastric retention occurred less frequently in the combined nursing group than in the control group (15.0% vs 30.0%), although the difference did not reach statistical significance (P = .053). The combined nursing group had lower incidences of abdominal distension (16.7% vs 36.7%, P = .011), nausea and vomiting (11.7% vs 26.7%, P = .038), and overall gastrointestinal intolerance (20.0% vs 43.3%, P = .006). Time to achievement of enteral nutrition targets, gastric residual volume, time to recovery of bowel sounds, and time to first defecation were also more favorable (all P < .001). Enteral nutrition interruption was less frequent (8.3% vs 23.3%, P = .022), and hospital and ICU stays were shorter (both P < .01). Good nutritional tolerance and nursing satisfaction were more frequent in the combined nursing group (both P < .05). Multivariable analysis showed that the combined nursing model was associated with lower odds of gastric retention. Enteral nutrition nursing combined with gastrointestinal function monitoring was associated with improved gastrointestinal tolerance, more efficient nutritional delivery, earlier gastrointestinal recovery, and shorter hospital and ICU stays. A lower observed incidence of gastric retention was also noted, and adjusted analysis suggested an association with reduced odds of gastric retention.

articles.title: Prevalence of Chronic Complications After Inaugural Admission in Intensive Care Unit for Type 1 Diabetes in the SFDT1 Cohort: The INAUGURAL Study.
articles.abstract: Inaugural presentation at type 1 diabetes onset, as ketoacidosis, has been associated with poorer glycaemic control, but its relationship to diabetes-related complications remains unclear. We assessed the association between inaugural intensive care unit (ICU) admission and long-term diabetes-related outcomes in adults. This cross-sectional analysis used data from the Société Francophone du Diabète-Cohorte Diabète de Type 1 (SFDT1) cohort. We compared participants with and without an inaugural ICU admission regarding chronic complications, recent acute events, and cardiometabolic risk factors. Models were adjusted for age, sex, diabetes duration, smoking status, socioeconomic vulnerability, education, insulin therapy, HbA1c, and centre; interaction terms were tested. Among 3548 adults with type 1 diabetes (median duration 20 years [IQR 10-30]), 377 (10.6%) reported inaugural ICU admission. Retinopathy was more prevalent in the ICU group (36.6 vs. 31.4%; p < 0.05), including proliferative forms (11.1 vs. 7.7%; p < 0.05). These differences remained significant after adjustment (p < 0.05). An association with retinopathy was observed among individuals diagnosed before the age of 17 (OR = 1.5; 95% CI, 1.1-2.1; p = 0.015). Severe hypoglycaemia in the previous year was more frequent in the ICU group (15.4% vs. 10.5%; p < 0.01) and remained significant after adjustment (p < 0.05). No significant differences were observed for the other variables. In this multicentre cohort of adults with long-standing type 1 diabetes, inaugural ICU was associated with at least a 50% higher odds of severe hypoglycaemia and retinopathy, including proliferative forms. The association with retinopathy was mainly observed among individuals diagnosed at a young age. ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04657783).

articles.title: Decades of intensive care medicine trials: what randomised evidence has changed, corrected, and still questions to resolve.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have reshaped intensive care medicine (ICM), a discipline defined by acute, interacting organ failures, time-sensitive decisions, biological uncertainty, and heterogeneous recovery trajectories. Many interventions supported by strong physiological rationale failed to improve patient-centred outcomes, whereas durable advances often emerged from optimisation of supportive care, avoidance of iatrogenic harm, and reassessment of established practices. METHODS: We conducted an interpretive historical review of landmark multicentre RCTs in adult ICM from the early 1990s onwards. PubMed searches, reference lists from major trials and reviews, and international guidelines were used to identify trials with conceptual influence on practice, guidelines, physiological reasoning, therapeutic strategy, research priorities, de-implementation, or outcome framing. Evidence was organised into overlapping paradigms rather than rigid chronological periods. FINDINGS: Across haemodynamic support, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, antimicrobial treatment, nutrition, glucose control, transfusion, and sedation, landmark RCTs describe more than therapeutic expansion. Early biological and haemodynamic trials exposed the limits of reductionist strategies in syndromic critical illness. Protocol-driven approaches improved timeliness and consistency, but later pragmatic trials showed that rigid targets and invasive algorithms often added little once high-quality usual care was established. More recent trials challenge the assumption that greater intervention intensity improves outcomes, emphasising timing, disease phase, baseline risk, heterogeneity, patient selection, and treatment-related harm. Modern ICM RCTs have clarified not only what works, but what can be reduced, delayed, avoided, or applied selectively. Future progress requires biologically informed, context-sensitive trials focussed on meaningful survival, recovery, and long-term function.

articles.title: Key principles for rehabilitation of critically ill patients with obesity.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Patients with obesity who are admitted to an ICU bring specific challenges for rehabilitation during and after critical illness. This narrative review explores impact of differences in body compositions and pathophysiology on outcomes to summarise interprofessional, patient-centred rehabilitation strategies across the trajectory of recovery. METHODS: The interprofessional expert panel reviewed major trials and guidelines, integrating their clinical expertise with the current evidence. RESULTS: Three distinct phenotypes potentially influence outcomes for survivors. Whilst patients with preserved muscle mass may have a survival advantage, the phenotypes characterised by ectopic visceral fat or sarcopenia are frequently complicated by multimorbidity and polypharmacy, likely increasing the risk of adverse effects such as suboptimal sedation, prolonged ventilation and immobilisation, malnutrition, and impaired recovery. Targeted respiratory interventions, including secretion-clearance techniques and appropriate patient positioning to prevent atelectasis, reduce the work of breathing. Optimisation of communication and swallowing function is an essential component for facilitating safe oral intake and promoting active patient participation in rehabilitation. Concurrently, targeted nutrition strategies combined with early, targeted, progressive mobilisation might mitigate ICU acquired weakness and support functional recovery. The availability of appropriate weight‑based equipment is fundamental to ensuring safe mobilisation for both patients and healthcare professionals. CONCLUSION: Interprofessional collaboration is central to optimising outcomes and should extend beyond the ICU to structured post-ICU follow-up to address persistent, worsening, or newly emerging health impairments. Early rehabilitation in critically ill patients with obesity should integrate physiological, logistical, and psychosocial considerations to support equitable and functional recovery.
articles.ai_summary: This study reviewed rehabilitation strategies for critically ill patients with obesity, identifying three distinct phenotypes that influence outcomes. Targeted interventions, including respiratory, nutrition, and mobilization strategies, can mitigate complications and support functional recovery.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings highlight the importance of interprofessional collaboration and early rehabilitation in critically ill patients with obesity, emphasizing the need to address physiological, logistical, and psychosocial considerations to support equitable and functional recovery.

articles.title: Net Ultrafiltration Rate and Mortality in Critically Ill Patients: A Multicenter Cohort Study With Analysis of Fluid Balance Changes.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To investigate the association between net ultrafiltration (NUF) rate and fluid balance changes with 28-day mortality in critically ill patients receiving continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). DESIGN: Multicenter retrospective observational study. SETTING: Data from two European mixed medical-surgical ICUs: University Hospital Bern, Switzerland, and Amsterdam University Medical Center, the Netherlands. PATIENTS: Adult critically ill patients receiving CRRT for at least 24 hours. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We studied 973 critically ill adults undergoing a total of 6914 days of CRRT. NUF rates and fluid balance changes were calculated from hourly data and categorized into four predefined groups. NUF rates were classified as no NUF, low (< 1.01 mL/kg/h), moderate (1.01-1.75 mL/kg/h), or high (> 1.75 mL/kg/h). Fluid balance change was stratified as negative (< -1.5 L/day), moderate negative (-1.5 to -0.5 L/day), neutral (-0.5 to 0.5 L/day), or positive (> 0.5 L/day). Using multivariable regression, random forest modeling, and mediation analysis, we observed no independent association between NUF rate and 28-day mortality after accounting for fluid balance. Mediation analysis suggested that the apparent survival advantage observed among patients with higher NUF rates was largely mediated through achievement of a more negative fluid balance, rather than a direct effect of NUF rate itself. In contrast, more positive fluid balance changes were linked to adverse clinical outcomes including 28-day mortality. CONCLUSIONS: In this two-center cohort of CRRT patients, NUF rate was not independently associated with mortality. Instead, the key determinant of outcome was fluid balance change. These findings suggest clinicians should not make NUF decisions in isolation, but rather should be using NUF as a means to achieve patient-specific fluid balance targets.
articles.ai_key_stats: n=973, no independent association between NUF rate and 28-day mortality, fluid balance change linked to adverse outcomes including 28-day mortality
articles.ai_summary: This study investigated the relationship between net ultrafiltration rate and fluid balance changes in critically ill patients receiving continuous renal replacement therapy. The results showed that fluid balance change, not net ultrafiltration rate, was the key determinant of outcome. The study found that more positive fluid balance changes were linked to adverse clinical outcomes.
articles.ai_significance: These findings suggest that clinicians should prioritize achieving patient-specific fluid balance targets over focusing solely on net ultrafiltration rate in critically ill patients receiving CRRT.

articles.title: From Formula Composition to Precision Nutrition: Who Benefits, From What, and When?
articles.abstract: Morowitz et al argue that the composition of enteral nutrition formulas deserves to be studied as an intervention in its own right. Building on this perspective, we consider how critical care nutrition research has progressively refined its questions from whether to feed to when and how much. We argue that enteral formula composition represents the next logical frontier in critical care nutrition research, while emphasizing the need for biologically informed, clinically meaningful, and practical interventions. We also highlight the importance of learning from previous translational challenges to ensure that future research identifies formulations that improve patient outcomes while remaining feasible for routine critical care practice.

articles.title: Perioperative Nursing Management of Patients Undergoing Nonsupercharged Cervical Roux-en-Y Esophagojejunostomy: A Single-Center Retrospective Descriptive Case Series.
articles.journal: Journal of perianesthesia nursing : official journal of the American Society of PeriAnesthesia Nurses
articles.abstract: Perioperative nursing after esophageal reconstruction is demanding, and nonsupercharged cervical Roux-en-Y esophagojejunostomy shifts nursing surveillance away from microvascular patency toward the more gradual signs of marginal conduit hypoperfusion. Nursing-focused reports describing phase-specific surveillance, documentation, and escalation for this reconstruction are lacking. This study aimed to describe an institutional perioperative nursing pathway together with the clinical outcomes and nursing process indicators observed in patients undergoing this procedure. This study adopted a single-center, retrospective descriptive case-series design. In this study, we reviewed 22 consecutive patients with esophageal cancer who underwent nonsupercharged cervical Roux-en-Y esophagojejunostomy between January 2021 and April 2025. Data were retrospectively abstracted from routinely maintained clinical and nursing records. An institutional perioperative nursing pathway combining routine esophageal perioperative care with procedure-specific surveillance of the cervical jejunal conduit was in use throughout the study period. No formal sample-size calculation was performed and no comparator group was available; therefore, clinical outcomes and nursing process indicators were summarized descriptively. The median operation time was 274.0 minutes (IQR 255.8-288.5), median mechanical ventilation time 18.0 hours (IQR 14.0-19.8), median intensive care unit stay 4.0 days (IQR 3.0-5.2), and median total hospital stay 12.0 days (IQR 8.8-14.0). Enteral nutrition was initiated at a median of postoperative day 5.0. The early mobilization target was documented in 86.4% (19/22) of patients by postoperative day 2, all patients ambulated by postoperative day 4, and respiratory exercises were recorded at a median of 4 sessions per day (IQR 3-5). Clavien-Dindo grade II or higher complications were recorded in 22.7% (5/22) of patients, anastomotic leakage in 18.2% (4/22, all endoscopically confirmed), and pulmonary complications in 4.5% (1/22). Perfusion warning events were documented in 31.8% (7/22) of patients; all were managed according to the predefined nursing escalation process and resolved or did not progress. No graft necrosis, re-exploration, or 30-day death occurred. This case series describes the implementation of a structured perioperative nursing pathway for nonsupercharged cervical Roux-en-Y esophagojejunostomy and the outcomes observed under it. Perfusion warning events and anastomotic complications were documented without graft necrosis or reoperation. These preliminary observational findings offer practical clinical insight but do not establish pathway effectiveness. Prospective multicenter studies are required to evaluate implementation fidelity, measurement reliability, clinical effectiveness, and generalizability.

articles.title: Sarcopenia in Hospitalized Patients: A Critical Narrative Review of Diagnostic and Nutritional Management Approaches.
articles.abstract: Sarcopenia is an independent predictor of adverse outcomes in hospitalized patients, associated with increased mortality, prolonged length of stay, and functional decline, yet it remains underdiagnosed owing to inconsistent diagnostic criteria and the practical challenges of assessing acutely ill patients. This narrative review summarizes current evidence on sarcopenia in hospitalized patients, with emphasis on diagnostic approaches, nutritional requirements, and optimal nutritional support strategies. Sarcopenia is particularly prevalent among critically ill patients and is driven by the convergence of systemic inflammation, immobility, and anabolic resistance. Diagnosis remains challenging: no ICU-specific framework exists, and the recent Global Leadership Initiative of Sarcopenia consensus established a unified, setting-independent conceptual definition as a foundation for future operational criteria, with ICU-specific frameworks yet to be developed. Bedside tools, including handgrip strength, bioelectrical impedance analysis, and ultrasound, retain strong prognostic value despite imperfect agreement with reference imaging. Nutritional intervention is a key component of management; however, large-scale trials have demonstrated that higher energy or protein delivery does not universally improve outcomes and may be harmful in selected critically ill patients. A gradual increase in energy and protein delivery according to the phase of illness, with protein targets of ≥1.2-1.5 g/kg/day, is recommended; leucine-enriched supplementation may help counteract anabolic resistance, although direct evidence in non-ICU hospitalized patients remains limited. Early mobilization is an essential complement, as nutrient provision without a mechanical stimulus cannot reverse immobility-induced muscle loss. A practical clinical algorithm integrating screening, nutritional target-setting, route selection, and reassessment is proposed to guide decision-making in this population. Future research should focus on improving the accuracy and feasibility of muscle assessment tools in critically ill patients to enable the timely diagnosis of sarcopenia and nutritional intervention, alongside the development of validated multi-marker panels and adequately powered trials examining the combined effect of nutrition and exercise in this population.

articles.title: Explainable Machine Learning for Prediction of Future High-Severity States Using Longitudinal APACHE-II Trajectories: Internal Validation and Cross-Cohort Portability Assessment.
articles.abstract: Background: Longitudinal severity assessment may provide more informative risk stratification than reliance on a single admission score in intensive care. This study developed and internally validated an explainable machine learning framework for predicting a subsequent APACHE-II-defined high-severity state using repeated APACHE-II assessments in intensive care unit (ICU) patients receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN). The endpoint was defined as an APACHE-II score of ≥ 20 at the final assessment (T10), while predictor information was restricted to measurements obtained at T0-T9. Methods: A retrospective institutional cohort of 844 adult ICU patients was analyzed, of whom 214 (25.4%) met the predefined high-severity endpoint. Four principal feature representations were evaluated: admission APACHE-II, longitudinal APACHE-II information combining the raw T0-T9 sequence with derived trajectory descriptors, longitudinal laboratory information, and multimodal combinations including baseline characteristics. Six machine learning algorithms were compared using stratified five-fold cross-validation and independent hold-out testing. Additional analyses included simpler APACHE-II comparators, sequential observation truncation, nested cross-validation, calibration assessment, threshold sensitivity analysis, and SHAP-based model interpretation. Because equivalent longitudinal APACHE-II measurements and an equivalent endpoint were unavailable in eICU, a separate harmonized XGBoost model was used only for exploratory cross-cohort portability assessment. Results: The longitudinal APACHE-II CatBoost model achieved the highest performance, with a cross-validated ROC-AUC of 0.924 and an independent hold-out ROC-AUC of 0.921 (95% CI: 0.878-0.960). Hold-out calibration was good (Brier score = 0.095, calibration intercept = - 0.03, slope = 0.98), and nested cross-validation yielded a pooled out-of-fold ROC-AUC of 0.908 and a mean outer-fold ROC-AUC of 0.920 ± 0.038. The latest APACHE-II assessment alone (T9; ROC-AUC = 0.553), change from baseline (0.576), ordinal slope (0.539), and logistic regression using engineered APACHE-II descriptors (0.633) performed substantially below the full longitudinal CatBoost model. Sequential truncation showed that discrimination was retained after removing later observations, although performance varied non-monotonically across truncated sequences. SHAP analysis showed that multiple APACHE-II observations contributed prominently to model predictions, with trajectory-derived descriptors providing complementary contributions. Adding laboratory trajectories or baseline characteristics did not improve discrimination over the longitudinal APACHE-II representation. Conclusions: Nonlinear modeling of repeated APACHE-II assessments provided strong internal discrimination of a subsequent APACHE-II-defined high-severity state in this TPN-treated ICU cohort and substantially outperformed single-score and simpler longitudinal comparators. However, the predictors and endpoint share the APACHE-II construct, observation indices were sequential rather than standardized clock-time intervals, and the primary model could not undergo conventional external validation in eICU. These findings therefore support the internal predictive value of longitudinal APACHE-II modeling for this specific severity-state task and warrant prospective multicenter evaluation using standardized timing and independent clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Epidemiology of Critically Ill Patients With Cirrhosis Undergoing Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy: A Contemporaneous Parallel Analysis of the HRS-HARMONY and CRRTnet Registries.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Describe the epidemiology of patients with cirrhosis/acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) receiving continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) pertaining to process factors including renal replacement dose, modality, and circuit anticoagulation. SETTING: Academic tertiary care hospitals in the United States and Canada. DESIGN AND PATIENTS: We performed a parallel study of contemporaneous data from the HARMONY and CRRT network (CRRTnet) databases to describe the epidemiology and process of CRRT care of cirrhosis/ACLF patients receiving CRRT in the ICU. We evaluated clinical and CRRT process factors (dialysis dose, anticoagulation) with the primary outcome of in-hospital mortality. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: The HARMONY cohort (n = 245; median age, 57 yr; 41% female) and CRRTnet cohort (n = 206; 58 yr; 39% female) demonstrated similar overall survival to hospital discharge (HARMONY, 34%; CRRTnet, 30%). In HARMONY, the two most common causes of acute kidney injury (AKI) requiring CRRT were acute tubular necrosis (73%) and hepatorenal syndrome-AKI (13%), with no significant difference between survivors and nonsurvivors (p = 0.24). In HARMONY, higher chronic liver failure-C ACLF scores (hazard ratio, 1.03 [95% CI, 1.01-1.05]; p < 0.001) were independently associated with increased in-hospital mortality. In CRRTnet, the most common CRRT modality was continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (83.8%), and the most common anticoagulation strategy was regional citrate anticoagulation (58.0%) or no anticoagulation (35.8%). CRRT prescribed dose greater than 30 mL/kg/hr was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (multivariable regression; odds ratio, 2.69; 95% CI, 1.3-5.64; p = 0.01). Of survivors in CRRTnet, 64% were transitioned to intermittent hemodialysis (IHD) before hospital discharge. CONCLUSIONS: Critically ill cirrhosis/ACLF patients initiated on CRRT in the absence of liver transplantation had high in-hospital mortality. These patients were prescribed higher initial CRRT doses (median total effluent > 30 mL/kg/hr), with higher CRRT dose independently associated with increased in-hospital mortality. Of ICU survivors, 64% were transitioned to IHD at ICU discharge. Despite concerns for citrate toxicity, citrate regional anticoagulation was commonly employed in these patients.

articles.title: Individualising blood glucose control in ICU patients: evidence and practical implementations.
articles.abstract: Many intensive care unit patients develop hyperglycaemia, and this is associated with an increased risk of adverse outcomes. Landmark randomised controlled trials (RCTs) suggest the impact of lowering blood glucose to the healthy, age-adjusted fasting range, hereafter called tight glucose control, depends on the accuracy of the glucose control protocol and the nutritional strategy. In the context of early parenteral nutrition, a condition that induces severe, iatrogenic hyperglycaemia, tight glucose control significantly reduced morbidity and mortality compared to tolerating severe hyperglycaemia. In the absence of early parenteral nutrition, hyperglycaemia was less severe; tight glucose control, applied with a computerised protocol that avoided severe hypoglycaemia, did not impact mortality nor the duration of ICU dependency as primary endpoint in a large multicentre RCT, but was associated with a less pronounced benefit on selected morbidity outcomes. Conversely, tight glucose control, using a protocol that considerably increased the risk of severe hypoglycaemic events, concomitantly increased mortality; nevertheless, the cause of excess mortality in this trial remains unproven and other mechanisms may have contributed as well. Altogether, evidence suggests that severe and iatrogenic hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia should both be avoided. From a pathophysiologic point of view, tight glucose control may be superior in selected settings if it can be applied with a validated protocol that avoids severe hypoglycaemia. In the absence of such a protocol, the increased risk of severe hypoglycaemia may offset any benefit of preventing hyperglycaemia, and tolerating intermediate blood glucose targets is likely the default setting. In the paper, we suggest specific blood glucose targets that differ according to the clinical context.
