articles.title: Vancomycin optimised dosing regimens for critically ill patients receiving renal replacement therapy.
authors: European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases (ESCMID) Study Groups for Infections in Critically Ill Patients (ESGCIP) and the ESCMID PK/PD of Anti-Infectives Study Group (EPASG)
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Optimal dosing of vancomycin in critically ill patients receiving renal replacement therapy (RRT) is uncertain due to high pharmacokinetic variability. We aimed to develop individualised vancomycin dosing recommendations that optimise efficacy while minimising toxicity. METHODS: Prospective, international, pharmacokinetic study enrolling critically ill patients treated with vancomycin and various RRT modalities. A population pharmacokinetic model was developed, externally validated and applied to perform Monte Carlo dosing simulations. We calculated the probability of each dosing regimen to achieve the efficacy target against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (ratio of the area under the concentration-time curve to the minimum inhibitory concentration (AUC0-24 h/MIC) ≥ 400) without exceeding the toxicity threshold (AUC0-24 h ≥ 700 mg.h/L). RESULTS: We enrolled 65 critically ill patients from 6 countries receiving continuous RRT (50.8%) or sustained low-efficiency dialysis (49.2%). The model was developed using 1318 pre- and post-filter plasma and effluent concentrations and validated with a new dataset (19 critically ill patients, 124 pre-filter plasma concentrations), with 47.4% patients concomitantly treated with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Predictive performance was high (median prediction error =-13.4%). Simulations showed that dosing requirements were dependent on actual body weight and RRT intensity and duration (p < 0.05). An optimised dosing nomogram was subsequently developed considering these clinical characteristics. CONCLUSIONS: Actual body weight and RRT intensity and duration are the main determinants of vancomycin dosing requirements in critically ill patients treated with RRT. Efficacious, non-toxic dosing may be guided by the optimised nomogram.

articles.title: Effects of a clinical metagenomics intervention on clinical outcomes, healthcare costs, and health-related quality of life in patients with sepsis or septic shock: results of the randomized-controlled DigiSep trial.
authors: German Society of Anaesthesiology and Intensive Care (GSAIC) Trials Group
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Early pathogen detection is crucial in sepsis. We hypothesized that detection of microbial circulating cell-free DNA by metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) improves clinical outcomes and health-related quality of life without increasing healthcare costs. METHODS: This randomized, controlled, interventional, open-label, multicenter trial was conducted in 24 intensive care units across Germany. The intervention group (n = 200) received mNGS diagnostics in addition to standard-of-care microbiology, compared with standard-of-care microbiology alone (control group; n = 189). The primary endpoint was the Desirability of Outcome Ranking/Response Adjusted for Duration of Antibiotic Risk (DOOR/RADAR) score. RESULTS: The DOOR/RADAR score was not significantly improved at 28 days after sepsis onset (intervention group: 3.21 ± 1.54; control group: 3.49 ± 1.51; 95% CI - 0.58 to 0.03). However, other secondary endpoints were improved, including a reduced duration of mechanical ventilation (intervention group: 6.6 ± 9.4 days; control group: 9.3 ± 10.6 days; 95% CI - 5.03 to - 0.34) and faster shock resolution (intervention group: 6.9 ± 7.4 days; control group: 8.8 ± 8.5 days; 95% CI - 3.75 to - 0.04). Health-related quality of life at 90 days (EQ-5D-5L) was improved in the intervention group (0.312 ± 0.386) compared with the control group (0.208 ± 0.373; p = 0.047). In the subgroup with available claims data (33.2% of participating patients), healthcare costs over 180 days did not differ. CONCLUSION: The DOOR/RADAR score as primary endpoint was not significantly improved by mNGS. Exploratory secondary analyses revealed improvements in secondary endpoints. (Funding: German Innovation Fund; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04571801, registration: 25.8.2020).

articles.title: Inflammatory Phenotypes In Severe Pneumonia: Clinical Evidence To Mouse Models For Precision Therapeutics.
articles.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
articles.abstract: RATIONALE: Hyperinflammatory and hypoinflammatory phenotypes previously identified in sepsis and ARDS may enable precision therapies, but their clinical relevance and translational modeling in severe pneumonia remain incompletely characterized. OBJECTIVES: To examine biomarker-defined hyperinflammatory and hypoinflammatory phenotypes in critically ill patients with pneumonia (pulmonary sepsis), test whether the biomarkers that define these phenotypes identify subgroups and outcomes in a mouse model of bacterial pneumonia, and determine whether the mouse phenotypes respond differently to therapeutic interventions. METHODS: We performed latent class analysis (LCA) in a cohort of 548 ICU patients with pulmonary sepsis to identify inflammatory phenotypes and test the association of these phenotypes with clinical outcomes using validated classifier models. We developed a mouse model of pneumococcal pneumonia which recapitulates key aspects of these phenotypes and tested responses to dexamethasone and IL-6 receptor blockade. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Two phenotypes were identified in patients with pulmonary sepsis: a hyperinflammatory phenotype with more lung injury and increased mortality, and a hypoinflammatory phenotype with more favorable outcomes. Despite uniform pathogen exposure and baseline conditions, LCA identified two phenotypes in the mice with divergent trajectories (lung injury and mortality). Therapeutic benefit from anti-inflammatory interventions was observed exclusively in the more inflamed mice. CONCLUSIONS: By integrating clinical data from human studies and experimental findings in a clinically relevant mouse model, this study provides a translational framework for developing phenotype-targeted therapies for critical illness, with the goal of improving patient outcomes.
articles.ai_key_stats: n=548, RR not reported, ARR not reported, ARR not reported, RRR not reported, NNT not reported, p not reported, CI not reported
articles.ai_summary: Researchers identified two inflammatory phenotypes in patients with severe pneumonia: a hyperinflammatory phenotype with worse outcomes and a hypoinflammatory phenotype with better outcomes. They also developed a mouse model that mimics these phenotypes and found that anti-inflammatory interventions only benefited the more inflamed mice. This study provides a framework for developing targeted therapies for critical illness.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings have the potential to improve patient outcomes by enabling precision therapies tailored to individual inflammatory phenotypes in severe pneumonia.

articles.title: Mucormycosis in critically ill patients: a 9-year multicenter cohort study of clinical features, management, and 90-day outcomes.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mucormycosis is a rare but life-threatening invasive fungal infection that primarily affects immunocompromised patients. Data on its presentation, management, and prognosis in the intensive care unit setting remain scarce. We aimed to evaluate 90-day mortality and to explore clinical, microbiological, therapeutic, and immunological factors associated with outcome in critically ill patients with mucormycosis. METHODS: This retrospective multicenter cohort study included patients diagnosed with mucormycosis and admitted to the ICUs of the Hospices Civils de Lyon between January 2014 and July 2023. Patients were identified through mycological records and hospital discharge codes. Univariable analysis and multivariable Cox model were performed to identify factors associated with 90-day mortality. RESULTS: Among 43 patients included, hematological malignancy and trauma were the most common underlying conditions (26% each), followed by solid organ transplantation (21%), and burns (16%). Cutaneous forms (49%) predominated, especially among trauma and burn patients, while pulmonary and rhinocerebral forms were mostly observed in previously immunocompromised individuals. The number of mucormycosis diagnoses increased nearly threefold over the study period, paralleling the implementation of Mucorales-specific polymerase chain reaction. Antifungal therapy was initiated in 39 patients (91%); first-line treatment was liposomal amphotericin B in 32 (74%), at a median maximum dose of 7.5 [3.5-9.4] mg/kg/day, and 12 (28%) received a combination therapy. The 90-day mortality was 47%. In the multivariable Cox model, older age, hematological malignancy, and a higher Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score at diagnosis were independently associated with mortality, while lower liposomal amphotericin B dosing was associated with mortality in univariable analysis. In eight patients without previous immunosuppression and uncontrolled disease, immune monitoring was performed and revealed decreased monocyte HLA-DR expression at 4556 [4194-6936] Ab/c, in favor of injury-induced immunosuppression. Among them, six patients received interferon-gamma as immunotherapy; four responded immunologically and survived. CONCLUSIONS: Mucormycosis in critically ill patients is associated with high mortality, particularly in those with hematological malignancies. Polymerase chain reaction-based diagnostics may allow earlier detection, and immune monitoring could help identify high-risk patients, particularly in trauma and burn settings.

articles.title: Consensus recommendations for patient selection and clinical implementation of polymyxin B hemoadsorption in endotoxic septic shock.
articles.abstract: Despite long-standing clinical use and emerging evidence, no structured framework exists guiding clinicians in identifying septic shock patients for endotoxemia assessment, interpretation of the Endotoxin Activity Assay (EAA), or practical implementation of polymyxin B hemoadsorption (PMX-HA) therapy. A modified Delphi consensus process was conducted with ten critical care and nephrology experts, compromising a pre-meeting survey, a one-day in-person consensus conference, and iterative voting on draft statements. Consensus was predefined as ≥ 80% agreement. Consensus was achieved on 20 statements across three domains: (1) operational criteria to prompt endotoxemia assessment in suspected or presumed septic shock, (2) role and interpretation of the EAA, and (3) logistics and clinical implementation of PMX-HA. Key recommendations included standardized criteria to identify eligible patients, EAA thresholds of ≥ 0.60 and < 0.90 to support PMX‑HA consideration, initiation of therapy as early as possible once eligibility is confirmed, with ≤ 36 h from septic shock onset proposed as a pragmatic implementation benchmark, and standardized treatment protocols consisting of two sessions, 24 h apart, targeting 120 min each. A multidisciplinary team model was endorsed for implementation. Identified research priorities were in treatment effect heterogeneity, EAA kinetics, clinical implementation, and healthcare system integration. These consensus recommendations provide a structured, implementation-focused framework for PMX-HA use in suspected endotoxic shock. The framework emphasizes stepwise operational criteria, biomarker-guided decision-making, multidisciplinary team-based implementation, and standardized protocols. It is intended to support institutions currently using PMX-HA and to assist U.S. clinicians and health systems in preparing for potential adoption pending regulatory approval.

articles.title: Assessing fluid responsiveness in mechanically ventilated patients with intra-abdominal hypertension: a two-center, prospective, observational study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) may reduce the diagnostic accuracy of the passive leg raising (PLR) test for predicting fluid responsiveness, with unclear mechanisms. The reliability of the end-expiratory occlusion (EEO) test and mini-fluid challenge in IAH remains unknown. This study explored the mechanisms underlying PLR impairment and assessed the accuracy of EEO and mini-fluid challenge in detecting fluid responsiveness in patients with and without IAH. METHODS: In this prospective study in two intensive care units (ICUs), we included ventilated patients with IAH ("IAH + "; intra-abdominal pressure [IAP] ≥ 12 mmHg) and without ("IAH-"), all monitored via transpulmonary thermodilution and receiving a 500-mL fluid challenge. Patients consecutively underwent a 1‑minute PLR, a 15‑second EEO, and a 1‑minute mini-fluid challenge of 100 mL, with cardiac index (CI) changes recorded during each maneuver. Following the mini-fluid challenge, the remaining 400 mL were infused over 14 min, and a ≥ 15% increase in CI was used to define fluid responders. The transmural pressure of the inferior vena cava was estimated by the central venous pressure (CVP) - IAP gradient. RESULTS: We included 88 patients, 44 IAH- (25 fluid responders and 19 non-responders) and 44 IAH + (22 responders and 22 non-responders). Baseline IAP was 9 ± 2 mmHg in IAH- and 17 ± 3 mmHg in IAH + (p < 0.001). In IAH- responders, CI increased by 19 ± 11% during PLR and 31 ± 17% after volume expansion, with PLR positive in 24/25 responders. In IAH + responders, CI increased by 6 ± 7% during PLR (p < 0.001 vs. IAH-) and 30 ± 18% after volume expansion (p = 0.907 vs. IAH-). The AUROC of the PLR for detecting fluid responsiveness was 0.96 (0.87-1.00) in IAH- and 0.71 (0.56-0.87) in IAH + (p = 0.009 vs. IAH-). Among IAH + , there were 16 false negatives and 6 true positives for PLR, both with negative baseline CVP-IAP gradients. During PLR, the gradient reversed in true-positives (from -2.4 ± 4.0 to + 2.2 ± 2.7 mmHg, p = 0.014), whereas it remained negative in false-negatives (from -6.3 ± 3.7 to -1.4 ± 3.4 mmHg, p < 0.001). AUROC between IAH- and IAH + was similar for either the EEO test (0.95 [0.87-1.00] vs. 0.89 [0.80-0.97], p = 0.332) or mini-fluid challenge (0.94 [0.87-1.00] vs. 0.90 [0.79-1.00], p = 0.514). CONCLUSION: In patients with IAH, the limited diagnostic value of PLR for fluid responsiveness may be related to persistently negative CVP-IAP gradients in false-negative cases, whereas EEO and mini-fluid challenge remain reliable alternatives.

articles.title: The ARDS, Pneumonia, and Sepsis Consortium: Rationale, Design, and Feasibility of a National Platform for Phenotyping Critical Illness Syndromes.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: To enhance biological understanding of ARDS, pneumonia, and sepsis and to accelerate therapeutic development in these areas, the National Institutes of Health developed the ARDS, Pneumonia, and Sepsis (APS) Consortium. RESEARCH QUESTION: Is the APS Consortium study rapidly generating data and biospecimens from a large cohort of critically ill adults with ARDS, pneumonia, and sepsis that will facilitate phenotyping of these syndromes? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: The APS Consortium Phenotyping Study is a multicenter, longitudinal, prospective, observational cohort study aimed at enrolling 4,000 critically ill adults with ARDS, pneumonia, sepsis, or a combination thereof over 4 years. Data and biospecimens are collected to characterize many aspects of each participant's chronic health, acute illness, and long-term recovery to facilitate phenotyping, that is, subclassifying ARDS, pneumonia, and sepsis into precise biologically based subsets with shared pathophysiologic characteristics. Feasibility of the study was assessed by evaluating the first 1,000 participants in terms of recruitment pace, participant characteristics, biospecimen collection, and proportion with confirmed ARDS, pneumonia, and sepsis based on expert adjudication. RESULTS: The first 1,000 participants were recruited ahead of schedule in < 13 months. Median age was 64 years, 75% received vasopressors, 50% received invasive mechanical ventilation, and 25% died in the hospital within 4 weeks of enrollment. Biospecimen collection rates were high, with 99% of participants with blood samples, 98% with upper respiratory swabs, 37% with lower respiratory samples, 80% with urine samples, and 65% with gastrointestinal samples. Expert adjudication resulted in 40% classified with ARDS, 52% classified with pneumonia, and 89% classified with sepsis. INTERPRETATION: The APS Consortium Phenotyping Study is producing a cohort of critically ill adults with ARDS, pneumonia, and sepsis with high severity of disease and a rich set of data and biospecimens. The study will continue to full enrollment of 4,000 participants. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov; No.: NCT06521502; URL: www. CLINICALTRIALS: gov.

articles.title: The molecular ICU: a primer on omics, informatics and the future of precision critical care.
articles.abstract: Critical care has produced hundreds of neutral randomized trials, in part because therapies have been tested in biologically incoherent populations that dilute meaningful treatment effects. Syndromic diagnoses such as sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and traumatic brain injury group distinct pathobiological states under a single label, limiting the ability to detect treatment-responsive subgroups. While high-dimensional omics technologies have revealed this biologic heterogeneity, the field lacks a practical framework to translate these insights into clinical trial design and bedside decision-making. This Review addresses the translational gap in precision critical care through a pathway-level framework. We synthesize advances in genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, highlighting their roles in capturing susceptibility, host response, effector function, and real-time physiology. We propose pathway-focused biomarkers as clinically translatable signatures that preserve biological mechanisms while enabling practical measurement. We outline how pathway enrichment, network analysis, and multi-omic integration can identify these programs, and how feature selection can derive parsimonious biomarker panels for clinical use. This approach also supports pathway-guided drug repurposing by linking dysregulated molecular programs to existing therapies. Together, these signatures provide a framework for predictive enrichment, aligning patient selection with therapeutic mechanisms and facilitating implementation within adaptive platform trials. This Review serves as a practical primer that outlines the concepts and methods needed to translate omics into clinically actionable tools. By shifting from syndromic classification to pathway-defined biology, it provides a framework for biomarker development, trial design, and precision critical care.
articles.ai_summary: This study reviews the current limitations in critical care research due to syndromic diagnoses and proposes a pathway-level framework to translate omics insights into clinical trial design and bedside decision-making.
articles.ai_significance: This framework has the potential to improve patient outcomes by enabling personalized treatment and more effective use of existing therapies in critical care settings.

articles.title: Optimizing β-lactam antibiotics with the highest concentration-for continuous infusion reduce carbon footprint in intensive care.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: β-lactam antibiotics are the most commonly used antibiotics to treat infection in critically-ill patients. The modalities of antibiotics reconstitution/preparation for continuous infusion are elaborated according to drug stability. In between 2 periods, a sustainable protocol for 4 common β-lactam antibiotics administration was implemented, consisting of preparing the highest stable concentration for continuous administration through a 50 mL syringe. RESULTS: Overall, 418 patients were treated (202 in 2024 and 216 in 2025), age, and SAPSII did not differed between both periods. A sustainable protocol implementation reduced the greenhouse gas emission (GHG) by 52% from 2760 [1380-4968]g to 1380 [552-2208]g/treatment, p < 0.0001. The global reduction of plastic consumed (syringes, tubing, solution bags, blister packs) was - 48% (-61 kg), and treatment cost was also reduced by 48% (-1324 €). The total nursing time for preparation was 145 h shorter during the second 6 months period. DISCUSSION: These results showed that implementation of a sustainable protocol for continuous β-lactam antibiotics can significantly reduce the environmental impact of antibiotic administration. CONCLUSION: A careful prescription of drug dilution, if continuous infusion of β-lactam antibiotics is used, can be efficient in reducing GHG emissions, consumables, waste, and costs.
articles.ai_summary: Researchers implemented a sustainable protocol for administering 4 common β-lactam antibiotics in ICU patients, using the highest stable concentration for continuous infusion. This reduced greenhouse gas emissions by 52%, plastic consumption by 48%, and treatment costs by 48%. The protocol also saved nursing time.
articles.ai_significance: This study highlights the potential for reducing the environmental impact of antibiotic administration in ICUs, which is crucial for sustainability and cost-effectiveness in critical care.

articles.title: Genomic dynamics of antimicrobial resistance transmission between bacteria from intensive care unit surfaces and from critically ill patients.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is an environment where multiple factors that predispose to the transmission of Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) coexist. Genomic sequencing is a technology that enables a better understanding of how AMR genes are transmitted within the ICU environment. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the genomic dynamics of the transmission of antimicrobial resistance genes between bacteria from ICU surfaces and bacteria from critically ill patients. METHODS: A cross-sectional analytical study. Surface swab samples were collected from the ICU, including suction units, infusion pumps, stethoscopes, dialysis machines, monitors, ventilators and gas valves, as well as samples from critically ill patients with infections. Species were identified using microbiological microplate panels; antibiotic susceptibility testing was carried out to assess AMR; and whole-genome sequencing was performed on isolates that were multidrug-resistant (MDR). The sequencing was carried out using a nanopore long-read sequencer and the results were analysed using specialised bioinformatics tools. RESULTS: A total of 130 positive isolates were identified, of which 96 (73.85%) were from environmental samples and 34 (26.15%) from patient samples. Forty (30.76%) MDR species were identified. The most common MDR species were Klebsiella pneumoniae and Acinetobacter baumannii. The most frequently detected AMR genes were blaNDM-5 and blaOXA-23. The most common plasmids were IncFIB(K)_1_Kpn3, Col440I and IncL/M(pMU407)_1_pMU407. A clonal outbreak of Acinetobacter baumannii ST 2 was detected on the dialysis machine, stethoscopes and patient samples. Evidence of horizontal transfer of resistance genes via plasmids conjugation was found in samples taken from suction units, oxygen valves and tracheal secretion in three cases. CONCLUSION: The findings of this research show that antimicrobial resistance genes are transferred between bacteria on surfaces and bacteria in critically ill patients, and that this transfer occurs in both directions.

articles.title: Decoding candidemia in critically ill patients: unsupervised clustering identifies three unique phenotypes.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Candidemia displays significant clinical heterogeneity in critically ill patients. This study aimed to identify distinct clinical phenotypes and to assess their association with 90-day mortality. METHODS: We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study of 492 intensive care unit (ICU) patients with candidemia from 16 French ICUs (2015-2023). We performed a factor analysis of mixed data (FAMD) incorporating both categorical and continuous baseline variables, followed by hierarchical clustering on principal components (HCPC). Survival analysis was performed with Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox proportional hazards models. RESULTS: Overall, 90-day mortality for the 492 patients (median age: 64 years, 69.1% male) with candidemia was 62.6%. Three different phenotypes emerged from FAMD followed by HCPC: Phenotype 1 (n = 70, 14.2%) comprised patients with severe immunosuppression, mostly due to hematological malignancies (82.9%), and high severity scores (SAPS II:70); Phenotype 2 (n = 223, 45.3%) corresponded to elderly cirrhotic patients (19.3%) with early-onset digestive candidemia; Phenotype 3 (n = 199, 40.5%) comprised younger patients with lower severity scores and catheter-related candidemia. Mortality differed significantly between phenotypes: 72.9% (Phenotype 1), 70.4% (Phenotype 2), and 50.3% (Phenotype 3) (p < 0.001). Independent predictors of mortality included age (aHR: 1.01, 95% CI: 1.00-1.02; p = 0.003), cirrhosis (aHR: 1.90, 95% CI: 1.39-2.60; p < 0.001), SAPS II (aHR: 1.01, 95% CI: 1.01-1.02; p < 0.001), echinocandin use (aHR = 0.49, 95% CI: 0.39-0.63; p < 0.001) and proven catheter-related candidemia (protective; aHR: 0.48, 95% CI: 0.33-0.69; p < 0.001). Immunodepression was not associated with mortality. CONCLUSION: Unsupervised clustering identified three clinically different candidemia phenotypes with different outcomes. Cirrhosis, higher age and illness severity were associated with mortality, whereas a catheter-related source of infection was protective.
articles.ai_summary: Researchers studied 492 ICU patients with candidemia and found three distinct phenotypes with different outcomes. Phenotype 1 had high mortality due to severe immunosuppression, Phenotype 2 had high mortality in elderly cirrhotic patients, and Phenotype 3 had lower mortality in younger patients with catheter-related candidemia.
articles.ai_significance: This study helps clinicians understand the heterogeneity of candidemia in ICU patients and identify patients at higher risk of mortality, allowing for more personalized treatment and care.

articles.title: Neutrophil EMR3 dynamics in critically ill patients with sepsis: an ICU experience.
4% Tetrasodium EDTA to Prevent Central Venous Access Device-Associated Complications: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Use of central venous access devices (CVADs) can result in catheter-associated bloodstream infection, catheter occlusion, and catheter-related venous thrombosis. EDTA is a potent anticoagulant, antimicrobial, and antibiofilm agent that can be instilled into inactive CVAD ports as a locking fluid to decrease the risk of infection and maintain patency. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether a 4% tetrasodium EDTA (t-EDTA) locking fluid reduces CVAD-associated infections, occlusions, and thrombolytic use in adults treated in an intensive care unit (ICU). DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Pragmatic, triple-blind, multicenter, cluster-randomized crossover trial including patients older than 18 years in the ICU with a CVAD in place and at least 1 lumen not in use. The trial was conducted in 6 Canadian hospitals (3 community hospitals and 3 academic centers). The first patient was enrolled on March 22, 2022, and the date of last follow-up occurred on September 25, 2024. INTERVENTIONS: The ICUs were randomized to use prefilled, identical, masked syringes containing 2.5 mL of t-EDTA (intervention) or control locking fluid (saline or 4% citrate for hemodialysis lines) for all trial participants over a 3.5-month period. After a 1-month follow-up period, ICUs crossed over to the opposing treatment group for another 3.5 months, with a subsequent 1-month follow-up. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was a composite incidence rate of CVAD-associated bloodstream infection, catheter occlusion requiring alteplase use, and/or catheter removal due to occlusion. Three of the 8 prespecified secondary outcomes included incidence rates of each component of the primary outcome separately. RESULTS: Of the 1574 eligible patients, 1468 (mean age, 60 [SD, 16.0] years; 37.7% female) were included in the analysis (696 receiving t-EDTA and 772 receiving control). The incidence rate of primary outcome events was 13.1 per 1000 catheter-days (74 events) in the t-EDTA group vs 19.9 per 1000 catheter-days (126 events) in the control group. In adjusted multivariate analysis, the incidence rate of the composite outcome was lower among patients receiving t-EDTA vs control (rate ratio, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.47-0.96; P = .03). Among the 3 components of the primary outcome, only the secondary outcome of CVAD occlusion requiring administration of alteplase significantly differed between the groups, with lower rates in the t-EDTA group vs control (66 vs 112; incidence rate, 11.67 and 17.73 per 1000 catheter-days, respectively; rate ratio, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.46-0.96). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Compared with control locking solution, use of 4% t-EDTA locking solution for CVADs reduced the incidence of a composite outcome of CVAD-associated bloodstream infection, catheter occlusion requiring alteplase use, and catheter removal due to occlusion among adult patients in the ICU. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04548713.

articles.title: The role of hemoadsorption in septic shock: toward a personalized approach.
articles.abstract: A dysregulated host response to infection is central to the pathophysiology of sepsis and may culminate in life-threatening organ dysfunction. Given that this process is largely characterized by concurrent pro- and anti-inflammatory activation, immunomodulatory strategies have long been explored in sepsis research. Among these, extracorporeal removal of circulating cytokines, inflammatory mediators and other soluble factors through non-specific hemoadsorption with macroporous styrene-divinylbenzene sorbents has been proposed as a potential therapeutic approach. Its adoption into clinical practice has largely been based on pathophysiological considerations rather than on evidence from large, well-designed randomized clinical trials. Over the past 15 years, most of the available evidence has been predominantly derived from small, single-center cohorts, reports from registries and heterogeneous prospective studies with substantial variability in patients' selection, timing, and treatment intensity. In addition, the precise mechanisms of action of hemoadsorption remain incompletely understood. Although several meta-analyses have attempted to synthesize the existing data, the overall quality and heterogeneity of the included studies limit the strength and reliability of their conclusions. As a result, current guideline recommendations are largely based on expert opinions rather than high-certainty evidence. This position statement aimed to provide a concise overview of the biological rationale, current evidence, and contemporary clinical practice related to hemoadsorption in critically ill patients.
articles.ai_summary: Researchers reviewed the evidence on hemoadsorption in septic shock, finding that current guidelines are based on expert opinions rather than high-certainty evidence. Hemoadsorption involves removing inflammatory mediators from the blood, but its effectiveness and mechanisms of action are not well understood. More research is needed to determine its role in treating septic shock.
articles.ai_significance: This study highlights the need for more robust clinical trials to establish the effectiveness of hemoadsorption in septic shock, which could lead to more personalized and effective treatment approaches in the ICU.

articles.title: Current concepts on feeding the critically ill patient: a narrative review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Nutritional therapy is a key component of critical care management, yet optimal strategies remain debated due to the heterogeneity of ICU patients, dynamic metabolic alterations, and the profound influence of inflammation on nutrient utilisation. Evidence from recent trials has challenged traditional one-size-fits-all approaches, emphasising the need for individualised, phase-specific nutrition throughout the continuum of critical illness and recovery. This manuscript summarises current concepts and emerging evidence in nutrition therapy presented at the 39th Annual Conference of the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM). Experts reviewed and critically discussed inflammation-driven metabolic changes, personalised energy and protein prescriptions, micronutrient management, macronutrient adaptation, ketogenic strategies in neurocritical care and sepsis, and nutritional considerations in post-ICU syndrome and outpatient recovery. This overview does not claim to be exhaustive; interpretations of individual study results partly reflect the views of the experts. Together with the inclusion of newer therapeutic approaches, this is intended to stimulate discussion and, at the same time, provide a basis for further studies. MAIN BODY: Inflammation and high disease severity strongly influence nutritional responsiveness, with highly inflamed patients demonstrating reduced benefit and heightened risk of overfeeding. Personalised strategies, including indirect calorimetry, fat-free mass-based protein dosing, and metabolic biomarkers such as the urea-creatinine ratio, offer a rational framework for tailoring therapy. Micronutrient deficiencies are common due to redistribution, pre-existing deficits, and extracorporeal losses, necessitating structured assessment and supplementation. Macronutrient delivery should be progressively escalated and regarded as a pharmacologic intervention aligned with disease phase and organ function. Early standardised ketogenic diet protocols show feasibility and potential clinical benefit in refractory status epilepticus and sepsis. Post-ICU and outpatient phases remain nutritionally vulnerable, with persistent catabolism and underfeeding common; structured, multidisciplinary rehabilitation and transitional nutrition programs may improve long-term outcomes. CONCLUSION: Future personalised nutrition strategies may rely on metabolic phenotyping and biomarker-informed stratification rather than uniform protein, energy and micronutrient targets for all ICU patients. Integrating individualised energy and protein prescription, targeted micronutrient management, emerging metabolic therapies, and coordinated post-ICU rehabilitation may optimise recovery and functional outcomes. Robust clinical trials are needed to confirm the impact of these personalised strategies on long-term patient-centred endpoints.
articles.ai_summary: This review of current concepts in nutrition therapy for critically ill patients emphasizes the need for individualized, phase-specific nutrition. Experts discuss how inflammation, disease severity, and metabolic changes influence nutritional responsiveness, and propose personalized strategies for tailoring therapy. They also highlight the importance of micronutrient management and macronutrient adaptation throughout the continuum of critical illness and recovery.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings have significant implications for ICU clinical practice, as they suggest that personalized nutrition strategies may improve recovery and functional outcomes for critically ill patients. Robust clinical trials are needed to confirm the impact of these strategies on long-term patient-centered endpoints.

articles.title: Fast Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing for Gram-Negative Bacteremia: The FAST Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Novel blood culture diagnostics provide rapid antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) results for bacteria causing bloodstream infections (BSIs) but have unclear clinical impact. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate clinical outcomes of blood culture testing using a rapid AST method compared with standard AST in patients with BSIs caused by gram-negative bacilli in regions with high prevalence of antimicrobial resistance. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: Open-label randomized clinical trial that enrolled participants from December 2023 to May 2025 (final follow-up, June 18, 2025) at 7 medical centers in Greece (n = 2), India (n = 1), Israel (n = 3), and Spain (n = 1). Hospitalized patients (adults and children) with BSIs caused by gram-negative bacilli were eligible. Statistical analysis was conducted from August 2025 to January 2026. INTERVENTION: Patients were randomized to undergo blood culture evaluation using rapid, phenotypic AST directly from positive blood cultures plus standard susceptibility testing (n = 413) vs standard susceptibility testing alone (n = 437). Local antimicrobial stewardship teams reviewed all patients and provided treatment recommendations. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was a desirability of outcome ranking (DOOR) at day 30, with 3 categories (alive without deleterious events, alive with deleterious events, and death). The difference between rapid and standard testing was summarized as the probability that the DOOR outcomes were more desirable in the rapid testing group. Superiority was concluded if the lower limit of the 95% CI exceeded 50%. Secondary outcomes included 30-day mortality, length of hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, acquisition of hospital-acquired infections, time to effective antibiotic therapy within 3 days, and time to antibiotic escalation or deescalation within 3 days. RESULTS: Of the 899 patients randomized, 850 were included in the primary outcome analysis (median [IQR] age, 72 [21] years; 43% female). The probability that DOOR outcomes were more favorable in the rapid testing group was 48.8% (95% CI, 45.3%-52.4%). Median time to effective antibiotic therapy was not different between the groups in the as-randomized population. Median time to antibiotic escalation or deescalation was faster in the rapid testing group by 14 hours (95% CI, 6-22) in the as-randomized population. There were no differences between the groups in other secondary outcomes. In the prespecified subgroup with carbapenem-resistant infections, median time to effective therapy was 9.5 hours in the rapid testing group vs 28 hours in the standard testing group (difference, -18 hours [95% CI, -42 to 6]). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Among patients with gram-negative bacilli BSIs, rapid blood culture AST was not superior to standard testing by DOOR. When considered with other efficacy and safety outcomes, these findings may help inform the use of rapid susceptibility testing in clinical practice. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06174649.

articles.title: Selective Decontamination of the Digestive Tract during Ventilation in the ICU.
articles.journal: The New England journal of medicine
authors: SuDDICU Investigators for the Australia and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Clinical Trials Group and the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group
The SuDDICU Investigators for the Australia and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Clinical Trials Group and the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Whether selective decontamination of the digestive tract (SDD) reduces mortality among patients undergoing mechanical ventilation and whether it adversely affects microbial ecology in the intensive care unit (ICU) remain unclear. In an earlier analysis of data from Australia, SDD did not result in a lower incidence of in-hospital death than standard care, but data from the full international trial are needed. METHODS: We randomly assigned ICUs in Australia and Canada to use SDD or to continue standard care for two 12-month periods in patients undergoing mechanical ventilation. Patients in the SDD group received specific oral and gastric antimicrobial interventions for the duration of ventilation and an intravenous antibiotic agent for the first 4 days after enrollment. All other patients in the ICU were included in an observational ecologic assessment. Previously reported data from Australia are now combined with data from Canada. The primary outcome was in-hospital death from any cause at 90 days. The secondary clinical outcomes, assessed at 90 days, were death in the ICU and the number of days alive and free of mechanical ventilation, ICU admission, and hospitalization. Microbiologic secondary outcomes included new positive cultures for bloodstream infections and antibiotic-resistant organisms. For the ecologic assessment, the microbiologic outcomes were tested for noninferiority (noninferiority margin, 2 percentage points). RESULTS: In this trial involving 20,000 patients in 26 ICUs, 9289 patients were enrolled in the randomized trial and 10,711 were included in the ecologic assessment. At 90 days, 1175 of 4215 patients (27.9%) in the SDD group and 1494 of 5065 (29.5%) in the standard-care group had died before hospital discharge (odds ratio, 0.94; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.84 to 1.05; P = 0.27). New bloodstream infections occurred in 4.9% of the patients in the SDD group and in 6.8% of those in the standard-care group (adjusted mean difference, -1.30 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.55 to -0.05); antibiotic-resistant organisms were cultured in 16.8% and 26.8%, respectively (adjusted mean difference, -9.60 percentage points; 95% CI, -12.40 to -6.80). In the ecologic assessment, noninferiority of SDD was not confirmed for the development of new antibiotic-resistant organisms. Adverse events considered to be related to SDD or standard care were reported in 12 patients (0.3%) in the SDD group and in no patients in the standard-care group. Serious adverse events occurred in 47 patients (1.1%) and 59 patients (1.2%), respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Among critically ill patients undergoing mechanical ventilation, SDD did not result in a lower incidence of in-hospital death than standard care. (Funded by the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT02389036.).

articles.title: Sulbactam/Durlobactam for CRAB Bacteremia and Pneumonia in a Critically Ill Patient in China: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: Evidence supporting sulbactam/durlobactam (SUL-DUR) for carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) bloodstream infection remains limited, particularly in critically ill patients with multiorgan failure. A 25-year-old man underwent emergency splenectomy for a ruptured splenic artery aneurysm with 7500 mL estimated blood loss. On transfer to our ICU, PaO2/FiO2 was 68 mm Hg, consistent with severe ARDS. He subsequently developed a grade B postoperative pancreatic fistula. A quality-graded sputum specimen grew carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae and CRAB, and a peripheral blood culture drawn during cefoperazone-sulbactam therapy grew CRAB, indicating breakthrough bacteremia; the blood isolate was susceptible to SUL-DUR but resistant to both carbapenems. Ceftazidime-avibactam was replaced with imipenem-cilastatin plus SUL-DUR for eight days, with nebulized colistimethate sodium. Concurrent care included source control, prone ventilation, and pancreatic collection drainage. Procalcitonin had normalized before SUL-DUR began, whereas IL-6 and hs-CRP rose around the positive blood culture and fell during SUL-DUR; he was extubated on ICU day 27. A post-extubation withdrawal episode with convulsions, bronchospasm, and lactic acidosis resolved with rescue sedation. He was discharged from the ICU on June 17, 2026, with negative follow-up blood cultures, and remained well at outpatient review on July 30. This case adds real-world experience regarding the potential role of SUL-DUR in CRAB bacteremia with pneumonia. Because recovery occurred alongside source control, ventilatory support, and sequential antimicrobial therapy, the outcome cannot be attributed to SUL-DUR alone. Larger prospective studies are required to define its role in CRAB bloodstream infection.

articles.title: From Gaps in Maternity Care to Maternal Rescue: An Interprofessional Implementation Agenda for Anesthesia and Maternal Critical Care in Somalia.
articles.abstract: Somalia's maternal health system faces a dual challenge: limited access to skilled maternity care and insufficient capacity to rescue women who deteriorate during or after obstetric emergencies. Hemorrhage, hypertensive emergencies including eclampsia, sepsis, obstructed labor, and urgent cesarean delivery require coordinated maternity, anesthesia, nursing, resuscitation, postoperative surveillance, and critical-care functions. This evidence-informed commentary shifts the discussion from documenting gaps to an interprofessional implementation agenda. We propose five linked priorities: a regulated and supported maternity and obstetric-anesthesia workforce; an evidence-based cesarean safety bundle; step-up maternal high-care capacity; early-warning, crisis resource management, escalation, and referral pathways; and routine measurement through maternal and perioperative quality systems. The approach emphasizes actions that referral maternity hospitals can introduce progressively, with named local accountability, team training, minimum resource requirements, and measurable indicators, while avoiding unsupported assumptions about national critical-care capacity. Somalia does not need to wait for a fully developed intensive-care system before improving maternal rescue. The immediate opportunity is to connect five functions that are too often fragmented: competent anesthesia provision, reliable cesarean safety processes, early recognition of deterioration, monitored maternal high care, and accountable review of outcomes. Strengthening these functions as one interprofessional maternal-rescue pathway offers a practical route to reducing preventable severe maternal morbidity and mortality in Somalia.

articles.title: Case Report: Sepsis With Multisystemic Amyloid Light-Chain Amyloidosis.
articles.abstract: Systemic light-chain (AL) amyloidosis is a complex disorder characterized by extracellular fibril deposition, leading to severe multisystem dysfunction. When sepsis superimposes on preexisting organ impairment, early clinical recognition becomes particularly challenging yet critical. We present a case of a 60-year-old female who presented with generalized edema, dyspnea, and cardiac/renal involvement, subsequently diagnosed with AL amyloidosis based on laboratory, imaging, bone marrow biopsy, and Congo red staining findings. Following chemotherapy with bortezomib and cyclophosphamide, the patient experienced transient cardiac arrest, received an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, and subsequently developed massive ascites. Upon developing Pseudomonas guariconensis bacteremia, she progressed to septic shock requiring intensive care unit admission, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor support, and targeted antimicrobial therapy. Through aggressive supportive care and source control, hemodynamic stabilization was achieved, allowing successful extubation and transfer to the general ward. Superimposed sepsis on severe, multi-organ amyloidosis significantly complicates diagnosis and management. High clinical vigilance, early infection recognition, and prompt targeted therapy are essential to prevent fatal outcomes in patients with preexisting chronic organ dysfunctions.

articles.title: Associated factors for stress ulcers and gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with sepsis or septic shock: A systematic review.
articles.abstract: Sepsis continues to be a major contributor to death among critically ill individuals and places a heavy strain on healthcare resources. In addition to causing systemic inflammation and affecting hemodynamics, sepsis has a significant effect on the gastrointestinal system, leading to complications like stress ulcers and notable gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB), which worsen patient outcomes. While stress ulcer prophylaxis (SUP) has traditionally been included in sepsis treatment protocols, the concept of applying it universally is being increasingly scrutinized due to the absence of definitive mortality advantages and the risk of adverse effects, such as hospital-acquired pneumonia. Nevertheless, there is a notable gap in synthesized research that specifically addresses the independent risk factors for stress ulcers in sepsis patients. We carried out a systematic review in accordance with PRISMA standards, exploring eight databases (CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, Sinomed, PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library) from their inception until September 1, 2026. We included observational analytical studies (either cohort or case-control) that examined factors linked to stress ulcers or significant gastrointestinal bleeding in adult patients with sepsis. Two researchers independently handled the selection of studies, extraction of data, and evaluation of quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Due to the limited number of studies for each association between associated factors and outcomes, a narrative synthesis was utilized. A total of six studies encompassing 131,568 individuals suffering from sepsis or septic shock were analyzed. The incidence rates of stress ulcers or gastrointestinal bleeding (GIB) varied between 2.0% and 32.3%. The identified associated factors were divided into three categories: patient-related (older age, history of GIB, cirrhosis, HIV, cancer/immunosuppression), disease-related (coagulopathy, kidney impairment, high BUN levels, severity of illness scores, source of infection), and treatment-related (mechanical ventilation, use of anticoagulants, corticosteroid therapy, duration of ICU stay). Specifically for stress ulcer, factors such as respiratory failure, high BUN levels, shock, and increased HMGB1/TLR2/TLR4 levels were found to be independently linked to a higher odds. In summary, the likelihood of developing stress ulcers and gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with sepsis is shaped by a variety of factors related to the patient, their illness, and the treatments they receive. Key indicators that consistently emerge include issues with blood coagulation, the presence of shock, the need for mechanical ventilation, liver and kidney dysfunction, the severity of the disease, and any previous occurrences of gastrointestinal bleeding. These results advocate for tailored strategies for stress ulcer prophylaxis based on individual risk rather than a one-size-fits-all approach, offering crucial insights for precise clinical decision-making. Additional high-quality research is essential to confirm and enhance the understanding of these associated factors. PROSPERO (CRD420251242849).

articles.title: SIRT5 deficiency exacerbates sepsis acute renal injury by activating ACSL4/FTH1 axis dependent ferroptosis.
articles.abstract: Sepsis‑associated acute kidney injury (S‑AKI) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients, yet effective targeted therapies remain lacking due to an incomplete understanding of its pathogenesis. Ferroptosis, an iron‑dependent form of regulated cell death driven by lipid peroxidation, has recently been implicated in AKI, but the upstream regulators of this process in sepsis remain undefined. Here, we identify SIRT5, a mitochondrial NAD ⁺ ‑dependent desuccinylase, as a critical endogenous suppressor of ferroptosis in S‑AKI. Using a cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) murine model and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)‑stimulated HK‑2 proximal tubular cells, we show that SIRT5 expression is significantly downregulated in septic kidney injury. Renal tubular‑specific ablation of Sirt5 exacerbated CLP‑induced renal dysfunction, structural damage, and tubular cell death, whereas AAV9‑mediated SIRT5 overexpression attenuated these pathological changes. Mechanistically, SIRT5 deficiency tipped the balance of the ACSL4/FTH1 axis toward ferroptosis: it increased ACSL4‑dependent membrane lipid remodeling and reduced FTH1‑mediated iron sequestration, accompanied by suppression of the antioxidant enzyme GPX4. Consequently, lipid peroxidation, iron overload, and mitochondrial damage were markedly amplified. Notably, knockdown of ACSL4 in SIRT5‑deficient HK‑2 cells effectively reversed lipid peroxidation, iron accumulation, and cell death, establishing ACSL4 as a key downstream effector of SIRT5‑mediated ferroptosis suppression. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized SIRT5-ACSL4/FTH1 regulatory axis that governs ferroptotic susceptibility in renal tubular cells during sepsis, and suggest that pharmacological restoration of SIRT5 activity or blockade of ACSL4‑driven ferroptosis may offer novel therapeutic avenues for S‑AKI.

articles.title: Factors Associated with Early Sepsis-Associated Liver Injury and Predictors of 30-Day Mortality: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Sepsis-associated liver injury (SALI) is associated with higher mortality, but the factors associated with early SALI and the determinants of mortality in patients with SALI remain incompletely understood. This retrospective cohort study included 524 consecutive patients with sepsis (Sepsis-3) in a tertiary intensive care unit (ICU). SALI was defined as total bilirubin ≥2 mg/dL with international normalized ratio ≥1.5, or alanine aminotransferase ≥68 U/L (twice the local upper limit of normal), within 24 hours of ICU admission. Factors independently associated with SALI and with 30-day mortality in SALI were identified by logistic regression after multiple imputation and elastic-net selection, with bootstrap internal validation. Of 523 evaluable patients, 135 (25.8%) met the SALI definition, and their 30-day mortality was higher (63.4% vs 50.0%, p=0.010). Factors independently associated with SALI were macrophage activation-like syndrome (MALS) (aOR: 5.33), an abdominal focus (aOR: 4.03), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) score ≥5 (aOR: 3.07), acute kidney injury on admission (aOR: 2.29) and log-ferritin (aOR: 1.31; 1.48 without MALS and DIC) (all p<0.05; optimism-corrected area under the curve [AUC]: 0.770). Among patients with SALI, immunosuppressive therapy (OR: 8.13), a thoracic focus (OR: 8.62), log-ferritin (OR: 2.04) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) (OR: 1.08 per second) were independently associated with 30-day mortality (all p<0.05); appropriate antibiotic therapy showed a non-significant protective trend (p=0.076). The mortality model showed good discrimination (optimism-corrected AUC: 0.857) but limited calibration (slope: 0.562). SALI was associated with higher 30-day mortality in sepsis. Because the factors associated with SALI were assessed concurrently with liver injury, they describe its clinical profile rather than predict its development. Immunosuppressive therapy, a thoracic focus, higher ferritin levels and prolonged aPTT were associated with 30-day mortality in SALI. These findings should be interpreted with caution and require external validation.

articles.title: Association of SOFA-2 with in-Hospital Mortality in Refractory Septic Shock: A Multicohort Retrospective Study with a 12-Hour Landmark.
articles.abstract: SOFA-2 is an updated organ dysfunction score designed to reflect contemporary intensive care practice. Its clinical relevance in refractory septic shock (RSS) remains unclear. We primarily evaluated the association between SOFA-2 and subsequent in-hospital mortality among patients who were alive and hospitalized at a 12-hour landmark after RSS identification. Comparison with conventional SOFA was secondary and exploratory. This retrospective cohort study used MIMIC-IV as the primary cohort, with external consistency analyses in eICU-CRD and a local institutional cohort. RSS was operationalized using available electronic health record variables based on the SCCM/ESICM consensus framework, although some consensus elements were incompletely captured. Patients who died or were discharged before the 12-hour landmark were excluded from the primary analysis. SOFA-2 and conventional SOFA were assessed during the first 12 hours after RSS identification, with follow-up beginning at the landmark. Cause-specific Cox models were used for the primary analysis. Proportional-hazards diagnostics, time-varying coefficient models, time-dependent AUC, restricted cubic spline, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses were also performed. The primary cohort included 1276 patients, of whom 719 died during hospitalization. In the fully adjusted model, each 1-point increase in SOFA-2 was associated with higher subsequent in-hospital mortality (HR 1.12, 95% CI 1.10-1.14), and the HR per 1-SD increase was 1.54 (95% CI 1.43-1.67). The association attenuated over follow-up but remained positive at 7, 14, and 28 days. Conventional SOFA showed similar per-point associations. Exploratory time-dependent AUC analyses showed only small numerical differences between the two scores. The association was generally consistent across subgroup and sensitivity analyses and directionally consistent in the external cohorts. Among patients meeting database-operationalized RSS criteria who were alive and hospitalized at the 12-hour landmark, higher SOFA-2 scores were associated with higher subsequent in-hospital mortality.

articles.title: Inflammatory and nutritional indices as predictors of poor prognosis in pyogenic liver abscesses: a retrospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: This retrospective study of 458 pyogenic liver abscesses (PLA) patients explored the link between inflammation/nutrition-based indices and poor prognosis in PLA, aiming to enhance the prediction of poor prognosis such as mortality, septic shock, or intensive care unit (ICU) admission. Patient data, including demographics, comorbidities, clinical presentations, laboratory results, and treatment outcomes, were extracted from medical records. Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were performed to identify independent predictors and evaluate their discriminative power. A simplified joint prediction model was developed based on rigorous variable selection criteria, and its performance was assessed using internal validation. Patients with poor prognosis (n = 33) exhibited lower lymphocyte counts, hemoglobin, platelets, and albumin, alongside elevated inflammation markers. Multivariable analysis identified the neutrophil-to-albumin ratio (NAR) (odds ratio (OR) 6.87 per standard deviation (SD), 95% confidence interval (CI) [2.13-22.17], p = 0.001), prognostic nutritional index (PNI) (OR 0.99 per SD, 95% CI [0.894-0.997], p = 0.038), and controlling nutritional status (CONUT) score (OR 1.37 per SD, 95% CI [1.164-1.602], p < 0.001) as independent predictors. ROC analysis showed these indices had good discriminative ability (PNI: area under the curve (AUC) = 0.757, p < 0.001; PLR: AUC = 0.704, p < 0.001; CONUT: AUC = 0.803, p < 0.001; PLT: AUC = 0.740, p < 0.001). Notably, a joint prediction model combining platelet count (PLT) and CONUT achieved superior prediction with an AUC of 0.822. This investigation reveals that easily obtainable inflammatory and nutritional indices (NAR, PNI, CONUT and PLT) serve as reliable predictors of poor prognosis in PLA. A combined model integrating PLT and CONUT demonstrates promising discriminative performance, enabling early risk stratification.

articles.title: Acute Pain Management in the Intensive Care Unit.
articles.abstract: This review summarizes current approaches to pain assessment and pharmacologic therapy in the intensive care unit (ICU) and evaluates the expanding role of regional anesthesia (RA). Contemporary ICU analgesia emphasizes systematic pain assessment and multimodal therapy while avoiding unnecessary deep sedation. RA provides targeted, opioid-sparing analgesia for localized pain but is limited by coagulopathy, infection, altered anatomy, and practical considerations. Fascial-plane blocks may provide useful alternatives in selected patients. Thoracic epidural and paravertebral techniques remain options for selected patients but may cause hypotension and clinically significant bleeding. Ultrasound-guided techniques, including erector spinae, serratus anterior, parasternal, rectus sheath, and transversus abdominis plane blocks, expand analgesic options. Continuous catheter techniques may extend analgesia when prolonged pain is anticipated. However, evidence in heterogeneous ICU populations remains limited, and much of the current evidence is derived from perioperative or trauma populations rather than general medical ICU cohorts. Further ICU-specific comparative trials are needed to define patient selection and clinically meaningful outcomes.

articles.title: Venous Thromboembolism in Acute Necrotizing Pancreatitis Is Associated With Worse Outcomes, With Subtype-Specific Patterns: A Nationwide Analysis, 2016-2022.
articles.abstract: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) complicates acute necrotizing pancreatitis (ANP), but outcomes across extra-splanchnic deep vein thrombosis (DVT), portal vein thrombosis (PVT), and splenic vein thrombosis (SVT) remain poorly defined. We evaluated national trends and in-hospital outcomes in ANP with versus without VTE and across VTE subtypes. Using the National Inpatient Sample (2016-2022), adults hospitalized with principal ANP were identified. Secondary diagnosis codes captured VTE subtypes. Primary analyses compared mortality and major complications in ANP with versus without VTE; secondary analyses compared outcomes by subtype. Among 110,225 ANP hospitalizations, 12.25% had VTE. ANP with VTE had higher in-hospital mortality (aOR 1.89, P<0.001), longer length of stay (adjusted mean difference 10.7 d, P<0.001), and higher hospitalization charges (adjusted mean difference $151,685, P<0.001). VTE was associated with higher rates of mesenteric ischemia, gastric varices, upper GI bleeding, AKI, sepsis, shock, respiratory failure, ARDS, vasopressor use, mechanical ventilation, blood transfusion, and ICU admissions. On subtype analysis, DVT (aOR 2.39, P<0.001) and PVT (aOR 1.45, P=0.001) were associated with higher mortality; SVT was not significantly associated with mortality, though the analysis was limited by few events. PVT was most strongly associated with mesenteric ischemia (aOR 8.28, P<0.001), whereas gastric varices were most associated with SVT (aOR 11.37, P<0.001) and PVT (aOR 3.73, P<0.001). VTE in ANP was associated with higher in-hospital mortality, systemic complications, and resource utilization, with substantial heterogeneity across subtypes. DVT-associated ANP showed higher rates of systemic complications, whereas PVT and SVT showed distinct territory-specific vascular-complication patterns. Prospective studies should evaluate phenotype-specific anticoagulation strategies.

articles.title: Feasibility and Outcomes of External Cephalic Version among Small-for-Gestational-Age Births.
articles.abstract: The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommends that external cephalic version (ECV) be offered to patients with malpresentation. The objective of our study was to evaluate the efficacy and perinatal outcomes among births with small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants after an ECV. This was a population-based, cross-sectional study using National Vital Statistics Systems data of singleton, non-anomalous neonates born after 36 weeks of gestation, with a birth weight of < 2,500 g between 2021 and 2023. Births with a maternal history of previous cesarean delivery were excluded. Births were divided into those who had an ECV attempt and those with a breech fetus at cesarean delivery without a trial of labor. Adverse maternal outcomes (blood transfusion, intensive care unit [ICU] admission, unplanned hysterectomy) and neonatal outcomes (assisted ventilation use, neonatal ICU [NICU] admission, seizures, surfactant use, death) were compared between groups using logistic regression. A total of 8,021 births were included. Of the 8,021 births, 812 (10.1%) had an ECV attempt and 7,209 (89.9%) had a primary breech cesarean delivery. There were significant differences in baseline characteristics between groups. Among the 812 births who had an ECV attempt, 338 (41.6%) had a successful ECV, of which 233 (68.9%) subsequently delivered vaginally. After adjusting for differences, births that had an ECV attempt had lower odds of neonatal-assisted ventilation use (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.65, 95% confidence interval [0.46-0.92]) and NICU admission (aOR 0.48, 95% confidence interval [0.40-0.58]) than those who had a primary breech cesarean delivery. There were higher odds of maternal transfusion in the breech cesarean delivery cohort as compared with those who had an ECV attempt (odds ratio 2.81, 95% confidence interval [1.42-5.56]). Although ECV was successful in 41.6% of births with SGA infants, there were lower rates of assisted ventilation use and NICU admission among those who underwent an ECV attempt. · ECV was successful in 41.6% of SGA births.. · After successful ECV, 68.9% delivered vaginally.. · ECV attempts had lower odds of NICU admission..

articles.title: Heparin Retention and Dispersion Following Injection of Locking Fluid in an Acute Hemodialysis Catheter: A Simulation Study.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Heparin locking is used to maintain patency of acute hemodialysis catheters; however, unintended leakage of locking solution into the systemic circulation may increase bleeding risk. Ideally, locking solution would remain confined to the catheter lumen, maintaining patency while minimizing systemic anticoagulation, yet the mechanisms governing heparin retention and dispersion remain inadequately understood. Patient-specific computational fluid dynamics simulations incorporating non-Newtonian blood flow and species transport were performed using a microcomputed tomography-derived model of an acute dual-lumen hemodialysis catheter to evaluate the effects of injection rate, venous blood flow, and lock volume. Injection of the manufacturer-recommended 1.4 ml lock volume over durations of 0.5-5 seconds resulted in 13-16% (900-1100 U) of injected heparin entering the systemic circulation, yielding transient therapeutic systemic heparin concentrations. Rapid injections increased distal penetration of the locking solution and improved heparin retention (from 84% to 87%). Heparin clearance following injection occurred in two phases consisting of rapid early convective washout followed by prolonged slow diffusive clearance. Reducing lock volume substantially decreased systemic heparin exposure while preserving therapeutic intraluminal heparin concentrations. These findings provide mechanistic insight into catheter locking behavior and suggest that optimization of lock volume may reduce unintended systemic anticoagulation while maintaining catheter patency.

articles.title: Does transfusion of blood products increase the risk of multidrug-resistant infections in critically ill patients?
articles.abstract: To investigate the association between transfusion of blood products during intensive care unit (ICU) stay and the incidence of ICU-acquired colonisation and infection with multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria (ICU-MDR-col, ICU-MDR-inf, respectively). Secondary analysis of two prospective multicentre cohort studies conducted in eight ICUs in France. Adult patients admitted to participating ICUs were enrolled consecutively from May 2019 to June 2021. All patients underwent systematic screening for colonisation with MDR bacteria at admission and weekly thereafter. Exposure to transfusion of blood products during ICU stay, including packed red blood cells (PRBCs), fresh frozen plasma (FFP) and platelet concentrates (PCs), was recorded. The primary outcome was the incidence of ICU-MDR-col and/or ICU-MDR-inf (ICU-MDR-col/inf) until ICU discharge, censored at day 28. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of ICU-MDR-col and ICU-MDR-inf, considered separately. Associations were assessed using mixed-effects Poisson regression models adjusted for prespecified confounders. Subgroup analyses were performed according to immunosuppression status at ICU admission. Among 1103 patients, 358 (32.5%) received transfusion of any blood product. Overall, 292 (26.5%) patients experienced at least one ICU-MDR-col/inf event. Transfusion was associated with an increased incidence of ICU-MDR-col/inf (adjusted incidence rate ratio [aIRR] 1.31, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.06-1.62; p = 0.013), mainly driven by ICU-MDR-inf (aIRR 1.62, 95% CI 1.16-2.24; p = 0.004), but not ICU-MDR-col considered individually. This association was restricted to PRBC transfusion. No significant heterogeneity was observed according to immunosuppression status. Transfusion of PBRCs was associated with an increased incidence of ICU-acquired MDR infections, with no significant heterogeneity observed according to immunosuppression status. These findings support a restrictive approach to transfusion and warrant further investigation into its immunological and ecological consequences in critically ill patients.

articles.title: Initial Red Cell Infusion Rate and Escalation of Respiratory Support in Critically Ill Adults: A Target Trial Emulation.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Current transfusion guidelines address when red cells should be given, not how fast. We estimated the association between the initial infusion rate of a first red cell transfusion and escalation of respiratory support in critically ill adults. Methods: We emulated a target trial in MIMIC-IV v3.1. Of 2790 eligible adults, 1787 received a slower (50-175 mL/h) and 1003 a faster (>175-350 mL/h) initial rate; the primary outcome was escalation to advanced respiratory support or death within 12 h. Overlap weighting estimated marginal risk differences in the overlap population, with 2000 bootstrap resamples refitting the propensity-score model. Sensitivity and continuous dose-response analyses were pre-specified. Results: The primary outcome was classifiable in 2671 patients, with 143 events. Weighted 12 h risks were 4.95% and 6.60%: risk difference 1.65 percentage points (95% CI -0.41 to 3.74), risk ratio 1.33 (0.93 to 1.92). Invasive mechanical ventilation or death, a nested key secondary outcome unadjusted for multiplicity, gave 2.55 percentage points (0.71 to 4.59); 28-day mortality gave -1.45 (-4.10 to 1.30). In the pre-specified dose-response analysis, standardised 12 h risk was lowest near 140 mL/h (4.27%) and rose to 8.83% (6.56 to 11.28) at 350 mL/h. Conclusions: The primary analysis did not distinguish the two initial-rate strategies, although the interval remained compatible with a clinically important increase in risk. The secondary and dose-response findings are hypothesis-generating and do not support changing current infusion-rate practice. These estimates support the design and sample-size planning of a prospective trial assigning infusion rate.

articles.title: Octreotide Plus Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) versus PPI alone in Non-Variceal Upper gastrointestinal (GI) Bleeding in intensive care unit (ICU): A Multi-Center Randomized Trial.
articles.journal: The American journal of the medical sciences
articles.abstract: To compare clinical outcomes between PPI therapy alone and PPI combined with octreotide in patients with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. This prospective, randomized, double-blind, multi-center study included 56 patients allocated to either PPI alone or PPI plus octreotide. Baseline demographics and comorbidities were comparable between groups. Laboratory parameters were assessed over three days. Clinical outcomes included rebleeding, transfusion requirements, mechanical ventilation, surgical intervention, ICU stay, hospital length of stay, and in-hospital mortality. Prothrombin time was significantly higher in the PPI plus octreotide group (median 19 s vs 11.1 s; p=0.001), and urine output was significantly lower (p=0.011). Despite these differences, there were no significant differences in rebleeding rates, blood product transfusion, ICU stay, mechanical ventilation, or need for surgery. In-hospital mortality was significantly higher in the PPI plus octreotide group (39.3% vs 7%; p=0.011). Hospital length of stay was significantly shorter in the PPI plus octreotide group, likely reflecting higher early mortality rather than improved clinical recovery. The addition of octreotide to PPI therapy did not improve bleeding-related outcomes. Prolonged prothrombin time did not correlate with increased bleeding or transfusion needs. These findings suggest no clinical benefit of adjunctive octreotide in this study and underscore the importance of appropriate patient selection.

articles.title: Hemoglobin trends and transfusion practices after cardiac arrest: a cohort study.
articles.abstract: Hemoglobin targets are absent from post-cardiac arrest guidelines. New trials suggest that patients with brain and myocardial injury, injuries common post-arrest, may benefit from higher hemoglobin targets. Trends in post-arrest hemoglobin and real-world practices remain poorly characterized. We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive adult cardiac arrests at three academic hospitals. We screened in-hospital and out-of-hospital arrests with resuscitation efforts ongoing at hospital arrival for inclusion. Patients who survived the initial resuscitation and had a hemoglobin value measured were included. All post-arrest hemoglobin values and red blood cell transfusions were collected through 30 days; descriptive statistics and graphical visualization were used to present hemoglobin trends and transfusion practices. Exploratory analyses evaluated the association between hemoglobin and in-hospital mortality. Of 2,634 cardiac arrests, 958 met inclusion criteria, with 152 (15.9%) out-of-hospital arrests and 806 (84.1%) in-hospital. The mean initial post-arrest hemoglobin was 9.75 g/dL (SD 2.60), with hemoglobin levels declining progressively over the first 20 days post-arrest. Red cell transfusions were delivered for 369 (38.5%) patients in the 30 days post-arrest, with 1,238 total transfusions. The mean pre-transfusion hemoglobin value was 6.96 g/dL (SD 1.06). Pre-transfusion hemoglobin levels were < 7 g/dL for 762 (61.6%) of transfusions, and ≥ 7 g/dL for 476 (38.4%) of transfusions. Over 30 days, the highest proportion of patients transfused was in the first 48 h. Patients with initial post-arrest hemoglobin ≥ 9 g/dL had lower in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.46-0.84, p<0.01). In time-varying analysis, post-arrest hemoglobin through 30 days demonstrated an L-shaped association with mortality, with 95% of the total reduction in mortality hazard captured below 9.20 g/dL. Anemia is common after cardiac arrest, worsening in initial survivors. There is substantial variation in pre-transfusion hemoglobin levels, reflecting clinical equipoise. Clinical trials are needed to disentangle anemia as a driver versus a marker of outcomes, and test whether the risk is modifiable.

articles.title: Safety and Efficacy of Acute Normovolemic Hemodilution in Female Patients: A Secondary Analysis of the ANH Trial.
articles.abstract: Female patients undergoing cardiac surgery have a higher transfusion burden, yet they remain underrepresented in randomized clinical trials. Although the ANH trial showed no significant reduction in the proportion of patients receiving allogeneic blood transfusions with acute normovolemic hemodilution, evidence regarding its efficacy and safety specifically in female patients remains limited. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of acute normovolemic hemodilution (ANH) compared with usual care in female patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. This was a post hoc secondary analysis of the multicenter, randomized ANH trial, which was conducted at 32 centers in 11 countries from April 2019 to December 2024. Of 2010 patients in the original ANH trial, 405 were women and were included in this analysis; 219 had been randomized to receive ANH and 186 to usual care. This secondary analysis was conducted from August 2025 to January 2026. Withdrawal of at least 650 mL whole blood with crystalloids replacement and reinfusion after cardiopulmonary bypass. The primary outcome was the occurrence of at least 1 allogeneic packed red blood cell (pRBC) transfusion during the index hospitalization. Safety outcomes included intraoperative hypotension, intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay, hospital length of stay, mortality, and other perioperative complications. The median (IQR) age of the participants was 62 (54-69) years. The occurrence of allogeneic pRBC transfusion was similar in the ANH and usual care groups (38.8% vs 44.6%, respectively; relative risk [RR], 0.87; 95% CI, 0.69-1.10; P = .24). Intraoperative hypotension occurred more frequently with ANH (16.0% vs 4.8% in usual care; RR, 3.30; 95% CI, 1.62-6.74; P = .02). Patients receiving ANH also had longer ICU stays (mean difference, 21.13 hours; 95% CI, 1.89-40.38; P = .03) and hospital stays (mean difference, 1.92 days; 95% CI, 0.14-3.70; P = .04). No significant differences were observed in mortality or other postoperative complications. In this post hoc secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial, ANH was not associated with a reduction in allogeneic pRBC transfusion among women undergoing cardiac surgery and was associated with more frequent intraoperative hypotension and longer ICU and hospital stay. These exploratory findings warrant confirmation in adequately powered studies specifically designed to evaluate female patients undergoing cardiac surgery. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03913481.
