Appreciation/respect was associated with attenuation of the indirect effect (ACME = 0.00007), whereas endorsement of enhanced reimbursement for two-therapist care of critically ill patients was associated with a larger indirect effect (ACME = 0.00637; 95% CI 0.00122-0.0100). Because the primary mediation analysis used a binary mediator and binary outcome with logistic link functions, a formal ρ-based sensitivity analysis for unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding was not available under this specification.Conclusions: Among Japanese physiotherapists, the association between direct COVID-19 patient contact and burnout was consistent with an indirect pathway operating through a stress-related behavioural mediator. Recognition appeared to buffer this pathway, whereas reimbursement-linked resource strain appeared to amplify it. These findings suggest potentially relevant organisational targets for future intervention, but should be interpreted cautiously given the cross-sectional design and the causal assumptions required for mediation analysis.
articles.ai_summary: This study looked at Japanese physiotherapists who worked with COVID-19 patients and found that direct contact with patients contributed to burnout, but this effect was partly buffered by appreciation and respect from patients and colleagues. The study suggests that organisational resources, such as reimbursement for care, may also play a role in burnout. Burnout prevalence was 19.4% among the physiotherapists.
articles.ai_significance: These findings are relevant for ICU clinical practice as they highlight the importance of organisational resources and staff appreciation in mitigating burnout among healthcare workers, particularly during high-stress situations like the COVID-19 pandemic.

articles.title: Impact of direct transfer to critical care on mortality for patients who undergo emergency colorectal cancer resection: a national population-based cohort study in England.
articles.abstract: It is recommended that patients receiving emergency surgery and with 'high-risk' of morbidity and mortality should be transferred directly from theatre to critical care. Using a national, population-based cohort study, we estimated the effect of direct transfer to critical care on 90-day mortality after emergency colorectal cancer resection, and the variation amongst English NHS hospitals. Patients who underwent emergency colorectal cancer resection between December 2016 and November 2019 according to Hospital Episodes Statistics, National Bowel Cancer Audit or National Emergency Laparotomy Audit were included. Patients were identified as having a direct transfer to critical care through linkage with the Intensive Care National Audit and Research Centre Case Mix Programme. Multivariable logistic regression and propensity score methods were used to measure the effect of direct transfer to critical care on 90-day mortality. In total, 10,441 patients underwent an emergency colorectal cancer resection. Unadjusted 90-day mortality was higher in the direct transfer to critical care cohort (10.9%) than in patients without direct transfer to critical care (3.7%) (odds ratio [OR]: 3.16, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.65-3.77). There was no evidence of an association after risk adjustment (adjusted OR: 1.16, 95% CI: 0.94-1.43) or after propensity score analysis (weighted OR: 0.94, 95% CI: 0.69-1.27). For patients at high risk with a predicted mortality ≥5%, the proportion of patients with a direct transfer to critical care varied widely amongst hospitals (interquartile range 68%-92%; median 83%). Our findings suggest that apparent higher postoperative mortality in patients having direct transfer to critical care can be mostly explained by characteristics of patients, tumours, physiology and surgery. However, the extent to which direct transfer to critical care is used varies widely amongst hospitals. Further work to understand this variation has the potential to improve patient outcomes after emergency colorectal cancer resection.

articles.title: Health economic evaluation of polytrauma treatment in the current aG-DRG system - Results of a Level I Trauma Center.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Resource-intensive polytrauma care is associated with high treatment and readiness costs and poses a financial challenge for hospitals. The aim of this retrospective single-center study of the years 2020 to 2022 was to analyze polytrauma reimbursements and costs. Based on billing and clinical data of 201 polytrauma cases from a German University Hospital and Level I Trauma Center, revenues and costs of the eleven MDC 21 A polytrauma DRGs were analyzed. Ratios of the revenue in relation to LOS, ventilation hours, OR time and implant costs as well as personnel costs were calculated. Contribution margins were determined as an upper-bound estimate. DRG reimbursement was highest for the most severely injured patients (50,852 €, DRG W36Z). It was lowest for patients who died within five days (2,214 €, DRG W60Z) or without surgeries (4,056 €, DRG W61B). The contribution margin was also highest for the most severely injured patients (52,775 €, DRG W36Z). Revenues in relation to ICU LOS (3,455 €/day, DRG W36Z) and ventilation time (238 €/hour, DRG W01B) were lowest for the most severe polytraumas. Regarding OR time and implant costs, reimbursement was lowest for injuries of the spine, pelvis and extremities with 62 €/min (DRG W02B) and 5 €/€ (DRG W02A). Treatment of polytrauma patients with long ICU stay, extended mechanical ventilation and multiple injuries of the extremities, pelvis and spine is not adequately reflected by the current per-case reimbursement in relation to the resources used (ICU days, ventilation hours, OR time and implant costs).

articles.title: Role of Mitochondrial Impairment in Sepsis-Induced Platelet Activation.
articles.abstract: Sepsis-induced mitochondrial impairment has been described in different organs, in both animal models and humans. Excessive radical oxygen species (ROS) could be involved in this phenomenon. As a result, antioxidants have been proposed as a potential therapeutic strategy, although results remain controversial. Platelet hyperactivation is considered a central pathogenic mechanism in the development of sepsis-induced organ damage. In this study, we aimed to determine whether mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to platelet hyperactivation during sepsis. We also evaluated the effect of ROS scavenging using the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoTEMPO. Laboratory investigation. University Hospital. Patients with sepsis/septic shock (n = 3/7), nonseptic burn patients (n = 10), and healthy control subjects (n = 10). Platelet mitochondria and isolated platelets from healthy donors were treated in vitro with plasma from patients with sepsis/septic shock and healthy subjects, before and after preincubation with MitoTEMPO. We measured platelet oxygen consumption rates in isolated human platelets using the Seahorse Extracellular Flux Analyzer. Platelet mitochondrial respiratory chain enzyme activity was measured in mitochondria-enriched fractions by spectrophotometry. Platelet aggregation in platelet-rich plasma was analyzed using light-transmission aggregometry, and leukocyte-platelet adhesion in whole blood by flow cytometry.We found that incubating platelets with septic plasma significantly reduced basal, maximal, and adenosine triphosphate-linked oxygen consumption rate. Incubation of platelet mitochondria with septic plasma also reduced platelet Complex I activity, compared with healthy plasma or plasma from nonseptic burn patients. This decrease was associated with an increase in Epinephrine-induced platelet activation. Preincubating platelets with the mitochondria-selective ROS scavenger MitoTEMPO significantly reversed these effects. Our results show that the mitochondria-selective ROS scavenger MitoTEMPO prevents mitochondrial dysfunction and enhances platelet activation induced by septic plasma in human platelets in vitro. This may help in designing new therapeutic approaches to prevent sepsis-induced organ damage mediated by mitochondrial dysfunction and platelet hyperactivation.

articles.title: Alcohol-positive polytrauma patients: injury patterns, ICU resource use and mortality at a German Level I trauma center.
articles.abstract: In most countries, alcohol consumption is so culturally ingrained that even small amounts are permitted while driving. Even at a blood alcohol concentration of 0.5 g/L, ethanol impairs mental and cognitive performance. Studies from the US and Europe estimate that elevated blood alcohol levels may be detected in 10%-40% of all emergency department patients. Against this background, we investigated the impact of alcohol consumption on injury severity, injury patterns, as well as primary and secondary outcomes in polytrauma patients. This retrospective, single-center cohort study included patients admitted to a Level I trauma center via the trauma room and documented in the TraumaRegister DGU® between 2015 and 2023. Serum ethanol was determined routinely in all adolescent and adult trauma room patients. Patients without serum ethanol measurement or younger than 13 years were excluded. Patients with detectable serum ethanol (> 1 mg/dL, detection limit of the laboratory; ALC) were compared with patients without (noALC) using the χ² and Mann-Whitney U tests. Multivariable logistic and linear regression analyses were adjusted for age, sex, Injury Severity Score (ISS), severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) and pre-injury ASA classification. A dose-response analysis was performed using serum ethanol categories. A total of 1,524 patients were analyzed: 431 (28.3%) were alcohol-positive (ALC) and 1,093 (71.7%) were not (noALC). ALC patients were younger, more often male and had a lower prehospital Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score (p < 0.001), whereas the ISS did not differ (p = 0.396). They were more frequently victims of violent crime and were overrepresented among pedestrians and falls from < 3 m, whereas motorcyclists were more often sober. Alcohol-positive patients were more often treated in the ICU (90.0% vs. 86.3%; p = 0.048), but this association was attenuated after multivariable adjustment (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.40; 95% CI 0.96-2.03). Length of ICU stay and duration of mechanical ventilation did not differ, and alcohol was not independently associated with mortality (aOR 0.91; 95% CI 0.56-1.47). Severe TBI was more frequent in alcohol-positive patients (38.5% vs. 29.5%), increased with serum ethanol concentration, and was the strongest predictor of ICU treatment and mortality. Nearly one in three severely injured patients had detectable serum ethanol. After adjustment for confounders, alcohol was not independently associated with mortality or intensive care resource use, and no dose-response relationship was found for these outcomes. The more frequent ICU treatment of alcohol-positive patients appears to be explained by their distinct injury pattern, particularly the concentration-dependent increase in severe TBI.

articles.title: Slow-tempo piano music listening and short-term anxiety and burnout trajectories in a predominantly nursing sample of ICU healthcare workers: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: Healthcare workers in intensive care units (ICUs) are chronically exposed to high-intensity, high-risk clinical environments, where anxiety and burnout are highly prevalent. Music listening is a low-burden, non-pharmacological supportive strategy with potential stress-reducing effects; however, randomized trials evaluating standardized slow-tempo piano music interventions among ICU healthcare workers remain limited. To compare short-term trajectories in self-reported generalized anxiety symptoms and weighted MBI-GS burnout index values between ICU healthcare workers assigned to a slow-tempo piano music intervention and those assigned to a passive control condition. This single-center, open-label, two-group parallel randomized controlled trial was conducted in the ICUs of a tertiary hospital in China. A total of 126 ICU healthcare workers were enrolled and randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to the piano music group or the passive control group, with 63 participants in each group. The piano music group received a 2-week standardized slow-tempo piano music listening intervention consisting of four 30-minute sessions per week, for a total of eight sessions. The listening sessions were conducted outside ICU working hours, after the end of the participant's shift and before bedtime. The passive control group maintained their usual routines and received neither the study-specified music intervention nor a study-arranged 30-minute rest period. Anxiety and burnout were assessed after the 1st, 4th, and 8th sessions using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 scale and the Maslach Burnout Inventory-General Survey. No outcome assessment was conducted before the first intervention session; therefore, the first assessment (T1) was a post-session assessment rather than a pre-intervention baseline. The study was retrospectively registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2500097216). All 126 randomized participants completed the three assessments. In the full sample, statistically significant group × time interactions were identified for GAD-7 scores (Wald χ2(2) = 46.29, p < .001) and the weighted MBI-GS burnout index (Wald χ2(2) = 6.78, p = .034). In the T1-adjusted analyses, the passive control group had higher GAD-7 scores than the piano music group at T2 (adjusted mean difference = 1.47, 95% CI [0.69, 2.25], p < .001), whereas the adjusted difference at T3 was not statistically significant (adjusted mean difference = 0.85, 95% CI [-0.03, 1.72], p = .057). The passive control group also had higher adjusted weighted MBI-GS burnout index values at T2 (adjusted mean difference = 0.52, 95% CI [0.24, 0.80], p < .001) and T3 (adjusted mean difference = 0.97, 95% CI [0.71, 1.24], p < .001). In the nurse-only sensitivity analysis, the group × time interaction remained statistically significant for GAD-7 scores but not for the weighted MBI-GS burnout index. The piano music and passive control groups showed different short-term trajectories in self-reported anxiety symptoms and the weighted burnout index. However, because the study lacked a genuine pre-intervention assessment and used a passive control condition, the findings should be regarded as preliminary associations in short-term outcome trajectories, not as evidence of intervention efficacy or a specific effect of piano music. Further trials incorporating a pre-intervention baseline, active comparison conditions, and longer follow-up are warranted.

articles.title: Perceived inappropriateness of care among ICU clinicians is associated with burnout and intention to leave the job.
authors: on behalf the PICNL-ICU study group

articles.title: Emergency surgery for blunt abdominal trauma in polytrauma - the impact of time to laparotomy on outcomes.
articles.journal: European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society
articles.abstract: Blunt abdominal trauma (BAT) is common in polytrauma patients. Emergency surgery is required for haemodynamically significant solid organ injury and intra-abdominal hollow organ injury. The effect of time to surgery on outcomes in patients requiring emergency laparotomy remains uncertain. Adult polytrauma patients (ISS > 16) who underwent emergency laparotomy for blunt abdominal trauma between 1996 and 2020 from a trauma registry of a single level one trauma centre were included. Patients were divided into two groups based on the time elapsed from admission to emergency laparotomy: "Super Early" (≤ 60 min) and "Early" (60-180 min). Length of stay (LOS), intensive care unit (ICU)-LOS, ventilation time, re-look operations and mortality were assessed. Adjusted logistic regression was used to determine the independent predictive parameters, including timing of surgery, for mortality. The study included 190 polytrauma patients with concomitant blunt abdominal trauma (mean age 42 years (± 17), median ISS of 36 (IQR: 19)). There were 95 patients in each group. Patients in the "Super Early" group had a compromised haemodynamic status and a higher ISS. Liver injury and serous membrane injury were more common in the super early group. The mortality rate was significantly higher in the "Super Early" group (51.6%) compared to the "Early" group (26.3%) (p < 0.001). Death due to haemorrhagic shock was significantly more frequent in the "Super Early" group (36.8%) compared to the "Early" group (13.7%) (p < 0.001). A regression model was adjusted to determine the independent predictors of mortality. Time to emergency laparotomy was not an independent predictor of mortality. However, increased ISS (OR = 1.04, p = 0.049), age (OR = 1.03, p = 0.037) and decreased systolic blood pressure (OR = 0.98, p = 0.025) were found to be significant predictors of mortality. The timing of surgery showed no independent association with mortality as long as an emergency laparotomy was performed within 3 h of admission. The data suggests that patient-specific characteristics, injury severity and clinical status are more important for survival than the timing of an early emergency laparotomy. Future research should focus on determining the role of delayed laparotomy on outcomes in specific subgroups of patients.

articles.title: Injury patterns, in-hospital outcomes, and resource utilization of acute cuboid and navicular fractures.
articles.journal: The Journal of foot and ankle surgery : official publication of the American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons
articles.abstract: Acute cuboid and navicular fractures can be serious injuries. However, multicenter data on their associated injuries and in-hospital course are limited. To characterize the demographics, injury patterns, in-hospital outcomes, and resource utilization of trauma center patients with acute cuboid and/or navicular fractures. Retrospective cross-sectional database study. The American College of Surgeons National Trauma Data Bank (2017-2019) was queried for acute cuboid and/or navicular fractures. Multivariable regression identified factors associated with discharge to post-acute care, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, and hospital length of stay in adults. Overall, 3,424 patients with 4,084 fractures were identified (2,327 with cuboid and 1,637 with navicular fractures, including 540 with both). Road-traffic mechanisms accounted for 64.5%, and 25.1% had polytrauma. Metatarsal, calcaneal, and talar fractures were the most common concomitant injuries. Combined fractures were more often ipsilateral than contralateral (457 vs 18 patients). Despite infrequent complications, 50.2% were discharged home without post-acute services (home health, inpatient rehabilitation, or skilled nursing care). In-hospital mortality was 1.1%. After adjustment, polytrauma (OR 3.75, 95% CI 3.04-4.61), bilateral involvement, and ankle, tibia, fibula, or metatarsal fractures were associated with discharge to post-acute care, whereas fracture pattern was not. Cuboid and navicular fractures are predominantly high-energy injuries that rarely occur in isolation. Post-acute care needs, ICU admission, and length of stay were associated with overall injury burden rather than the specific bone fractured.

articles.title: Influence of Perioperative Variables on Surgical Site Infection in Patients With Frailty and Prefrailty Undergoing Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting: Retrospective Multicenter Study.
articles.abstract: Surgical site infection (SSI) in patients with frailty undergoing myocardial revascularization is a major clinical challenge, and there is a gap in the literature related to this topic. This study aimed to identify perioperative variables associated with SSI in patients with frailty and prefrailty undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting within 30 days of the procedure. This retrospective observational study included 467 patients with frailty or prefrailty aged 60 years and older who underwent coronary artery bypass grafting in 6 Brazilian centers between January 2018 and December 2024. Frailty was defined using the Fried criteria. SSI was defined as a wound with exposed tissue with positive culture requiring antibiotic treatment. Univariate and multivariate analyses were carried out. The rate of SSI was 5.6% (26/467). The New York Heart Association classification (P=.02), Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI; P=.01), use of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB; P=.003), CPB time (P=.02), total surgery time (P<.001), occurrence of bleeding (P=.04), mechanical ventilation time (P=.001), length of hospital stay (P<.001), intensive care unit stay (P<.001), and need for reoperation (P<.001) variables were associated with SSI in unadjusted comparisons. In the multivariate model, the CCI (odds ratio 1.58, 95% CI 1.25-1.99; P<.001) and use of CPB (odds ratio 4.89, 95% CI 1.71-13.94; P=.003) were independently associated with SSI. The CCI and the use of CPB were independently associated with SSI.

articles.title: Esophageal resonance Raman spectroscopy tracks mixed venous oxygenation in experimental shock and hypoxemia.
articles.abstract: Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) reflects the balance between systemic oxygen delivery and consumption and is widely used as an indicator of tissue oxygenation in critically ill patients. However, its measurement requires invasive venous access. We evaluated whether a customized probe applied to the esophageal mucosa could provide a continuous measurement of regional capillary hemoglobin oxygen saturation (SEsO2) that tracks changes in mixed venous oxygen saturation for early detection of experimental shock with minimal invasiveness. A miniaturized 405 nm resonance Raman spectroscopy (RRS) probe was developed to quantify esophageal regional capillary hemoglobin saturation (SEsO2) based on spectral decomposition of oxy- and deoxy-hemoglobin Raman peaks. Two rat models were investigated: progressive hemorrhage (n = 12) and graded hypoxia (n = 9). At each stage, SvO2, SEsO2, arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2), and serum lactate were measured. Tracking ability and diagnostic accuracy compared to SvO2 and transabdominal near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models (animal random intercepts), (cluster-bootstrapped) receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) analyses, and Pearson correlation. In both models, baseline SEsO2 was ~20% higher than SvO2, consistent with a regional capillary measurement distinct from mixed venous blood. In hemorrhage, LME showed SEsO2 was positively associated with SvO2 (β = 0.53, 95% CI 0.43-0.62; p < 0.0001) and inversely associated with lactate (β = -0.15, 95% CI -0.18 to -0.12; p < 0.0001). In ROC analysis, SEsO2 discriminated SvO2 < 40% with AUC 0.98 (95% CI 0.95-1.00). For transabdominal NIRS, the AUC was 0.82 (95% CI 0.70-0.95). During graded hypoxia, SEsO2 was also positively associated with SvO2 (β = 0.51, 95% CI 0.43-0.60; p < 0.0001) and inversely associated with lactate (β = -0.11, 95% CI -0.13 to -0.09; p < 0.0001). Discrimination of SEsO2 for SvO2 < 40% was AUC 0.92 (95% CI 0.82-1.00). Transabdominal NIRS demonstrated discrimination with high uncertainty (AUC 0.56, 95% CI 0.23-1.00). Esophageal RRS enables molecularly specific measurement of regional capillary hemoglobin oxygen saturation and thereby tracks SvO2 across distinct experimental shock paradigms. These preclinical findings support further investigation of esophageal RRS as a potential minimally invasive monitoring approach for detection of systemic oxygen imbalance.

articles.title: Characteristics and outcomes of haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury and combined injuries from a South African Trauma Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: To describe and compare injury severity, clinical management and mortality among haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury (TBI) and combined haemorrhage+TBI cohorts in a South African trauma population. Secondary analysis of data from the Epidemiology and Outcomes of Prolonged Trauma Care (EpiC) multicentre observational cohort study, April 2021 to December 2024. Six government health facilities and affiliated government ambulances across the Western Cape, South Africa. 18 840 adult patients with blunt and/or penetrating traumatic injuries enrolled in the EpiC registry were eligible for this secondary analysis. Patients <18 years of age and prisoners are excluded from EpiC. Burn injuries, non-haemorrhage and non-TBI injuries were excluded from this analysis. Patients were assigned to one of three mutually exclusive cohorts (haemorrhage, TBI or haemorrhage+TBI) using anatomic and physiologic criteria. The primary outcome was crude, all-cause prehospital or in-hospital mortality. Mantel-Haenszel risk ratios (RRs) for mortality were adjusted for injury severity, injury force type and mode of prehospital transportation. Secondary outcomes included critical interventions, hospital admission, length of stay and time from injury to death. A total of 7614 patients met inclusion: 5146 (67.6%) haemorrhage, 1556 (20.4%) TBI and 912 (12.0%) haemorrhage+TBI. The majority were male (85.1%) with a median age of 31 years. Patients with haemorrhage+TBI received more intensive care, including airway interventions (38%), transfusions (41%) and intensive care unit admissions (36%). Crude mortality was highest in haemorrhage+TBI (31.3%), followed by TBI (7.7%) and haemorrhage (5.4%). After injury-pattern specific severity adjustment, mortality risk remained significantly higher in haemorrhage+TBI than in TBI (RR 1.87, 95% CI 1.60 to 2.19) and haemorrhage (RR 3.38, 95% CI 2.96 to 3.85). Estimates were similar after additional adjustment for injury force and prehospital transportation (RR 1.84 and 2.98). In this South African population, haemorrhage+TBI was the least prevalent but most high-risk cohort with greater morbidity and mortality compared with haemorrhage or TBI alone, even after adjusting for injury severity. These findings may inform system level planning and resource allocation particularly in resource-limited settings.

articles.title: Fibrinolytic Activation and Its Association with Mortality After Traumatic and Thermal Injury.
articles.abstract: Characterize plasma markers of fibrinolytic activation and their associations with mortality in burn and trauma patients from hospital admission through 48 hours. Fibrinolytic activation following burn and non-burn trauma is associated with increased mortality. Whether fibrinolytic activation differs between burn and non-burn injury is unknown. Adult patients aged 18 years and older who presented to one of two regional trauma centers or one regional burn center within 4 hours of injury were included. Blood was collected at admission and at hours 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24, 36, and 48. Plasmin-antiplasmin complex (PAP), D-dimer, and plasminogen concentrations in plasma were determined. Of 590 patients, 58.3% presented with blunt, 27.1% with thermal, and 14.6% with penetrating injury. Admission PAP and D-dimer were higher in trauma (blunt and penetrating groups combined) than in burn patients (p<.001). Non-survivors (injury types combined) had higher PAP and D-dimer and lower plasminogen (p<.001) at admission and over time. After adjusting for age, injury severity and % total body surface area burned, admission PAP ≥1645.6 ng/mL was associated with 7.0 times higher odds for mortality (p=.002) and D-dimer ≥6.5 µg/mL was associated with 5.0 times higher odds for mortality (p=.01). Changes in biomarkers over time were similar between trauma and burn patients. Higher fibrinolytic activation was associated with mortality in trauma and burn patients. Trauma patients had higher fibrinolytic activation markers than burn patients, while patterns of change were similar. Data suggest potential for use of similar resuscitative adjuncts to mitigate early fibrinolytic dysfunction in trauma and burns.

articles.title: Bioactive adrenomedullin dynamics and microcirculatory changes in a porcine model of hemorrhagic shock.
articles.abstract: Hemorrhagic shock is a leading cause of preventable trauma death, marked by impaired oxygen delivery and endothelial dysfunction. Bioactive adrenomedullin (bio-ADM) regulates endothelial barrier integrity, but its dynamics during hemorrhagic shock and resuscitation remain unclear. This secondary analysis of a porcine hemorrhagic shock model investigated bio-ADM and its association with macro- and microcirculatory parameters during resuscitation. All animals received crystalloid infusion (10 mL/kg/h) from anesthesia induction onward. Shock was induced by blood withdrawal to maintain MAP at 40 ± 5 mmHg for 60 min (T5), before randomization to control (n = 7), fluid (n = 6), or noradrenaline (n = 7) groups, with intervention groups titrated to MAP targets of 65 then 90 mmHg (60 min each). Macrocirculation was assessed via vital signs and pulse contour analysis; microcirculation via hyperspectral imaging (tissue oxygenation, hemoglobin, water index). Fluid resuscitation improved macrohemodynamics and microcirculatory oxygenation versus control and noradrenaline, which failed to sustain perfusion and impaired microcirculatory oxygenation. Bio-ADM increased after shock induction (p < 0.001), peaking at T9 (120 min of therapy). At T5, levels were comparable among control (16.8 [13.6-18.9] pg/ml), fluid (15.65 [15.43-16.55] pg/ml), and noradrenaline (14.3 [7.85-18.95] pg/ml). Thereafter, bio-ADM continued to rise in control (19.7 [17.4-32.6] pg/ml) and noradrenaline (21.2 [14.4-33.45] pg/ml), while stabilizing in the fluid group (12.05 [10.65-15.18] pg/ml); accordingly, the T5-T9 increase was smaller in the fluid group than in control (p = 0.022) or noradrenaline (p = 0.003). The fluid group received ~3-fold more fluid by T9. Higher bio-ADM correlated with lower MAP, higher lactate, and lower ScvO₂, but not oxygen delivery (DO₂); a higher tissue water index correlated with a smaller rise. Bio-ADM increased during hemorrhagic shock, extending previous observations from cardiogenic and septic shock, and represents a comparatively non-specific marker of endothelial and microcirculatory stress rather than specific to any single shock etiology. Effective resuscitation was associated with stabilization, rather than a clear decrease, of bio-ADM levels, though this coincided with higher fluid administration, and dilution cannot be excluded. Whether bio-ADM offers therapeutic utility to guide resuscitation remains unclear, warranting further prospective evaluation in animal and human studies.

articles.title: Nursing management of postoperative hemorrhagic shock: A case study in intensive care.
articles.abstract: Postoperative hemorrhagic shock is a time-critical complication associated with high morbidity and mortality, particularly in older surgical patients, requiring rapid, coordinated management in the intensive care unit (ICU). This case report describes specialized nursing management guided by the International Classification for Nursing Practice (ICNP®/CIPE®) and Benner's Clinical Wisdom Theory. An 89-year-old woman underwent emergency gastrojejunostomy for intestinal obstruction and subsequently developed hemorrhagic shock with profound anemia (hemoglobin nadir 5.8 g/dL), severe hyperlactatemia (12 mmol/L), hypothermia (33.6 °C), peripheral hypoperfusion, and hypotension (mean arterial pressure <65 mmHg). She required orotracheal intubation, invasive mechanical ventilation, and deep sedation. Diagnostic reassessment included serial hemoglobin and arterial blood gas analyses, lactate trending, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, and surgical re-exploration with intraoperative upper endoscopy, which suggested an upper gastrointestinal source (suspected Mallory-Weiss type lesion) treated endoscopically. Nursing priorities, structured using ICNP®, focused on perfusion restoration and correction of the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy), multimodal analgesia, continuous monitoring, prevention bundles (infection and pressure injury prevention), and structured family communication. The patient progressively stabilized, with hemoglobin increasing to 9.6 g/dL, lactate decreasing to <1 mmol/L, normothermia recovery, discontinuation of vasopressors, and no documented ICU-acquired complications during the ICU stay. This case highlights how standardized nursing language (ICNP®/CIPE®), combined with advanced clinical reasoning and evidence-based ICU bundles, can improve the structure, traceability, and continuity of nursing care in postoperative hemorrhagic shock.

articles.title: Designing a hybrid surgical ICU to avoid intrahospital transport in selected critically Ill patients: the CUHK-SZ institutional concept.
articles.journal: World journal of emergency surgery : WJES
articles.abstract: Intrahospital transport for surgery exposes critically ill patients to equipment failure, displacement of tubes and lines, interrupted monitoring, and physiologic instability. Although transport protocols can reduce these hazards, they do not address the underlying physical decoupling of surgical infrastructure from the critical care environment. This institutional perspective describes the rationale and design of a hybrid surgical ICU planned for the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen (CUHK-SZ) Medical Center: a dedicated clinical space designed to function as both a critical care unit and a procedural suite, bringing surgery to the patient rather than transporting the patient to the operating room (OR). The model is presented as an illustrative, hypothesis-generating concept rather than a validated clinical pathway. The design concept, which is a patient-centered approach, should guide healthcare delivery in modern medicine by placing the patient at the forefront of all decisions and mobilizing all available resources to serve them. This approach addresses all three domains: personnel, environment, and equipment. Overlapping anesthesiology and critical care competencies support integrated staffing. Connectable ICU rooms, adequate space and electrical capacity, anterooms, and switchable HEPA-filtered positive-pressure ventilation meet environmental requirements. Total intravenous anesthesia, portable surgical platforms, and minimally invasive or robotic techniques reduce dependence on fixed OR infrastructure. At CUHK-SZ, the concept is planned as a prototype in the trauma building using two adjacent ICU rooms with an openable partition and switchable ventilation. Candidate patient groups, procedural levels, and implementation requirements are presented as provisional, expert-derived proposals, and engineering testing and simulated drills are planned before any clinical use. The hybrid surgical ICU is a technically plausible option for carefully selected patients at high risk from transport, but its clinical effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness remain unproven. The CUHK-SZ concept is intended to generate hypotheses for prospective evaluation, and its transferability to existing hospitals is likely to depend on incremental adaptation rather than direct replication.

articles.title: Determinants of Adoption of a Mechanical Ventilation Dashboard in Intensive Care: Measurement Instrument for Determinants of Innovations-Based, Single-Center, Cross-Sectional Evaluation.
articles.abstract: Lung-protective ventilation (LPV) reduces complications of mechanical ventilation, yet adherence in intensive care units (ICUs) remains inconsistent. Digital dashboards may support LPV by improving situational awareness and supporting protocol adherence. However, adoption of such tools in high-acuity clinical environments depends on a range of cognitive, professional, and contextual determinants. The Measurement Instrument for Determinants of Innovations (MIDI) provides a validated framework to systematically assess these factors. This study aims to identify determinants influencing the adoption of a newly piloted mechanical ventilation dashboard in the ICU using the MIDI framework. We conducted a single-center, cross-sectional evaluation among ICU health care professionals during a dedicated survey period within a pilot introduction of a mechanical ventilation dashboard at Amsterdam University Medical Center. Participants completed a structured questionnaire consisting of 24 MIDI items adapted to the ICU context rated on a 5-point Likert scale ("completely disagree" to "completely agree"), supplemented by open-ended questions on perceived barriers and facilitators to its use. Determinants were classified as facilitators when ≥80% of respondents selected "agree" or "completely agree" and as barriers when ≥20% selected "disagree" or "completely disagree." Open-ended responses were analyzed using a general inductive thematic approach. A total of 71 completed questionnaires were analyzed, including responses from nurses, physicians, intensivists, ventilation specialists, and researchers in mechanical ventilation. Six determinants met the criteria for facilitators: outcome expectations, self-efficacy, procedural clarity, low complexity, correctness, and observability. Two determinants met the criteria for barriers: relevance for client and professional obligation. Analysis of open-ended responses highlighted perceived barriers such as additional workload, the need for an extra device, overlap with existing systems, and limited role-specific relevance. Facilitators included improved situational overview, educational value, easier trend monitoring, and increased efficiency. This evaluation identified key determinants influencing the adoption of a mechanical ventilation dashboard in the ICU. While the dashboard was generally perceived as useful and easy to understand, adoption was shaped by determinants related to workflow integration, role-specific relevance, and professional responsibility. These findings suggest that successful introduction of digital clinical support tools in intensive care requires attention not only to technical design, but also to how such tools align with users' roles, daily work processes, and shared clinical responsibilities. Systematic assessment of determinants provides actionable insights into the adoption of digital decision-support tools in high-acuity care settings.

articles.title: VIDD or CIADD? The ventilator remains a bona fide culprit.
articles.abstract: Rosà and colleagues recently proposed that mechanical ventilation (MV) may not be the primary driver of diaphragm dysfunction in critically ill patients, advocating the term "critical illness-associated diaphragm dysfunction" (CIADD) over "ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction" (VIDD). While we support distinguishing VIDD from CIADD, we contend that the review's central conclusion underestimates the causal role of MV itself.This commentary addresses three questions in turn. First, does MV injure the diaphragm under controlled conditions? Here the evidence is strong: brain-dead donor studies-dismissed by the authors as a "unique patient category"-are a uniquely informative, though not pure, human model of controlled MV exposure, and their dismissal creates an unfalsifiable position. Second, how much does MV contribute to diaphragm dysfunction in critically ill patients? This is considerably less certain: the molecular abnormalities observed in critically ill patients (ubiquitin-proteasome activation, RyR1 calcium leak, mitochondrial oxidative stress) coincide with pathways that MV reliably induces in controlled animal experiments, providing biological plausibility-though not proof-that MV contributes to the molecular phenotype of critical illness. Third, do MV and critical illness interact? We propose that CIADD should serve as an umbrella term encompassing VIDD as a distinct mechanistic subtype-rather than replacing it-analogous to how "pneumonia" subsumes VAP, HAP, and CAP, and we propose three differentiated model types for future research: pure VIDD models, pure CIADD models, and combined models with factorial design.VIDD and CIADD are mechanistically distinct but interacting entities. Future research should employ models that minimize confounding from critical illness to isolate ventilation-specific injury pathways. Importantly, establishing that VIDD exists is not equivalent to establishing that preventing VIDD is beneficial; clinical trials are needed to demonstrate the feasibility and benefit of diaphragm-protective strategies. Diminishing MV's role risks undermining the mechanistic foundation of diaphragm-protective ventilation strategies.

articles.title: Respiratory mechanics modifies the impact of ventilator settings on clinical outcome in patients with acute brain injury.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate whether respiratory system elastance (ERS) modifies the associations of tidal volume (VT) and respiratory rate with clinical outcomes in mechanically ventilated patients with acute brain injury. METHODS: In this post hoc analysis of the VENTIBRAIN study, ERS was computed as the ratio of driving pressure (ΔP) to VT/PBW. Effect modification by ERS on outcome associations was assessed. RESULTS: In 1158 patients, VT was similar across ERS tertiles (median 7.9, 7.6 and 7.1 mL/kg), resulting in a marked ΔP gradient across tertiles (median 5, 9, and 12 cmH2O). Higher VT was associated with lower ICU mortality in patients with low ERS (OR 0.52, 95%CI 0.36-0.74) but not in those with high ERS (OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.89-1.51; Pint < 0.001). Higher respiratory rate was associated with worse outcomes, particularly at low ERS, with the association attenuating at higher ERS. The Bayesian optimal VT/PBW decreased continuously with ERS, from 11.4 mL/kg at ERS 0.5 cmH2O/(mL/kg) (≈ ΔP 6 cmH2O) to 4.4 mL/kg at ERS 2.5 cmH2O/(mL/kg) (≈ ΔP 11 cmH2O), while the optimal respiratory rate increased from 15 to 19 breaths/min. At constant alveolar ventilation, 1-cmH2O ΔP increase had comparable prognostic impact to ≈ 3 breaths/min respiratory rate increases. These results were consistent irrespective of ARDS diagnosis. CONCLUSIONS: The impact of ventilator settings is modulated by ERS. A physiological framework for VT adjustment could consider ΔP along with the respiratory rate required to maintain isocapnia, with outcome effects governed by a trade-off of ≈ 3 breaths/min per 1-cmH2O change in ΔP.

articles.title: Intracranial pressure physiology, monitoring and individualized management in the acute brain injured patient.
articles.abstract: Acute brain injury (ABI), including traumatic brain injury, ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke, is associated with high morbidity and mortality, which is driven not only by the primary brain injury, but also by the development of secondary cerebral insults. Among these, raised intracranial pressure (ICP) plays a central pathophysiological role, acting both as a consequence and a driver of ongoing brain injury through mechanical deformation and cerebral ischemia. Although invasive intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring has a longstanding and ongoing role in neurocritical care management, the interpretation and clinical use of ICP remain controversial. Traditional management strategies rely on fixed ICP thresholds (e.g., > 22 mmHg) to trigger a standardized stepwise escalation of therapy; however, growing clinical evidence indicates that tolerance to ICP elevation varies widely across patients, disease entities, and physiological contexts. This review summarizes the physiological determinants of ICP, including intracranial compliance, cerebrospinal fluid dynamics, cerebral blood volume, and systemic factors, and describes the mechanisms underlying intracranial hypertension. We discuss limitations of using fixed ICP thresholds and highlight emerging concepts, such as ICP burden, waveform morphology, cerebral autoregulation, and functional brain monitoring, as tools to individualize ICP interpretation. The role of invasive and noninvasive ICP monitoring (nICP) modalities is reviewed, emphasizing the complementary value of nICP in guiding decision-making when invasive monitoring is unavailable or contraindicated. Particular attention is given to the integration of ICP within multimodal neuromonitoring frameworks assessing cerebral perfusion, oxygenation, and metabolism. Finally, we explore future perspectives, including the potential of artificial intelligence-based approaches to analyse complex neuromonitoring data, predict secondary insults, and move toward actionable, patientspecific therapeutic strategies. Collectively, these advances support a shift from a uniform, threshold-driven approach toward individualized, physiology-informed management of intracranial hypertension.

articles.title: Postintensive Care Frailty of Older Patients With Septic Shock: A Post Hoc Analysis of a Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Postintensive care frailty impairs quality of life in survivors of severe illness. While anabolic hormone deficiency and prolonged inflammation are considered key physiologic mechanisms, specific features associated with frailty progression remain unclear. This study aimed to elucidate clinical characteristics associated with frailty deterioration following recovery from septic shock in older adults. DESIGN: Post hoc analysis of a randomized controlled trial. SETTING: ICUs in Japan. PATIENTS: Adults of 65 years or older with septic shock. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Data were analyzed from a randomized controlled trial investigating optimal blood pressure targets in patients of 65 years or older with septic shock. Frailty at 90 days after intensive care was classified as no-to-mild, moderate, and severe based on the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) scores of less than or equal to 4, 5-6, and greater than or equal to 7, respectively. Baseline characteristics, treatments, and outcomes were compared across these frailty categories. Factors associated with postintensive care frailty were identified using ordinal logistic regression fitted with a generalized estimating equation model. Among 513 eligible patients, 339 patients survived to 90 days; 103 patients (30.4%) had no-to-mild frailty, 114 patients (33.6%) had moderate frailty, and 122 patients (36.0%) had severe frailty, respectively. Higher presepsis CFS scores (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.03 [1.72-2.40] per 1-point increase; p < 0.001), higher sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) scores (aOR, 1.16 [1.06-1.26] per 1-point increase; p < 0.001), and corticosteroid use (aOR, 1.72 [1.14-2.61]; p < 0.001) were independently associated with frailty. Subgroup analyses revealed that corticosteroid use was associated with frailty deterioration in patients with baseline frailty (CFS ≥ 5), whereas SOFA scores were associated with frailty in patients with tissue hypoperfusion (lactate, ≥ 2 mmol/L). CONCLUSIONS: Baseline frailty before sepsis, organ dysfunction severity, and corticosteroid therapy independently predict severe postintensive care frailty in older adults with septic shock.

articles.title: Targeted Temperature Management at 35°C vs. 37°C for Heatstroke in ICU: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
authors: Heatstroke Research Group in Southwest China
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the feasibility of conducting a trial comparing targeted temperature management (TTM) at 35°C-37°C in intubated heatstroke patients, while collecting preliminary data on safety and clinical outcomes. DESIGN: Pilot multicenter randomized clinical trial (June to December 2024). SETTING: Ten tertiary ICUs in China. PATIENTS: Thirty-five intubated adults (18 yr or older) with heatstroke meeting predefined diagnostic criteria. Key exclusions: nonenvironmental hyperthermia, expected death within 24 hours, or contraindications to temperature management. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to two TTM strategies. The therapeutic hypothermia group received protocolized rapid cooling using a combination of ice packs, precooled blankets, and ice-cold IV saline to achieve the target of 35.0°C within 2 hours, which was then maintained for 48 hours. The controlled normothermia group received conventional cooling measures (ice packs, 32°C blankets) only if body temperature exceeded 38.0°C, with the goal of maintaining core temperature between 36.5°C and 37.5°C. Shivering was managed according to a stepwise protocol, with a "lytic cocktail" (chlorpromazine, promethazine, and meperidine) available as rescue therapy for refractory shivering in both groups. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Recruitment rate was 83.7%, retention rate was 97.2%, and protocol adherence exceeded 88%. For clinical outcomes, no significant differences were observed in 28-day poor functional outcome (17.6% vs. 16.7%) or survival (82.4% vs. 83.3%). However, therapeutic hypothermia was associated with significantly higher rates of severe gastrointestinal injury (Acute Gastrointestinal Injury grade 3-4: 52.9% vs. 0%; p < 0.001) and arrhythmias (41.2% vs. 11.1%; p = 0.045). The lytic cocktail was required in 100% of hypothermia-group patients vs. 27.8% in the normothermia group ( p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: This pilot study confirms the operational feasibility of a large-scale randomized clinical trial. However, therapeutic hypothermia was associated with significantly worse gastrointestinal injury and higher arrhythmia incidence, without evidence of neurologic or survival benefit. The universal requirement for pharmacological shivering control in the hypothermia group raises additional safety considerations. Based on current evidence, this strategy should not be routinely adopted in ICU heatstroke management.

articles.title: Post-Extubation Recall of Thirst During Mechanical Ventilation Among Intensive Care Unit Patients: A Conventional Content Analysis.
articles.abstract: In ICU patients, particularly after extubation, thirst is a common and troubling symptom. Although earlier research has focused mainly on quantifying thirst severity and its clinical correlates, less is known about the subjective experiences of patients, including their emotional responses, sense of helplessness, help-seeking actions, and the challenges they face in obtaining relief within the ICU. Therefore, this study aimed to examine how post-extubation ICU patients experience thirst and the strategies they use to manage or alleviate it. Between January and August 2024, this qualitative research was carried out in Tehran, Iran, using conventional content analysis. Participants were recruited through purposive sampling, and data were collected via semi-structured interviews conducted in Persian with 20 patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) following extubation. Interviews proceeded until data saturation occurred, and even though they were held after extubation, the thirst experiences participants reported mostly pertained to the time of mechanical ventilation and intubation. The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guideline was followed in this study. Three main categories were identified in this study: 'Unrelieved Thirst' (Hope despite Disappointment and Cognitive and Emotional Burden of Thirst), 'Seeking Relief' (Spiritual Coping and Endurance and Non-Verbal Pleading for Water), and 'Emotional Collapse and Withdrawal' (Resigned Withdrawal and Emotional Isolation and Perceived Neglect). Participants experienced persistent thoughts about water, employed spiritual coping strategies, used gestures without words to express thirst, and eventually emotionally withdrew when their needs were persistently ignored. The study revealed that post-extubation thirst is experienced as a deeply upsetting phenomenon affecting physical, psychological, and existential levels, where patients face physical discomfort, emotional distress, challenges in communication, and a sense of being overlooked in the ICU. The findings highlight the urgent necessity for systematic thirst assessment, improved non-verbal communication techniques, and compassionate, patient-focused nursing care to reduce thirst-related distress. Healthcare providers must be trained to identify both verbal and non-verbal thirst signals and to incorporate patients' cultural and spiritual resources into supportive care. The research delivers a comprehensive understanding of the multifaceted nature of thirst in ICU patients, demonstrating that unresolved thirst may result in emotional collapse and withdrawal. It highlights the significance of managing thirst as an essential human requirement in critical care. The study followed the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) guideline. No patient or public contribution.

articles.title: Perme Mobility Scale Is Associated With Morbidity and Mortality in Patients Undergoing Lung Transplant: 1-Year Follow-Up.
articles.journal: Physiotherapy research international : the journal for researchers and clinicians in physical therapy
articles.abstract: Lung transplantation (LTx) is an effective treatment for patients with advanced chronic lung disease who are unresponsive to other therapies. Functional capacity is increasingly recognized as an important prognostic indicator in transplant candidates and recipients. To assess functional status using the Perme Mobility Scale in patients undergoing LTx, and to examine its association with mechanical ventilation (MV) duration, ICU and hospital length of stay, and mortality over a 1-year follow-up. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of patients admitted to the ICU at Dom Vicente Scherer Hospital, Porto Alegre, following lung transplantation between January 2018 and December 2019. Perme Mobility Scale scores were recorded at ICU admission and hospital discharge. Data on MV duration, ICU and hospital length of stay, readmissions, and mortality were collected from medical records and follow-up calls. Sixty-seven patients were included (median age 57 years; 52.2% female). Higher Perme scores were significantly associated with shorter MV duration, shorter ICU and shorter hospital stay. Specifically, the total Perme score at hospital discharge was negatively correlated with mechanical ventilation duration (r = -0.408; p = 0.001) and ICU length of stay (r = -0.314; p = 0.01). Additionally, mechanical ventilation duration categories were significantly associated with 1-year mortality (p = 0.005), with the highest mortality observed in patients requiring mechanical ventilation for > 48 hours. Improved functional status as measured by the Perme Mobility Scale was associated with better clinical outcomes in lung transplant recipients. The Perme Mobility Scale represents a potentially useful prognostic marker that warrants further validation in prospective multicenter studies before being established as a tool for prognostic risk stratification.

articles.title: Management of renal failure in earthquake-related crush syndrome: Multicenter intensive care outcomes.
articles.journal: Ulusal travma ve acil cerrahi dergisi = Turkish journal of trauma & emergency surgery : TJTES
articles.abstract: Crush syndrome (CS) is a clinical condition associated with multisystem organ dysfunction that develops after traumatic rhabdomyolysis and primarily affects the kidneys. The aim of this study was to characterize the incidence, risk factors, and treatment patterns of acute kidney injury (AKI) in earthquake victims with CS, with a particular focus on renal replacement therapy (RRT) use and clinical outcomes. In this retrospective multicenter study, 247 adult patients with earthquake-related CS who were admitted to intensive care units (ICUs) in 22 hospitals after the Kahramanmaraş 2023 earthquakes were analyzed. Demographic data, injury patterns, laboratory parameters, treatment protocols, and outcomes were evaluated during the first 15 days following ICU admission. AKI developed in 78.5% (n=194) of patients, and RRT was required in 62.4% (n=121) of those with AKI. Multiple logistic regression analysis demonstrated that myoglobin and creatinine levels were associated with an elevated risk of developing AKI (odds ratio [OR]: 1.001; 95% confidence interval CI: 1.000-1.001 and OR: 1.735; 95% CI: 1.151-2.615, respectively). Similarly, creatinine level and reasons for ICU admission were identified as factors influencing RRT administration. (OR: 1.7; 95% CI: 1.28-2.15 and OR: 2.9; 95% CI: 1.26-6.90, respectively). The 30-day mortality rate was higher in patients with AKI than in those without AKI. Mortality rates were similar between patients with AKI who received RRT and those who did not. This study demonstrates the high incidence of AKI in earthquake-related CS, underscores the need for improved disaster preparedness with adequate dialysis capacity and early risk stratification using serum myoglobin and creatinine levels for optimal management.

articles.title: Clinical burden and predictors of hospitalization in extremity gunshot wounds: A single-center retrospective study.
articles.journal: Ulusal travma ve acil cerrahi dergisi = Turkish journal of trauma & emergency surgery : TJTES
articles.abstract: This study aimed to retrospectively evaluate the clinical characteristics, temporal admission patterns, and clinical outcomes of patients with extremity gunshot wounds (GSW) presenting to a tertiary care teaching and research hospital. A total of 123 patients presenting with GSWs affecting at least one extremity between January 2024 and December 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. Injury characteristics, interventions, and clinical outcomes were evaluated. Factors independently associated with hospital length of stay (LOS) and intensive care unit (ICU) admission were identified using negative binomial regression and multivariate logistic regression analyses, respectively. Of the patients, 116 (94.3%) were male, with a mean age of 29.9±11.9 years. The lower extremity was the most frequently affected region (69.1%), and 42 of 43 fractures (97.7%) were open fractures. The ICU admission rate was 26.0% (n=32), and in-hospital mortality was 4.1% (n=5). A total of 43.1% of admissions occurred between 18: 00 and 23: 59. In negative binomial regression, concomitant injury (incidence rate ratio [IRR]=6.93; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.82-12.57; p<0.001), fracture (IRR=5.02; 95% CI: 2.82-8.93; p<0.001), and reoperation (IRR=2.73; 95% CI: 1.44-5.16; p=0.002) were independently associated with length of hospital stay. In logistic regression, neurovascular injury (odds ratio [OR]=28.12; 95% CI: 7.60-104.09; p<0.001) and concomitant injury (OR=20.36; 95% CI: 5.62-73.81; p<0.001) independently predicted ICU admission. Extremity GSWs predominantly affect young males and cluster during evening hours. Concomitant injury and fracture were independently associated with length of hospital stay, whereas reoperation was associated with prolonged hospitalization during the clinical course, while neurovascular injury and concomitant injury independently predict ICU admission.

articles.title: Pulmonary Herpes Simplex Virus Reactivation in Invasively Mechanically Ventilated Patients With COVID-19 in Intensive Care Unit.
articles.abstract: Patients in intensive care units (ICU) under mechanical ventilation, particularly those with SARS-CoV-2 infection, are highly susceptible to Herpes simplex virus (HSV) reactivation. Given the lack of data on the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron and Delta variants, this study aimed to assess the prevalence of pulmonary HSV reactivation in mechanically ventilated patients with SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia. The impact of HSV replication on SARS-CoV-2 replication, and conversely, was investigated, along with the susceptibility of HSV strains to antiviral therapies. This retrospective study included 381 mechanically ventilated ICU patients in Lyon. Overall, 103 patients (27.0%) experienced HSV reactivation, with a trend toward a higher prevalence among SARS-CoV-2-positive patients (32.8%) compared to SARS-CoV-2-negative (24.1%; p value = 0.058). HSV reactivation was significantly higher with the Delta variant (46.2%) compared to Omicron (27.1%; p value = 0.045); the Delta variant was associated with a 2.38-fold increased risk of HSV reactivation. HSV-positive patients exhibited a 1-log lower SARS-CoV-2 viral load compared to HSV-negative patients, a finding indicative of the natural course of SARS-CoV-2 infection followed by HSV reactivation, rather than viral interference. Unexpectedly, acyclovir resistance mutations appeared in the UL23 gene in at least 13.6% of HSV-1 strains in patients with an HSV load above 105 copies/mL. Complementary phenotypic and genotypic approaches allowed to identify three novel substitutions in UL30: Q217R, D741A, and E756K, classified as polymorphisms. Further optimization is needed in the management of mechanically ventilated ICU patients with pulmonary HSV reactivation, especially regarding antiviral resistance testing.

articles.title: Critical Care Nurses' Encounters With Multicultural Patients and Families in Saudi Arabia: A Qualitative Study.
articles.abstract: To examine the perceptions and experiences of local and expatriate critical care nurses when interacting with multicultural patients and their families in Saudi healthcare settings. A descriptive qualitative exploratory design was employed to gain an in-depth understanding using purposive sampling. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, conducted in English, with 18 nurses from intensive care, cardiac care, burn and emergency units. We operationally defined multicultural patients and families as those whose nationality, language, religion, or cultural background differed from that of the treating nurse (see Section 1 for the full definition). Interviews explored nurses' perceptions and encounters with multicultural patients and families. Transcribed data were analysed using thematic analysis. Four major themes emerged. Communication barriers, particularly language differences, were the most frequently reported and, according to participants, the most immediately consequential challenge, since language determined whether basic clinical information could be exchanged at all; cultural and religious beliefs, limited health literacy and organisational constraints shaped how well that information was received and acted upon. Nurses employed adaptive strategies, including teamwork, translation technologies and institutional support (e.g., embassies, social workers), largely in the absence of formal interpreter services. Nurses described a strong personal and professional commitment to diversity, equity and inclusion; however, most reported little or no structured training in cultural competence, relying instead on informal, experience-based learning and identified specific system-level gaps in interpreter provision and culturally adapted policy. Critical care nurses face substantial challenges in caring for multicultural patients. Enhancing cultural competence requires tailored training, adequate resources and system-level support. These findings underscore the importance of organisational policies and infrastructure that promote culturally sensitive, patient-centred care. Structured cultural competence training and access to system-level resources, including professional interpreters and culturally adapted policies, are essential. These measures enable nurses to communicate effectively, respect patients' cultural and religious practices, and deliver equitable, patient-centred care. The study highlights key communication barriers and effective strategies for culturally competent care in post-Vision 2030 Saudi healthcare settings. Findings may inform education, policy and practice and support efforts to strengthen patient-family-nurse interactions and culturally responsive care. We adhered to the relevant EQUATOR Network reporting guidance using the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ); the completed COREQ checklist is provided in Table S1. No patient or public contribution.

articles.title: Effect of Virtual Reality Relaxation on Alarm Fatigue and Professional Quality of Life Among Nurses in Intensive Care Units.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit nurses are faced with a large number of equipment alarms daily, which can increase the likelihood of errors and threaten their professional quality of life. Today, the use of virtual reality to create relaxing experiences in stressful environments has received attention. This study aimed to determine the effect of virtual reality relaxation on alarm fatigue and the professional quality of life among ICU nurses. This is an intervention study with a pretest-posttest design with a control group. ICU nurses who met the inclusion criteria were selected conveniently and were randomly assigned to two intervention and control groups (30 people in each group). The intervention was implemented as three 20-min virtual reality relaxation sessions over a week. The data collection tools included the Alarm Fatigue Scale (AFS) and the Professional Quality of Life (ProQOL) questionnaire. The questionnaires were completed before and immediately after the intervention. The results showed that the mean AFS score improved significantly after the intervention (p < 0.001), and there was a significant difference between the intervention and control groups (p = 0.014). The mean dimensions of ProQOL also improved significantly in all three dimensions of compassion satisfaction, burnout, and secondary trauma stress after the intervention (p < 0.001). There was a significant difference between two groups in all dimensions after the intervention (p < 0.001). The significant improvement in AFS and ProQOL scores indicates that the use of new technologies, such as virtual reality can be considered as a complementary tool in promoting the mental and professional health of nurses in stressful environments.

articles.title: Risk Factors for Poor Outcomes of Mild and Moderate Traumatic Brain Injury Patients in Tanzania: A Retrospective Cohort Study Using Latent Class Analysis.
articles.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major global health concern, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). LMICs have higher injury rates and limited quality of care. TBI patients can be stratified as mild, moderate, and severe risk based on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). Although most poor outcomes are from severe TBIs, mild and moderate TBI patients significantly contribute to the overall morbidity and mortality, and may benefit from early monitoring to identify deterioration of status. Our goal was to identify unique subgroups within the mild and moderate TBI population at a high risk for poor outcomes. We selected mild (GCS 14-15) and moderate (GCS 9-13) TBI patients from a TBI registry collected at a small city, regional referral hospital in Moshi, Tanzania, from May 2014 to April 2017. With these subsets (mild: n = 1738, moderate: n = 346), we performed a latent class analysis (LCA) to define unique patient classes based on clinical course, vital signs, and demographics. We then performed a survival analysis using a Cox proportional hazard model to examine the association of the defined latent classes with clinical outcome. The predictor variables were demographic variables, hospital interventions, and vital signs. The outcome of interest was a dichotomized discharge Glasgow outcome scale extended score (good outcome 7-8 and poor outcome 1-6). The LCA identified five classes among mild TBI patients: Adolescent (18.8%), Assault (31.5%), Young Adult Polytrauma (32.7%), Adult Polytrauma (9.2%), and RTI with ICU (7.8%). Three classes were identified among moderate TBI patients: Assault (20.2%), RTI with ICU (26.3%), and RTI without ICU (53.5%). Road traffic injury was the predominant mechanism in both severity groups (67% and 68%, respectively), and poor outcomes occurred in 4% of mild and 16% of moderate TBI patients. Relative to the lowest-risk reference class, all other mild TBI classes had higher hazards of poor outcomes. Among moderate TBI classes, RTI with ICU had a higher hazard of poor outcome than RTI without ICU (HR 2.58, 95% CI 1.26-5.24). We identified clinically distinct latent classes within GCS-defined mild and moderate TBI groups, with differences in discharge outcomes across classes. These findings suggest that combining GCS category with demographic, physiological, injury, and care-process information may provide additional prognostic stratification. The results do not establish that GCS is inadequate; rather, they support further evaluation of complementary, context-appropriate risk-stratification approaches.

articles.title: A Case of Hemorrhagic Shock Due to Abdominal Hemorrhage in Hemophilia A: The Role of Laboratory Medicine in Multidisciplinary Team.
articles.abstract: Spontaneous abdominal hemorrhage due to hemophilia A is one of the most lethal complications, progressing rapidly and potentially leading to hemorrhagic shock or death. We report a case of a 38-year-old male patient with hemophilia A who presented with massive spontaneous abdominal hemorrhage, leading to a large hematoma and severe hemorrhagic shock. Upon admission, the patient showed unstable vital signs and a significant decline in hemoglobin levels, indicating an extremely perilous condition that required immediate multidisciplinary collaborative intervention. A multidisciplinary team was assembled, including specialists from emergency medicine, intensive care, hematology, cardiothoracic surgery, laboratory medicine, and radiology. The team quickly diagnosed active abdominal hemorrhage and performed successful catheter-directed arterial embolization. Despite ongoing hemoglobin decline after the procedure, the multidisciplinary team employed targeted laboratory monitoring and assessments to identify underlying causes and adjust coagulation factor replacement and transfusion strategies, effectively stabilizing hemoglobin levels. During recovery, the patient developed progressive jaundice, which was determined to be due to the absorption of the large hematoma, thus preventing unnecessary invasive procedures. This case underscores the importance of a multidisciplinary approach in managing complex critical conditions and highlights the vital role of laboratory medicine in accurate diagnosis, decision-making, and management of complications.

articles.title: A specialist-led interprofessional weaning program to prevent weaning failure in high-risk patients: the PRiVENT study.
articles.abstract: Effective strategies to prevent weaning failure and prolonged invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in patients at high risk of weaning failure are limited. We evaluated a structured, specialist-led interprofessional weaning program. In this prospective, multicenter, non-randomized interventional study, mechanically ventilated patients were screened 96 h to 11 days after intubation. Patients meeting predefined high-risk criteria received a specialist-led interprofessional weaning program, while a parallel control group was derived from health insurance claims data. The primary outcome was successful weaning at ICU discharge. The primary analysis included 349 intervention patients and 1,768 controls. Successful weaning occurred in 58.3% of intervention patients and 51.7% of controls. In the adjusted primary analysis, the odds ratio for successful weaning was 1.46 (95% CI, 0.99-2.17; P = 0.057), and the difference did not reach statistical significance. In prespecified propensity score-matched analysis, successful weaning occurred in 58.3% of intervention patients and 46.4% of matched controls (OR, 2.90; 95% CI, 1.61-5.24; P < 0.001). An exploratory analysis restricted to ICU survivors also showed higher odds of successful weaning in the intervention group (OR, 2.10; 95% CI, 1.09-4.04; P = 0.026). Overall, 16.3% of intervention patients were transferred to a specialized weaning center. These patients had longer ventilation durations, contributing to a longer overall duration of IMV in the intervention group. The PRiVENT intervention was feasible and successful weaning was numerically more frequent in the intervention group, although the prespecified adjusted primary analysis did not reach statistical significance. These findings suggest a potential benefit of structured, multidisciplinary weaning support. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05260853, registered on March 2, 2022.

articles.title: Duration of antibiotic therapy in sepsis and severe infections in critically ill patients.
articles.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
articles.abstract: Antibiotic treatment duration in critically ill patients has undergone major reevaluation. Historically concerns for short therapy included a lower cure rate and emergence of resistance, whereas prolonged courses raised risks of microbiome disruption, superinfection, Clostridioides difficile colitis, and resistance. Defining optimal duration of therapy in sepsis and severe infections remains challenging due to heterogeneity in host immunity, pathogen virulence, infection site and source control. Mechanistic insights from microbiology and PK/PD highlight how bacterial inoculum, biofilms, mutant selection windows and altered drug distribution in critical illness influence bacterial clearance and resistance selection. Experimental models and PK-optimized dosing strategies underscore the potential to shorten therapy by accelerating pathogen eradication. Across a range of serious infections, randomized trials consistently show that short course therapy (<7 days) is noninferior to longer courses, including bacteremia, intra-abdominal infections and ventilator-associated pneumonia. Biomarker guided strategies-particularly procalcitonin-based algorithms-might further individualize duration of therapy and safely reduce exposure. Uncertainty remains for S. aureus bacteremia, infections caused by non-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli, difficult to treat multidrug-resistant organisms, invasive candidiasis and immunocompromised patients. Robust evidence supports markedly reduced duration of therapy for uncomplicated bloodstream infections after effective source control, intra-abdominal infections and ventilator-associated pneumonia. Infections involving retained prosthetic material or devices often require prolonged therapy or long-term suppressive regimens. Future research must include adequately powered trials across diverse populations, and evaluate rapid diagnostics, host-response profiling, and individualized response-guided strategies. Optimizing antibiotic duration in critically ill patients ultimately requires integrating mechanistic understanding, individual clinical evolution, and stewardship principles to balance potential efficacy and potential harm.

articles.title: Comparison of two automated pupillometry indices in patients with acute brain injury: the prospective multicentre LYNX cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Automated pupillometry quantifies the pupillary light reflex in acute brain injury. The neurological pupil index (NPi) is the established composite index and carries prognostic value. A second index from a different device, the quantitative pupil index (QPi), has recently become available, but whether it conveys equivalent information in non-anoxic acute brain injury is unknown. METHODS: LYNX was a prospective cohort study in three European intensive care units (September 2022-July 2024). Consecutive adults with traumatic brain injury, subarachnoid or intracerebral haemorrhage, or ischaemic stroke ventilated for more than 12 h were enrolled and followed for 6 months. Paired NPi (NPi-300) and QPi (NeuroLight) measurements were obtained at least every 6 h to day 7. Ancillary cohorts of healthy volunteers (dark vs. bright light) and surgical patients (before and after sufentanil and propofol) were also studied. The primary outcome was the correlation between the two indices; secondary outcomes were their association with intracranial hypertension and unfavourable 6-month outcome (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended ≤ 4). Values below 3 were considered abnormal, with QPi thresholds of 2 and 4 as sensitivity analyses; multivariable models were adjusted for age, sex, admission Glasgow Coma Scale score and focal deficit. RESULTS: Among 108 patients (median age 57 years [IQR 44-67], 60.2% male), 7089 paired measurements were obtained. The two indices were moderately to strongly correlated (r = 0.717, 95% CI 0.705-0.730). Each 10-percentage-point increase in abnormal values independently predicted unfavourable outcome (NPi: OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.09-2.04, p = 0.013; QPi: OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.31-2.37, p < 0.001). QPi was associated with intracranial hypertension (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.04-1.82, p = 0.025), whereas NPi was not. Ambient lighting and contralateral eye opening had no meaningful effect in 75 volunteers. In 20 sedated non-brain-injured patients, propofol reduced QPi to a median of 1 (IQR 1-3) and NPi to 4.0 (IQR 3.6-4.3). CONCLUSIONS: NPi and QPi were correlated and both predicted 6-month outcome, but QPi was far more sensitive to anaesthetics, which probably confounds its association with intracranial hypertension. The indices are not interchangeable in sedated critically ill patients. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05567978. Registered 5 October 2022.

articles.title: Burn mechanism does not predict ICU mortality beyond the Abbreviated Burn Severity Index: A 24-year registry analysis.
articles.journal: Journal of plastic, reconstructive & aesthetic surgery : JPRAS
articles.abstract: Flame burns are consistently associated with higher mortality than scald injuries; however, it is unclear whether burn mechanism independently influences outcome or primarily reflects differences in injury severity. Therefore, we performed a retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained registry by including 1069 adult patients with flame or scald burns who were admitted to a tertiary burn intensive care unit between 2000 and 2024. The primary outcome was intensive care unit (ICU) mortality. Logistic regression analyzes evaluated the association between burn mechanism and mortality before and after adjustment for Abbreviated Burn Severity Index (ABSI) and calendar year, with an additional model incorporating the individual ABSI components and calendar year. Patients with flame burns had significantly larger burns, higher ABSI scores, more frequent inhalation injury, and higher prevalence of full-thickness burns (all p < 0.001). Crude ICU mortality was significantly higher following flame burns than scald injuries (27.8% vs. 10.3%; OR 3.36, 95% CI 2.26-5.01; p<0.001). However, burn mechanism was no longer independently associated with mortality after adjusting for ABSI and calendar year (OR 1.03, 95% CI 0.63-1.69; p=0.913) or after adjusting for the individual ABSI components and calendar year (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.57-1.71; p=0.967). Age, total body surface area burned, inhalation injury, and full-thickness burns remained independently associated with mortality. These findings indicate that the higher mortality observed after flame burns is attributable to greater injury severity rather than burn mechanism.
