The National System for Knowledge-Driven Healthcare Management (NPO) in Sweden commissioned the development of a practice recommendation for the follow-up of critically ill adults. Multidisciplinary experts in ICU survivorship formed a task force group. A systematic literature search in four databases was conducted in 2024 to identify pre-existing systematic reviews on the topic. The literature was reviewed, assessed for quality and recommendations were developed based on the literature evidence. The draft was discussed among multiprofessional groups involved in follow-up, in workshops with critical care nurses (n = 30) and professionals responsible for follow-up clinics (n = 74) and among patient representatives (n = 4). The final draft underwent external peer review by representatives from relevant professional organisations, the national registry for intensive care and governmental agencies in Sweden. The consensus recommendation suggests that all adult patients with an ICU length of stay ≥ 48 h are recommended for follow-up, with an initial contact within 1 week of ICU discharge to assess clinical status, identify early problems and ensure continuity of care. Patients and their families are recommended to be offered an outpatient follow-up visit at 2-3 months after discharge, led by ICU clinicians and, when possible, delivered by a multidisciplinary team. Validated screening tools and objective tests are recommended to assess relevant outcomes, including post-traumatic stress, anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment, physical function and Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) as appropriate. Patients with identified problems should be referred to appropriate healthcare providers or specialist services for further management. This consensus recommendation provides a framework for patient selection, timing and assessment to support a more structured and equitable management of post-intensive care syndrome. Systematic follow up of ICU survivors after hospital discharge is needed in order to assess long-term patient-centred outcomes. This is a consensus set of recommendations and not a GRADE-based clinical practice guideline for doing this, which can be considered by relevant ICUs.

articles.title: Bedside pharmacist interventions for managing intravenous drug incompatibilities in critically ill patients.
articles.journal: Exploratory research in clinical and social pharmacy
articles.abstract: Patients admitted to intensive care units are at increased risk of intravenous drug incompatibilities, owing to polypharmacy and the limited number of available venous access devices. To evaluate bedside pharmacist interventions for managing drug incompatibilities identified during intravenous administration in intensive care unit patients. A cross-sectional study with prospective data collection was conducted between June and December 2025 in five intensive care units of a university hospital. Two pharmacists assessed medication administration at the bedside and checked compatibility using the Micromedex and American Society of Health-System Pharmacists (ASHP) Injectable Drug Information databases. The type and number of central venous access devices, infusion modality, proposed interventions, and the healthcare team's response were recorded. Data were described using absolute and relative frequencies. A total of 887 infusions were analyzed in 88 patients, of which 159 corresponded to occurrences of incompatibility or lack of compatibility data (73 distinct drug combinations). Of these 159 occurrences, 135 (84.9%) were incompatible, and 24 (15.1%) lacked compatibility studies. Most of the pharmacist interventions performed were accepted by the healthcare team (130/159; 81.8%). The high frequency of incompatibilities observed is related to the large number of intravenous medications and the complexity of therapeutic regimens used in intensive care. Bedside pharmacist involvement proved feasible and contributed to safer medication administration practices in these units.

articles.title: Preserved anabolic skeletal muscle capacity in response to exercise and protein intake after critical illness.
articles.abstract: Low muscle mass and persistent weakness are common after critical illness, but the mechanisms behind impaired recovery are incompletely understood. The aim of this study was to investigate the skeletal muscle anabolic response to combined resistance exercise and protein intake in intensive care unit (ICU) survivors, compared to matched controls without a history of critical illness. We hypothesised that residual anabolic resistance limits muscle regeneration after ICU stay. Former patients were enrolled within 3 to 6 months of intensive care unit discharge. Muscle biopsies were obtained before and after resistance exercise using a flywheel leg extension ergometer, combined with ingestion of 24 g hydrolysed protein. Muscle protein fractional synthetic rate was determined from the incorporation of [ring-²H₅]phenylalanine into mixed-muscle protein during a primed continuous intravenous infusion. Anabolic and proteolytic pathways were measured using standard assays. Group-by-time differences were analysed using linear mixed models. The primary comparison was the between-group difference in pre-to-post change in muscle protein synthesis. Twenty ICU survivors (60 ± 12 years, 30% female, BMI 26.9 (IQR 22.9-28.7), SAPS 3 62.3 ± 15.8) and 20 age- and sex-matched controls were included. ICU survivors had significantly lower quadriceps muscle thickness (p = 0.02) and handgrip strength (p = 0.04) than controls. In ICU survivors, muscle protein synthesis from plasma precursor amino acids was higher at baseline than in controls (0.041%/hour vs. 0.030%/hour, p = 0.009), but increased less (Δ 0.031 vs. Δ 0.040%/hour, p = 0.04). Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis was similar between groups (0.071%/hour vs. 0.070%/hour, p = 0.70). At baseline, ICU survivors showed lower activation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway. In both groups, the intervention increased anabolic signalling, decreased initiation of autophagy and increased parts of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. In ICU survivors with persistent muscle loss and weakness, the increase in muscle protein synthesis after combined resistance exercise and protein intake was smaller than in controls, in the context of a higher baseline fractional synthetic rate. Post-intervention muscle protein synthesis rates were similar between groups. These findings provide the first mechanistic support for structured exercise-nutrition rehabilitation to promote muscle recovery after critical illness. This study was prospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05261984), 2022-02-20.

articles.title: Risk Factors for Admission to the Intensive Care Unit and Mortality in Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplant Recipients with Acute Myeloid Leukemia.
articles.abstract: Adults with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are at risk of requiring intensive care unit (ICU)-level care following allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT). Risk factors for admission to the ICU and outcomes are, however, poorly defined. To assess risk factors associated with ICU admission in such patients, identify variables associated with ICU mortality, and analyze the outcome of ICU survivors in comparison to HCT recipients not admitted to the ICU. Here, we retrospectively analyzed a cohort of 1,265 adults with MDS/AML or AML who received an allograft while in first or second remission between 2006 and 2023. The cumulative incidence of ICU admission was 9.2% on day +100 after HCT. HCT-comorbidity index (hazard ratio [HR]=1.15, P=0.005), treatment-related mortality (TRM) score (HR=1.07, P=0.004), and graft from an HLA-mismatched donor (HR=2.19, P=0.018) were independently associated with ICU admission. Within 100 days of ICU admission, 50 patients (43%) died; poor performance status (odds ratio [OR]=5.45, P=0.005), higher TRM score (OR per one unit increase=1.14, P=0.035), and secondary AML (OR=2.71 P=0.035) were associated with increased day +100 mortality after ICU admission. In a landmark analysis, patients admitted to the ICU during the first 100 days after HCT and alive at day +150 had significantly higher NRM (HR=2.36, P<0.001) after multivariable adjustment. Together, these results highlight that ICU admission is common after allografting in adults with AML and is associated with high mortality. Identification of patients at increased risk may, ultimately, help develop possible preventive strategies and allow testing in particularly vulnerable individuals.

articles.title: Biomarker tests for invasive Candida infection in critically ill patients in the UK (A-Stop): a multicentre diagnostic test accuracy study.
articles.abstract: The current practice of empirical antifungal treatment for suspected invasive Candida infection in the intensive care unit (ICU) leads to overtreatment. Biomarkers might better target treatment; however, their diagnostic accuracy in this patient group is uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate whether a biomarker or a combination of biomarkers has sufficiently high negative predictive value (NPV) to enable early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in patients in ICUs. In this prospective, multicentre, diagnostic test accuracy study, we recruited patients who had been started on empirical antifungal treatment for suspected candidiasis and had blood cultures drawn within 24 h of starting treatment from 43 UK ICUs. We tested a research blood sample, collected within 24 h of the standard-of-care care blood culture (ie, within 48 h of starting empirical antifungal treatment), with three DNA detection tests (Fungiplex, T2Candida, and CandID) and one (1,3)-β-D-glucan test (Fungitell). We assessed the accuracy of these tests against an international consensus definition of proven invasive Candida infection and a constructed reference standard for proven or probable infection. The primary outcome was NPV for exclusion of proven Candida infection; we also reported sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios. Among 4005 patients screened, 1251 were enrolled. A total of 1225 participants, recruited between April, 2018 and Feb, 2023, were evaluable, among whom 54 (4·4%) had proven invasive Candida infection. The median duration of antifungal treatment was 9 days (IQR 5-15), and survival at 28 days was 76·8%. The index tests had similar NPVs: 96·6% (95·3-97·6) for Fungiplex, 97·1% (94·7-98·6) for T2Candida, 96·7% (95·4-97·8) for CandID, and 97·2% (95·5-98·4) for Fungitell; however, sensitivity varied widely among the tests, from 27·5% to 68·6%. The optimal test combination was Fungitell and CandID, which had an NPV of 97·5% (95·7-98·7) and a sensitivity of 75·0%. Combining these biomarkers with standard-of-care blood culture testing further increased the NPV to 98·6% (97·0-99·4), with a sensitivity of 85·1%. No single biomarker had sufficiently high sensitivity to justify stopping empirical antifungal treatment. Combining Fungitell and CandID with standard-of-care blood culture testing could provide a sufficiently high NPV to allow early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in this patient group, thereby reducing overtreatment, although this gain in sensitivity is accompanied by a reduction in specificity. Randomised trials are needed to confirm the clinical and cost-effectiveness of this diagnostic strategy before it is adopted in practice. UK National Institute for Health and Care Research Health Technology Assessment Programme and the Research Charitable Trust Fund of the Belfast Health & Social Care Trust.

articles.title: Knowledge and attitudes toward advance directives among ICU nurses.
articles.abstract: End-of-life decision-making in Intensive Care Units (ICUs) may be hindered not only by the absence of advance directives (ADs), but also by limited knowledge among ICU nurses. The aim of this study was to analyse knowledge and attitudes regarding advance directives among ICU nurses. An observational, descriptive, cross-sectional and multicentre study was conducted among ICU nurses working in public hospitals in Las Palmas (Spain). An anonymous electronic questionnaire was used. Statistical analysis was performed using R Core Team 2024. A total of 229 responses were obtained from a population of 260 professionals, yielding a response rate of 88.1%. Most participants were women (75.6%) and had a median of 6 years of ICU experience (interquartile range: 3-14). Overall, 87.7% reported not having received specific training on advance directives (ADs). Although attitudes toward ADs were highly favorable (scores above 9/10), the level of knowledge was limited, particularly regarding legal aspects, procedures, documentation, and content. A discrepancy exists between nurses' favorable attitudes toward ADs and their limited practical knowledge. The implementation of targeted training programs, along with the development of institutional protocols, could enhance the integration of ADs into ICU clinical practice.

articles.title: What's new in trauma critical care?
authors: ESICM Trauma and Emergency Medicine Section

articles.title: Principles of drug dosing for obese patients in the intensive care unit.
articles.abstract: The increasing prevalence of severe obesity in intensive care unit (ICU) patients has led to several challenges with medication dosing. Doses listed in product labels or tertiary references typically do not account for the pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic variability encountered with obesity, leading to the potential for treatment failure or an adverse effect. The purpose of this review is to provide guidance for ICU clinicians when crafting pharmacotherapy regimens in critically ill patients with extreme obesity. A literature search was performed to identify relevant articles pertaining to the pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics of medications in obese patients. Articles describing both general treatment principles and medication specific assessments were retrieved. Bibliographies were searched for additional publications. Evidence guiding medication use in critically ill obese patients is limited by the small number of patients with more extreme forms of obesity, the lack of clinical outcome measurements, and the few studies that are specific to the ICU. Obesity-related alterations in pharmacokinetic parameters, such as apparent volume of distribution and drug clearance, may hinder attainment of pharmacodynamic targets. Individualized dosing strategies are essential to optimize therapeutic outcomes. This review provides dosing recommendations for selected ICU medications and proposes a practical framework to guide medication dosing decisions in this patient population. Drug dosing in critically ill obese patients should be individualized by assessing pharmacokinetic variability and whether pharmacodynamic goals can be achieved. Selecting the correct weight for weight-based calculations or dose for fixed regimens is paramount for achieving these goals. Consultation with a clinical pharmacist may be beneficial.

articles.title: UNOS Registry Analysis: How Does Heart Transplant Recipient Weight Affect Waitlist Days?
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Body weight of heart transplant (HTx) recipients affects waitlist days. However, no prior report exists to articulate this in detail. The aim of this study is to analyze the effect of recipients' weight to HTx. The United Network of Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry was analyzed under the current allocation from 2018 to 2023. The cohort was divided into three even weight groups: low (<77.1 kg), middle (77.1-92.1 kg), and high (>92.1 kg). Candidate/donor demographics, weight distributions, waitlist days in UNOS Status, cumulative incidence of HTx and delisting, post-HTx survival, and cutoff weight for earlier HTx were analyzed. A total of 16,664 HTx recipients were included (5,535: low, 5,537: middle, and 5,592: high). Donors and recipients had a weight distribution mismatch (p = 0.003). For waitlist days, status 1 was comparable; however, the high group with status ≥2 had approximately twice longer waitlist days than the low group. The high group had a lower incidence of HTx (p < 0.001) and higher delisting (p = 0.02) than the low group. One year survival was comparable (p = 0.28). The weight cutoff for earlier HTx was 80 kg with a 21.6% increased rate of HTx (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.216; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.171-1.263, p < 0.001). Recipients weighing <80 kg had earlier HTx and a higher incidence of HTx. The effect of pre-HTx weight management requires further study.

articles.title: Ex Vivo Heart Perfusion Versus Cold Storage in Prolonged Preservation Period: A Juvenile Porcine Experimental Model.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Cross-clamp times greater than or equal to 4 hours are critical for donor heart viability. We compared cold storage (CS) and normothermic ex vivo heart perfusion (EVHP) during prolonged preservation using a juvenile porcine model. Twenty-two piglet hearts (~10 kg) were assigned to CS or EVHP for 6 or 8 hours, followed by 2 hours of working-mode (WM) perfusion. Metabolism, cardiac function, and cell damage were compared using two-sample t-tests or Fisher's exact tests, and temporal changes during perfusion were assessed using linear mixed-effects models and generalized estimating equations. During EVHP, the minimal rate of pressure change decreased, and arterial lactate levels increased after 5-6 hours. Compared to CS, EVHP hearts showed higher left atrial pressure (6 vs. 0 mm Hg, p = 0.011), arterial lactate levels during WM (p < 0.001), and NFκB-p65 levels (p = 0.002) at 6 hours, and lower cardiac output (90 vs. 120% of normal, p = 0.026), higher left atrial pressure (7 vs. 3 mm Hg, p = 0.009), higher arterial lactate levels during WM (p < 0.001), and increased neutrophil infiltration (p = 0.033) at 8 hours. Ex vivo heart perfusion hearts deteriorated beyond 5-6 hours and showed greater hemodynamic, metabolic, and inflammatory changes at both 6 and 8 hours. Ex vivo heart perfusion enhancements reducing immune response and inflammation are crucial for expanding the donor pool.

articles.title: Sensitivity of Damage Markers for Mechanical Trauma to Erythrocytes in Mechanical Circulatory Support Devices: A Multispecies Study.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Mechanical circulatory support (MCS) advancement relies on fully understanding remaining hemocompatibility issues, including identifying and monitoring a variety of damage markers, as hemolysis alone is insufficient to understand the full scope of total blood damage. It is also important to understand how these alternative markers vary between species, as animal surrogates are often used in device development. This work focuses on evaluating erythrocyte-derived extracellular vesicles (ErEVs) released during MCS perfusion as an alternative marker for monitoring erythrocyte damage. Porcine, bovine, and human washed red blood cells (RBCs) were perfused through a blood circulatory loop using the CentriMag pump. Both hemolysis and ErEV production were monitored over time to compare the sensitivity of both to mechanically induced trauma and to observe species-dependent differences. All species produced significant increases in ErEV concentrations, while only human and bovine erythrocytes produced significant increases in free hemoglobin. There were no differences in the normalized index of hemolysis between species, but bovine RBCs produced significantly more ErEVs than human or porcine, which were similar. Regarding damage marker sensitivity, ErEV generation appears to be a promising complementary marker to hemolysis and potentially more sensitive for porcine and bovine models, while more testing is needed for human.

articles.title: Alarm fatigue levels and associated factors among intensive care unit nurses: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: To estimate the pooled mean alarm fatigue score among intensive care unit nurses and to synthesise evidence on factors associated with alarm fatigue. Eight Chinese and international databases were systematically searched to identify original observational studies of alarm fatigue among ICU nurses published between January 2017 and February 2026. Two reviewers independently screened the records, appraised the methodological quality of the included studies, and extracted the data. A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted using Stata version 14 to pool mean alarm fatigue scores and their 95% confidence intervals. Sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the robustness of the findings, and potential publication bias was evaluated using Begg's and Egger's tests. Sixteen studies were included in the systematic review, of which 15 provided data suitable for meta-analysis, comprising 4084 intensive care unit nurses. The meta-analysis revealed a pooled mean alarm fatigue score of 25.93 (95% CI, 24.38-27.48). Subgroup analysis indicated that higher levels of alarm fatigue were observed in female nurses (25.89, 95% CI: 22.72-29.06), those aged ≤25 years (26.80, 95% CI: 23.26-30.34), unmarried individuals(24.56, 95% CI: 22.70-26.43), junior-level nurses (27.42, 95% CI: 23.60-31.24), and those with a master's degree (27.15, 95% CI: 24.32-29.99). Elevated alarm fatigue was also observed among nurses without a critical care specialty (24.09, 95% CI: 22.75-25.44), those engaged in rotating night shifts (24.07, 95% CI, 21.98-26.16), nurses without alarm management training (31.52, 95% CI, 25.97-37.07), and those working in general ICUs (26.80, 95% CI, 22.27-31.34). The pooled mean alarm fatigue score among ICU nurses fell within the moderate range. Hospitals and nursing managers should strengthen standardised alarm management procedures and provide alarm management training for all ICU nurses. These measures may help mitigate alarm fatigue, improve the quality of nursing care, and promote patient safety.

articles.title: Nurse-led continuity-oriented family support across the adult ICU trajectory: a systematic review and meta-analysis of PICS-F-related outcomes.
articles.abstract: Family members of adult ICU patients are at risk of post-intensive care syndrome-family (PICS-F), but the psychological effects and optimal timing of nurse-led support remain uncertain. To evaluate nurse-led, continuity-oriented family support for PICS-F-related psychological outcomes and explore differences by intervention phase and nurse type. PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, PsycINFO, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to May 2026. Randomized and quasi-experimental studies were eligible if they evaluated nurse-led family support in adult ICUs and assessed at least one family-level PICS-F psychological outcome. Short-term outcomes assessed from 2 weeks to 3 months after ICU discharge formed the primary analyses. Random-effects meta-analyses used Hedges' g standardized mean differences (SMDs). Subgroup analyses were conducted by primary intervention phase and nurse type. Risk of bias and certainty of evidence were assessed using validated tools and GRADE. Seventeen reports representing 16 independent studies and 3,887 family participants were included. Nurse-led support was not associated with short-term anxiety (SMD = -0.05, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.14; very low certainty), depression (SMD = -0.01, 95% CI -0.23 to 0.21; very low certainty), or post-traumatic stress disorder-related symptoms (SMD = 0.02, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.15; moderate certainty). In-ICU support was associated with lower depression scores (SMD = -0.40, 95% CI -0.67 to -0.12), although phase comparisons included few studies. No ICU transition study contributed an eligible short-term primary outcome. Nurse-type analyses showed no consistent differences. Nurse-led, continuity-oriented family support was not associated with improvements in short-term PICS-F-related psychological outcomes. Current evidence does not identify an optimal intervention phase or nurse type. Intervention timing should be considered, although the optimal phase remains uncertain. Nurse-led support may strengthen family-centred care, but persistent distress may require tailored psychological support and referral.

articles.title: Cluster Versus Individual Randomization in Prehospital, Emergency and Critical Care Trials: A Meta-Epidemiological Study.
articles.abstract: Cluster-randomized clinical trials (cRCTs) are pooled with individually randomized clinical trials (iRCTs) in meta-analyses. However, cRCTs are associated with methodological characteristics potentially inducing systematic differences compared with iRCTs. In acute settings, trial inclusion is time-sensitive, exacerbating inclusion-based biases. We conducted a meta-epidemiological study to assess deviations in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs in these settings. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed and Embase. We screened and identified all meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, or critical care within the last decade that included at least one cRCT and one iRCT. Data were extracted in duplicate from the meta-analyses. If overlapping trials were identified, results were pooled. The primary outcome was mortality; the secondary outcome comprised length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes. Using absolute ln(odds ratio [OR]) for mortality and absolute Hedges' g for the secondary outcome, mean differences (MDs) in effect estimates between cRCTs and iRCTs were analyzed using mixed regression models, presented with 95% CIs. We identified 94 eligible meta-analyses; 44.7% reported on randomization type (cRCT or iRCT). We included 65 meta-analyses in quantitative analyses, encompassing 212 randomized clinical trials (39 cRCTs and 173 iRCTs) and 315,276 patients. No statistically significant difference in absolute ln(OR) for mortality between cRCTs and iRCTs was found (MD, -0.110; 95% CI, -0.093 to 0.313). For length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, a significant difference in absolute Hedges' g was found (MD, -0.202; 95% CI, -0.392 to -0.012). A systematic difference between cRCTs and iRCTs in length-of-stay- or days-alive-type outcomes, but not mortality, was identified, with cRCTs reporting smaller effect size magnitudes than iRCTs. With under half of identified meta-analyses reporting on randomization modality, these results highlight the need for improved transparency and statistical consideration of randomization type in future meta-analyses in prehospital, emergency, and critical care.

articles.title: Bacterial contamination of mobile phones used by healthcare workers in intensive care units in Sudan: A cross-sectional study.
articles.abstract: To determine the prevalence and bacterial profile of contamination on mobile phones used by healthcare workers (HCWs) in intensive care units (ICUs) and to evaluate mobile phone disinfection practices in hospitals in Khartoum State, Sudan. A descriptive cross-sectional laboratory-based study was conducted among 44 HCWs from ICUs in four hospitals in Khartoum State, Sudan. Mobile phone swabs were cultured on Blood and MacConkey agar, and bacterial isolates were identified using conventional methods. Factors associated with bacterial contamination were assessed. Bacterial growth was detected in 31 (70.5%) mobile phones. Staphylococcus epidermidis was the predominant isolate (61.3%), followed by Staphylococcus aureus (12.9%), Micrococcus spp. (9.7%), Bacillus cereus (9.7%), and Klebsiella pneumoniae (6.5%). No significant associations were found between bacterial contamination and gender, healthcare worker category, duration of phone use, or phone use inside the ICU (p > 0.05). Regular phone disinfection was significantly associated with lower bacterial contamination (33.3% vs 80.0%, p = 0.012). Mobile phone contamination among HCWs in ICUs was common. Regular phone disinfection significantly reduced bacterial contamination, emphasizing the importance of routine mobile phone decontamination as part of infection prevention and control practices.

articles.title: Current Status and Future Directions of Cardiovascular Intensive Care in Japan: Workforce, Structure, Education, and Regional Disparities - Report of the Japan Critical Care Cardiology Committee (J4CS).
articles.journal: Circulation journal : official journal of the Japanese Circulation Society
authors: Japanese Circulation Society Emergency and Critical Care Committee
articles.abstract: Rapid population aging has increased the number of patients with severe acute cardiovascular diseases requiring intensive care. Contemporary cardiovascular intensive care has evolved beyond traditional management of acute coronary syndromes to encompass hemodynamic instability, multiple organ dysfunction, and advanced life-support technologies. Accordingly, cardiovascular intensive care units (CICUs) must provide comprehensive, tailored critical care for increasingly complex clinical conditions. In Japan, cardiovascular intensive care remains heterogeneous, with critically ill patients managed in various critical care settings. Structured care systems and specialist training remain underdeveloped. To clarify the current status, we reviewed nationwide survey data from the JROAD-DPC database. Substantial variability in institutional care systems, limited availability of dedicated cardiac care units/CICUs, and marked regional disparities in infrastructure and human resources were identified. Intensive care unit admission was associated with lower in-hospital mortality in cardiovascular emergencies, although these observational findings should be interpreted with caution because of potential residual confounding, differences in patient characteristics, and end-of-life care pathways. These findings support the need for appropriate triage and resource allocation according to patient acuity and institutional capability, rather than the uniform establishment of dedicated CICUs. Addressing these challenges will require optimized resource allocation, strengthened regional coordination, and structured training programs to establish sustainable cardiovascular intensive care systems in Japan.

articles.title: Temporal Trends in Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis Among Critically Ill Patients: Serum Galactomannan Testing Intensity and Host Risk Status.
articles.journal: International journal of infectious diseases : IJID : official publication of the International Society for Infectious Diseases
articles.abstract: We evaluated temporal trends in invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) incidence in relation to serum galactomannan (GM) testing intensity and compared outcomes by classical host-risk status. Adults with ICU stays ≥72 hours during 2017-2024 were retrospectively screened for proven/probable IPA. Consensus EORTC/MSGERC and FUNDICU definitions defined the primary cohort. Modified criteria were exploratory. Negative binomial and Cox regression assessed incidence and 30-day mortality. Among 11,707 ICU stays, 135 patients met consensus definitions; 55 (40.7%) lacked classical host risk factors, rising to 48.9% under modified criteria. IPA incidence increased over time (IRR/year 1.40; 95% CI 1.06-1.85). After adjustment for serum GM testing intensity, the calendar-year IRR was 0.73 (95% CI 0.54-0.98), whereas testing intensity was strongly associated with measured incidence (IRR 6.15; 95% CI 2.81-13.43). Patients without classical host risk factors received antifungal therapy less often (12.7% vs 67.5%) and had higher crude 30-day mortality (58.2% vs 36.2%). The adjusted host-status association was attenuated (aHR 1.48; 95% CI 0.82-2.66). The temporal rise in measured IPA incidence was associated with serum GM testing intensity, underscoring diagnostic ascertainment. Patients without classical host risk factors were treated less often and had higher mortality, although the adjusted association was attenuated.

articles.title: Development, implementation and evaluation of a sustainable medication-use process in the intensive care unit: a lean-based quality improvement study.
articles.abstract: In the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), substantial quantities of medication are wasted, negatively affecting ecological and economic sustainability. This study aimed to develop, implement, and evaluate an ecologically and economically sustainable medication-use process to reduce medication waste in the ICU of a Dutch academic hospital. This lean-based quality improvement study comprised three phases: (I) Three-week baseline medication waste assessment in terms of quantity (i.e., disposed medication units) and economic value per 100 ICU beds per day. (II) Development and implementation of a sustainable medication-use process using lean principles. Causes of medication waste were identified among hospital staff using qualitative methods, and targeted interventions were identified and implemented accordingly. (III) Post-implementation effect evaluation of the sustainable medication-use process on medication waste. At baseline, a mean total of 113 units, worth €1037, were wasted daily per 100 ICU beds. Causes for medication waste were: insufficient knowledge among hospital staff about quantities and impacts of medication waste; suboptimal medication ordering, supplying and preparing, resulting in unnecessary medication waste; and patient's therapy changes/discontinuation. Interventions implemented were: awareness campaigns on medication waste; adjustment of protocols and work processes to prevent excess order, supply and preparation of medication; and dispensing individually labelled medication to the patient following transfer or discharge. Implementing these interventions reduced medication waste by 31.8% to 77 units per 100 ICU beds per day, and economic losses decreased by 18.4% to €846. Implementation of a sustainable medication-use process targeting staff's knowledge and work processes, reduced the extent of wasted medications in the ICU and associated costs.

articles.title: An Attending-Directed Intervention to Enhance Interprofessional Teaching on ICU Rounds.
articles.abstract: Interprofessional teaching (IPT) during rounds may enhance teamwork and collaborative patient care, but previous studies have shown low rates of IPT during intensive care unit (ICU) rounds. We designed a study to explore contributions by interprofessional providers (IPPs) during ICU rounds and an attending-targeted intervention to promote IPT. Using a novel observation tool, we collected details regarding contributions made by IPPs during rounds in two ICUs at an academic medical center. A study team member conducted observations for six weeks before and after implementation of an attending-directed intervention. Comparisons were made between pre- and post-intervention data. Before the intervention, six attendings were observed for 59 patient-rounds with 309 contributions recorded, and after, eleven attendings were observed for 94 patient-rounds with 512 contributions recorded. The majority of contributions from IPPs were classified as "reporting" (pre/post: 42.7% vs. 43.6%) and "observing" (pre/post: 29.1% vs. 29.7%). "Teaching" contributions were rare, but increased from 3.9% (12/309) to 4.7% (24/512) of all contributions (p > 0.05). The mean number of contributions per patient did not change after the intervention (5.24 vs. 5.45), and the types of contributions were similar across different attendings. When an IPP spontaneously provided a recommendation (pre: 33, post: 55), the contribution often changed the care plan (pre/post: 97.0% (32/33), 83.6% (46/55)). IPPs predominantly contribute to rounds by reporting data and providing observations. An intervention to improve attending facilitation of IPT did not affect rates of teaching. However, recommendations made by IPPs consistently impacted the patient care plan.

articles.title: Geo-economic variations in structure and organization of intensive care units: the ISOREA survey.
articles.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
articles.abstract: Little is known on critical care services globally. This study aimed to describe ICU resources and organization across countries and assess variability by income group, between countries, and within countries. Participating centers provided structured data on hospital and ICU characteristics via electronic case report form (January 2018 to July 2020). Questionnaire included 237 items covering general characteristics (2 topics) and ICU resources and organization (18 topics). We computed standardized functional domain scores (ISOREA score), classified ICUs using Marshall criteria, and readiness for essential emergency and critical care using a modified Schell score. A total of 1,426 ICUs from five continents were recruited, and 1,225 were analyzed, from high-income countries (HICs, 58%), upper-middle-income (20%), and low/lower-middle-income countries (LLMICs, 22%). Most ICUs were in referral centers (90%) and large urban areas (80%). Most variables (93%) were significantly associated with income group, Most variables (93%) were significantly associated with income group, with 88% showing higher levels in HICs and lower levels in LLMICs. Six domains showed major disparities: extracorporeal support, respiratory support, emergency access to interventional radiology and surgery, neurology and trauma care, patient file and general monitoring, and cardiovascular and hemodynamic monitoring. According to the Marshall classification, 79% of ICUs in HICs were classified as level III, whereas 55% of ICUs in LLMICs were classified as level I. Domains with higher ISOREA scores varied primarily between countries, whereas lower-performing domains exhibited greater variability across ICUs within the same country. Adjustment for income group reduced, but did not eliminate, country-level clustering. Substantial disparities exist in ICU resources and organization across income groups, countries, and ICUs. ICU capacities appeared multidimensional, extending beyond resource limitations.

articles.title: Intensivists' Perspectives and Practices on Palliative Care in the ICU: A Nationwide Survey in Korea.
articles.abstract: While many countries have made progress in integrating palliative care into intensive care units (ICUs), implementation remains highly context-dependent. In Korea, palliative care integration within ICUs remains limited, and intensivists' perspectives on its role and applicability have not been well studied. We conducted a nationwide, cross-sectional online survey of certified intensivists and fellows registered with the Korean Society of Critical Care Medicine between April and May 2024. The questionnaire explored knowledge and confidence in palliative care, current ICU practices, referral patterns, perceived barriers, and preferred strategies for integration. A total of 241 intensivists responded (response rate, 23.9%). Most agreed that palliative care should be incorporated into ICU care (97.1%) and were willing to make referrals (98.3%). Advance care planning, symptom management, and family decision-making were the most expected domains of support. However, fewer reported involvement in psychological support, end-of-life care, or bereavement services. Referral practices were more frequent in institutions with palliative care teams, while lack of resources, unsupportive institutional culture, and unclear processes were commonly cited barriers. Clinical guidelines, professional education, and reimbursement reform were identified as priority strategies for integration. Korean intensivists widely recognize the need for palliative care in the ICU but apply it within a limited scope. To strengthen integration, consensus on definitions, clear referral criteria, and supportive institutional and policy frameworks are required.

articles.title: Structured communication interventions for families of patients in the intensive care unit: A scoping review.
articles.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
articles.abstract: The aim of this study was to map structured communication interventions for families or surrogate decision-makers of adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients, describe their main characteristics and reported outcomes, and organise reported intervention components into a descriptive communication-domain map. A scoping review using descriptive evidence mapping and a combined deductive-inductive synthesis of communication domains. Sources of evidence included PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and reference list screening. Eligibility criteria included primary studies reporting structured communication protocols, frameworks, checklists, bundles, tools, or reproductible interventions implemented by ICU clinical teams to support communication with families or surrogate decision-makers of adult ICU patients. Two reviewers independently extracted study and intervention characteristics, outcomes, measurement approaches, and quantitative findings, and reported limitations using a standardised form. Reported intervention components were charted and organised into descriptive communication domains through a combined deductive-inductive synthesis process; disagreements were resolved by consensus. Nine studies (2010-2022) were included and grouped into structured communication frameworks, educational/training interventions, and multicomponent bundles. Reported communication components were unevenly represented across included sources. Empathy/emotional support, knowledge transmission, summarisation, and value elicitation were among the most frequently described components, whereas ethical considerations, cultural adaptation, time management, nonverbal communication, and supportive aids were less frequently reported in published intervention descriptions. Outcomes were predominantly perceptual and process related. Structured ICU family communication interventions are heterogeneous in design, delivery, and outcome assessment. This review provides an evidence map of intervention types and a descriptive-domain map of reported communication components. These findings may support the development and reporting of more comprehensive, context-sensitive ICU family communication interventions.

articles.title: Navigating the translational chasm: a scoping review of large language models and hybrid architectures in intensive care.
articles.abstract: Foundation models, particularly large language models, can process the unstructured data central to the intensive care record, yet their clinical readiness remains poorly defined. This study aimed to map foundation-model and large language model applications in adult intensive care, characterise their architectural paradigms, and chart their validation and deployment features. Empirical studies applying a large language model or other foundation model to adult intensive care tasks were eligible for inclusion. Traditional machine-learning-only, non-intensive care, and paediatric studies were excluded. PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched (January 2022-February 2026). A supplementary preprint and conference search through mid-2026 was analysed separately. Data were extracted in duplicate using an operationalised taxonomy (generative large language models, clinical language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and hybrid pipelines). Evidence-maturity mapping was performed without formal risk-of-bias appraisal. Sixty-four studies addressed decision support (51.6%), clinical NLP (23.4%), predictive analytics (20.3%), and ICU operations (4.7%). Standalone configurations predominated (79.7%); retrieval-augmented generation (6.3%) and hybrid (14.1%) architectures concentrated in higher-stakes tasks. Maturity was limited: 46.9% relied solely on retrospective MIMIC data, 6.3% reported external validation, 90.6% remained internally retrospective, and only 3.1% achieved prospective evaluation. Hybrid and retrieval-augmented architectures appear better aligned with high-risk ICU tasks, though no comparative synthesis was performed. Prospective validation and a risk-stratified 'clinical co-pilot' framework are needed.

articles.title: Emotional experiences of workplace violence in the intensive care unit.
articles.abstract: BackgroundWorkplace violence is common in intensive care units and is often regarded as an inevitable aspect of the job. This normalisation may obscure the emotional impact of violence on healthcare professionals and the ethical tensions that arise when altruistic caregiving values conflict with personal safety. Therefore, this study was conducted to explore healthcare professionals' emotional experiences of workplace violence within the context of intensive care.Research designThis study constitutes a secondary, inductive analysis of data originally collected in 37 semi-structured interviews. The interviews were conducted between November 2024 and March 2025 in intensive care units across five hospitals in Sweden. Data were interpreted using Reflexive thematic analysis.Ethical considerationsEthical aspects were carefully considered throughout the study in line with established ethical principles. Participation was voluntary, and informed consent was obtained from all individuals before the interview. Data confidentiality was ensured, and all direct quotes were anonymised.FindingsParticipants' descriptions of their emotional experiences generated three themes. A conflict between professional obligation and human vulnerability captured how participants experienced a tension between the expectation to remain composed in their professional roles and their human vulnerability. Balancing core values of caregiving with safety illustrated the professional and moral dilemmas that emerged when violence or escalating aggression forced healthcare professionals to reconcile their commitment to compassionate care. Organisational conditions influencing emotional responses reflected the conditions that either support or undermine ICU healthcare professionals' emotional resilience when they encounter violence.ConclusionsWorkplace violence in intensive care was experienced as more than a threat to personal safety; participants described how it challenged their professional identity and caring values. Organisational conditions influenced how healthcare professionals experienced and managed these challenges.

articles.title: A Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii Outbreak in an Intensive Care Unit: Detection Before Recognition and Persistence After Containment.
articles.abstract: We analyzed a carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) outbreak in an intensive care unit (ICU) to improve insight into how this pathogen spreads within health care facilities and to inform the development of targeted control procedures. A CRAB outbreak in a tertiary referral center was investigated over a 5-month window with clinical data, molecular typing (AP-PCR, PFGE), and one month of environmental sampling. All ICU patients (n=31) were compared-epidemic-clone-positive (n=7) versus -negative (n=24)-using Mann-Whitney/Fisher tests and Firth penalized logistic regression. Although the outbreak spanned 6 days clinically, index patients had been colonized up to 41 days earlier. CRAB was recovered from high-touch surfaces; 6/7 patients developed pneumonia/VAP and 6/7 died (4 CRAB-attributable). Prior A. baumannii isolation (57% vs 0%) was the only independent risk factor (Firth odds ratio 34.7; P=.004). Despite treatment, infected patients redeveloped epidemic-clone infection up to 3.5 months later. In CRAB outbreaks, spread may begin weeks before clinical recognition, and-even months after the outbreak is contained-the epidemic clone can cause reinfection in previously treated patients; only high-resolution analyses spanning an extended period can document this. Multidisciplinary and administrative collaboration, extended and effective environmental disinfection, and effective isolation of positive patients are important for containing CRAB outbreaks.

articles.title: Promoting equity, diversity and inclusion in intensive Care: a position paper of the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine.
Infections Acquired in the ICU Among Cancer and Other Immunosuppressed Patients: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: To compare the cumulative incidence of ICU-acquired infections (ICU-AIs) across distinct immunosuppression diagnostic categories (solid cancer, hematological cancer, other immunosuppression) and nonimmunosuppressed patients, accounting for competing risks of death and discharge. Retrospective cohort study using prospectively collected data. A total of 50 participating ICUs in Brazil. A total of 38,126 adult patients admitted between October 2019 and December 2021 with an ICU stay exceeding 48 hours and no infections diagnosed within the first 48 hours. None. The primary outcome was the incidence of the first ICU-AI during the ICU stay, evaluated using Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratios (sHR). In the multivariable competing-risk analysis, patients with hematological malignancies (sHR, 1.64; 95% CI, 1.01-2.65) and other immunosuppressive conditions (sHR, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.02-2.54) were associated with an increased cumulative incidence of ICU-AI, while solid malignancy was not significantly different from non-immunosuppressed patients (sHR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.68-1.14). Patients with hematological malignancies and other immunosuppressive conditions face a significantly higher risk of ICU-AIs.

articles.title: When Human Tissue Meets the Driveline: Implications of Tissue Integration to Combat Driveline Infections.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Driveline infection remains a common complication of ventricular assist device (VAD) therapy. These infections often progress from the exit site through the subcutaneous tract to the deeper tunnel and, in severe cases, the pocket, underscoring the vulnerability of the driveline-tissue interface. In this review, we examine the biological and mechanical factors governing tissue-driveline interactions and their implications for tissue integration of the implanted driveline. Dysregulated inflammation, impaired vascular maturation, abnormal extracellular matrix remodeling, repetitive micromotion and traction, and biomaterial-tissue mismatch may all compromise optimal tissue ingrowth of the driveline. Insufficient tissue integration can lead to the formation of microgaps within the driveline tunnel, providing a potential niche for microbial colonization and biofilm formation, thereby contributing to persistent driveline infections. Recognizing the potential association between inadequate tissue integration and the occurrence of driveline infection shifts the focus from microbial eradication alone toward optimizing driveline-tissue interactions across different segments of the driveline. Such an approach may help reduce the incidence of driveline infections in patients requiring long-term VAD support. Finally, strategies to promote tissue integration and long-term driveline stability, including driveline surface engineering, modulation of physicochemical properties, and optimization of surgical techniques, are discussed.

articles.title: What's new in point-of-care lung ultrasound: reading the new recommendations.
Early dietitian-led nutrition intervention and unplanned intensive care unit transfer in hospitalized adults with nutritional risk: A retrospective cohort study.
articles.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition
articles.abstract: Malnutrition and nutritional risk are common among inpatients and are associated with adverse outcomes. Although dietitian-led individualized nutrition intervention is recommended, evidence from routine practice among non-critically ill inpatients remains limited. We aimed to evaluate the association between early dietitian-led nutrition intervention and deterioration-related outcomes among adults at nutritional risk. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using electronic medical records from a Chinese tertiary hospital (2016-2023). Adults aged 18-90 years with Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 scores ≥3 were included; patients directly admitted to intensive care unit were excluded. Patients receiving early dietitian-led nutrition intervention within 72 h after hospital admission were propensity score matched 1:1 to comparators. Outcomes were unplanned intensive care unit transfer, major gastrointestinal events after admission, and predefined clinically meaningful changes in laboratory indicators. Associations were estimated using logistic regression and reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Among 96,532 eligible patients, 16,661 (17.3%) received early dietitian-led nutrition intervention. After matching, 16,419 pairs were analyzed. Early dietitian-led nutrition intervention was associated with lower odds of intensive care unit transfer (3.0% vs. 3.4%; OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77-0.99), major gastrointestinal events (4.0% vs. 4.4%; OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.80-0.99), and higher odds of clinically meaningful reduction in C-reactive protein (12.6% vs. 10.9%; OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.11-1.27). Early dietitian-led nutrition intervention was associated with lower odds of deterioration-related outcomes among hospitalized adults at nutritional risk. Limited early dietitian involvement despite routine nutritional risk screening suggests an implementation gap and warrants further prospective evaluation.

articles.title: Clinical course and outcomes of diabetic ketoacidosis in pregnancy: a single-center experience.
articles.abstract: We evaluated the obstetric and perinatal outcomes of pregnant women hospitalised with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and examined the association between clinical and laboratory parameters and admission to the intensive care unit (ICU). This retrospective observational study included 32 pregnant women managed for DKA between May 2019 and December 2025 at Ankara Bilkent City Hospital, comparing those admitted to the ICU with those who were not. The association of arterial pH and serum bicarbonate with ICU admission was examined using ROC analysis and logistic regression, and biochemical severity markers were compared between pregnancies with and without DKA-related adverse outcomes. Given the sample size, all inferential analyses were regarded as exploratory. Twenty women (62.5%) were admitted to the ICU. They were older and had lower arterial pH and serum bicarbonate, whereas plasma glucose did not differ between groups. Thresholds examined were ≤ 18.5 mmol/L for bicarbonate (AUC 0.80, 95% CI 0.65-0.95) and ≤ 7.33 for pH (AUC 0.72, 95% CI 0.53-0.90). In a two-variable logistic regression model, lower bicarbonate (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.37-0.91) and older age (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.07-2.08) were associated with ICU admission. Women with DKA-related adverse outcomes had lower pH (7.20 versus 7.34; p = 0.004) and lower bicarbonate (8.0 versus 17.0 mmol/L; p = 0.014). In this small single-centre cohort, the depth of maternal acidosis rather than the degree of hyperglycaemia was associated with ICU admission and with adverse obstetric outcomes. These findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating; the thresholds reported here require validation in larger, multicentre cohorts before any clinical application.

articles.title: Mobility in ICU survivors: A concept analysis.
articles.abstract: Mobility limitations are common and clinically important among ICU survivors, yet the concept of mobility remains inconsistently defined and is often conflated with physical capacity, functional status, and activities of daily living. This study aimed to clarify the concept of mobility in ICU survivors using Walker and Avant's concept analysis methodology. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and Web of Science from database inception to August 15, 2026. Walker and Avant's eight-step framework guided the identification and synthesis of uses, related concepts, defining attributes, antecedents, consequences, and empirical referents. Thirty-eight studies were included. One defining attribute of mobility was identified: purposeful transition in body position or spatial location. Antecedents comprised predisposing factors, critical illness-related factors, physical prerequisites and limiting conditions, and contextual and modifying factors. Consequences spanned functional and daily-life, psychosocial and participation, and care and service domains. Mobility-focused task measures were the most conceptually aligned empirical referents, whereas measures of muscle strength, exercise capacity, activities of daily living, disability, participation, and quality of life assessed related but distinct constructs. Mobility in ICU survivors is defined as patient-generated or patient-controlled movement that produces a purposeful transition in body position or spatial location following critical illness. Such transitions may be performed independently or with assistance. This definition distinguishes mobility from enabling physical capacities, passive repositioning, contextual influences, and broader functional and social outcomes. This concept analysis may help nurses and rehabilitation professionals distinguish mobility from physical capacity and broader functional outcomes, supporting more consistent mobility assessment, individualized rehabilitation planning, and the development of nursing-sensitive mobility outcomes.

articles.title: Where are the female manikins? Representation of female anatomy across two European resuscitation congresses.
Beyond Selection Bias: Post-Event Video Deletion and Trust in Healthcare.
Impact of portal hypertension on clinical outcomes in critically Ill adult patients: A retrospective study: Outcomes in critically Ill patients with portal hypertension.
articles.abstract: Liver dysfunction is a common complication in critically ill patients, and portal hypertension (PHT) represents a severe hepatic pathological condition closely associated with adverse patient outcomes. This study aims to investigate the impact of PHT on clinical outcomes in critically ill adult patients. Data were extracted from the Medical Information Market for Intensive Care IV database. All critically ill patients admitted to the hospital were included in this study. Logistic regression analysis was used to assess the correlation between PHT and hospital mortality, length of stay in the intensive care unit (LOS-ICU), and length of stay in hospital in critically ill patients, and multiple collinearity checks were performed. Propensity score matching was used to minimize group differences, and subgroup analyses were conducted. A total of 46,804 adult critically ill patients were included in this study. The hospital mortality rate for critically ill patients with PHT was 19%, significantly higher than the 8.8% mortality rate for patients without PHT (P < .05). Critically ill patients with PHT also had longer LOS-ICU and length of stay in hospital and higher total bilirubin levels (P < .05). Furthermore, multivariate logistic regression analysis showed that PHT was significantly associated with hospital mortality (OR: 2.716, 95% CI: 2.330-3.158, P < .001). After propensity score matching, the baseline differences between the 2 groups were significantly reduced, and the results showed that critically ill patients with PHT had worse clinical outcomes. However, the LOS-ICU was not significantly different after matching. PHT is a significant predictor of poor prognosis in critically ill adult patients, necessitating enhanced clinical monitoring and management to improve their clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Development and Psychometric Validation of the Geriatric Patient Safety Culture Questionnaire for Intensive Care Nurses.
articles.abstract: Background: Critically ill geriatric patients represent a unique group with specific care needs due to the physiological and pathological changes associated with aging, which make them susceptible to adverse events and complications during their stay in the Intensive Care Units. This study aimed to develop and psychometrically validate the Geriatric Patient Safety Culture Questionnaire (GPSC-Q), which assesses ICU nurses' knowledge, attitudes, self-reported practices, and perceptions of the work environment related to the safety of critically ill geriatric patients. Method: A methodological study was conducted among 330 ICU nurses to develop and evaluate the psychometric properties of the multidimensional GPSC-Q. The psychometric evaluation included content validity, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, internal consistency, and convergent and discriminant validity assessments. Results: The final questionnaire comprised 43 items: 15 Knowledge, 7 Attitude, 12 Practice, and 9 Work Environment items. Exploratory factor analysis identified four, one, four, and three factors, respectively. Internal consistency coefficients were 0.902, 0.936, 0.749, and 0.721, respectively. Knowledge and Practice showed satisfactory primary CFA fit, whereas Attitude showed mixed fit, including an elevated RMSEA of 0.083. Work Environment showed weaker fit (CFI = 0.907, TLI = 0.855, RMSEA = 0.089) and lower reliability and convergent validity in two domains. The second-order CFA showed mixed fit (CFI = 0.936, TLI = 0.930, RMSEA = 0.048, SRMR = 0.070), with CFI and TLI below the prespecified criteria. Conclusions: The GPSC-Q provides preliminary psychometric support for assessing ICU nurses' knowledge, attitudes, self-reported practices, and perceptions of the work environment related to geriatric patient safety. However, support varied across subscales, with weaker findings for Work Environment. Further refinement and validation in independent samples are needed before recommending broad application. Implications for Practice: The GPSC-Q provides a structured approach to assessing nursing and work environment dimensions relevant to geriatric patient safety in intensive care. Further validation may support its use in identifying educational priorities and informing organizational safety initiatives.

articles.title: Association of the Vasoactive-Inotropic Score with Postoperative Intensive Care Unit Stay Following Arterial Switch Operation.
articles.journal: Journal of cardiovascular development and disease
articles.abstract: Transposition of the great arteries (TGA) is one of the most common cyanotic congenital heart diseases in the neonatal period, and arterial switch operation (ASO) is the standard surgical treatment. Postoperative low cardiac output syndrome remains an important cause of morbidity. This study evaluated the association between serial vasoactive-inotropic score (VIS) measurements and postoperative intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay in neonates with TGA undergoing ASO. This retrospective study included neonates with TGA who underwent ASO and were followed in a tertiary Pediatric Cardiac Intensive Care Unit between 1 August 2020, and 1 August 2022. ICU length of stay was analyzed as a continuous primary outcome. Prolonged ICU stay, defined as the upper quartile of ICU length of stay in the study cohort (≥9 days), was evaluated as a secondary exploratory outcome. VIS values were recorded at ICU admission and at 24, 48, and 72 h after surgery. Associations between VIS parameters and continuous ICU length of stay were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation. ROC analysis and logistic regression were performed for prolonged ICU stay. A total of 60 neonates were included, and 15 patients (25%) had a prolonged ICU stay. Admission VIS values were similar between groups. However, VIS values at 24 and 48 h were significantly higher in the prolonged ICU stay group (p = 0.005 and p = 0.001, respectively), whereas no significant difference was observed at 72 h. VIS at 48 h showed the strongest correlation with ICU length of stay (Spearman's r = 0.52, p < 0.001), followed by ΔVIS48 (r = 0.48, p = 0.001) and VIS at 24 h (r = 0.44, p = 0.002). In secondary exploratory analyses, VIS at 48 h demonstrated a numerically higher AUC than VIS at 24 h (0.82 vs. 0.74). ΔVIS48 was associated with prolonged ICU stay in multivariable logistic regression (OR, 1.18 per unit increase; 95% CI, 1.05-1.33; p = 0.006). Firth's penalized logistic regression yielded a similar estimate (OR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.03-1.30; p = 0.012). In neonates with TGA undergoing ASO, higher VIS during the first 24-48 postoperative hours, particularly an increase from admission to 48 h, was associated with longer ICU stay. These findings support serial VIS assessment as a marker of early postoperative clinical trajectory. Cohort-derived VIS thresholds should be considered exploratory and require external multicenter validation before clinical application.

articles.title: Baseline AI Economic Literacy and Enacted Adoption of Artificial Intelligence Tools by Oncology and Critical Care Professionals.
articles.abstract: We examined whether baseline artificial intelligence (AI) economic literacy was associated with sustained use of oncology AI tools. This prospective cohort included 96 oncology and critical care professionals at two centres in Timișoara, Romania, followed for 12 months after institutional roll-out. Participants were classified by AI Economic Literacy Index (AIELI) scores as high (≥14) or low (<14). Sustained use required log-verified activity in at least two of the final three months. Analyses included regression, inverse probability of treatment weighting and exploratory indirect-association analysis through return-on-investment (ROI) confidence. Among 91 completers, sustained use occurred in 29/53 high-literacy participants (54.7%) and 7/38 low-literacy participants (18.4%; risk ratio 2.97, 95% confidence interval 1.46-6.06). The weighted risk ratio was 2.24 (1.15-4.34), and the profession-stratified risk ratio was 2.80 (1.36-5.76). Median time to first use was 5.8 months in the high-literacy group and was not reached in the low-literacy group. Nine participants (eight high-literacy, one low-literacy) had recorded use before the baseline assessment; in a delayed-entry analysis restricted to the 87 participants unused at assessment, the crude hazard ratio for subsequent first use was 2.98 (1.62-5.48) and the crude risk ratio for sustained use after excluding prior users was 3.01 (1.36-6.64); the corresponding covariate-adjusted estimates were less precise (hazard ratio 1.81, 0.89-3.69; risk ratio 2.19, 0.99-4.86) and their confidence intervals included the null. Roll-out-based time-to-first-use comparisons are descriptive because they include events preceding measurement. Sustained use increased across literacy bands. An indirect association through ROI confidence was observed but was not interpretable as causal mediation. Higher baseline economic literacy was associated with earlier and more sustained recorded AI-tool use, although opportunity for use differed by profession, and the adjusted timing-corrected estimates leave the independent contribution of literacy uncertain. Larger multicentre studies should evaluate whether literacy training improves adoption and whether adoption translates into clinical or economic benefit.

articles.title: Patient and family engagement in patient safety in resource-limited intensive care units: A qualitative exploratory study.
articles.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses
articles.abstract: Patient and family engagement (PFE) in the intensive care unit (ICU) enhances patient safety through detection and reporting of safety incidents that may be missed by healthcare professionals, providing an important and additional safeguard against harm. However, empirical evidence to inform policy and practice in resource-limited critical care settings remains scarce. The aim of this study was to explore the perspectives and experiences of patients, families, and healthcare professionals on PFE in patient safety in Ethiopian ICUs. A pragmatic, exploratory qualitative descriptive study was conducted using in-depth interviews guided by a semistructured interview protocol. Participants were purposively selected and included patients, families, and healthcare professionals. Participants were recruited from four ICUs, including both adult and paediatric/neonatal ICUs in a major university hospital in Eastern Ethiopia. Reflexive thematic analysis with inductive orientation guided by Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach was employed. Convergence and divergence of perspectives across participant groups were identified and reported. Criteria for rigour and trustworthiness including credibility, dependability, transferability, confirmability, and integrity guided the research process. The consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research were followed to ensure the transparency and consistency of reporting. Fifty-nine in-depth interviews were conducted, including patients (5; 9%), families (15; 25%), and healthcare professionals (39; 66%). Three overarching themes were identified: First, contested safety roles reflected the competing views on engagement, which were endorsed rhetorically but constrained in practice due to structural and hierarchical power dynamics. Second, sociocultural logics of engagement underscored inequities between rural and urban patients/families shaped by sociocultural attributes and faith-based sense-making. Third, tensions inpatient safetyincident disclosure highlighted the discordance between the expectation of transparency and hesitancy to involve patients and families in incident disclosure due to fear of reprisals. PFE in patient safety in Ethiopian ICUs was endorsed in principle yet remained constrained by sociocultural contexts, hierarchical power dynamics, and limited institutional support mechanisms. Clearly defining patient safety roles, implementing family-activated escalation pathways, and strengthening formal patient safety incident reporting and disclosure systems are essential to promote inclusive, equitable, and sustainable PFE in patient safety across Ethiopian ICUs and beyond.

articles.title: A Quality Improvement Initiative to Achieve Provincial Implementation of a Web-Based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) Survey to Inform Patient-Centered Care.
articles.abstract: To review the web-based Family Satisfaction in ICU (FS-ICU) survey across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs to capture patient and family experiences with critical care, and to evaluate feasibility, participation, and satisfaction scores. A province-wide, multisite quality improvement study using an electronic, key-based FS-ICU survey with prospectively collected anonymous data linked to encounters through a centralized database. All 83 adult level 3 ICUs (52 community, 31 academic) in ON, Canada, from July 1, 2019, to May 31, 2024. The population comprised adult ICU patients, family members, or substitute decision-makers, with one survey per ICU encounter regardless of length of stay or number of family members. ICUs implemented a web-based FS-ICU using a unique seven-digit key in three formats (Staff-Provided, Quick Response-Driven, Website-Code), supported by training, resources, and tablets, with no clinical care interventions beyond routine practice. Feasibility metrics included onboarding (keys generated per ICU admission), opening, participation, and completion rates, calculated for different centers using provincial data. Over the study period, 24,679 unique keys were generated for 353,400 ICU admissions (onboarding rate, 7.0%), 13,596 keys were opened (opening rate, 55.1%), and 7,542 surveys met the greater than or equal to 70% completion threshold (completion rate, 57.6% among opened surveys; reflection rate, 2.1% of ICU encounters). Survey initiation was highest with the Staff-Provided format (88.4% of keys initiated), and overall satisfaction was high, with mean FS with Care, 87.8; FS with Decision-Making, 84.4; and FS-TOTAL 86.5 on a 0-100 scale, with nursing care rated highest and adequacy of time for questions rated lowest. A provincial, web-based FS-ICU was implemented across all adult level 3 Ontario ICUs, producing a large dataset with high satisfaction scores. A small proportion completed the survey, highlighting feasibility and workflow barriers. Future efforts should improve activation and completion rates and integrate FS-ICU data into routine quality improvement to enhance patient- and family-centered care.

articles.title: ICU Physical Environments Used for Family Conferences: A Multimodal Qualitative Evaluation with ICU Team Members.
articles.abstract: Family-clinician communication is central to high-quality care for critically ill patients. Although previous work has focused on improving how and what is communicated, little is known about where this high-stakes communication takes place and how it is shaped by the physical environment. Our objectives were to characterize ICU spaces typically used for family conferences and identify modifiable environmental features that influence communication. We conducted a multimodal qualitative study of 17 spaces typically used for family conferences across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center. Healthcare design and architecture experts independently assessed architectural plans and photographs to characterize spatial features. Then, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 23 ICU team members (nurses, social workers, case managers) to elicit perspectives on and experiences within these spaces. We conducted qualitative content analysis using a combined inductive and deductive approach. A total of 17 family conference spaces across four adult ICUs in a U.S. academic medical center. A total of 23 ICU team members. None. The 17 analyzed spaces included designated family-communication rooms (n = 2), multipurpose rooms (n = 6), visitor lounges (n = 4), and public areas (n = 5; lobbies/hallways). Study participants preferred designated spaces, as they provide privacy, prevent interruption, and facilitate emotional support. Conversely, multipurpose and public areas are prone to distractions and interruptions from conflicting uses. We identified key environmental features that support communication: proximity to patients, flexible furniture layout, and nonclinical ambiance. Family conferences occur in a variety of physical environments in and around adult ICUs, ranging from intentionally designed rooms to elevator lobbies. ICU team members perceive that physical environments have an important influence on communication quality, and we identified pragmatic opportunities to improve existing spaces.

articles.title: Nutritional Status at Admission and Clinical Outcomes in Hospitalized Patients with COVID-19: Results from the MODIeCOSe in Italy Study.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Poor nutritional status is common among hospitalized patients and may adversely affect the response to severe acute illness. We investigated the association between nutritional status at hospital admission and clinical outcomes in patients hospitalized with COVID-19 during the first two pandemic waves in Italy. Methods: This retrospective multicenter study included 1187 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 across nine Italian centers participating in the MODIeCOSe in Italia registry. Nutritional status was assessed using the Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) score, the Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI), and available anthropometric measures. The primary outcome was a composite of in-hospital death or transfer to an intensive care unit (ICU). Multivariable logistic regression was used to assess the independent association between nutritional status and outcome. Results: Overall, 275 patients (23.2%) experienced the composite adverse outcome. CONUT score was higher in patients with an adverse than in those with a favorable outcome (4.4 ± 2.3 vs. 3.4 ± 1.8; p < 0.001), whereas PNI did not differ significantly. Patients with an adverse outcome also had lower body weight, BMI, waist circumference, and waist-to-height ratio, although anthropometric data were available only in subsets of the cohort. In the main multivariable model adjusted for admission PaO2/FiO2 and relevant clinical covariates, higher CONUT remained independently associated with adverse outcome (OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.12-2.45 per 1-SD increase; p = 0.01). The association was similar in a sensitivity analysis excluding PaO2/FiO2 (OR 1.79, 95% CI 1.28-2.49; p < 0.001). Conclusions: A higher CONUT score at admission was independently associated with an increased risk of in-hospital death or ICU transfer, supporting its prognostic relevance as an immuno-nutritional index in hospitalized patients with COVID-19.

articles.title: Association of Tele-Critical Care Capability With Interhospital Transfers and Potentially Low-Value Transfers Among Critically Ill Medicare Beneficiaries.
articles.abstract: Interhospital transfer is essential for accessing specialized critical care services, yet it poses clinical risk and substantial burden for patients and the healthcare system. Tele-critical care (TCC) programs extend expertise to resource-limited hospitals and may influence transfer decisions by identifying patients requiring escalation or supporting local management. We examined the association between TCC capability at index ICU hospitalizations, interhospital transfer, and post-transfer outcomes. Nationwide retrospective cohort study using 2021-2023 Medicare claims linked to the American Hospital Association Annual Survey Database (AHAASD). U.S. acute care hospitals. Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries with ICU hospitalizations between 2022 and 2023. None. TCC capability was identified by AHAASD reporting and/or the presence of five or more TCC claims annually. The primary outcome was interhospital ICU transfer. Exploratory post-transfer outcomes included receipt of specialty procedures, death or hospice discharge within 1 day of transfer, in-hospital and 30-day mortality, and discharge disposition. Hierarchical logistic regression adjusted for patient demographics, comorbidities, acute organ failures, and transferring/accepting hospital characteristics, with transferring hospitals as random intercepts. Among 2,140,919 ICU hospitalizations, 33.4% occurred at 1,066 TCC-capable hospitals. Absolute transfer rates were similar (2.5% vs. 3.0%), but TCC capability was associated with higher adjusted odds of transfer (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.08; 95% CI, 1.01-1.14). In exploratory post-transfer analyses, transferred patients from TCC hospitals had greater illness severity yet were less likely to die or be discharged to hospice within 1 day of transfer (4.6% vs. 6.6%; aOR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.76-0.97) and more likely to be discharged home within 2 days (4.7% vs. 3.7%; aOR, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.03-1.33). TCC capability was associated with modestly increased transfer rates, fewer potentially low-value transfers, and improved post-transfer outcomes, suggesting improved transfer selection.

articles.title: Tools Measuring Health Literacy in Critically Ill Patients and Their Caregivers: A Scoping Review.
