articles.abstract: Health literacy, the ability to understand and use health information, is important for critically ill patients and their caregivers in the neonatal ICU (NICU), PICU, and adult ICU to make informed decisions and navigate complex care. This review aimed to identify and summarize tools used to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO through July 24, 2025. Included articles reported on tools to assess health literacy in critically ill patients or their caregivers. Two reviewers independently performed screening and data extraction. Two independent reviewers extracted data in Covidence. Data items included study characteristics (country in which the study was conducted, study funding, study setting) and health literacy tool characteristics (tool user, types of questions in the tool, method of tool administration, if the tool was created by the study team, and if a full version was available in the publication). We included 92 articles describing 84 health literacy tools. Tools measured: 1) topic-specific clinical knowledge (e.g., organ donation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation; n = 24/84, 29%; NICU: n = 9; PICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 14); 2) ICU prognosis, diagnosis, and treatment (n = 23/84, 27%; NICU: 6; PICU: 3; ICU: n = 15); 3) neonatal and parenting (n = 13/84, 15%; all NICU); 4) general health literacy abilities (n = 11/84, 13%; NICU: n = 6; PICU: n = 2; ICU: n = 7); 5) information needs (n = 4/84, 5%; NICU: n = 1; PICU: n = 0; ICU: n = 3); 6) readiness for discharge (n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 7) decision-making (n = 3/84, 4%; all NICU); 8) health-related behaviors (n = 2/84, 2%; NICU: n = 1; ICU: n = 1); and 9) research participation (n = 1/84, 1%; NICU). Although several health literacy tools exist, they often focus on individual knowledge of specific aspects of ICU care, with less attention to how understanding is produced within the clinical context through interactions among patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers. This may limit their ability to reflect how health literacy functions in critical illness. Assessment of health literacy requires pairing the appropriate tools with interaction-focused approaches to guide communication and support informed decision-making in ICU settings.

articles.title: Infection Control Knowledge, Job Stress, and Self-Efficacy in Relation to Infection Control Performance Among Intensive Care Unit Registered Nurses: A Descriptive Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.abstract: Healthcare-associated infections remain a critical patient-safety concern in intensive care units (ICUs), where invasive procedures and immunocompromised patients elevate infection risk. Infection control knowledge, job stress, and self-efficacy have each been linked to infection control performance, but few studies have examined these factors simultaneously among ICU registered nurses (RNs). This study aimed to investigate ICU RNs' infection control knowledge, infection control job stress, self-efficacy, and infection control performance, and to identify factors associated with infection control performance. This descriptive cross-sectional study surveyed 191 ICU RNs (of 219 recruited) with ≥6 months of ICU experience at two tertiary hospitals in the Republic of Korea (December 2024-January 2025) using structured, validated questionnaires. Data were analyzed with descriptive statistics, independent t-tests, one-way ANOVA (Scheffé/Games-Howell post hoc), Pearson correlation, and hierarchical multiple regression (SPSS 22.0). Mean scores were 19.16 ± 1.07 (of 20) for infection control knowledge, 3.23 ± 0.67 (of 5) for infection control job stress, 3.62 ± 0.53 (of 5) for self-efficacy, and 4.82 ± 0.26 (of 5) for infection control performance. Infection control performance was positively correlated with knowledge (r = 0.151, p = 0.037), job stress (r = 0.161, p = 0.026), and self-efficacy (r = 0.178, p = 0.014). Hierarchical regression showed that current ICU department (surgical, cardiac, emergency, trauma, and general ICU vs. internal medicine ICU as reference), infection control job stress (β = 0.188, p = 0.008), and self-efficacy (β = 0.157, p = 0.022) significantly predicted infection control performance, together explaining 17.4% of the variance (F = 5.995, p < 0.001); infection control knowledge was a nominally significant predictor in this model (β = 0.164, p = 0.016), but this association was not robust to sensitivity analyses (Spearman ρ = 0.034, p = 0.636; heteroscedasticity-robust regression p = 0.095) or to a covariate-adjusted robustness check (p = 0.091), and should be interpreted with caution. Infection control job stress, self-efficacy, and current department were robustly associated with infection control performance among ICU RNs across all sensitivity analyses; infection control knowledge showed a comparatively weaker, fragile association that did not survive rank-based, heteroscedasticity-robust, or covariate-adjusted sensitivity checks. Effect sizes were small to moderate overall, and the final model explained only 17.4% of variance. Department-tailored education and organizational support strategies-channeling job stress constructively and strengthening self-efficacy through hands-on training and mentoring-may help sustain and improve infection control performance; recommendations regarding knowledge-related training should be treated as preliminary given the fragility of this association.

articles.title: Cognitive types of research learning barriers among ICU clinical nurse specialist trainees: A Q methodology study.
articles.abstract: This study used Q methodology to identify cognitive types of research learning barriers among intensive care unit (ICU) clinical nurse specialist (CNS) trainees and to uncover the attributional structure underlying these perceptions, thereby informing type-specific training. The research capacity of clinical nurse specialists is a core marker of their professional development. Existing studies have mainly used conventional questionnaires to assess the severity of barriers, without revealing how different trainees perceive the same barriers, which limits the ability to target training interventions. A Q methodology study. A 40-statement Q sample was developed and 84 trainees completed valid Q sorts on a nine-point forced distribution from -4 to + 4. Factors were extracted by principal component analysis with varimax rotation and post-sort interviews were conducted to aid interpretation. Four cognitive types were identified: Skill-Anxious (42.9%), Double-Jeopardy (19.0%), Growth-Oriented (17.9%) and Time-Constrained (8.3%). A "same score, different meaning" pattern emerged, with the same barrier attributed in systematically different ways across types. Among trainees with research experience, 52.9% belonged to the Growth-Oriented type. The factor solution was robust despite the P-set exceeding the Q-set (composite reliabilities 0.97-0.99; 88.1% clean single-factor assignment). The perceptions of research barriers among ICU CNS trainees fall into four distinct cognitive types. Training should shift from standardised delivery to type-specific targeted intervention, with particular emphasis on institutional research support for Double-Jeopardy trainees after they return to their clinical posts. The single-site, single-cohort sample limits the generalisability of these findings.

articles.title: Beyond information delivery: Candidate competencies for ICU nurses navigating prognostic uncertainty with patients and families.
articles.abstract: Prognostic uncertainty is intrinsic to critical illness, yet communication education often treats the clinician's task as accurate information transfer. This Discussion Paper presents and critically examines author-derived candidate competencies for intensive care unit (ICU) nurses supporting adult patients and families when prognosis remains uncertain. A four-step, author-led narrative synthesis integrated uncertainty theory, adult patient and family evidence, ICU communication literature, and nursing role constraints. Recurrent nursing functions were compared, grouped, and cross-checked against reported needs, harms, and role boundaries. The resulting domains are: align roles and messages; map patient participation, uncertainty, and preferences; name what is known, unknown, and next; respond to emotion and verify understanding; and revisit uncertainty across time and transitions. Their enactment depends on trust, interdisciplinary coherence, staffing, continuity, interpreter access, family-centred policies, and a suitable communication environment. The process was interpretive rather than systematic and did not include independent coding or patient and family partners. The domains are a transparent conceptual proposal for education and debate, not a disclosure protocol or validated standard. Patient and family co-design, content validation, context-sensitive behavioral assessment, and testing of learner, relational, and system outcomes are required before implementation.

articles.title: Interpreting the HISTAP trial: the role of AKI criteria and cumulative exposure to hypotension. Author's reply.
Rapid molecular diagnostics in VAP: when faster results do not mean faster decisions.
Frontal cortical neuroinflammation and circulating biomarkers following cardiopulmonary bypass in sheep.
articles.abstract: Cerebral hypoxia and neuroinflammation have been implicated in neurocognitive disorders following cardiac surgery, but their postoperative trajectory and relationship with circulating biomarkers are poorly defined. We investigated cerebral tissue oxygenation, neuroinflammation, and plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration over 4 weeks after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) in sheep. Sixteen adult Merino ewes underwent CPB with a 2-h aortic cross-clamp and recovered for either 48 h (n = 8) or 4 weeks (n = 8). Cerebral tissue oxygenation was monitored. Neuroinflammation was quantified by morphometric analyses of microglia and astrocytes in the frontal cortex in both CPB groups and a naïve control group (n = 8). Plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) were measured serially. Compared with pre-CPB baseline, cerebral tissue oxygenation did not change significantly in the 48-h or 4-week period. In the 48-h post-CPB group, microglial soma sphericity was reduced (0.79 ± 0.04 vs. 0.83 ± 0.02, P = 0.018) compared with naïve controls, indicating microglial activation. Astrocytic GFAP-positive area was also elevated (17 ± 2% vs. 10 ± 2%, P = 0.026). In the 4-week post-CPB group, these measures did not differ significantly from naïve controls. Plasma NfL rose from 138 [96-185] pg/mL at baseline to 198 [149-265] pg/mL at 48 h (P = 0.0007), while GFAP peaked at the end of CPB (14.4 [4.7-32.4] vs. 3.0 [1.3-4.5] pg/mL, P < 0.0001) and normalised by 48 h. CPB induced neuroinflammation characterised by frontal cortical microglial activation and astrogliosis, accompanied by temporal elevations in plasma GFAP and NfL. These findings identify microglial activation as a response to CPB in the setting of preserved tissue oxygenation and provide preliminary evidence of an association between perioperative neuroinflammatory changes and circulating biomarkers GFAP and NfL, supporting further investigation.

articles.title: How commercial "agenda laundering" is shaping critical care.
Multiterritorial ischaemic strokes with unexplained hypoxaemia.
Acute myelopathy following chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy: an unusual diagnostic challenge.
Training for humanization in intensive care: a competency-based educational continuum for patient- and family-centred practice.

Delivery fidelity was high with variable uptake of optional components in a remote multicomponent rehabilitation intervention in intensive care unit survivors (iRehab): a mixed-methods fidelity assessment.
articles.abstract: What was the fidelity of a remote multicomponent rehabilitation intervention in intensive care unit survivors (iRehab) across the National Institutes of Health Behavior Change Consortium Treatment Fidelity framework domains (design, training, delivery, receipt and enactment)? iRehab participants (n = 429; 231 intervention, 198 standard care); interviews involved 20 intervention participants, 15 standard care participants and six intervention staff. A mixed-methods fidelity assessment was embedded within the process evaluation of a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Quantitative fidelity was assessed using structured checklists, participant-level tracking data and longitudinal monitoring of potential drift. Qualitative interviews explored fidelity processes across domains. Study design fidelity was maintained, with clear differentiation between the experimental intervention and standard care. Provider training included structured training, competency assessment and ongoing multidisciplinary support. Delivery fidelity was high for one-to-one sessions, with no systematic drift in sampled sessions. Of 231 participants allocated to iRehab, 169 (73%) attended at least five one-to-one appointments. The uptake of optional group-based components was more variable. Qualitative findings indicated participant understanding and engagement, whereas tracking data and participant accounts provided evidence of strategies being applied in daily life. The iRehab intervention was delivered with high delivery fidelity while allowing individualisation to patient needs. For physiotherapists, monitoring of fidelity should extend beyond attendance and exercise prescription to whether patients can independently apply rehabilitation strategies when symptoms, fatigue and everyday demands fluctuate. Defined core components, staff training, staff competency assessment, ongoing support and fidelity monitoring may help support consistent remote delivery.

articles.title: Evaluating Humanisation in Intensive Care Nursing Practice: An Exploratory Study Using the HUMAS Scale.
articles.journal: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
articles.abstract: Humanised care is central to nursing practice, yet sustaining relational and emotionally responsive care may be particularly challenging in intensive care environments characterised by technological complexity, clinical instability and repeated exposure to suffering. Humanisation should therefore be understood not as a single professional attribute, but as a multidimensional and context-dependent aspect of nursing practice. To explore humanisation-related dimensions among nurses working in an adult intensive care unit using the Healthcare Professional Humanisation Scale (HUMAS). An exploratory cross-sectional study was conducted among 32 nurses working in an adult intensive care unit. Humanisation-related dimensions were assessed using the Healthcare Professional Humanisation Scale (HUMAS). Descriptive analyses were used to examine scores across the dimensions evaluated by the instrument. Sociability showed the highest mean score (4.4), followed by self-efficacy (3.9), optimistic disposition (3.7), affection (3.6) and emotional understanding (2.9). These aggregated means describe a numerical pattern within this sample. In the absence of reported measures of variability or statistical comparisons, they cannot establish differences between dimensions or explain how nurses expressed these attributes in clinical practice. The findings provide an exploratory description of humanisation-related dimensions among intensive care nurses and suggest that humanisation in this setting should be considered as a multidimensional construct. Further research using larger samples and more comprehensive statistical analyses is needed to examine these dimensions and their expression in intensive care practice.

articles.title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practice Behaviours Regarding Intravenous Drug Incompatibilities Among Intensive Care Unit Healthcare Professionals: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.journal: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
articles.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the knowledge, clinical attitudes, and behavioural responses of healthcare professionals regarding IV drug incompatibility, identify gaps between knowledge and practice, and determine areas for improvement. A cross- sectional online survey was conducted in Türkiye among physicians and nurses with intensive care unit (ICU) experience. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire assessing knowledge levels, attitudes, and perceived barriers. A total of 380 healthcare professionals participated. Overall knowledge levels were moderate to high (mean score: 10.4 ± 2.2). Most participants recognised the serious clinical consequences of IV drug incompatibility and emphasised its importance for patient safety. However, adherence to standard guidelines was limited, and time constraints and workload were reported as major barriers. Multivariate analysis revealed that nurses had significantly lower knowledge scores than physicians (β = -1.64; 95% CI: -2.15 to -1.13). Despite high awareness, knowledge was not consistently translated into practice. These findings highlight the importance of system-level interventions rather than solely individual-focused training. However, the findings should be interpreted in light of the cross-sectional design, convenience sampling, and reliance on self-reported data.

articles.title: Intensive Care Nurses' Self-Reported Adherence to Evidence-Informed Microaspiration-Prevention Practices and Potential Implementation Determinants: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study.
articles.abstract: To assess intensive care nurses' self-reported adherence to recommended microaspiration-prevention practices and explore potential implementation determinants. Multicentre, cross-sectional. From December 2024 to February 2025, nurses in 31 intensive care units at 17 hospitals in Henan Province, China, completed a questionnaire on 22 preventive practices and 43 implementation-related items informed by the Theoretical Domains Framework. Bivariate analyses, a fully adjusted three-level mixed-effects model accounting for unit and hospital clustering, and generalised estimating equation sensitivity analyses examined associations. Of 510 respondents, 476 were analysed. Mean adherence was 77.17/110 (70.15% of maximum), with basic care scoring highest (73.6%) and risk management lowest (67.2%). After adjustment, adherence was lower in units with 10-14, 15-19 and ≥ 20 beds than in those with < 5 beds; the 5-9-bed group did not differ. Both training exposures were associated with higher adherence in the primary analysis; only evidence-based practice training remained significant in the 14-item analysis. The lowest-scoring items concerned near-term implementation intention (3.10), competing priorities (3.21), and professional responsibility (3.29); the highest concerned time efficiency (4.19), workflow compatibility (4.15) and interest (3.94). Self-reported adherence varied across practices and domains. Intensive care unit bed capacity and training exposure were associated with adherence, and implementation-related findings identified potential areas for further investigation. Findings may guide intensive care unit nurses, nurse managers, and educators in strengthening targeted microaspiration-prevention training, clarifying responsibilities, integrating preventive practices into routine workflows, and reinforcing bedside supervision, particularly in units with 10-14, 15-19, or ≥ 20 beds. The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidelines were followed. Patient or Public Contribution: None.

articles.title: Integrated Single-Myofibre Multi-Omics Correlates Inflammatory State to Myosin Energetics in ICU-Acquired Weakness.
articles.journal: Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle
articles.abstract: Skeletal muscle atrophy is a pervasive complication of critical illness that worsens survival and recovery, yet remains poorly explained by current clinical or molecular markers. To directly connect disease-associated molecular states to the contractile machinery, this study combined sequential functional, transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of the same single human skeletal myofibres from critically ill patients in the intensive care unit with acquired weakness (ICU-AW) and controls. This integrated approach provides a framework for validating molecular signals directly within the cellular and biomechanical context. Differential expression analyses between control and ICU-AW myofibres show marked donor-level heterogeneity, with no differentially expressed features (FDR < 0.05). Ranked gene set enrichment analyses revealed distinct transcriptional and proteomic signatures between conditions, as well as a subtle yet conserved myofibre state enriched in ICU-AW, characterised by inflammatory and chemotactic gene programmes, intracellular structural remodelling and bioenergetic adaptation. Nineteen features were significantly (FDR < 0.05) altered at both RNA and protein levels from the same myofibre. Overall, these 19 overlapping features link an inflammatory transcriptional landscape to a proteomic shift toward mitochondrial and translational machinery, revealing a coordinated stress-adaptation programme with selective post-translational control in fibres from patients with ICU-AW. Further integration with the functional dataset revealed fibres in this state displayed selectively disrupted myosin dynamics, evidenced by prolonged ATP turnover time of myosin heads in their super-relaxed conformation, suggesting altered myosin energetics as a contributor to muscle dysfunction. These findings define a discrete, disease-associated myofibre state and validate a proof-of-concept integrative single-fibre framework for connecting multi-omic heterogeneity to molecular motor function in complex human disease. The identification of coordinated transcriptomic and proteomic programmes, validated through functional measurement, suggests that targeting this fibre state may offer new therapeutic opportunities in ICU-acquired dysfunction and related muscle disorders.

articles.title: Lived Experiences and Coping Strategies of Newly Recruited ICU Nurses in a Resource-Constrained Hospital in Ghana.
articles.abstract: To explore the lived experiences and coping strategies of newly recruited intensive care unit (ICU) nurses in a resource-constrained setting in Accra, Ghana. An exploratory, descriptive qualitative study was conducted. We purposively recruited 12 newly recruited nurses from the ICUs of a teaching hospital in Accra. The participants were interviewed using a pilot-tested interview guide. The interviews were audio-taped, transcribed verbatim, and analysed using thematic analysis with the aid of Nvivo 11. The main themes identified were experiences and coping strategies of the newly recruited nurses. On the sub-themes under experiences, we identified the following: shift mismatches, unavailability of mentors and lack of supportive learning environment. On the coping strategies, the following sub-themes were identified: self-directed learning, the expectation of implementation of structured orientation programmes, regular evaluation and peer support networks. There is ineffective mentorship of newly recruited ICU nurses due to the absence of institutional mentorship protocols. Peer mentoring, periodic competence-based assessment, and protected mentorship time are useful strategies that can be harnessed to promote nursing skills transfer in newly recruited nurses. Nursing heads of hospitals should ensure structured mentorship protocols are put in place as well as protected mentor time to ensure effective nursing mentorship. Furthermore, heads of in-service training units of hospitals need to institute competence-based orientation programmes and periodic competence-based assessment to help newly recruited nurses' transition effectively into the work environment. This study explored gaps in mentorship and identified strategies to promote effective nursing skills transfer. The findings will help nurse managers in hospitals ensure effective mentorship of newly recruited nurses. We adhered to COREQ guidelines. Twelve newly recruited nurses actively participated in the study.

articles.title: Bridging Critical Care and Mental Health: Jordanian ICU Nurses' Self-Reported Knowledge, Skills, Attitudes and Confidence in Caring for Patients With Mental Illness.
articles.abstract: Intensive Care Unit (ICU) nurses frequently care for patients with mental illness, yet many report feeling insufficiently prepared to address mental health needs in critical care settings. Understanding nurses' knowledge, skills and attitudes toward mental health care is essential to improving the quality and safety of care. This study assessed Jordanian ICU nurses' self-reported knowledge, skills and attitudes regarding the care of patients with mental illness and examined factors associated with their perceived competence in managing mental health conditions in critical care settings. A cross-sectional descriptive design was used, involving 502 ICU nurses from 20 public, private and university hospitals in Jordan. The primary outcomes were nurses' self-reported perceived knowledge and preparedness, self-reported skills and attitudes toward caring for patients with mental illness. The questionnaire also assessed previous experience and receipt of formal training specifically related to mental health care for critically ill patients. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Kruskal-Wallis test, Pearson correlations and multiple regression. Instrument reliability was acceptable (Cronbach's α = 0.81-0.92). Nurses reported moderate self-reported perceived knowledge and beliefs (mean = 3.19 ± 0.70), self-reported skills (mean = 3.20 ± 0.51) and attitudes (mean = 3.28 ± 0.44). Important gaps were identified in knowledge of psychotropic medication use, clinical assessment tools and legal aspects of mental health care, as well as confidence in managing suicidal behaviour, psychotic symptoms and mental status assessment. Only 32% of nurses had received formal training specifically in mental health care for critically ill patients, whereas 79% reported that they could be better prepared to manage such situations with additional education. Perceived knowledge-and-beliefs scores, skills and attitudes were strongly and positively correlated (r = 0.606-0.790, p < 0.001). Higher educational qualification (β = 0.129, p = 0.011) and longer professional nursing experience (β = 0.229, p = 0.005) were associated with higher self-reported skills. More positive attitudes were associated with educational qualification (β = 0.174, p < 0.001), years as a qualified nurse (β = 0.362, p < 0.001) and ICU experience (β = 0.211, p < 0.001). Jordanian ICU nurses reported moderate perceived competence in mental health care, alongside important gaps in perceived knowledge, perceived preparedness, self-reported clinical assessment skills and confidence in managing complex mental health situations. Some responses also indicated potentially stigmatizing beliefs that require attention in future education. The strong associations among knowledge, skills and attitudes suggest that these domains should be addressed together through structured mental health education, practical skills training and organizational support. Objective assessment of clinical competence is warranted to complement self-reported preparedness.

articles.title: Between Beliefs and Reality: How to Help Family Members Deal With Prognostic Expectations for Critically Ill Patients.

Evaluating plasma ferritin and suPAR as treatable traits for critically ill patients with COVID-19 treated with anakinra: an exploratory analysis of the immune modulation domain of the REMAP-CAP randomised clinical trial.
articles.abstract: Identifying treatable traits in critically ill patients offers potential to enable a precision medicine approach to treatment. The aim of this exploratory analysis of the REMAP-CAP immune modulation domain was to evaluate whether plasma ferritin or soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (suPAR) represent treatable traits for anakinra in critically ill patients with coronavirus disease (COVID-19). An exploratory analysis of patients randomised within the COVID-19 immune modulation domain of the REMAP-CAP trial was conducted. Adults within 24 h of receiving respiratory or cardiovascular organ support in an ICU with suspected or microbiologically confirmed COVID-19 were included. Plasma ferritin was measured at study sites, and plasma suPAR measured in stored plasma samples. The primary outcome was organ support-free days (OSFD) until day 21. Analyses were performed using a Bayesian cumulative logistic regression model, and results are presented as the posterior median odds ratio (OR), along with 95% credible intervals (CrI), for anakinra being superior to control. In ferritin analyses, 1243 patients were included. Patients with increasing ferritin levels had numerically fewer OSFDs. The posterior probabilities of anakinra having benefit (OR > 1) were 64%, 71%, and 21% across increasing ferritin terciles, compared to 53% in analyses that did not adjust for ferritin levels. 145 patients were included in the suPAR analyses. Patients with high baseline plasma suPAR (≥ 6 ng/ml; n = 85) had numerically fewer OSFDs than patients with low plasma suPAR (-1.0 (-1.0, 9.0) vs. 13.0 (-1.0, 17.0)). The posterior probabilities of anakinra having benefit (OR > 1) were 94.8% (OR 2.28 [0.85-6.06]) in patients with low baseline suPAR, and 38.6% (OR 0.88 [0.39-2.00]) in patients with high baseline suPAR. Plasma ferritin does not identify patients with COVID-19 who benefit from treatment with anakinra, whilst anakinra may be beneficial in patients with low, rather than high, baseline plasma suPAR. These hypothesis-generating findings contrast with the results of clinical trials in non-critically ill patients with COVID-19. NCT02735707. Date of trial registration: 06/04/2016.

articles.title: Restrictive Potassium Supplementation Strategy in a General Intensive Care Unit: A Before-and-After Quality Improvement Audit in a Mixed Critical Care Population.
articles.abstract: Potassium supplementation thresholds in intensive care vary widely and have historically lacked strong supporting evidence. The TIGHT K trial demonstrated non-inferiority of a restrictive potassium threshold in cardiac surgical patients; applicability to general intensive care populations is unclear. Retrospective before-and-after quality improvement audit in a mixed adult intensive care unit (ICU), comparing two one-week periods before (May 2025) and after (September 2025) reducing the intravenous potassium supplementation threshold from <4.5 to <3.6 mmol/L. Forty-eight patients were included (22 pre-, 26 post-guideline) with comparable baseline characteristics. Mean intravenous potassium administrations per patient fell by 17.4% (from 9.41 to 7.77 administrations per patient), and the proportion of supplementation episodes initiated at K⁺ ≥4.0 mmol/L fell from 32.9% to 11.4% (a 21.5 percentage-point absolute reduction, equivalent to a 65.2% relative reduction). Pre-supplementation potassium was lower post guideline (3.44 vs 3.83 mmol/L; p <0.001), but potassium correction (ΔK) was unchanged (p = 0.51), and arrhythmia burden did not increase. A restrictive potassium supplementation threshold reduced potassium use without evidence of harm in a general intensive care population, supporting wider applicability beyond cardiac surgery, although larger prospective studies are needed.

articles.title: Perioperative Management of Decompensated Peripartum Cardiomyopathy With Severe Left Ventricular Dysfunction: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a potentially life-threatening cause of heart failure that may be difficult to distinguish from the physiological symptoms of pregnancy. We report the case of a 42-year-old woman at 34 weeks of gestation who presented with progressive dyspnea and was found to have severe global left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of approximately 20%. Despite initial improvement with diuresis, she developed recurrent acute decompensated heart failure requiring intensive care unit readmission. Point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) demonstrated pulmonary congestion and reduced forward flow, with a left ventricular outflow tract velocity-time integral (LVOT VTI) of 10 cm. Following hemodynamic optimization with diuresis and inotropic support, cesarean delivery was performed under general anesthesia with invasive monitoring and titrated vasoactive support. Postoperatively, LVOT VTI increased to 15 cm with corresponding clinical improvement. This case highlights the value of serial hemodynamic assessment, including POCUS, and multidisciplinary perioperative management in severe PPCM with recurrent decompensation.
