authors: European Society of Intensive Care Medicine-Society of Critical Care Medicine (ESICM-SCCM) Consensus Group

articles.title: Advancing a New Method of Care: The Scientific and Business Development of the eICU.
[Research progress on the role of geniohyoid muscle ultrasound in the assessment of swallowing function in critically ill elderly patients].
articles.journal: Zhonghua wei zhong bing ji jiu yi xue
articles.abstract: Swallowing dysfunction severely affects the quality of life in elderly individuals. In China, the prevalence of dysphagia among people aged 80 years or older is 41%, with even higher rates seen in critically ill elderly patients. Currently, available methods for assessing swallowing function are complex to perform and inconvenient for bedside evaluation. However, this functional disorder, which is common and has a significant impact on prognosis in critically ill elderly patients, has not received widespread attention from intensivists. With the increasing use of ultrasound in critical care, identifying a convenient and reliable ultrasound method for evaluating swallowing function will offer more tools for precise monitoring, scientific intervention, therapeutic assessment, and prognostic evaluation of swallowing function in critically ill patients. Atrophy of the geniohyoid muscle is an important factor in reduced swallowing safety and aspiration in the elderly. Using ultrasound to measure the cross-sectional area, movement, and muscle quality changes of the geniohyoid muscle in the sagittal plane to evaluate swallowing function has demonstrated good accuracy and operability. This article summarizes the pathogenesis of swallowing dysfunction, the role of the geniohyoid muscle in swallowing, the progress of research on ultrasound detection of the geniohyoid muscle, and the methods of ultrasound measurement of the geniohyoid muscle. The aim is to provide a reference for research and application of ultrasound evaluation of swallowing function in critically ill elderly patients.

articles.title: Parental perspectives on clinician guidance in value-laden NICU conversations: a qualitative study.
articles.abstract: Value-laden decisions about life-sustaining treatment for critically ill infants in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) present profound emotional and ethical challenges for parents and clinicians. In such situations, clinicians must balance providing guidance with respecting parental autonomy. We explored parental perspectives on clinician guidance and effective communication during these decisions. We conducted a secondary qualitative analysis within a randomized clinical trial using parental free-text responses to a simulated neonatal decision-making scenario. The study was carried out online between February and April 2024 in Switzerland, Germany, and Austria. Eligible participants were German-speaking parents of preterm infants with prior NICU experience, recruited through patient and parent organizations. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis. Among 128 participants (84% female), parents emphasized the importance of clear, detailed, and evidence-based information about their child's condition and treatment options, as well as empathetic, honest, and individualized communication. They valued sufficient time for discussion and reflection, access to second opinions, and attention to the child's quality of life. Parents appeared to retain a sense of decision ownership, while differing in their preferences regarding clinician guidance. Some welcomed explicit recommendations, whereas others preferred neutral, value-sensitive communication that preserved space for independent deliberation. Parents facing complex medical decisions value both high-quality information and empathetic and honest communication. While they generally retain decision ownership, preferences regarding clinician guidance vary, suggesting that clinicians should actively explore how much direction parents want and tailor their communication accordingly. ISRCTN registry under number ISRCTN16123073, registration date: 17/01/2024, ( https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN16123073 ).

articles.title: Serial ultrasound assessment of flexor carpi ulnaris and biceps brachii cross-sectional area in critically ill patients: A prospective cohort study.
articles.abstract: Serial ultrasound measurements may help characterize muscle wasting in critically ill patients. The flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) is a superficial forearm muscle that may provide an additional assessment site. We described longitudinal FCU and biceps brachii (BB) cross-sectional area (CSA) changes and explored between-muscle differences and clinical associations. This prospective two-center observational study enrolled 23 intensive care unit (ICU) patients; 20 were included in the analysis (median age, 57 years; range, 33-82). CSA was measured on days 0, 5, 7, and 14 after ICU admission. Analyses used Friedman tests, exact conditional Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction, and exploratory Spearman correlations. Post hoc between-muscle comparisons assessed participant-level percentage changes. Mean FCU CSA decreased from 1.36 to 1.08 cm² and mean BB CSA from 6.08 to 5.09 cm² over 14 days, corresponding to reductions of 20.9% and 16.4% in the unrounded group means. The median paired difference in percentage change (FCU minus BB) was -11.9 percentage points on day 7 (unadjusted p = 0.0023), meeting the Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/3. Differences on days 5 and 14 did not meet this threshold (p = 0.1429 and p = 0.2024). Baseline CSA values were correlated (ρ = 0.845, p < 0.001), as were 14-day percentage changes (ρ = 0.549, p = 0.0122); correlation p-values were unadjusted. Serial ultrasound documented decreases in FCU and BB CSA in this small cohort, with an exploratory direct comparison identifying a greater proportional FCU decrease on day 7. These findings support further evaluation of FCU ultrasound as an additional muscle-monitoring measure. Its value for earlier detection of muscle wasting or diagnosis of ICU-acquired weakness requires direct validation.

articles.title: Reducing Noise and Alarm Burden in Adult Intensive Care Units: An Integrative Review of Interventions and Implications for Nursing Management.
articles.abstract: To synthesise evidence on noise-reduction and alarm-management strategies in adult intensive care units and examine their implications for nursing management. ICU noise and alarm burden present challenges for patient rest, clinical surveillance, nursing workflow and staff experience. Intervention effectiveness and sustainability remain uncertain. An integrative review guided by Whittemore and Knafl's framework synthesised empirical, implementation and review-level evidence identified through PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL and reference screening. Interventions addressed alarm management, environmental modification, quiet-hour practices, staff engagement and multicomponent implementation. Reported benefits varied across studies, and available evidence did not establish the superiority of bundled approaches. Direct evidence concerning workforce well-being, nursing leadership, clinical surveillance and sustained improvement was limited. Quiet ICU interventions may improve selected acoustic and alarm-related outcomes, but their comparative effectiveness and long-term sustainability remain uncertain. Nurse leaders may consider context-sensitive interventions supported by alarm governance, workflow integration, staff participation and ongoing evaluation. Future studies should assess nursing workload, clinical surveillance, patient safety and sustainability alongside acoustic outcomes.

articles.title: Association of a structured prevention algorithm with nurse knowledge and device-related pressure injury severity in critical care: A pre‑post study.
articles.abstract: Medical Device-Related Pressure Injuries (MDRPI) are a serious complication in intensive care units (ICUs), yet structured prevention algorithms are lacking. This single-group, pre-test/post-test quasi-experimental study was conducted in the General Intensive Care Unit from February 2025 to April 2025. The sample comprised 38 nurses and 77 patients (39 pre-intervention, 38 post-intervention). Nurses' knowledge was assessed using the MDRPUKQ questionnaire, and patient outcomes were monitored using baseline and post-intervention data on pressure injury prevalence and severity. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 26, employing descriptive and inferential statistics including paired t-tests, independent t-tests, chi-square tests, Fisher's exact tests, and multivariable logistic regression. The mean knowledge score increased significantly from 57.74 (SD = 11.15) before training to 89.55 (SD = 5.17) afterward (mean difference: 31.81, 95% CI: 28.35-35.27, P < 0.001, Cohen's d = 3.02). Overall, MDRPI prevalence decreased from 38.5% (95% CI: 24.9-54.1%) pre-intervention to 28.9% (95% CI: 17-44%). However, this difference was not statistically significant using Pearson's chi-square test (χ2 = 0.82, P = 0.365). The distribution of pressure injury stages before implementation was: Stage 1 (28.2%), Stage 2 (7.7%), and Stage 3 (2.6%). Following the intervention, prevalence dropped to Stage 1 (21.1%) and Stage 2 (5.3%), with no new Stage 3 injuries reported. After adjusting for potential confounders (age, Braden score, ICU length of stay, and device exposure duration), implementation of the algorithm was associated with reduced MDRPI occurrence (adjusted OR = 0.42, 95% CI: 0.19-0.91, P = 0.026). Implementation of the MDRPI prevention algorithm was associated with significant improvement in nurses' knowledge. A numerically lower prevalence was observed. This suggests that injuries caused by medical equipment are largely absent from current mandatory continuing education or postgraduate nursing curricula, reinforcing the need for a thorough review and the integration of this topic into standard educational programs.

articles.title: Fungal Versus Gram-Negative Bloodstream Infection and 30-Day Mortality in Critically Ill Patients: A Propensity Score-Matched MIMIC-IV Analysis with an Allo-HSCT Comparison Cohort.
articles.abstract: Fungal bloodstream infections (BSIs) are linked to substantial morbidity and mortality among critically ill patients; however, comparative analyses with Gram-negative BSIs remain scarce. In this retrospective MIMIC-IV v3.1 study, adults were included if their first bloodstream infection (BSI) occurred during an ICU stay. The primary propensity score model included age, sex, Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score within 24 hours of ICU admission (SOFA_24hours), Simplified Acute Physiology Score II (SAPS II), Charlson comorbidity index, and immunosuppressive therapy within 30 days before the index culture. Patients were matched 1:1 using a 0.2-SD logit caliper. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), doubly robust, extended-window, and SOFA_24hours ≥2 analyses were performed. The primary endpoint was 30-day all-cause mortality. An independent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) comparison cohort was also analyzed. The ICU-stay BSI cohort included 363 patients (129 fungal and 234 Gram-negative; 123 deaths). Unadjusted analysis showed higher 30-day mortality with fungal BSI (hazard ratio [HR], 2.89; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.02-4.13). In the primary expanded matched cohort (119 pairs; n = 238), fungal BSI remained associated with higher mortality (HR, 1.96; 95% CI, 1.35-2.86). Results were consistent in expanded IPTW (HR, 1.86; 95% CI, 1.27-2.74), doubly robust (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.38-2.87), and sensitivity analyses. In the external allo-HSCT comparison cohort (n = 186; 14 fungal cases), mortality was 42.9% versus 7.6% (adjusted HR, 7.58; 95% CI, 2.74-20.99); precision was limited. Among patients with BSI during an ICU stay, fungal BSI was associated with higher 30-day mortality than Gram-negative BSI. These hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation; causality and treatment benefit were not assessed.

articles.title: Combined Case-Based and Problem-Based Learning in a Cardiothoracic ICU: A Retrospective Nonrandomized Comparative Educational Study.
articles.journal: Advances in medical education and practice
articles.abstract: To compare immediate knowledge improvement, simulation performance, and participant satisfaction between combined case-based learning and problem-based learning (CBL-PBL) and traditional lecture-based training among cardiothoracic intensive care unit (ICU) professionals in a single-center retrospective nonrandomized comparative study. This single-center retrospective nonrandomized comparative study reviewed training records for 46 healthcare professionals at Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital, China, from January to December 2024. Training-group membership was preference-based, with 23 participants per group. Outcomes included pre-to-post knowledge change, simulation performance, and satisfaction. Additional unadjusted comparisons used the Welch method. Exploratory logistic regression examined membership in a median-defined higher post-training score category, adjusting for age, sex, professional experience, and baseline knowledge. Clinical indicators were reported descriptively. The between-group difference in knowledge improvement favored CBL-PBL by 7.60 points (approximate 95% CI 1.01-14.19; P = 0.025). Simulation-score differences favored CBL-PBL across three scenarios, ranging from 1.60 to 1.90 points (all P ≤ 0.001). Satisfaction was higher by 2.80 points (95% CI 1.91-3.69; P < 0.001). CBL-PBL was associated with higher odds of membership in the higher-score category (adjusted OR 8.961; 95% CI 1.861-43.156; P = 0.006), although the estimate was imprecise. Structured case discussion and collaborative problem-solving warrant further evaluation as components of cardiothoracic ICU training. Prospective studies with validated assessments and delayed follow-up are needed before recommending routine adoption or claiming sustained learning or patient benefit.

articles.title: From Gaps in Maternity Care to Maternal Rescue: An Interprofessional Implementation Agenda for Anesthesia and Maternal Critical Care in Somalia.
articles.abstract: Somalia's maternal health system faces a dual challenge: limited access to skilled maternity care and insufficient capacity to rescue women who deteriorate during or after obstetric emergencies. Hemorrhage, hypertensive emergencies including eclampsia, sepsis, obstructed labor, and urgent cesarean delivery require coordinated maternity, anesthesia, nursing, resuscitation, postoperative surveillance, and critical-care functions. This evidence-informed commentary shifts the discussion from documenting gaps to an interprofessional implementation agenda. We propose five linked priorities: a regulated and supported maternity and obstetric-anesthesia workforce; an evidence-based cesarean safety bundle; step-up maternal high-care capacity; early-warning, crisis resource management, escalation, and referral pathways; and routine measurement through maternal and perioperative quality systems. The approach emphasizes actions that referral maternity hospitals can introduce progressively, with named local accountability, team training, minimum resource requirements, and measurable indicators, while avoiding unsupported assumptions about national critical-care capacity. Somalia does not need to wait for a fully developed intensive-care system before improving maternal rescue. The immediate opportunity is to connect five functions that are too often fragmented: competent anesthesia provision, reliable cesarean safety processes, early recognition of deterioration, monitored maternal high care, and accountable review of outcomes. Strengthening these functions as one interprofessional maternal-rescue pathway offers a practical route to reducing preventable severe maternal morbidity and mortality in Somalia.

articles.title: Feature-token clinical transformer for 24-h landmark mortality risk stratification in critically ill patients with heart failure: development and multicenter external validation.
articles.abstract: The first 24 h after ICU admission in critically ill patients with heart failure yield heterogeneous EHR evidence across vital signs, laboratory tests, treatments, organ support, and nurse-charted monitoring. Conventional scores and flat-vector ML models may not preserve individual variable identity or context. We developed FTCT, encoding each predictor recorded during the first 24 h after ICU admission as a clinically tagged token (value, missingness, identity, group). MIMIC-IV (2008-2019) served for development, validation, and internal testing; eICU-CRD (2014-2015) served for external validation. Included were adults with heart failure, a complete 24-h ICU observation window, and known discharge status. The endpoint was in-hospital all-cause death. MIMIC-IV included 11,156 stays and 1,484 deaths, partitioned into training (n = 7,809), validation (n = 1,673), and internal test (n = 1,674) sets. eICU-CRD included 9,837 stays and 1,319 deaths. FTCT achieved an AUROC of 0.849 (95% CI, 0.835-0.863) internally and 0.804 (0.788-0.820) externally. Patient-paired AUROC differences vs. XGBoost were 0.027 (0.011-0.043) internally and 0.032 (0.014-0.050) externally. A matched FT-Transformer-style baseline achieved an external AUROC of 0.781 (0.760-0.801). In eICU-CRD, FTCT achieved an AUPRC of 0.296 (0.278-0.314), Brier score of 0.091 (0.085-0.097), and expected calibration error of 0.036 (0.030-0.042). In a post hoc cohort-specific descriptive operating analysis targeting approximately 85% specificity, external sensitivity was 0.662 (0.636-0.687), positive predictive value 0.406 (0.385-0.427), negative predictive value 0.942 (0.937-0.947), and F1 score 0.503. Removing feature-token encoding produced the largest ablation loss in external AUROC (-0.031). FTCT combines established feature-token Transformer modeling with clinical-group embeddings, explicit missingness representation, and group-aware pooling for 24-h landmark mortality risk stratification from structured EHR data recorded during the first 24 h after ICU admission. Its external validation and ablation results support prospective investigation, but do not yet demonstrate clinical utility, workflow integration, admission-time applicability, or autonomous use.

articles.title: Enhancing High-Fidelity Simulation Flight-Based Training for Critical Care Paramedics in EMS Aviation: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: High-fidelity simulation (HFS) is used with critical care paramedics (CCPs) to enhance preparedness in high-stake scenarios. This systematic review aims to assess the evidence on the role and effectiveness of HFS flight-based training, evaluating its application in education for CCPs operating within emergency medical services aviation settings. A systematic literature search was performed using a set of inclusion and exclusion criteria, resulting in 7 articles which were appraised using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme tool. HFS training equips learners with skills relevant to their practice. CCPs register improved expertise, engagement and motivation, responsiveness, and general mood. There was insufficient evidence on whether this modality enhances self-awareness. HFS learning is feasible in training CCPs in emergency medical services aviation. However, there is limited evidence on the performance of CCPs trained using HFS learning in the prehospital setting. The findings suggest that standardizing training and assessment methods is recommended to optimize skill acquisition, improve team performance, and enhance patient safety in high-acuity emergencies.

articles.title: Serum ammonia improves early risk stratification beyond West Haven criteria in acute liver failure.
articles.journal: Liver transplantation : official publication of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and the International Liver Transplantation Society
authors: US Acute Liver Failure Study Group
articles.abstract: The prognosis of patients with acute liver failure (ALF) presenting with low grade hepatic encephalopathy (HE) defined by the West Haven criteria (WHC) is difficult to establish. We studied the association between HE severity, assessed by WHC and serum ammonia, with outcomes across different age groups. Retrospective analysis of the prospective multicentre United States ALF Study Group registry (2000-2016). Exposures were WHC and serum ammonia on day 1 post inclusion. Endpoints were transplant-free survival (TFS) and mortality due to cerebral events on day 21. Findings were validated in a different and more recent (2010-2023) European cohort. Among 1092 patients, median age was 39 years and 526 (48.2%) had acetaminophen toxicity. On day 1, 968 (88.6%) patients were in the intensive care unit and 669 (61.3%) were receiving any specific organ support (ventilation vasopressors, or renal replacement therapy). TFS and cerebral mortality on day 21 were 45.2% and 6.3%, respectively. Patients with hyperammonemia (≥50 µmol/L) on day 1 had lower TFS on day 21 than others, both for WHC grades 1-2 (53.0% vs. 65.2%) and 3-4 (31.8% vs. 60.9%). Higher ammonia on day 1 was independently associated with lower TFS on day 21, irrespective of WHC grade (odds ratio of 0.958 per each 10 µmol/L increment). Ammonia on day 1 of ≥100 µmol/L showed a significant threshold effect for TFS or cerebral mortality on day 21. Patients with <40 years had the highest probability of cerebral mortality on day 21. In ALF, serum ammonia may help to define HE and assess prognosis earlier, irrespective of WHC grade. Patients with early serum ammonia of ≥100 µmol/L require optimized monitoring and treatment.

articles.title: Principles of drug dosing for obese patients in the intensive care unit.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The increasing prevalence of severe obesity in intensive care unit (ICU) patients has led to several challenges with medication dosing. Doses listed in product labels or tertiary references typically do not account for the pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic variability encountered with obesity, leading to the potential for treatment failure or an adverse effect. The purpose of this review is to provide guidance for ICU clinicians when crafting pharmacotherapy regimens in critically ill patients with extreme obesity. METHODS: A literature search was performed to identify relevant articles pertaining to the pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics of medications in obese patients. Articles describing both general treatment principles and medication specific assessments were retrieved. Bibliographies were searched for additional publications. RESULTS: Evidence guiding medication use in critically ill obese patients is limited by the small number of patients with more extreme forms of obesity, the lack of clinical outcome measurements, and the few studies that are specific to the ICU. Obesity-related alterations in pharmacokinetic parameters, such as apparent volume of distribution and drug clearance, may hinder attainment of pharmacodynamic targets. Individualized dosing strategies are essential to optimize therapeutic outcomes. This review provides dosing recommendations for selected ICU medications and proposes a practical framework to guide medication dosing decisions in this patient population. CONCLUSION: Drug dosing in critically ill obese patients should be individualized by assessing pharmacokinetic variability and whether pharmacodynamic goals can be achieved. Selecting the correct weight for weight-based calculations or dose for fixed regimens is paramount for achieving these goals. Consultation with a clinical pharmacist may be beneficial.

articles.title: Music Therapy During Weaning From Invasive Mechanical Ventilation in the ICU: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The study examined the effect of daily music therapy on weaning from invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in the ICU, with a primary focus on weaning duration. Secondary agitation, sedation, and analgesia doses, pain, delirium, and perceived stress after 90 days were assessed. Additionally, total IMV and ICU stay durations and tracheostomy rates were studied. Physiologic parameters were assessed in the music therapy group (MG). The study also aimed to promote the humanization of critical care through a biopsychosocial and creative music therapy approach. DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups: control group receiving standard care during weaning and MG receiving music therapy additionally. SETTING AND PATIENTS: Adult critically ill patients (n = 100) admitted to a general ICU who received IMV for at least 48 hours. INTERVENTIONS: MG received daily, individualized music therapy sessions averaging 25 minutes, based on patient needs and musical preferences, which included music relaxation, music listening, and clinical improvisation. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: No significant difference in weaning duration was observed between groups (p = 0.97). Patients in the MG group showed significant improvements in agitation and sedation levels (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) on days 1 and 3 (p = 0.048, 0.005, and 0.024) and a lower percentage required propofol (p = 0.028). No significant difference in perceived pain (Visual Analog Pain Scale). The MG obtained lower Perceived Stress Scale-14 scores (p = 0.24). Additionally, MG significantly reduced tracheostomy rates (14%; p = 0.025). Median total IMV and ICU stay duration were shorter in the MG group, but not significantly (p = 0.206 and 0.203). Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygenation showed no significant difference before and after music therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Music therapy may serve as a nonpharmacological complementary adjunct during weaning by reducing agitation, sedation, and tracheostomy rate. It may potentially decrease perceived stress and IMV and ICU stay durations. Further research is warranted.

articles.title: Ex Vivo Assessment of Lamotrigine Clearance During Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy.
articles.abstract: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) provides renal support for unstable ICU patients but significantly alters drug concentrations. For patients on long-term antiepileptics such as lamotrigine, CRRT may increase risk for breakthrough seizures due to subtherapeutic levels. Conversely, CRRT may aid in lamotrigine overdose. While partial clearance of lamotrigine by intermittent hemodialysis has been reported, CRRT clearance is not well studied. This study determined lamotrigine extraction by CRRT in an ex vivo system. Medication was administered at two concentrations: one therapeutic and one supratherapeutic to closed-loop, blood-primed, ex vivo CRRT circuits. Drug concentrations were measured in plasma, hemofiltrate (effluent), and matching control samples at specific time points. For each time point, percent recovery of lamotrigine was calculated, and differences between CRRT circuits and controls were analyzed using two-sample t-tests. Plasma lamotrigine concentrations decreased rapidly, with 10% (n = 3, SD = 4%) and 17% (n = 2, SD = 3%) recovery at four hours for therapeutic and supratherapeutic doses, respectively. Although lower starting concentrations trended toward greater clearance, differences were not statistically significant (P = .13). Control concentrations remained stable, with approximately 100% recovery. Lamotrigine concentrations were significantly affected by CRRT circuits. Patients receiving lamotrigine who require CRRT may need dosing adjustments to maintain clinical efficacy. Additionally, CRRT effectively clears lamotrigine, suggesting potential utility in overdose management.

articles.title: Developing Models for Complicated Outcomes in Acutely Intoxicated ICU Patients With and Without Toxicity Information.
authors: and the INTOXICATE Study Investigators Group
articles.abstract: To assess the prognostic value of the mean Lethality Risk Score (LRS), reflecting the toxicity of substances involved in an exposure, and to develop prediction models for complicated outcomes in ICU patients with acute intoxication. Multicenter prospective cohort study. Seventy-eight ICUs in Europe, Australia, and the Eastern Mediterranean (2020-2023). A total of 2265 adult patients were admitted to the ICU with acute intoxication as the main reason for admission for at least 4 hours. None. The primary outcome was defined as ICU complications or death (22.5%). Clinical data were collected in an electronic capture system. We developed two prediction models: one incorporating laboratory variables ("Laboratory Model"), and one including the mean LRS ("Expo Model"). The mean LRS was calculated as the average of the individual LRS values assigned to the toxicants involved in the exposure. Key predictors were age, severity at presentation, systolic blood pressure, Glasgow Coma Scale score, and hospital type. The mean LRS remained significant only when laboratory variables were not considered. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC), calibration plots, likelihood ratio tests, and decision curve analysis. Internal validation demonstrated good performance for both models (AUROCs of 0.79 and 0.77; calibration slopes of 0.94 and 0.95; intercepts of -0.06 and -0.06), with minimal overfitting. Decision curve analysis revealed clinically relevant threshold probability ranges of 0-50% for the Laboratory Model and 0-40% for the Expo Model. The mean LRS had prognostic value only in the absence of laboratory test results. Both models may aid decision-making regarding the management of acutely intoxicated patients in the ICU.

articles.title: Harm reduction opportunities following ICU admission for prescription opioid overdose: An 8-year comparative audit at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.
articles.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) admission following prescription opioid overdose represents an important opportunity for multidisciplinary intervention and harm reduction, yet Australian data describing inpatient management are limited. A retrospective audit was conducted of 70 adults admitted to the ICU at the Royal Melbourne Hospital with prescription opioid overdose between 2021 and 2024. The primary outcome was provision of take-home naloxone (THN) before discharge among patients meeting institutional eligibility criteria. Secondary outcomes included opioid education, multidisciplinary involvement and discharge opioid management, with comparison with the previous institutional audit where comparable data were available. Only five patients (7.5%, 95% confidence interval 3.2-16.3) were supplied with THN despite all meeting institutional eligibility criteria. Polypharmacy overdose was common (77%). Most patients received at least one specialist referral (83%), although 15% received no inpatient specialist referral. Opioid education was documented in 58 patients (87%) compared with 17% previously (P <0.001), although content and documentation were inconsistent. These findings demonstrate persistent gaps in THN provision, structured opioid education and coordinated discharge planning, highlighting ICU admission as an important opportunity for prescription opioid harm reduction. Strengthening guideline-based multidisciplinary interventions during admission may improve patient outcomes and inform harm reduction strategies nationally.

articles.title: Immobilized Neuroglobin Scavenges Carbon Monoxide From Circulating Carboxyhemoglobin.
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
articles.abstract: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning is responsible for around 50,000 emergency department visits per year in the United States alone. Currently, there is no available antidote for CO poisoning. We have previously developed an antidotal therapy based on an engineered hemeprotein, human neuroglobin (Ngb-H64Q-CCC). Intravenous infusion of Ngb-H64Q-CCC removes CO from circulating red blood cells and improves survival in a lethal CO poisoning mouse model. However, the infusion of heme-containing proteins has inherent heme toxicity risks that may limit the dose that can be used safely without liver or kidney toxicity. To overcome these problems, we have investigated the development of immobilized Ngb in a solid matrix. This approach allows for the development of a CO removal system using an extracorporeal blood-circulating system coupled with a stationary matrix with immobilized Ngb-H64Q-CCC. Such a system avoids drug infusion and possible organ injury, allows for antidote recycling, and provides advantages for storage and handling of the antidote. Here we have developed Ngb-H64Q-CCC covalently bound to N-hydroxysuccinimide agarose. The immobilized protein shows preserved heme redox activity and retains its CO removal capacity after successive regeneration cycles. We expect that this novel approach will advance the development of new scavenger-based therapies for CO poisoning.

articles.title: Association between leukocytosis and adverse clinical outcomes in thrombocytopenic patients with acute pesticide poisoning: a cross-sectional study from a referral poisoning center in Iran.
articles.journal: International journal of environmental health research
articles.abstract: This study evaluated the association between leukocytosis and adverse clinical outcomes in patients with pesticide poisoning who also had thrombocytopenia. This cross-sectional study used medical records of patients who presented between 2016 and 2021, including 241 adult patients with confirmed pesticide poisoning. We extracted demographic data, clinical signs, laboratory parameters, and outcomes. We categorized hospitalization duration as >72 hours, 24-72 hours, and <24 hours. Leukocytosis was present in 43.2% of patients (n = 104). The overall mortality rate was 25.3% (n = 61), with 49.8% requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission (n = 120) and 44.4% requiring intubation (n = 107). Patients with elevated WBC had higher odds of prolonged hospitalization than those with normal counts: OR = 3.36, p = 0.004 for 24-72 h; and OR = 4.63, p < 0.001 for hospitalizations longer than 72 h. Leukocytosis was also strongly associated with intubation (OR = 3.50, p < 0.001) and ICU admission (OR = 3.58, p < 0.001). After adjustment, only ICU admission and leukocytosis remained significantly associated (OR = 2.20, p = 0.024). Leukocytosis may be a valuable parameter in predicting ICU admission and hospitalization duration in thrombocytopenic patients with acute pesticide poisoning. Further prospective multicenter studies are needed.

articles.title: Fulminant multi-organ failure associated with cereulide-producing Bacillus cereus after consumption of improperly stored rice.
articles.abstract: A male in his 20s with no medical history was found with generalised seizures and profound hypoglycaemia after consuming improperly stored, reheated rice.Initial laboratory tests showed acute liver failure with hyperammonaemia, acute kidney injury and lactic acidosis, which rapidly progressed to multi-organ failure requiring urgent liver transplantation evaluation.With maximal supportive therapy, including glucose, ammonia and glutamine scavengers, renal replacement therapy, haemodynamic and respiratory support, he gradually improved, avoiding transplantation and achieving full neurological recovery. Toxicological analysis of the rice and serum revealed high concentrations of cereulide, a toxin produced by Bacillus cereus This case illustrates that cereulide intoxication can be associated with potentially fatal multi-organ failure, particularly after ingestion of improperly stored starchy foods.Early recognition through targeted dietary history, focused laboratory evaluation and prompt supportive therapy are essential. Increasing awareness among healthcare professionals and safe food storage practices are key preventive measures.

articles.title: Key principles for rehabilitation of critically ill patients with obesity.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Patients with obesity who are admitted to an ICU bring specific challenges for rehabilitation during and after critical illness. This narrative review explores impact of differences in body compositions and pathophysiology on outcomes to summarise interprofessional, patient-centred rehabilitation strategies across the trajectory of recovery. METHODS: The interprofessional expert panel reviewed major trials and guidelines, integrating their clinical expertise with the current evidence. RESULTS: Three distinct phenotypes potentially influence outcomes for survivors. Whilst patients with preserved muscle mass may have a survival advantage, the phenotypes characterised by ectopic visceral fat or sarcopenia are frequently complicated by multimorbidity and polypharmacy, likely increasing the risk of adverse effects such as suboptimal sedation, prolonged ventilation and immobilisation, malnutrition, and impaired recovery. Targeted respiratory interventions, including secretion-clearance techniques and appropriate patient positioning to prevent atelectasis, reduce the work of breathing. Optimisation of communication and swallowing function is an essential component for facilitating safe oral intake and promoting active patient participation in rehabilitation. Concurrently, targeted nutrition strategies combined with early, targeted, progressive mobilisation might mitigate ICU acquired weakness and support functional recovery. The availability of appropriate weight‑based equipment is fundamental to ensuring safe mobilisation for both patients and healthcare professionals. CONCLUSION: Interprofessional collaboration is central to optimising outcomes and should extend beyond the ICU to structured post-ICU follow-up to address persistent, worsening, or newly emerging health impairments. Early rehabilitation in critically ill patients with obesity should integrate physiological, logistical, and psychosocial considerations to support equitable and functional recovery.
articles.ai_summary: This study reviewed rehabilitation strategies for critically ill patients with obesity, identifying three distinct phenotypes that influence outcomes. Targeted interventions, including respiratory, nutrition, and mobilization strategies, can mitigate complications and support functional recovery.
articles.ai_significance: This study's findings highlight the importance of interprofessional collaboration and early rehabilitation in critically ill patients with obesity, emphasizing the need to address physiological, logistical, and psychosocial considerations to support equitable and functional recovery.

articles.title: Decades of intensive care medicine trials: what randomised evidence has changed, corrected, and still questions to resolve.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have reshaped intensive care medicine (ICM), a discipline defined by acute, interacting organ failures, time-sensitive decisions, biological uncertainty, and heterogeneous recovery trajectories. Many interventions supported by strong physiological rationale failed to improve patient-centred outcomes, whereas durable advances often emerged from optimisation of supportive care, avoidance of iatrogenic harm, and reassessment of established practices. METHODS: We conducted an interpretive historical review of landmark multicentre RCTs in adult ICM from the early 1990s onwards. PubMed searches, reference lists from major trials and reviews, and international guidelines were used to identify trials with conceptual influence on practice, guidelines, physiological reasoning, therapeutic strategy, research priorities, de-implementation, or outcome framing. Evidence was organised into overlapping paradigms rather than rigid chronological periods. FINDINGS: Across haemodynamic support, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, antimicrobial treatment, nutrition, glucose control, transfusion, and sedation, landmark RCTs describe more than therapeutic expansion. Early biological and haemodynamic trials exposed the limits of reductionist strategies in syndromic critical illness. Protocol-driven approaches improved timeliness and consistency, but later pragmatic trials showed that rigid targets and invasive algorithms often added little once high-quality usual care was established. More recent trials challenge the assumption that greater intervention intensity improves outcomes, emphasising timing, disease phase, baseline risk, heterogeneity, patient selection, and treatment-related harm. Modern ICM RCTs have clarified not only what works, but what can be reduced, delayed, avoided, or applied selectively. Future progress requires biologically informed, context-sensitive trials focussed on meaningful survival, recovery, and long-term function.

articles.title: Antiseizure medication dosing and monitoring in the intensive care unit: a practical narrative review.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Antiseizure medications (ASMs) are commonly used in the intensive care unit (ICU) and often exhibit pharmacokinetics that differ substantially from those in healthy volunteers or in the outpatient setting. Organ dysfunction, polypharmacy, exogenous devices, and greater severity of illness all influence ASM pharmacokinetics, dosing decisions, and monitoring parameters. It is essential for critical care clinicians to familiarize themselves with the pharmacokinetics, dosing considerations, effects of exogenous devices, and therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)-all covered in this narrative review-to incorporate in their approach to ASMs in the critical care setting. METHODS: We identified relevant literature from MEDLINE from inception to March 2026 related to ASMs in the ICU. Data on pharmacokinetics, dosing in the ICU, the effect of renal replacement therapy, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and plasmapheresis (PLEX) on ASM exposure, and the role of TDM in the ICU were collected and summarized. RESULTS: Considerations for 15 ASMs (brivaracetam, cannabidiol, carbamazepine, cenobamate, clobazam, lacosamide, lamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, perampanel, phenobarbital, phenytoin, topiramate, valproate, and zonisamide) were included in the review. Dosing considerations for TDM, including indications and target reference ranges, and specific settings such as organ dysfunction, illness severity, renal replacement therapy, ECMO, and PLEX are discussed. CONCLUSION: The use of ASMs in the ICU require a distinct approach from outpatient settings. Severity of illness, organ dysfunction and replacement devices, and frequent drug-drug interactions warrant tailored agent selection, dosing, and monitoring.

articles.title: Ethylene Glycol Poisoning Without Fomepizole in a Regional Australian Intensive Care Unit: The Lactate Gap as the Diagnostic Key and the Consequences of Nasogastric Ethanol Therapy.
articles.abstract: A 62-year-old man presented comatose with pH 6.88 and no ingestion history. A point-of-care lactate above 31 mmol/L with a laboratory lactate of 0.8 mmol/L revealed a lactate gap, diagnosing ethylene glycol poisoning despite a near-normal osmolar gap. High-dose continuous renal replacement therapy corrected the acidosis; he survived.

articles.title: Integrated Use of Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation and Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System for Refractory Cardiotoxic Ingestion: A Single-Center Case Series.
articles.abstract: Cardiotoxic ingestions of calcium-channel blockers and beta-adrenergic antagonists are highly lethal, often causing refractory vasoplegic shock and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. While venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a recognized rescue therapy for cardiogenic shock, the roles of venovenous ECMO and albumin dialysis-specifically the molecular adsorbent recirculating system (MARS)-as well as the effectiveness of linking patients to therapy through a coordinated referral process remain underexplored. We describe five consecutive patients with severe cardiotoxic ingestions managed via a regionally triggered transfer pathway. Patients presented with profound hypotension and respiratory failure despite standard therapies. All five patients received MARS for drug clearance and vasoplegia management; two required venovenous ECMO for refractory hypoxemia. One patient died due to profound myocardial poisoning; four survived to discharge. Complications included continuous renal replacement therapy filter clotting and catheter-associated thrombosis. A coordinated regional protocol enabling early access to ECMO and MARS is feasible in massive cardiotoxic ingestions.

articles.title: Comparison of two automated pupillometry indices in patients with acute brain injury: the prospective multicentre LYNX cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Automated pupillometry quantifies the pupillary light reflex in acute brain injury. The neurological pupil index (NPi) is the established composite index and carries prognostic value. A second index from a different device, the quantitative pupil index (QPi), has recently become available, but whether it conveys equivalent information in non-anoxic acute brain injury is unknown. METHODS: LYNX was a prospective cohort study in three European intensive care units (September 2022-July 2024). Consecutive adults with traumatic brain injury, subarachnoid or intracerebral haemorrhage, or ischaemic stroke ventilated for more than 12 h were enrolled and followed for 6 months. Paired NPi (NPi-300) and QPi (NeuroLight) measurements were obtained at least every 6 h to day 7. Ancillary cohorts of healthy volunteers (dark vs. bright light) and surgical patients (before and after sufentanil and propofol) were also studied. The primary outcome was the correlation between the two indices; secondary outcomes were their association with intracranial hypertension and unfavourable 6-month outcome (Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended ≤ 4). Values below 3 were considered abnormal, with QPi thresholds of 2 and 4 as sensitivity analyses; multivariable models were adjusted for age, sex, admission Glasgow Coma Scale score and focal deficit. RESULTS: Among 108 patients (median age 57 years [IQR 44-67], 60.2% male), 7089 paired measurements were obtained. The two indices were moderately to strongly correlated (r = 0.717, 95% CI 0.705-0.730). Each 10-percentage-point increase in abnormal values independently predicted unfavourable outcome (NPi: OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.09-2.04, p = 0.013; QPi: OR 1.76, 95% CI 1.31-2.37, p < 0.001). QPi was associated with intracranial hypertension (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.04-1.82, p = 0.025), whereas NPi was not. Ambient lighting and contralateral eye opening had no meaningful effect in 75 volunteers. In 20 sedated non-brain-injured patients, propofol reduced QPi to a median of 1 (IQR 1-3) and NPi to 4.0 (IQR 3.6-4.3). CONCLUSIONS: NPi and QPi were correlated and both predicted 6-month outcome, but QPi was far more sensitive to anaesthetics, which probably confounds its association with intracranial hypertension. The indices are not interchangeable in sedated critically ill patients. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05567978. Registered 5 October 2022.

articles.title: Hemodynamic Effects of Interfacility Dexmedetomidine Infusions During Transport of Patients with Alpha-2-adrenergic Agonist Withdrawal.
articles.journal: The western journal of emergency medicine
articles.abstract: In the Philadelphia region, there has been an increase in the potency of illicit opioids as well as the addition of nonopioid adulterants. Currently, medetomidine, a veterinary anesthetic that acts as an alpha-2-adrenergic agonist, is a common adulterant in the illicit opioid supply, causing both unique overdose and withdrawal syndromes. Although opioid withdrawal alone is not deadly, with added adulterants, especially medetomidine, this is no longer the case. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2-adrenergic agonist frequently used for sedation in the emergency department and intensive care unit. Dexmedetomidine is also used off-label to treat the life-threatening withdrawal from alpha-2-agonists. This study describes the dosing and hemodynamic effects associated with the interfacility administration of dexmedetomidine in patients with alpha-2 adrenergic agonist withdrawal. Secondarily, we describe the safety of dexmedetomidine in this patient population. We conducted a retrospective case review of patients receiving dexmedetomidine infusions in the interfacility setting for presumed alpha-2-adrenergic agonist withdrawal. Demographic data, dosing, and vital signs were analyzed descriptively. Over a six-month period, of 217 cases identified, 182 contained complete hemodynamic data. The average age was 39.5 years, and 67% were male. The average transport time was 15.7 minutes (range, 5-40 minutes). The mean dexmedetomidine infusion rate was 1.32 (0.31) mcg/kg/hr. The average mean arterial pressure decreased from 122.1 mm Hg (21.7) at the time of initial patient contact to 118.3 mm Hg (21.7) (mean difference, 3.80; 95% CI, 1.96-5.64) at final patient interaction. Heart rate also showed a minimal change from 104.9 (23.7) to 103.6 (21.8) beats/min (mean 1.3; 95% CI, -0.48 to 3.08). No cases of severe hypotension or clinically significant bradycardia requiring intervention were documented (one-sided 95% CI, 0-1.7%). In this case series of patients, prehospital dexmedetomidine infusions to treat alpha-2-agonist withdrawal were associated with stable hemodynamics without significant bradycardia or hypotension. These findings support the safety of dexmedetomidine infusions for interfacility transport and provide a rationale for examining whether advanced life support clinicians can safely transport patients receiving dexmedetomidine infusions for this indication.

articles.title: Impact of Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System Therapy on Piperacillin Concentration in Critically Ill Patients: An Observational Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To assess the impact of Molecular Adsorbent Recirculating System (MARS) therapy on total plasma piperacillin concentrations in critically ill patients with acute liver failure or acute-on-chronic liver failure. DESIGN: Retrospective, single-center observational cohort study. SETTING: University ICU. PATIENTS: Consecutive adult patients treated with MARS therapy and piperacillin-tazobactam between March 2023 and June 2025. INTERVENTIONS: MARS therapy was delivered as 8-hour sessions for up to three consecutive days. Piperacillin-tazobactam was administered by continuous infusion following a loading dose. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Venous blood samples were collected immediately before and after each MARS session. Total piperacillin concentrations were quantified using ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography. The primary endpoint was the relative reduction in plasma piperacillin concentration induced by MARS therapy. Thirty patients (121 piperacillin measurements across 77 sessions) were analyzed. Seventy-three percent had cirrhosis (median Model for End-Stage Liver Disease Score 31 [23-38]). The mean relative reduction in piperacillin concentration per session was 34% (± 7.9%; p < 0.05). In univariable mixed-effects analysis, MARS session (β -47.49 mg/L; p < 0.001) and creatinine clearance (β -0.37 mg/L per mL/min; p < 0.001) were associated with lower concentrations. In multivariable modeling, higher creatinine clearance was independently associated with greater intra-session piperacillin loss ( p < 0.001), whereas higher bilirubin levels were associated with reduced drug loss ( p = 0.01). Overall, 31.6% of post-session concentrations were less than 80 mg/L, and 38% of patients had at least one concentration outside the predefined target range. CONCLUSIONS: MARS therapy was associated with a one-third reduction in total plasma piperacillin concentrations per session. These findings support systematic therapeutic drug monitoring and individualized antibiotic dose adjustment during MARS therapy.

articles.title: A Case of Suspected Scombroid Poisoning in Intensive Care Staff: Is It Anaphylaxis?
articles.abstract: Scombroid poisoning (histamine fish poisoning) is an uncommon foodborne illness that frequently mimics immunoglobulin E-mediated anaphylaxis. We report a case of a previously well 28-year-old intensive care nurse who developed abrupt facial flushing, wheeze, dizziness, and hypotension after consuming canned tuna. Initial observations demonstrated sinus tachycardia and hypotension. She was treated according to established anaphylaxis guidelines with two doses of intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous crystalloid resuscitation, and subsequent adrenaline infusion in intensive care. She recovered rapidly and was discharged the following day. Serial serum mast cell tryptase measurements at approximately one hour, six hours, and 24 hours after symptom onset were all within normal limits. In the absence of previous allergy history and given the temporal association with tuna ingestion, scombroid poisoning was considered as a possible diagnosis. This case highlights the difficulty of distinguishing severe histamine fish poisoning from anaphylaxis in the acute setting and reinforces that life-threatening presentations should initially be managed according to anaphylaxis protocols until an alternative diagnosis can be established.

articles.title: Severe and Prolonged Paroxetine Intoxication With Delayed Absorption and Extreme Serum Concentrations: A Case Report.
articles.abstract: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are commonly prescribed antidepressants, known for their relatively safe pharmacological profile and mild symptoms in cases of overdose compared with other antidepressants. In this case report, we describe a near-fatal case of a 70-year-old woman who ingested multiple drugs with suicidal intent, including an unknown quantity of celecoxib 200 mg, clorazepate acid 5 mg, omeprazole 20 mg, and immediate-release paroxetine 30 mg tablets. The patient developed severe serotonin syndrome complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and required admission to the intensive care unit (ICU). Because of progressive respiratory deterioration, she required intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation. Serotonin syndrome persisted for an unusually long period, with serum paroxetine concentrations of 4805 µg/L at admission that continued to rise to a maximum of 7824 µg/L on day four, both well above the lethal threshold. Intensive therapeutic interventions aimed at lowering paroxetine concentrations and resolving serotonin syndrome included activated charcoal, whole-bowel irrigation lavage, and rifampicin. Paroxetine concentrations gradually declined and reached the therapeutic range after 16 days. Following further ICU treatment, including prone ventilation and corticosteroids, the ARDS resolved, and the patient was extubated 21 days after ingestion. This case highlights that paroxetine overdose may present more severely than commonly reported in the literature, with delayed and prolonged toxicity, including serotonin syndrome and ARDS. Paroxetine overdose may be life-threatening and underscores the need for close monitoring of serum paroxetine concentrations and timely consideration of activated charcoal and whole-bowel irrigation.

articles.title: Fatal Fruit: Unveiling the Risks and Responses to Ackee Poisoning in a South Florida Inpatient Unit.
articles.abstract: The ackee fruit is a staple in many Afro-Caribbean diets. Yet, when consumed in its unripe form, it can induce Jamaican vomiting sickness, a potentially fatal condition caused by hypoglycin, a toxin that disrupts fatty acid oxidation and gluconeogenesis. Although cases are well-documented in endemic regions, reports outside the Caribbean remain rare. We report the case of a 33-year-old male with no comorbidities who presented in South Florida with acute metabolic encephalopathy, severe hypoglycemia, and profound electrolyte disturbances following the ingestion of unripe ackee fruit. Despite early recognition and aggressive interventions, including glucose administration, supportive therapy, and management coordinated by internal medicine, neurology, nephrology, toxicology, intensive care, and palliative care teams, the patient's clinical condition continued to deteriorate over 21 days post-exposure. This case is distinctive for its occurrence in a non-endemic region, the absence of comorbidities, and the refractory course despite multidisciplinary intervention. It highlights both the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of ackee poisoning in unfamiliar clinical settings. Increased globalization and the availability of culturally specific foods in diverse regions may increase the likelihood of similar presentations outside endemic areas. Awareness among healthcare providers is therefore essential. Ackee poisoning should be considered in patients presenting with unexplained hypoglycemia and encephalopathy, particularly in communities with Afro-Caribbean dietary practices. Early recognition, timely intervention, and interdisciplinary collaboration remain critical to improving patient outcomes. This case underscores the importance of provider awareness regarding culturally specific dietary exposures and their potential for severe toxicological consequences.

articles.title: Induction Agents for Tracheal Intubation of Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tracheal intubation is a common yet high-risk procedure in critically ill patients, with as many as one-half experiencing peri-intubation adverse outcomes. RESEARCH QUESTION: What is the comparative effectiveness and safety of various sedative agents used for endotracheal intubation of critically ill patients in the emergency department (ED), ICU, operating room, and prehospital setting? STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: We conducted a network meta-analysis and systematic review of randomized controlled trials. We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, PubMed, Cochrane, and trial registries from inception through December 10, 2025, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing ≥ 2 sedative agents in critically ill adults or children undergoing endotracheal intubation. Outcomes of interest were hemodynamic instability during intubation, hypoxemia, cardiac arrest, mortality, ICU and hospital length of stay, vasopressor use, adrenal insufficiency, and first-pass success. Reviewers screened, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool independently and in duplicate. We performed frequentist random-effects model network meta-analysis and used the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach to rate certainty in estimates. RESULTS: We included 21 RCTs enrolling 6,031 patients across ICU, ED, operating room, and prehospital settings. Compared with etomidate, more hemodynamic instability exists during intubation with ketamine (relative risk [RR], 1.31; 95% CI, 1.15-1.48; moderate certainty). Ketamine-propofol may decrease hemodynamic instability during intubation compared with etomidate (RR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.27-0.72; low certainty) and ketamine (RR, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.21-0.56; low certainty). Compared with etomidate, ketamine may decrease the need for the initiation of postintubation continuous infusion vasopressors (RR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.50-1.28; low certainty). Etomidate caused increased adrenal suppression compared with other agents. INTERPRETATION: Our results show that when considering sedation agents for endotracheal intubation of critically ill patients, etomidate probably causes less hemodynamic instability during intubation when compared with ketamine. However, etomidate may increase the need for the initiation of postintubation continuous infusion vasopressors when compared with ketamine and increases adrenal suppression. The clinical importance of these competing effects remains uncertain. Ketamine-propofol may decrease hemodynamic instability during intubation when compared with etomidate and ketamine, although the available evidence is too limited and uncertain to support firm conclusions, and further randomized trials are needed. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews; No.: CRD42024600739; URL: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/.

articles.title: Determinants of Delayed Recovery of Consciousness After Analgosedation Discontinuation in the ICU: Insights From Patients With COVID-19 Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Prolonged disorders of consciousness are common in critically ill patients receiving mechanical ventilation and are often attributed to prolonged sedative exposure in the setting of decreased drug clearance and/or reduced metabolism. Here, in a large sample of critically ill COVID patients obtained over a short period, we tested the assumption that prolonged unconsciousness following benzodiazepine and/or propofol sedation can be attributed to residual exposure. Further, we examine associations between clinical variables on time to recovery of consciousness (RoC) as a framework for the broader critically ill population. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study. SETTING: Massachusetts General Hospital, Weill Cornell Medicine, Columbia University Irving Medical Center. PATIENTS: Seven hundred eighty-four patients with COVID-19 critical illness in Spring-Summer 2020. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We estimated the latest expected RoC (LERoC) using models of sedation exposure that account for sedative-specific pharmacokinetics and critical illness. Our primary exposure variable was a time-weighted dose of analgosedative agents at benzodiazepine and/or propofol cessation; our primary outcome was time to RoC. We estimated relative risks for late RoC (i.e., after LERoC) via multinomial logistic regression. Among individuals with late RoC, we fit a multivariate subdistribution hazard model for time to RoC. Seventy-three percent of patients had RoC before hospital discharge, yet 34% of patients achieving RoC did not do so within pharmacologically plausible sedative elimination times. Patients with late RoC were older and exhibited hypoxemia and acute kidney injury. Patients with dexmedetomidine as an adjunct sedative had a disproportionately larger incidence of early recovery. Patients with early vs. late RoC did not have significantly different discharge dispositions. CONCLUSIONS: In our cohort, the time to RoC was commonly prolonged beyond that expected from sedation exposures alone. These data may aid clinicians and families with expectations of RoC and warrant investigation of alternative determinants of delayed RoC in this population.

articles.title: Reducing Physical Restraint in the ICU: Multicenter Phase II Randomized Trial of a Novel Device Versus Traditional Wrist Restraints.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate a novel device, developed under a National Institutes of Health Small Business Technology Transfer program grant, designed as an alternative to traditional wrist restraints. DESIGN: Within-patient crossover phase II randomized trial. SETTING: Four U.S. academic medical centers. PATIENTS: ICU patients ( n = 54) who were verbally responsive with a provider order for wrist restraints and expected stay greater than or equal to 2 days. INTERVENTIONS: Alternating use of novel device vs. traditional restraint during 4-hour assessment periods over 2 days (four assessment periods), with randomization of initial allocation to novel device vs. restraint. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Upper extremity activity (measured via wrist actigraphy) was the primary outcome, with safety, sedation, delirium, satisfaction (via Quebec User Evaluation of Satisfaction with Assistive Technology [QUEST] survey), and qualitative analyses of survey data as secondary outcomes. Analysis of actigraphy data demonstrated similar mean activity counts per 4-hour session for the novel device vs. traditional restraints, with a range of mean activity across the four sessions of 2930-4395 vs. 3898-4910, respectively, with relative mean total activity count per session of 0.93 (95% CI, 0.76-1.13; p = 0.45). Across 98 sessions using the novel device, 2 (2%) potential safety events were reported. No statistically significant differences were observed in sedation/agitation, or delirium status and severity. Of the QUEST satisfaction surveys completed by patient/family ( n = 25) and clinicians ( n = 79), 58% and 51%, respectively, indicated high satisfaction with qualitative analyses demonstrating four positive and six constructive themes. CONCLUSIONS: No differences in upper extremity activity, delirium, sedation, or agitation were demonstrated between the novel device and traditional wrist restraints. The novel device had overall moderate patient/family and clinician satisfaction, and qualitative analyses provide important insights for advancing the development of novel restraint alternative devices.

ai_appraisal.clinical_question: Does a novel device reduce physical restraint in ICU patients compared to traditional wrist restraints?
ai_appraisal.background: Physical restraints are often used in ICU settings to prevent patient harm, but they can have negative consequences. A novel device was developed as an alternative to traditional wrist restraints.
ai_appraisal.design: Within-patient crossover phase II randomized trial
ai_appraisal.setting: Four U.S. academic medical centers

articles.title: Clinical Severity and Serotonin Toxicity in Antidepressant Self-Poisoning: Implications for Clinical Risk Assessment.
articles.abstract: Background: Antidepressant self-poisoning is a common form of intentional self-harm, and comparisons across antidepressant groups are complicated by differences in ingested dose and coexposures. Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study reviewed emergency department presentations coded with International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) X61/X64 between 01 January 2023 and 15 May 2025. Among 15,160 screened records, 168 patients with documented antidepressant ingestion with self-harm/suicidal intent were included. Antidepressant exposures were classified by group and standardized using defined daily dose (DDD). Clinical presentation, serotonin toxicity based on the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria, management, and short-term outcomes were evaluated. Multivariable logistic regression was used to adjust for log-transformed DDD. Results: The median age was 27.0 years, and 66.7% of patients were female. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) were the most frequently ingested antidepressants (79.8%). Symptomatic presentation occurred in 33.3% of patients and was more frequent in non-SSRI than in SSRI exposures (55.9% vs 27.6%; adjusted OR, 3.40; 95% CI, 1.55-7.43; P = .002). Serotonin toxicity was identified in 7.7% and was also more frequent in non-SSRI exposures (23.5% vs 3.7%; adjusted OR, 8.17; 95% CI, 2.45-27.26; P = .001). Serotonin toxicity was associated with intensive care unit (ICU) admission (53.8% vs 10.3%; P < .001). Conclusion: Non-SSRI antidepressant exposures were associated with greater short-term clinical severity than SSRI exposures. Because non-SSRI subgroups were small and heterogeneous, class-specific findings should be interpreted as exploratory. The early clinical pattern of toxicity may inform short-term risk assessment.

articles.title: High-dose regular insulin as a potential rescue therapy in severe aluminum phosphide poisoning: a case report.
articles.abstract: Aluminum phosphide (rice tablet) can cause cardiocirculatory collapse and has negative cardiac inotropic effect. Positive inotropic effect of insulin on the cardiac myocytes is through calcium flux. Insulin increases the intramyocytes calcium concentration by increasing conductance of calcium through the L-type calcium channels and by increasing intramyocytes concentration of cyclic adenosine monophosphate. In addition to increasing the intramyocytes calcium level, insulin also enhances the responsiveness of the cardiac cells to calcium. High-dose insulin is a potential therapy for hypodynamic and hypotensive septic shock due to its positive inotropic qualities. In this paper, a critical aluminum phosphide poisoning patient (a 25-year-old Iranian young woman), presented with mixed severe metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypotension. In contrast to our previous experiences that ingestion of aluminum phosphide tablets associated with multiple organ failure and severe shock in approximately all critical poisoning patients, early initiation of high-dose intravenous regular insulin for this patient prevented multiorgan dysfunction and death. Treatment with high-dose intravenous insulin associated with IV fluids, sodium bicarbonate, hydrocortisone, potassium, dextrose therapy and supportive care resolved completely signs and symptoms of patient after 3 days in ICU. High-dose intravenous regular insulin may be act as a rescue therapy for aluminum phosphide poisoning patients. While this single case suggests a potential benefit, further studies are required to confirm these findings.

articles.title: Disparities in Finding Delirium in Critically Ill Latinos.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Delirium is common in the ICU and is associated with devastating consequences. However, the accuracy of delirium detection tools has not been evaluated when patient-provider language discordance is present. This study aimed to assess the accuracy of delirium screening practices in Spanish-speaking ICU patients, evaluate whether caregiver-administered tools improve detection amid language barriers, and examine language-based differences in delirium care. DESIGN: Prospective observational cohort study. SETTING: Two MICUs at the University of California, San Diego. PATIENTS: 142 ICU patients and 100 caregivers were enrolled between August 2024 and January 2025. INTERVENTIONS: Usual-Care (Confusion Assessment Method [CAM]-ICU completed by bedside providers), Reference-standard (English or Spanish-language CAM-ICU performed by research staff), and FAM-CAM (English or Spanish-language Family-CAM administered by caregivers). MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Among 71 English-speakers, 34 female (47%), with a mean ( sd ) age of 62 years (16). Among 71 Spanish-speakers, 26 female (37%) and the mean age was 60 years (15). The prevalence of delirium was 39% overall, affecting 26 (37%) English-speakers and 32 (45%) Spanish-speakers. Agreement between Usual-Care and Reference-standard was higher in English-speakers than in Spanish-speakers (κ=0.71 vs. κ=0.11; z=-4.98, p < 0.01), with 72% of delirium missed in Spanish-speakers. Among Spanish-speakers, FAM-CAM showed higher agreement with Reference-standard than did Usual-Care (κ=0.68 vs. κ=0.11; z= -4.69, p < 0.05) and reduced the rate of missed delirium by 47%. Spanish-speakers were more deeply sedated (mean Richmond Agitation Sedation Scale -1.46 [ sd 1.38] vs. -0.77 [ sd 1.31]; mean difference 0.69; 95% CI, 0.24 to 1.14, p < 0.01) and had higher odds of restraint use (odds ratio 4.53; 95% CI 1.91 to 10.74; p < 0.01) than English-speakers. CONCLUSIONS: Usual-Care demonstrated poor accuracy in delirium detection among Spanish-speakers, who also experienced deeper sedation and more frequent restraint use than English-speakers. FAM-CAM improved delirium detection among Spanish-speakers and may help overcome language barriers to equitable delirium detection.

articles.title: Sex Disparities in the Clinical Management and Outcomes of Critically Ill Adults Undergoing Electroencephalography Monitoring.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sex-related discrepancies concerning the treatment of patients in intensive care are increasingly described. However, information about management and outcome of critically ill patients undergoing electroencephalography is scarce. OBJECTIVES: This study explores sex-related disparities in management and clinical outcomes in critically ill patients needing electroencephalography for clinical purposes. DESIGN, SETTING, PATIENTS, AND INTERVENTIONS: In this post hoc analysis of the multicenter Continuous Electroencephalography Randomized Trial in Adults (CERTA), which included patients with impaired consciousness requiring electroencephalography, we explored correlations between sex and the timing of electroencephalography, detection of electroencephalography abnormalities, mechanical ventilation, sedation, antiseizure therapy, mortality, and favorable functional outcome (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) at 6 months, using univariable and multivariable analyses. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Among 364 patients (33.8% women), women showed a higher prevalence of intracranial hemorrhage (women 30.9%, men 19.5%; p = 0.015) and epileptiform electroencephalography discharges (women 27.6%, men 21.2%; p = 0.008), but use of sedation, antiseizure medication and mechanical ventilation was similar between sexes. Although mortality was similar (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 0.70; 95% CI, 0.39-1.28), women were less likely to reach CPC 1-2 (adjusted OR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.28-0.90). CONCLUSIONS: Critically ill women and men requiring electroencephalography appear to receive similar clinical management and have comparable mortality, although long-term functional outcome in surviving women is worse. These findings warrant further investigation to identify modifiable factors contributing to sex-related outcome differences.

articles.title: Early inhaled isoflurane sedation in neurocritical patients with invasive intracranial pressure monitoring: the NEURO-CONDA randomized pilot trial.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Evidence on inhaled sedation in neurocritically ill patients remains limited, mainly due to concerns about potential increases in intracranial pressure (ICP). We aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of early isoflurane sedation compared with propofol in invasively monitored neurocritical patients without intracranial hypertension. METHODS: NEURO-CONDA is a phase IV, randomized, open-label, parallel-group pilot trial conducted in a tertiary ICU (May 2024-October 2025). Adult neurocritical patients requiring ICP monitoring and without intracranial hypertension were randomized to receive either propofol or isoflurane. The primary endpoints were efficacy (assessed with RASS and BIS™) and safety, defined as the occurrence of serious adverse drug reactions (ADRs), including sustained ICP elevation or cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) < 60 mmHg requiring increased vasopressor support. Nociception (NOL®) and other systemic parameters were recorded for up to 72 h. Analyses were performed according to the intention-to-treat principle. RESULTS: Thirty patients were included (15 per group), and baseline characteristics were comparable; 19 had traumatic brain injury. Sedation efficacy was 100% in both groups throughout the study period. No serious ADRs occurred. ICP and CPP remained stable throughout the study period without requiring higher doses of vasopressors in the isoflurane sedated group. CONCLUSIONS: In this randomized pilot trial, early sedation with isoflurane was feasible and achieved reliable deep sedation without compromising intracranial or cerebral perfusion parameters in invasively monitored neurocritical patients without intracranial hypertension. Larger randomized studies are warranted to confirm these findings and assess long-term neurological outcomes.
